records.title: Plasma-Enhanced Multilayer Coatings on Metal Bipolar Plates for Corrosion Resistance and High Electrical Conductivity
records.abstract: Abstract Metal bipolar plates are central to lowering the cost and weight of proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC) stacks, yet their long-term use is limited by aggressive corrosion in the acidic, humid, low-pH cathode environment. Multilayer protective coatings combining adhesion-promoting metal interlayers with chemically inert graphitic carbon are widely regarded as a promising solution, but they have historically been deposited slowly and from precursors such as titanium tetrachloride that are difficult to scale safely. Here, we report the design and operation of a showerhead plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) reactor that deposits Ti/TiCx/amorphous-carbon (a-C) multilayer coatings on 304 stainless steel using the comparatively safe titanium isopropoxide (TiPO) precursor in combination with a hydrogen plasma. Both continuous radio frequency (RF) and nanosecond-pulsed glow discharges were tested at 10 W and at substrate temperatures up to 300 °C. Cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and Raman scattering confirm uniform, pinhole-free multilayers in which Ti is reduced from TiPO by atomic hydrogen and the carbon top layer is sp2-rich and graphitic. Carbon deposition rates of 200–237 nm min–1 were obtained, matching or exceeding the best values reported in the literature. A coupled plasma kinetics and showerhead transport model rationalizes these rates, the distinct microstructures obtained under continuous and nanosecond-pulsed excitation, and the measured coating uniformity. The best carbon coatings reach interfacial contact resistance (ICR) values of 5.4–13.5 mΩ·cm2 at 1.10 MPa, with the lowest well below the 2025 U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) target of 10 mΩ·cm2. The coatings showed no detectable Raman or morphological degradation after accelerated thermal cycling between 30 and 100 °C in pH 3 H2SO4, demonstrating their potential as a fast, safe, and scalable coating route for next-generation PEMFC bipolar plates.

records.title: Effect of lubricant oxidation on tribological performance of gear contact interfaces in three gorges ship lift: experiments and simulation
records.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to investigate the high-temperature degradation behavior of lubricating oils used in the gearboxes of the Three Gorges ship lift, which operate under harsh environmental conditions. The study seeks to understand the correlation between the evolution of physicochemical properties, oxidation mechanisms and the resulting tribological performance to address excessive gear wear. Design/methodology/approach High-temperature oxidation experiments were conducted to simulate the degradation process. The evolution of physicochemical properties was characterized by monitoring color, acid number and kinematic viscosity. Oxidation products were analyzed using Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy and GC-MS chromatography. Furthermore, ReaxFF reactive molecular dynamics simulations were used to reveal microscopic reaction pathways. Finally, the tribological performance of the degraded oil was evaluated using a friction tester and a 3D profilometer and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis was performed on the worn surface to characterize the compositional changes of the friction film, thereby revealing the friction-induced damage mechanism of the oxidized lubricating oil. Findings The results indicate that thermal oxidation leads to the formation of acidic polar molecules, such as carboxylic acids, aldehydes and esters, resulting in an increasing trend in both acid number and kinematic viscosity. ReaxFF simulations revealed that high-temperature oxidation proceeds through multiple specific reaction pathways. Crucially, the study confirms that the decline in tribological performance is directly related to these physicochemical changes and the accumulation of oxidation products. Originality/value This study uniquely combines macroscopic experimental characterization with microscopic ReaxFF molecular dynamics simulations to provide a comprehensive understanding of lubricant degradation in the specific context of large-scale ship lift gearboxes. The findings offer theoretical support for optimizing oil monitoring indicators and maintenance strategies for critical hydraulic engineering equipment.

records.body_text:
JIT Industries Acquires Birmingham-Based Chrome Plating Facility
JIT Industries, a full-service diversified company specializing in fluid power manufacturing and repair, large-scale machining, engineering support, and automation, has acquired Precision Plating in Birmingham, Alabama.
Precision Plating specializes in industrial hard chrome plating, machining, grinding, roll repair, and surface restoration. The facility can also chrome large components up to 23 feet long and up to 28 inches in outside diameter.
Precision Plating has served Birmingham and the surrounding region for more than 40 years. As part of JIT Industries, Precision Plating continues to expand its capabilities and provide customers with additional hydraulic and fluid power support.
Precision Plating is led by Operations Manager Charlie Butler, who brings more than 40 years of experience in the chrome plating industry. Together, the Precision Plating team has more than 90 years of industry experience.
“I’m proud to lead this new chapter for Precision Plating,” Butler says. “I believe we can accomplish a lot as part of JIT Industries, and I’m excited to see what the future holds as we continue to grow and support our customers in new ways.”
Matt McComb, COO of JIT Industries, was happy with the agreement.
"We are thrilled to welcome Precision Plating to the JIT Industries team as we continue our aggressive expansion focused on providing localized, immediate support and expanded capabilities across our network," McComb says.
The addition of Precision Plating expands JIT Industries’ industrial hard chrome plating capabilities while strengthening its ability to provide comprehensive fluid power solutions. Precision Plating is one of seven locations owned and operated by JIT Industries across four states.
Founded in 2001 in Hartselle, Alabama, JIT Industries began as a local hydraulic repair shop. Over the past 25 years, the company has grown into a full-service fluid power provider with seven Southeast locations. JIT Industries provides cylinder manufacturing, fluid power repair, CNC machining, engineering, research and development, and industrial hard chrome plating services to customers across heavy and critical industries.

records.body_text:
Navigating the Shift: Trivalent Chromium Plating in the Automotive Steel Market
MKS Atotech details the path to success to adopting trivalent chromium plating for automotive steel bumpers and exterior components.
Share
Read Next
This paper is based on a presentation originally given at SUR/FIN 2026 in Rosemont, Illinois on June 2, 2026, in Session 3: Automotive Surface Finishing. Decorative trivalent plating processes have been available for several decades, yet widespread adoption has faced significant industry hurdles. Debates regarding chloride-based chemistries versus sulfate-based chemistries, coupled with rigorous requirements for interior and exterior performance, have created a complex landscape for suppliers, applicators and OEMs alike.
This article reviews the strategic transition of automotive steel into the trivalent chromium market. By examining barriers to entry and the technical evolution of these processes, it outlines how the industry is successfully navigating regulatory and performance demands to implement sustainable, high-quality plating solutions.
The full presentation can be accessed and printed at short.pfonline.com/NASF26-Nov2.

Debates regarding chloride-based chemistries versus sulfate-based chemistries, coupled with rigorous requirements for interior and exterior performance, have created a complex landscape for suppliers, applicators and OEMs alike.
This article reviews the strategic transition of automotive steel into the trivalent chromium market. By examining barriers to entry and the technical evolution of these processes, it outlines how the industry is successfully navigating regulatory and performance demands to implement sustainable, high-quality plating solutions.
The full presentation can be accessed and printed at short.pfonline.com/NASF26-Nov2.

What Successful Hard Chrome Platers Need
The hard chrome industry is respected for its unique plating methods, diverse applications, and importance to America’s economy and defense.
This trade requires skill sets that differ greatly from more common types of electroplating, such as zinc, copper, nickel, or decorative coatings.
The following is a list of items necessary for hard chrome plating. Some overlap with other plating types, while others, like chromic acid, lead, and sometimes stop-offs, are unique to hard chrome. While most of these are obvious, they are all vital for uninterrupted production. Sadly, some platers overlook these necessities and only pay attention to them when production stops.
These items are not listed in any order of particular importance; however, a defect in any one of them will negatively affect the business. A productive hard chrome operation should address and manage each of these to keep the business successful and sustainable.
Electricity
Electroplating obviously requires electricity. High voltages like 480 VAC at significant amperage are typically required for industrial applications. The AC amperage needed is determined by the sizing of the various rectifiers and the electrical support equipment being used.
Rectifiers are used to convert this AC into DC, which is what’s used for the actual plating processes. The recent trend is to upgrade older SCR rectifiers to newer switch-mode units. Switch-mode rectifiers offer significant benefits, including more efficient power conversion, cleaner DC waveforms, lower ripple, and much better process control through programmable controls. The switch-mode units are also much smaller, which saves floor space.
Annual electrical savings are significant because hard chrome draws a lot of amperage. These units can automatically reverse current, saving time and eliminating the need for bussing changes and bulky reversing switches.
Switch mode units use stacked modules, typically 1,000 amps each. These units continue operating if a module ever malfunctions, which is rare, because they use solid-state technology. Keeping a spare module on hand lets you replace it quickly and easily. The defective module can then be returned for repairs without ever losing production. Switch mode rectifiers are a savior for modern hard chrome platers. Most operations replace their old SCR units when they crash. In contrast, others replace them to take advantage of energy savings, programmable controls, and better chrome deposits from the improved waveform and very low ripple.
Electricity can also be saved by keeping the bath impurity levels under control. Excessive bath impurities, such as high trivalent, iron, and copper, can add Thousands of Dollars to annual electrical costs. Since zero impurities are impossible, the best approach is to keep them within the recommended 4.8–7.2 TCL (total contaminant level). Fortunately, practical, cost-saving methods can achieve this.
Bussing
Bussing is used to connect the rectifier(s) to the various electrified tanks. Solid copper is typical, although aluminum is sometimes used instead. An alternative to solid copper is using high-capacity cable, which is much easier to route and install.
The optimum bussing sizing is one square inch of copper as a minimum cross section per 1,000 DC amperes being transmitted. It’s often recommended to oversize the bussing by 5-10% as a safeguard. Undersizing the bussing to save on initial cost is a mistake because it increases resistance, generates heat, and wastes expensive energy. That wasted energy, which can be as much as 50%, needlessly drives up electrical costs year after year.
Water
Water is another critical component; the plating process cannot operate without an adequate, reliable supply. It’s a necessity for the plating and process baths, the rinsing, and often for the cooling systems. Using city water is recommended because well water typically contains extremely high mineral levels that harm the plating bath.
The best operations purify the city water used in plating. Typical purification systems include RO and DI components that remove sulfate, chloride, metals, and minerals. This prevents these ions from continually building up in the plating baths until their levels cause serious plating problems.
Chromic Acid
Chromic acid is the most critical chemical ingredient used in hard chrome operations. The operation would be out of business without it. It is a vital chemical for our industry and our national defense. There are only three chromic acid sources in the world today: China, India, and Turkey. None of these are particularly friendly toward our nation; they could easily restrict our supply or drastically increase prices.
Most of the material produced in India and Turkey is poor quality because of high impurity levels, notably excess sulfate, chloride, iron, and copper. Some of the Chinese chrome has similar impurity defects. Using high-purity chromic acid is important because these contaminants build up in the plating bath and poison it, making it impossible to deposit suitable chrome. Those impurities end up in the products because of inadequate refining during manufacturing.
There is a limited quantity of chromic acid inventoried in the USA. Chemical suppliers keep only a few months' supply on hand, and there’s no national stockpile. Chromic acid availability is limited to what’s imported, either as chromic acid or as its ore.
Most of the chromic acid our industry uses comes from China, and they have no desire to support our industry. China could easily restrict supply or drastically raise prices. They have a history of doing this with critical goods.
There are two ways to resolve the cost, quality, and availability problems with chromic acid:
Buy Certified HCP Grade Chrome
Use only chromic acid material that’s been certified as HCP Grade. This eliminates impure material dumped on our market. HCP Grade is meticulously assayed for purity, so the material is free of impurities that harm your plating bath(s).
This step goes a long way toward preventing excessive and costly bath dumping caused by iron, copper, and other impurities. It also limits the barium carbonate treatments needed to remove excess sulfate and the dummying needed to lower the chloride levels. The HCP Grade doesn’t cost much more than the impure grades do, so there’s nothing to lose and everything to gain by using it. This step solves the quality issues.
Another suggestion is buying the newer beaded type of chromic acid instead of the older flake material. Besides being higher purity, the beaded material pours almost like a liquid, so it’s much easier to add to the tanks. It also reduces splashing because it resists absorbing moisture, so it doesn’t clump up like the older flake material.
Stockpile a Year’s Supply
Many hard chromers purchase chromic acid only when it’s needed and in the amount required to restore their bath concentrations. Others rarely keep more than a month’s supply in inventory. This is a mistake on two very important fronts – the cost and the availability.
It’s much better to purchase your chromic acid in larger bulk quantities. This provides several distinct and important benefits. The first is the huge cost savings involved, which are provided in two important ways:
- Buying in larger quantities provides lower prices because of the bulk discounts available. The cost savings can be significant when buying 5,000 pounds instead of 1,200, or 40,000 pounds instead of 5,000, etc. This also lowers your shipping costs.
- Keeping a large inventory of chromic acid on your floor helps you avoid the inevitable price increases that occur throughout the year. This can add to your savings by another 20-30% or more. Chromic acid is also often in short supply, and prices can rise even more during these shortages.
The issue now becomes what the ideal quantity is to buy at one time. Innovative managers want to keep at least a one-year supply of chromic acid in inventory at all times. There are several ways this concept can be approached. Start by determining your average monthly usage, then multiply it by 12 to get the quantity. This is what’s recommended as your minimum inventory.
This solves both the availability and the cost issues. A stockpile of chromic acid also lets you keep plating when others can’t because of a shortage.
Some critics will say that’s wasting assets by tying up so much capital in inventory.
They would be wrong because, over time, the cost savings percentage often exceeds the operation’s normal profit margin. This wouldn’t be wasted money because chromic acid is an asset while it sits in your inventory. This tactic reduces your costs and provides a buffer that could save your business when the next shortage occurs.
Lead, Stop-Off and Fixtures
Lead alloys are another necessary item for the hard chrome operation. Some platers buy ready-made tank or conforming anodes while others prefer to fabricate their own. Either way, lead alloys are a must-have item.
Those that make their own anodes will want to keep an inventory of the various ingots, cast grids, sheet, and wire stock needed. As with chromic acid, keeping a year’s inventory of these materials provides an adequate safety net against shortages and price increases.
Companies that purchase ready-made anodes should maintain an adequate back-up of the anode types used. It’s also recommended to maintain a good relationship with the anode supplier. Like chromic acid, lead has also faced environmental scrutiny, so the number of anode suppliers has become limited. Only a few remain, and their support is fundamental to your well-being.
There’s no shortage of stop-off suppliers, but that doesn’t negate the need to maintain an adequate inventory of the materials used. Depending on the type of parts being plated, this can include tapes (conductive and non-conductive), various vinyl shapes, waxes, lacquers, permanent PVC or CPVC shapes, and a host of other items.
Keeping a larger supply on hand ensures availability when needed. Each operation should evaluate its stop-off needs because they vary drastically with the part requirements. A captive shop typically uses the same stop-off materials, while a job shop needs to inventory all types so it can plate anything that comes in the door.
The type of fixtures used varies with the parts configurations being plated. For captive operations, this is typically a set of standardized fixtures dedicated to a particular part. Job shops, on the other hand, need a more varied set of fixtures to plate a wide variety of parts. They also need the ability to fabricate specialty fixtures for unusual parts.
Regardless of the operation, it’s important to keep an adequate inventory of backup fixtures and the materials needed for fabrication.
Skilled Labor
Labor is a clear necessity; this includes tank-side workers and their supervisor(s). Education for both is important if efficiency and success are expected, but each requires a different skill set. The tank-side workers need knowledge of the basic processing skills related to the parts being plated. This includes recognizing when conditions change and when questions should be asked. Supervisors need a deeper understanding of the process, its quirks, the specifications they must follow, the many variables involved, and insights into troubleshooting and problem-solving.
Unfortunately, schools don't teach hard chrome plating as a trade, yet it is of significant importance to our industry. Older-vintage hard chromers became skilled through trial and error; their knowledge was gradually passed down to their replacements. However, valuable information is always lost at every transition. That training method worked well enough until around the mid-1970s.
Unfortunately, the last batch of skilled ‘old-timers’ retired years ago, which left an education gap in today’s workforce. To make matters worse, very little written material on hard chrome plating explains the skills needed.
A lack of education and know-how in any industrial process always results in inefficiencies, typically:
- A decrease in the overall product quality.
- An increase in the rework volume.
- A decrease in the production efficiency.
- Lost business and lower profit margins.
Hard chrome plating is no different. In fact, these defects are amplified in our industry because, unlike other trades, it’s hard to find people with these skills. These employees usually need to be trained in-house.
Operating with a poorly trained workforce is a costly mistake. This applies to both the tank-side workers and their supervisors. On the other hand, trained, highly skilled workers can greatly improve throughput and increase the company’s profits.
We addressed the training issue using three approaches:
1. On-Site Training
Remote schools are sometimes available for processes like anodizing and electroless nickel plating, but nothing viable exists for hard chrome. NASF offers a course, but it barely covers the basics and provides no hands-on training. In addition, off-site schooling creates production issues when valuable employees are away for an extended period. Off-site schooling also adds costs for travel, housing, and living expenses.
Fortunately, there’s an alternative. Hard chrome training can be provided at your plant, on-site using your parts, your equipment, and your processes. This training comes to you, so there are no work stoppages or travel expenses, and you can train multiple employees at the same time.
This training can be tailored to your specific needs and can even include troubleshooting for various problems or difficult parts. This can be provided as classroom instruction, tank-side training, or a combination of both. Most scenarios include a mixture of these and can also incorporate an evaluation of the equipment and procedures being used.
This training is also available to bring new employees up to speed and help them get off to the right start. Another option that some corporations find attractive is annual refresher training. This helps eliminate the gradual efficiency reduction that seems to plague certain operations. You can combine annual refresher training with an equipment and maintenance evaluation to ensure everything is functioning at its peak.
2. Technical Manuals
Two manuals are available that cover the entire knowledge base needed for a successful hard chrome operation. These are recent publications with the latest up-to-date information.
Hard Chrome University Book (the Red Book): This book is used for generalized hard chrome training and is a valuable resource for both the tank-side plater and the supervisor. It covers every topic involved with the trade and provides valuable process control information. It’s complete with color illustrations and graphs for clarity. The text covers both the fundamentals and detailed advanced information.
Hard Chrome Secrets Book (the Blue Book): This book contains closely held technical knowledge in an easy-to-read format. It covers every aspect of the art and science, from both the practical and technical viewpoints. It includes scientific information, technical advice, and numerous tricks of the trade developed by experts over the years. It covers how to apply high-quality hard chrome deposits at the lowest cost. Hard Chrome Secrets is most valuable to the plating supervisor and should be on the shelf of every hard chrome operation whose objective is producing a quality hard chrome deposit most efficiently at the lowest cost.
These manuals have a limited publication and are not inexpensive. However, they provide incredibly valuable information that could easily save your operation six figures annually. They are only available to companies with a commercial hard chrome operation.
3. Online School Development
Plating Resources, Inc. is considering developing an on-line training program specifically for hard chrome technology. This is currently in the planning stage and only needs confirmation from the hard chrome industry that it would be useful. This online school would include several development levels, such as Tank-Side Plater, Plating Supervisor, and Hard Chrome Technician.
These levels would provide the knowledge needed for those positions, with each level building on the previous one. The program will use an easy-to-follow format, and each course should take around 40 hours to complete. Students can complete the course at home in the evenings, with instructor interaction so they can ask questions and gain clarity.
This would be an industry first because an online hard chrome school hasn’t existed before. This is a better approach than using a remote classroom because it eliminates travel and living expenses, as well as lost production while employees are away. An online school seems like a better approach because it eliminates expenses and time away, and students can learn at their own pace.
Laboratory
Many platers use an outside laboratory for controlling their bath concentrations, often their chemical supplier. This is generally a mistake on several fronts unless the operation is small and has minimal throughput. The worst case is when the company delays bath analysis until plating problems appear and the rework rate increases.
Relying on vendor-based laboratories for bath control has two problems.
- There’s a significant time delay from when the sample was taken and when you receive the results. The bath changes during that time lapse, so the results are never current, and the bath remains unbalanced.
- Many of today’s laboratories use automated analysis equipment, and the results are often unreliable. This primarily depends on when and how often instruments are calibrated and maintained. The reliability of these results is always in question.
Establish a routine analysis frequency so bath chemistry stays within a reasonable variance. This variance mostly applies to the chromic acid, sulfate, and any secondary catalyst used. Most experts recommend limiting this variance to 2-5% for best performance and repeatability.
The best way to control the chromic acid and sulfate is by in-house testing. A small laboratory set-up doesn’t need to be large or elaborate. Forget using Baume’ or Kocour kits for this because these are inaccurate. Using professional lab glassware, reagents, and procedures is much better. Weekly testing works well for most small- to medium-sized operations. Several baths can be tested in less than an hour.
A reliable outside laboratory or your vendor should then be used for back-up testing once the in-house analysis program is established. This will confirm your results while also controlling the impurities like trivalent, iron, copper and chloride. Those impurities don’t typically build up quickly, so monthly testing for these is usually sufficient.
Maintenance
Many platers overlook equipment maintenance until a breakdown occurs, then it’s a mad rush to get back in production. Some breakdowns require replacing a component, which invariably has a lengthy delivery time, sometimes exceeding 6-8 weeks or more. Meanwhile, the plating system is down, and production stops until the repair is completed. Equipment breakdowns are very costly in terms of lost income.
A regular maintenance program is critical to business success. These should be established for daily, weekly, monthly and annual requirements. The Hard Chrome University book published by Plating Resources, Inc. has a chapter on System Operation and Maintenance that outlines the various requirements in detail. Each plating system has its own particular requirements, but many generalities apply across the board.
Assign equipment maintenance to one person, using written instruction forms for each maintenance period.
Another part of a smart maintenance program is maintaining an inventory of critical spare parts. Having these on hand can save weeks of downtime because you can replace the failed component immediately instead of waiting for delivery. A replacement can then be ordered to restore your inventory.
Stocking the following spare parts should be considered, in no particular order of importance:
- Immersion Heaters
- Pumps
- Chemicals
- Anodes
- Fixtures
- Fan Belts
- Stop-Off Supplies
- Gaskets & Seals
- Polishing & Grinding Supplies
- Laboratory Supplies
- Ventilation HEPA Filters
- Filter Media
- Rectifier Modules & Parts
- Lubricants
- PPE Gear
- Others specific to your system
Profits
A business should generate a profit on every part plated, not just here and there. One of the problems is that the actual plating costs are often unknown. It’s relatively easy to calculate the general overhead, but a lot more complicated to detail specific job costs. This is especially true when multiple tanks are used, and several jobs are plated at the same time, each with different quantities, chrome thicknesses, and preparation steps.
A plating job should only be quoted once the actual costs are known; then the desired profit margin is applied. Typical hard chrome profit margins vary all over the map, but these seem to be typical:
- 20%: Considered a low margin
- 30%: An average margin
- 50%: Or more is a high margin
Margins above 50% can apply to unusual jobs where the part is excessively large, requires a thicker or tight-tolerance deposit, is overly complicated, or has unusual specification constraints. Another area where high margins apply is when you can repair an expensive part instead of replacing it, or when your shop is the only one that can handle the job.
A plating operation must detail its exact costs on every job it handles. Guessing costs or using estimates typically leads to losses. A costing program is now available in Excel that details all costs, both overhead and those related to plating a specific job, regardless of its requirements. This program
includes suggested profit margins and even generates the selling price for quoting, all based on the actual costs and the desired profit margin. Both job and captive operations would benefit from using this. Many job shops will be surprised by how much profit they leave on the table.
Capital
Many business managers consider setting aside a portion of profits as a capital reserve a good business practice. This amount is dedicated to the plating operation for maintenance, capital expansions, and unknowns. This may also include the future costs for any changes in the regulatory requirements. The exact amount of the capital reserve varies from operation to operation and is considered a strategic practice for future unidentified costs. There’s nothing worse in business than needing capital and not having it available.
Compliance
Regulatory compliance for environmental and worker safety issues is an ongoing requirement for hard chrome operations. You can’t sidestep this requirement because violations can be very costly and, if excessive, can even shut down the operation. The biggest issue usually involves meeting the air discharge limits.
Most hard chrome operations today rely on the Zero Discharge Recovery approach for their sewer regulations. This system is easy to understand and inexpensive to operate. It functions by reclaiming and reusing all of the operation’s rinsates, thereby bypassing the need for a waste treatment system and a sewer connection.
Tackling the air discharge has been both challenging and costly until a recent design innovation. Many operations rely on a complex ventilation system and/or expensive fume suppressants. A new approach provides a design that produces ZERO chrome discharge to the atmosphere – without needing to use a fume suppressant. This is the Sustainable Hard Chrome concept. It is not a marketing gimmick or tactic and has been proven in Real-World hard chrome shops operating at 20,000 amperes. The air discharge was shown to be ‘Zero’ by an EPA-approved laboratory.
This was accomplished without using a fume suppressant. This technology is easiest to apply to new system installations and plating system upgrades. The beauty of this approach is that authorities can’t regulate below zero, so the operation stays in compliance regardless of any regulatory tightening. Other features include improving the operator’s safety and lowering the operation’s chemical costs.
We hope this article opened some eyes and offers direction for improving your hard chrome operation.
Eric Svenson Sr. is CEO of Plating Resources and a Master CEF and IUSF member. Visit www.Plating.com. If you have any questions or wish to explore this topic further, please get in touch with Vicky at Vicky@Plating.com.

\#\#\#\# Lead\, Stop\-Off and Fixtures

Lead alloys are another necessary item for the hard chrome operation\. Some platers buy ready\-made tank or conforming anodes while others prefer to fabricate their own\. Either way\, lead alloys are a must\-have item\.

Those that make their own anodes will want to keep an inventory of the various ingots\, cast grids\, sheet\, and wire stock needed\. As with chromic acid\, keeping a year’s inventory of these materials provides an adequate safety net against shortages and price increases\.

Companies that purchase ready\-made anodes should maintain an adequate back\-up of the anode types used\. It’s also recommended to maintain a good relationship with the anode supplier\. Like chromic acid\, lead has also faced environmental scrutiny\, so the number of anode suppliers has become limited\. Only a few remain\, and their support is fundamental to your well\-being\.

There’s no shortage of stop\-off suppliers\, but that doesn’t negate the need to maintain an adequate inventory of the materials used\. Depending on the type of parts being plated\, this can include tapes \(conductive and non\-conductive\)\, various vinyl shapes\, waxes\, lacquers\, permanent PVC or CPVC shapes\, and a host of other items\.

Keeping a larger supply on hand ensures availability when needed\. Each operation should evaluate its stop\-off needs because they vary drastically with the part requirements\. A captive shop typically uses the same stop\-off materials\, while a job shop needs to inventory all types so it can plate anything that comes in the door\.

The type of fixtures used varies with the parts configurations being plated\. For captive operations\, this is typically a set of standardized fixtures dedicated to a particular part\. Job shops\, on the other hand\, need a more varied set of fixtures to plate a wide variety of parts\. They also need the ability to fabricate specialty fixtures for unusual parts\.

Regardless of the operation\, it’s important to keep an adequate inventory of backup fixtures and the materials needed for fabrication\.

\#\#\#\# Skilled Labor

Labor is a clear necessity\; this includes tank\-side workers and their supervisor\(s\)\. Education for both is important if efficiency and success are expected\, but each requires a different skill set\. The tank\-side workers need knowledge of the basic processing skills related to the parts being plated\. This includes recognizing when conditions change and when questions should be asked\. Supervisors need a deeper understanding of the process\, its quirks\, the specifications they must follow\, the many variables involved\, and insights into troubleshooting and problem\-solving\.

Unfortunately\, schools don\'t teach hard chrome plating as a trade\, yet it is of significant importance to our industry\. Older\-vintage hard chromers became skilled through trial and error\; their knowledge was gradually passed down to their replacements\. However\, valuable information is always lost at every transition\. That training method worked well enough until around the mid\-1970s\.

Unfortunately\, the last batch of skilled ‘old\-timers’ retired years ago\, which left an education gap in today’s workforce\. To make matters worse\, very little written material on hard chrome plating explains the skills needed\.

A lack of education and know\-how in any industrial process always results in inefficiencies\, typically\:

\- A decrease in the overall product quality\.
\- An increase in the rework volume\.
\- A decrease in the production efficiency\.
\- Lost business and lower profit margins\.

Hard chrome plating is no different\. In fact\, these defects are amplified in our industry because\, unlike other trades\, it’s hard to find people with these skills\. These employees usually need to be trained in\-house\.

Operating with a poorly trained workforce is a costly mistake\. This applies to both the tank\-side workers and their supervisors\. On the other hand\, trained\, highly skilled workers can greatly improve throughput and increase the company’s profits\.

We addressed the training issue using three approaches\:

1\. On\-Site Training

Remote schools are sometimes available for processes like anodizing and electroless nickel plating\, but nothing viable exists for hard chrome\. NASF offers a course\, but it barely covers the basics and provides no hands\-on training\. In addition\, off\-site schooling creates production issues when valuable employees are away for an extended period\. Off\-site schooling also adds costs for travel\, housing\, and living expenses\.

Fortunately\, there’s an alternative\. Hard chrome training can be provided at your plant\, on\-site using your parts\, your equipment\, and your processes\. This training comes to you\, so there are no work stoppages or travel expenses\, and you can train multiple employees at the same time\.

This training can be tailored to your specific needs and can even include troubleshooting for various problems or difficult parts\. This can be provided as classroom instruction\, tank\-side training\, or a combination of both\. Most scenarios include a mixture of these and can also incorporate an evaluation of the equipment and procedures being used\.

This training is also available to bring new employees up to speed and help them get off to the right start\. Another option that some corporations find attractive is annual refresher training\. This helps eliminate the gradual efficiency reduction that seems to plague certain operations\. You can combine annual refresher training with an equipment and maintenance evaluation to ensure everything is functioning at its peak\.

2\. Technical Manuals

Two manuals are available that cover the entire knowledge base needed for a successful hard chrome operation\. These are recent publications with the latest up\-to\-date information\.

Hard Chrome University Book \(the Red Book\)\: This book is used for generalized hard chrome training and is a valuable resource for both the tank\-side plater and the supervisor\. It covers every topic involved with the trade and provides valuable process control information\. It’s complete with color illustrations and graphs for clarity\. The text covers both the fundamentals and detailed advanced information\.

Hard Chrome Secrets Book \(the Blue Book\)\: This book contains closely held technical knowledge in an easy\-to\-read format\. It covers every aspect of the art and science\, from both the practical and technical viewpoints\. It includes scientific information\, technical advice\, and numerous tricks of the trade developed by experts over the years\. It covers how to apply high\-quality hard chrome deposits at the lowest cost\. Hard Chrome Secrets is most valuable to the plating supervisor and should be on the shelf of every hard chrome operation whose objective is producing a quality hard chrome deposit most efficiently at the lowest cost\.

These manuals have a limited publication and are not inexpensive\. However\, they provide incredibly valuable information that could easily save your operation six figures annually\. They are only available to companies with a commercial hard chrome operation\.

3\. Online School Development

Plating Resources\, Inc\. is considering developing an on\-line training program specifically for hard chrome technology\. This is currently in the planning stage and only needs confirmation from the hard chrome industry that it would be useful\. This online school would include several development levels\, such as Tank\-Side Plater\, Plating Supervisor\, and Hard Chrome Technician\.

These levels would provide the knowledge needed for those positions\, with each level building on the previous one\. The program will use an easy\-to\-follow format\, and each course should take around 40 hours to complete\. Students can complete the course at home in the evenings\, with instructor interaction so they can ask questions and gain clarity\.

This would be an industry first because an online hard chrome school hasn’t existed before\. This is a better approach than using a remote classroom because it eliminates travel and living expenses\, as well as lost production while employees are away\. An online school seems like a better approach because it eliminates expenses and time away\, and students can learn at their own pace\.

\#\#\#\# Laboratory

Many platers use an outside laboratory for controlling their bath concentrations\, often their chemical supplier\. This is generally a mistake on several fronts unless the operation is small and has minimal throughput\. The worst case is when the company delays bath analysis until plating problems appear and the rework rate increases\.

Relying on vendor\-based laboratories for bath control has two problems\.

\- There’s a significant time delay from when the sample was taken and when you receive the results\. The bath changes during that time lapse\, so the results are never current\, and the bath remains unbalanced\.
\- Many of today’s laboratories use automated analysis equipment\, and the results are often unreliable\. This primarily depends on when and how often instruments are calibrated and maintained\. The reliability of these results is always in question\.

Establish a routine analysis frequency so bath chemistry stays within a reasonable variance\. This variance mostly applies to the chromic acid\, sulfate\, and any secondary catalyst used\. Most experts recommend limiting this variance to 2\-5\% for best performance and repeatability\.

The best way to control the chromic acid and sulfate is by in\-house testing\. A small laboratory set\-up doesn’t need to be large or elaborate\. Forget using Baume’ or Kocour kits for this because these are inaccurate\. Using professional lab glassware\, reagents\, and procedures is much better\. Weekly testing works well for most small\- to medium\-sized operations\. Several baths can be tested in less than an hour\.

A reliable outside laboratory or your vendor should then be used for back\-up testing once the in\-house analysis program is established\. This will confirm your results while also controlling the impurities like trivalent\, iron\, copper and chloride\. Those impurities don’t typically build up quickly\, so monthly testing for these is usually sufficient\.

\#\#\#\# Maintenance

Many platers overlook equipment maintenance until a breakdown occurs\, then it’s a mad rush to get back in production\. Some breakdowns require replacing a component\, which invariably has a lengthy delivery time\, sometimes exceeding 6\-8 weeks or more\. Meanwhile\, the plating system is down\, and production stops until the repair is completed\. Equipment breakdowns are very costly in terms of lost income\.

A regular maintenance program is critical to business success\. These should be established for daily\, weekly\, monthly and annual requirements\. The Hard Chrome University book published by Plating Resources\, Inc\. has a chapter on System Operation and Maintenance that outlines the various requirements in detail\. Each plating system has its own particular requirements\, but many generalities apply across the board\.

Assign equipment maintenance to one person\, using written instruction forms for each maintenance period\.

Another part of a smart maintenance program is maintaining an inventory of critical spare parts\. Having these on hand can save weeks of downtime because you can replace the failed component immediately instead of waiting for delivery\. A replacement can then be ordered to restore your inventory\.

Stocking the following spare parts should be considered\, in no particular order of importance\:

\- Immersion Heaters
\- Pumps
\- Chemicals
\- Anodes
\- Fixtures
\- Fan Belts
\- Stop\-Off Supplies
\- Gaskets \& Seals
\- Polishing \& Grinding Supplies
\- Laboratory Supplies
\- Ventilation HEPA Filters
\- Filter Media
\- Rectifier Modules \& Parts
\- Lubricants
\- PPE Gear
\- Others specific to your system

\#\#\#\# Profits

A business should generate a profit on every part plated\, not just here and there\. One of the problems is that the actual plating costs are often unknown\. It’s relatively easy to calculate the general overhead\, but a lot more complicated to detail specific job costs\. This is especially true when multiple tanks are used\, and several jobs are plated at the same time\, each with different quantities\, chrome thicknesses\, and preparation steps\.

A plating job should only be quoted once the actual costs are known\; then the desired profit margin is applied\. Typical hard chrome profit margins vary all over the map\, but these seem to be typical\:

\- 20\%\: Considered a low margin
\- 30\%\: An average margin
\- 50\%\: Or more is a high margin

Margins above 50\% can apply to unusual jobs where the part is excessively large\, requires a thicker or tight\-tolerance deposit\, is overly complicated\, or has unusual specification constraints\. Another area where high margins apply is when you can repair an expensive part instead of replacing it\, or when your shop is the only one that can handle the job\.

A plating operation must detail its exact costs on every job it handles\. Guessing costs or using estimates typically leads to losses\. A costing program is now available in Excel that details all costs\, both overhead and those related to plating a specific job\, regardless of its requirements\. This program

includes suggested profit margins and even generates the selling price for quoting\, all based on the actual costs and the desired profit margin\. Both job and captive operations would benefit from using this\. Many job shops will be surprised by how much profit they leave on the table\.

\#\#\#\# Capital

Many business managers consider setting aside a portion of profits as a capital reserve a good business practice\. This amount is dedicated to the plating operation for maintenance\, capital expansions\, and unknowns\. This may also include the future costs for any changes in the regulatory requirements\. The exact amount of the capital reserve varies from operation to operation and is considered a strategic practice for future unidentified costs\. There’s nothing worse in business than needing capital and not having it available\.

\#\#\#\# Compliance

Regulatory compliance for environmental and worker safety issues is an ongoing requirement for hard chrome operations\. You can’t sidestep this requirement because violations can be very costly and\, if excessive\, can even shut down the operation\. The biggest issue usually involves meeting the air discharge limits\.

Most hard chrome operations today rely on the Zero Discharge Recovery approach for their sewer regulations\. This system is easy to understand and inexpensive to operate\. It functions by reclaiming and reusing all of the operation’s rinsates\, thereby bypassing the need for a waste treatment system and a sewer connection\.

Tackling the air discharge has been both challenging and costly until a recent design innovation\. Many operations rely on a complex ventilation system and\/or expensive fume suppressants\. A new approach provides a design that produces ZERO chrome discharge to the atmosphere – without needing to use a fume suppressant\. This is the Sustainable Hard Chrome concept\. It is not a marketing gimmick or tactic and has been proven in Real\-World hard chrome shops operating at 20\,000 amperes\. The air discharge was shown to be ‘Zero’ by an EPA\-approved laboratory\.

This was accomplished without using a fume suppressant\. This technology is easiest to apply to new system installations and plating system upgrades\. The beauty of this approach is that authorities can’t regulate below zero\, so the operation stays in compliance regardless of any regulatory tightening\. Other features include improving the operator’s safety and lowering the operation’s chemical costs\.

We hope this article opened some eyes and offers direction for improving your hard chrome operation\.

Eric Svenson Sr\. is CEO of Plating Resources and a Master CEF and IUSF member\. Visit www\.Plating\.com\. If you have any questions or wish to explore this topic further\, please get in touch with Vicky at Vicky\@Plating\.com\.

records.title: Data-Driven Modelling of an Electroplating Process
records.abstract: Electroplated zinc-nickel (Zn-Ni) coatings are commonly applied as corrosion protection for steel components in demanding industrial environments.
records.summary: This article reports a data-driven machine-learning study of an alkaline zinc-nickel (Zn-Ni) barrel electroplating process, aimed at improving process transparency and predictive control where chemical monitoring is irregular. The authors built a cyber-physical production system framework linking a controlled 20 L test bath (186 experiments, 12 months) with an industrial 13,000 L plant (151 batches, 43 part types), using only routinely available inputs (current density, temperature, coating time, and pre-coating Zn and Ni concentrations). Supervised models (Random Forest, XGBoost, SVR, MLP, linear regression, Gaussian Process Regression, 1D-CNN) were trained for process-level targets (post-coating Zn and Ni concentrations) and product-level targets (coating thickness, nickel ratio, binary OK/NOK quality). In the test environment, best models exceeded 86% R2 (e.g., Random Forest Zn R2 = 87%, MAE = 0.28 g/L; linear regression Ni R2 = 91%, MAE = 0.04 g/L; Random Forest thickness R2 = 88%, MAE = 0.45 µm; nickel ratio R2 = 86%, MAE = 0.53%; quality classifier accuracy 92%). Transfer results differed by level: industrial-only process-level models performed well (Zn R2 = 92%, Ni R2 = 94%), but augmenting with test data was not feasible because unrecorded zinc anode dosing altered concentration dynamics; product-level models improved with augmentation (thickness R2 61% to 74%, nickel ratio 35% to 74%, quality ROC 0.75 to 0.95).
records.why_it_matters: The study shows that whether lab-generated data can be transferred to an industrial plating line depends on the modelling target: product-level predictions benefit from experimental augmentation, but process-level bath-composition models require explicit recording of dosing interventions such as zinc anode immersion, so plants should instrument those actions before relying on cross-scale models.

records.body_text:
Electroplated zinc-nickel (Zn-Ni) coatings are commonly applied as corrosion protection for steel components in demanding industrial environments.
However, due to high process complexity, coupled with a limited process transparency and irregular chemical monitoring, achieving resource efficiency and predictive control remains challenging. This paper presents a data-driven approach for monitoring and modelling of an alkaline Zn-Ni barrel plating process at the process and product levels using machine learning (ML) techniques.
A methodology was developed within a cyber-physical production system framework for training the models based on a controlled laboratory environment (20 L bath volume) and knowledge transfer on an industrial electroplating plant (13,000 L bath volume). Different supervised algorithms were trained with a limited set of input features to predict metal concentrations of the bath, coating thickness, nickel ratio in the coating and aggregated coating quality indicator.
Despite data scarcity and process variability, the selected best models demonstrate accurate prediction rates (>86%). The results show that experimentally generated data can improve product-level modelling in the industrial environment, while process-level transfer remains limited when relevant industrial interventions, such as zinc dosing, are not recorded.
1. Introduction
Electroplated finishes play a vital role in significantly prolonging the lifespan of parts and tools by adding thin metallic layers on their surface to improve corrosion and wear resistance. By increasing component lifetime, electroplating also contributes to waste reduction and resource conservation (Leiden et al., 2020). At the same time, maintaining process stability is challenging, as electroplating systems are characterized by a large number of interacting influencing factors, including electrolyte composition, current density, temperature, and additive concentrations. Even small variations in these parameters can significantly affect coating quality, leading to defects, non-uniform layer thickness, and increased production costs. Against this background, there is growing interest in data-driven modelling approaches that enable predictive monitoring and optimization of electroplating processes.
In recent years, machine learning (ML) methods have increasingly been applied to model electrochemical processes and predict coating properties. Several studies have demonstrated successful prediction of coating thickness, composition, hardness, and defect formation using algorithms such as XGBoost, Random Forest, Support Vector Regression, and k-Nearest Neighbors (Katirci et al., 2021; Oliveira et al., 2025; Sánchez Lasheras et al., 2014; Zhai et al., 2025). In addition, image-based approaches have been developed to automatically classify coating quality based on surface features, including convolutional neural networks and segmentation methods such as Mask R-CNN (Katirci and Danaci, 2023; Katirci and Tekin, 2022; Katırcı et al., 2022). These approaches enable automated visual quality inspection and have been partially integrated into optimization frameworks, for example for controlling additive concentrations and process parameters. Furthermore, advanced optimization strategies such as reinforcement learning and hybrid neuro-fuzzy models have demonstrated the potential to simulate complex electrochemical behaviour and derive optimal operating conditions (Ren et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2024). Overall, these studies highlight the considerable potential of ML-based methods to improve process control and support the development of intelligent electroplating systems.
Despite these advances, a key limitation of many existing studies lies in the selection of input variables, which often do not reflect industrial practice. Numerous investigations rely on laboratory-scale datasets, highly controlled experimental conditions, or input features that are difficult to measure reliably in production environments, such as detailed additive concentrations, microstructural descriptors, or image-based surface features obtained under specialized optical conditions (Katırcı et al., 2022; Ren et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2024). In industrial electroplating plants, however, process monitoring is typically based on continuously recorded equipment data, such as current density, voltage, temperature, and flow conditions, as well as metal ion concentrations in the bath. This discrepancy between experimentally available variables and industrially measurable process data represents a major barrier to transferring ML-based modelling approaches into real manufacturing environments. In addition, limited data availability under production conditions further restricts the application of many ML approaches, as data acquisition costs, process interruptions, and variability between production lines hinder the creation of large, standardized datasets. Models developed under laboratory conditions therefore often require extensive adaptation before they can be deployed in industrial systems, where disturbances, equipment aging, and process variability introduce additional complexity.
Against this background, the present work develops ML models for an alkaline Zn-Ni barrel plating process using only input variables that are routinely available in industrial electroplating operations. The study distinguishes between two modelling scenarios: process-level modelling of Zn and Ni concentrations in the electrolyte after coating, and product-level modelling of coating thickness, nickel ratio in the coating, and a binary coating quality indicator. A controlled 20 L test environment was used to generate systematic parameter variations and deliberately broaden the represented process window, while an industrial 13,000 L environment provided production data under realistic operating conditions. The central objective is to evaluate which modelling targets can benefit from knowledge transfer between both environments and where transferability is limited by unrecorded industrial process interventions. Overall, the proposed modelling framework is consistently based on industrially available process and material data, ensuring direct compatibility with existing monitoring systems. The study is therefore characterized by its strict alignment with industrial constraints, the simultaneous consideration of product- and process-level predictions, and the deliberate enhancement of model robustness through enriched datasets. It contributes to bridging the gap between laboratory-scale research and industrial application and supports the development of intelligent, data-driven manufacturing systems with improved process transparency, higher resource efficiency, and reduced environmental impact.
The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews ML applications in electroplating and identifies the research gap. Section 3 introduces the CPPS-based methodological framework, the physical Zn-Ni electroplating systems, data acquisition, target variables, and modelling scenarios. Section 4 presents modelling results in the test environment. Section 5 evaluates knowledge transfer and industrial transferability. Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines future work.
2. State of research
Fig. 1 summarizes recent ML applications in electroplating from 2014 to 2026. Most studies are based on bench-scale experiments, typically using Hull cells, beaker-based setups, or cuvette-type configurations with virgin, self-prepared electrolytes. Consequently, industrial constraints such as commercial electrolyte chemistry, bath ageing, chemical consumption, and production-related variability are rarely represented. In addition, only a few studies discuss whether the identified model relationships are physically plausible.
Fig. 1. State of the art of ML modelling in electroplating classified by process scale, modelling target, data type, and discussion of physics.
2.1. Modelling at product level
Regarding modelling at product level, some studies focus on coating quality and defect prediction, often using image-based data. For zinc coating, Katirci et al. used Random Forest models to predict coating brightness from Hull cell experiments and reported high classification performance (Katırcı et al., 2022). Similarly, Katirci and Tekin modelled zinc bath states through image-based classification of coating outcomes, again in a Hull cell setup (Katirci and Tekin, 2022). For nickel systems, Katirci and Danaci combined Mask-R-CNN and Random Forest models to classify surface quality and infer additive requirements from Hull cell experiments (Katirci and Danaci, 2023). Sun et al. modelled coating defects and colour in black nickel electroplating using machine learning methods in a beaker-based setup (Sun et al., 2024). These studies demonstrate strong predictive performance for quality-related targets, but they are largely restricted to small-scale experimental systems and frequently rely on image-based rather than process integrated numerical data. Ren et al. modelled defect-related coating quality in black nickel electroplating by combining lightness and uniformity into a pass/fail target, alongside plating rate as a continuous output, and used the resulting virtual process model for reinforcement-learning-based current-density optimization (Ren et al., 2026).
A second group of studies addresses coating thickness prediction. Katirci et al. predicted Zn-Ni coating thickness in Hull cell experiments using machine learning models trained on electrolyte composition data (Katirci et al., 2021). De Oliveira et al. predicted zinc coating thickness using XGBoost based on experimental Hull cell data and reported high predictive accuracy (Oliveira et al., 2025). Sánchez Lasheras et al. developed an evolutionary support vector machine approach for hard chromium thickness prediction and included selected pre-treatment and bath related parameters as model inputs (Sánchez Lasheras et al., 2014). Although these studies show that coating thickness can be modelled effectively, most are still based on controlled laboratory conditions and do not systematically address industrial scale transferability.
A third group of articles has a focus on prediction of metal composition in coating (metal ratio), which is more closely related to the present study. Katirci et al. additionally to coating thickness predicted also nickel ratio in the deposited layer and identified key electrolyte components affecting the response variables (Katirci et al., 2021). Rai and Gupta modelled process-dependent responses in Cu-Zn alloy deposition, including alloy composition related effects, using ANN, RSM, and ANFIS approaches (Rai and Gupta, 2025). However, studies explicitly addressing alloy composition remain limited, and only one identified work specifically focuses on a Zn-Ni electroplating bath.
2.2. Modelling at process level
In regard to modelling of bath composition, several studies focus either on metal or additive concentrations in a bath. However, most of this work addresses organic additives or indirect descriptors of electrolyte performance rather than the concentrations of the main metallic elements under industrially relevant conditions. For zinc electroplating, Katirci and Tekin investigated additive-related bath states using image-based classification in a Hull cell setup (Katirci and Tekin, 2022). In nickel electroplating, Katirci and Danaci combined surface quality classification with Random-Forest-based prediction of bath composition and subsequent additive optimization (Katirci and Danaci, 2023). Luo et al. predicted Gutmann donor numbers of electrolyte additives from molecular descriptors and linked them to the electrochemical performance of zinc anodes (Luo et al., 2025). Zhai et al. analyzed Ni-W alloy deposition and identified bath chemistry related variables and process parameters influencing coating hardness (Zhai et al., 2025). Jo et al. focused on Cu bath monitoring and trained ANN models on voltammetric profiles to quantify the organic additive concentrations of DPS and PEG-PPG (Jo et al., 2025). Kumar et al. used convolutional LSTM models to predict the future image-based morphology of dendritic Cu electrodeposition from real-time image sequences rather than bath composition (Kumar et al., 2022).
These studies highlight the relevance of electrolyte composition for process behaviour, but they also show that previous machine learning approaches have mainly focused on additives and secondary bath descriptors. In contrast, the direct modelling of Zn and Ni concentrations in electroplating baths remains insufficiently addressed.
Taken together, the presented studies demonstrate that machine learning can successfully model several electroplating targets, particularly coating quality, thickness, and additive related bath behaviour. At the same time, three major gaps remain. First, most studies are conducted at bench scale and therefore only partially represent industrial process conditions. Second, the majority rely on virgin or simplified electrolytes rather than aged commercial baths under production load. Third, no identified study models metal bath concentrations together with coating related targets across both test and industrial environments. This is where the present work contributes by developing and comparing process-level and product-level black-box models for Zn-Ni electroplating across a controlled test environment and an industrial-scale production environment.
3. Materials and methods
This study evaluates the transferability of ML models between a controlled test environment and an industrial Zn-Ni electroplating environment. The methodological approach is organised according to a cyber-physical production system (CPPS), consisting of four elements: physical system, data acquisition, cyber system, and decision support/control (Thiede et al., 2016). The proposed framework to structure the CPPS builds on previous work (Lindner et al., 2025), and includes two physical systems, a test environment (a) and an industrial environment (b) (Fig. 2). Within this framework, the test environment is used for systematic parameter variation and targeted generation of different coating results, whereas the industrial environment provides realistic production data under normal operating conditions.
Fig. 2. Framework of the cyber-physical production system (CPPS), including knowledge transfer and transferability assessment between the test and industrial environment (adapted from (Lindner et al., 2025)).
The methodological approach distinguishes between two modelling scenarios. Scenario 1 refers to process-level modelling and targets Zn and Ni concentrations in the electrolyte after the coating process. Scenario 2 refers to product-level modelling and targets coating thickness, nickel ratio in the coating, and coating quality. Depending on the modelling objective and the available data, either one of these scenarios or both can be implemented.
3.1. Physical system: Zn-Ni barrel electroplating process
An electroplating process chain for alkaline zinc-nickel coatings on workpieces such as steel caps using barrel plating technology is investigated. Barrel plating is a widely used electroplating technique for processing small parts such as screws, nuts, washers, and other fasteners in large quantities. The process is efficient, cost-effective, and particularly suited for achieving uniform coatings on small, irregularly shaped components. The components to be coated are filled into a barrel. The barrel is continuously rotated and immersed in the active and rinsing baths of the entire process chain. The process begins with a pre-treatment consisting of a hot degreasing with 60 g L−1 potassium hydroxide (KOH) at 60 °C and then a pickling with 15 - 20% concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl) to remove heavy contamination from oils and rust. Afterwards, electrolytic degreasing (cathodic) with 120 g∙L−1 KOH at 40 °C, takes place, whereby the gaseous hydrogen formed on the component surface is released and fine impurities, including those in pores, are detached. This is followed by a mild pickling with 3-5% HCl, in which residues of KOH solution are neutralized and a newly formed thin oxide coating is removed. In the coating phase, the barrel with workpieces is placed in an alkaline zinc-nickel electrolyte of type SLOTOLOY ZN 210 VX from company Dr.-Ing. Max Schlötter GmbH & Co. KG. The electrolyte contains zinc and nickel salts, sodium hydroxide (NaOH) as conductive salt as well as a complexing agent and brighteners, see Table 1.
Table 1. Composition of zinc-nickel electrolyte ZN 210 VX according to manufacturer specifications.
| Component | Function | Concentration |
| Zinc | Metal ion | 6.5-8.5 |
| Nickel | Metal ion | 0.9-1.2 |
| NaOH | Conductive Salt | 110-130 |
| Slotoloy ZN 211 | Complexing Agent | 90-140 |
| Slotoloy ZN 212 | Leveler | 25-40 |
| Slotoloy ZN 214 | Brightener | 0.5-2 |
| Slotoloy ZN 216 VX | Top brightener | 0.1-0.3 |
Manufacturers do not disclose the exact additive composition. Typically, alkaline Zn-Ni electrolytes contain complexing agents, brighteners, levelers, wetting agents, and buffers, which influence metal ion stabilization, grain refinement, layer homogeneity, gas bubble formation, and pH stability (Jeon et al., 2023; Lotfi et al., 2018; Praveen and Venkatesha, 2012; Son et al., 2023; Zaky et al., 2011). Since these additive concentrations are not routinely available in the industrial environment, they were not included as model inputs. This reflects a typical limitation of industrial electroplating data. Furthermore, manufacturers use additive packages containing several substances in order to exploit their synergistic effects.
An electric current facilitates the deposition of a uniform Zn-Ni alloy coating, known for its excellent corrosion resistance and ductility. The rotation of the barrel ensures uniform exposure and prevents clumping of caps, promoting consistent coating thickness. Post-treatment includes passivation based on a chromium (III) conversion bath using the transparent coating Slotopas ZN-T-80 from Dr.-Ing. Max Schlötter GmbH & Co. KG to improve corrosion resistance. Conversion coatings are very thin coatings on a metal surface, which are usually produced by the chemical reaction of an aqueous treatment solution with the metallic substrate. This step is followed by drying and curing to further improve the coating's durability and performance.

3.1.1. Test and industrial environments
Data was obtained, on the one hand from a test environment with a manual electroplating system with a 20 L bath volume and on the other hand from an industrial environment with an automatic system with 13,000 L bath volume. Both environments fulfil different functions in data acquisition. The industrial environment provides a large amount of practical data. However, due to ongoing production, process parameters can only be varied to a limited extent. In the test environment, high throughput cannot be achieved, but the variation possibilities are almost unlimited. In this environment, for example, reject parts can also be generated in order to examine the limits of the process more specifically.
To best compare the two environments and the data generated there, the industrial process was evaluated by thorough inspections of the electroplating plant, in-depth interviews, available industrial data and then replicated in the test environment, as far as feasible, taking into account the given scaling differences. This includes the same sequence of individual process steps, the use of the same process parameters as well as the chemicals and anode material (“VX 1 special anode” which should reduce the formation of cyanide and degradation processes). The same product, see Fig. 3, was also coated in a smaller version (1 cm vs. 3 cm in diameter).
Fig. 3. (left) Photo of the caps that were defined in the study as the product to be coated. (right) Photo of the holder for 20 caps each for the XRF measurements on the top and bottom of the cap.
The main differences, apart from the different scaling and the automatic vs. manual electroplating, are on the one hand in the provision of the zinc salt: in the industrial environment there is an additional zinc dissolving station with soluble zinc anodes. This station supplies a total of nine electrolyte baths with zinc. The amount of dissolved zinc is determined by raising and lowering the anode rails. In the test environment only one electrolyte bath is used and the zinc salt is added via a metal salt solution due to the significantly lower throughput. Furthermore, two baths are used in the industrial plant for pickling and hot degreasing, as many different products with varying degrees of contamination are used in production, whereas only the caps are coated in the test environment. The first bath initially removes the majority of the contamination and the second bath ensures the required cleaning quality.
3.1.2. Target variables and parameter selection
To enable knowledge transfer from the test environment to the industrial environment, it is essential that the parameters required for monitoring are already established and routinely collected in a typical industrial electroplating plant. Therefore, only typical electroplating process parameters, structural characteristics and product properties were considered in the proposed approach: i) coating time, current density, temperature, and zinc and nickel concentrations, ii) coating thickness and nickel ratio in coating, and iii) corrosion protection (Fig. 4).
Fig. 4. Multi-level modelling approach at the process and product levels, depicting process-product-interdependencies between process parameters, structural characteristics and product properties.
The purpose of the galvanic Zn-Ni coating is to provide corrosion protection for the components. According to the literature, this is expected when the coating has a nickel ratio between 10 and 18 at.% due to the formation of a γ-phase, which has high corrosion resistance, hardness, and strength (Burliaev et al., 2021). This is also specified in various standards (DIN 50979; ASTM B841; DIN EN ISO 4526), which also define a permissible lower coating thickness range of 8 to 15 μm. Both the nickel ratio and the coating thickness were the target values, whose specified ranges had to be met with the respective parameter variations.
The current density was varied because, among others, it determines the deposition rate of the coating and that of the alloy components, and thus the composition of the coating. In addition to kinetics and mass transport, the temperature influences the conductivity of the electrolyte and affects the consumption of electrolyte additives. The additives are cathodically reduced and compete with metal deposition. As the temperature rises, their consumption increases disproportionately, which in turn also influences the layer properties (Kanani, 2020). Since the Zn-Ni bath heats up during production, it was necessary to clarify how warm the bath could become in order to continue to meet the target ranges. Also, the Zn and Ni concentrations and the coating time were varied, as these directly influence the coating composition and coating thickness.
3.2. Data acquisition
During the data acquisition phase (II) datasets are collected from both systems (Fig. 2). The sampling frequency corresponds to one observation per coating process. Consequently, the time resolution is limited to the process level, since an individual coating process over time is typically not being recorded in an industrial practice, even though higher sampling frequencies on the order of seconds would be technically feasible.
In addition to the coating process implementation, the bath and coating analysis were also coordinated between the two environments. In both environments, zinc and nickel concentrations were sampled before and after the coating process. In the test environment the sampling was done manually and analyzed with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) spectrometer in an in-house analysis laboratory. To measure the Zn and Ni bath concentrations, a bath sample was taken and measured a total of five times. An average value was then calculated from these measured values. In comparison, in the industrial environment, automatic sampling and concentration determination were performed every 15 min on the plant using an online XRF spectrometer. At an element specific crystal and detector angle, the device records the metal characteristic fluorescence in counts per second. For each angle, at least three replicate measurements are taken, outliers are checked and repeated if necessary, and the final value is the mean of the accepted measurements which is then converted to concentration using a prior calibration curve.
The coating thickness and composition were measured after every coating process in both environments using XRF analysis in an in-house laboratory. For this purpose, a holder was designed and manufactured using additive manufacturing. The holder enables a reproducible examination of the top and bottom of 20 caps per batch, see Fig. 3. Both parts of the holder can be plugged together so that the top and bottom of the caps can be aligned with defined positioning by turning the top and bottom of the holder without manual repositioning.
3.2.1. Test environment dataset
This section focuses on the data processing from the test environment and, in particular, of data generated during the coating process. The following parameters were varied extensively:
- Current density (0.4 – 0.8 A dm−2)
- Temperature (20 – 42 °C)
- Zn concentration (4 – 6 g L−1)
- Ni concentration (0.5 – 1.5 g L−1)
- Barrel speed (3.5 – 6 rpm)
- Coating time (65 – 80 min)
All other pre- and post-treatment process steps were carried out with the same parameter settings. This data is not considered in this approach. For each experiment conducted in the test environment, 20 caps were manually sampled by the operator. The coating thickness and composition were measured on both the top and bottom sides of each cap, resulting in a total of 40 measurements per experiment. The mean of all measurements was then calculated and used for further analysis as “Mean Coating Thickness” and “Mean Nickel Ratio” respectively. Current density and temperature are automatically set parameters, whereas the coating time was set manually by the operator by removing the barrel from the electroplating bath after 80 min.
A total of 186 experiments were conducted, whereas experiments affected by missing values or invalid data were excluded, and therefore are not part of this final dataset (Fig. 5). In 18 experiments the standard process parameters were tested as initial data. In further 57 experiments the temperature and in 40 experiments the current density was varied. On the one hand, variations in current density were combined with changes in zinc concentration and nickel concentration in 15 experiments in each case. On the other hand, exclusively metal concentrations were varied (zinc in 11 experiments; nickel in 12 experiments). Furthermore, 9 experiments were carried out with different barrel speeds, while in a further 9 experiments the barrel speed and the coating time were varied simultaneously. The experimental data was acquired within the period of 12 months.
