3.2.2. Industrial environment dataset
Similarly to the test data, the industrial data was gathered over several weeks during normal coating operations, resulting in a dataset of 151 coating batches across 43 different parts. The variables “Mean Coating Thickness” and “Mean Nickel Ratio” were both assessed as a mean value of multiple measurements after a coating process in an in-house laboratory via X-ray. Five repeated measurements were performed at each of three distinct locations on the parts, namely the top, bottom, and side, resulting in 15 measurements for each coating batch. Current density, coating time and temperature were automatically set in the plant control system, whereas as already described, the zinc and nickel concentrations were automatically sampled before and after the coating by an online XRF spectrometer.
3.3. Cyber system: modelling scenarios
Further, the datasets are modelled within the third element (Fig. 2, III Cyber System), addressing two primary scenarios:
- Modelling at the process level of process parameters, focusing on the aspects relevant for the maintenance of the tank electrolyte, especially on Zn and Ni concentrations in the electrolyte after the coating process.
- Modelling at the product level, specifically focusing on structural characteristics coating thickness and nickel ratio in coating, as well as product properties based upon labelled coating thickness, and corrosion protection. Corrosion protection is derived from defined required properties of the coating thickness and the nickel ratio in the coating (further referred to as coating quality).
Process parameters serve as input features at both the product and process levels. Metal concentrations are modelled using input samples collected prior to the coating process, with the target values corresponding to the concentrations obtained after the coating process.
Different algorithms have been applied and compared, including Random Forest, Support Vector Regression, Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Linear Regression, XGBoost, Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) and 1D-CNN (Breiman, 2001; Chen and Guestrin, 2016; Ding et al., 2021; Ige and Sibiya, 2024; LeCun et al., 2015; Rasmussen, 2006). Additionally, in regression models, a GPR approximation with 95% confidence band was added to address prediction uncertainty. All models used an 80/20 data-split, and a random_state was used by starting the random split always from the same seed and producing the identical random sequence to ensure reproducible results across different algorithms. Additionally, stratified sampling was applied in most models, in order to include the data from all experiments in the training dataset. Furthermore, the application of synthetic data was additionally investigated to improve modelling performance. Since no significant performance gains were achieved, this approach was discontinued and is not examined further in this study.
3.4. Digital assistance and decision support
The fourth element of the framework (Fig. 2, IV Digital Assistance Systems), closes the loop by providing deeper process understanding and decision support for the worker. The test environment loop of the CPPS serves as the foundation for knowledge discovery and transfer, as experimental investigations involving systematic variation of process parameters are only feasible in controlled testing environments. The knowledge discovery includes the modelling pipelines for different target variables in the Cyber System, as well as the selection of suitable algorithms for the respective task. Furthermore, deploying the models in the industrial environment enables monitoring at both the process and product-levels, thereby providing decision support.
4. Modelling results in test environment
This section presents the modelling results obtained in the test environment for Scenario 1a and Scenario 2a. The aim is to evaluate whether process-level and product-level targets can be predicted under controlled but industrially inspired experimental conditions.
4.1. Scenario 1a: modelling at process level in test environment
To model the post-coating metal concentrations in the Zn-Ni tank, following input parameters are used:
- Coating time [min],
- Temperature [°C],
- Current density [A∙dm−2],
- Zinc concentration before the coating [g∙L−1]
- Nickel concentration before the coating [g∙L−1].
The typical duration of a coating process is 80 min. It should be noted that in this case the models performed better without the data with a simultaneous parameter variation of barrel speed and the coating time (Fig. 5, area I), so the final dataset contained 177 experiments.
4.1.1. Zinc concentration after the coating [g∙L−1]
For modelling the Zn concentration, different regression algorithms were applied and quantitatively compared via R2 and MAE (Fig. 7a). The Random Forest model achieves the highest predictive performance with an R2 = 87% and lowest MAE = 0.28 g L−1 indicating a generalization capability. Following, Linear Regression and Gaussian Process algorithms also indicate a high performance, outperforming several other nonlinear models (MLP, SVR and 1D-CNN). Furthermore, Fig. 7b shows the predicted Zn concentration after the coating on test data and demonstrates that this model is able to closely follow the overall level and the local trends, including regions with varying Zn concentration across most experiments. Additionally, the approximate 95% predictive interval from the GPR model gives an overview of the predictive uncertainty, with a mixed-length-scale kernel for capturing multi scale behaviour. The width of the uncertainty band is mostly constant and it quantifies the confidence envelope of the model, meaning that the model is robust in most regions. The parity plot in Fig. 7c compares the predicted Zn concentrations with the measured ground truth concentrations. Most predictions are located around the ideal line with minor deviations. The deviations can be attributed to a smaller data density and increased experimental variability in these regions. Overall, the ensemble-based ML models provide accurate predictions of Zn concentrations after the coating.
Fig. 7. Comparison of different algorithms for predicting the concentration of Zn in the electrolyte after coating.
4.1.2. Nickel concentration after the coating [g∙L−1]
The results for Ni concentration prediction show a strong and consistent model performance across most algorithms with multiple R2 values above 80% (Fig. 8a). The Linear Regression model achieves the highest score on the test dataset with an R2 = 91%, and the lowest MAE of 0.04 g L−1. Since the target variable lies in the range of 0.5 to 1.5 g L−1, the low MAE indicates a high level of predictive precision of the model. Furthermore, as depicted in Fig. 8b, the predictions of Linear Regression are closely following the true values, suggesting that the relationship between the process parameters and the Ni concentration is predominantly linear within this process window. The GPR based approx. predictive interval (Fig. 8b) remains narrow and mostly stable over the test data range, indicating a high level of confidence, and limited epistemic uncertainty which normally occurs with limited or unbalanced datasets. The last plot (Fig. 8c) provides additional analysis of the best model with a parity plot, where model predictions are scattered tightly around the ideal predictions with no visible outliers.
Fig. 8. Comparison of different algorithms for predicting the concentration of Ni in the electrolyte after coating.
4.2. Scenario 2a: modelling at product level in test environment
In this research, the coating quality is defined through the corrosion protection requirements either with the coating thickness [μm], nickel ratio in coating [%] or a combination of both as a binary coating quality [OK, NOK]. The coating thickness and nickel ratio are modelled with regression algorithms, whereas these values can be labelled and assigned to the classes “OK” and “NOK” in a classification task. If both the coating thickness and the coating composition are in a good quality range, the binary coating quality is set as OK.
4.2.1. Mean coating thickness [μm]
For modelling the mean coating thickness, the following parameters were used as input variables with applied stratified sampling:
- Temperature [°C],
- Current density [A∙dm−2],
- Zn concentration before the coating [g∙L−1]
- Ni concentration before the coating [g∙L−1]
Fig. 9 illustrates the performance of different algorithms, as well as the overall prediction trend of the best model, along with supplementary details regarding the quality classes. Fig. 9a shows that nonlinear models perform best for this target variable, with the Random Forest achieving R2 of 88% and slightly outperforming XGBoost with R2 of 87%. Taken into the consideration, that coating thickness values range between 5 and 12.5 μm, an MAE of 0.45 μm can be regarded as a good predictive performance. Even though the experiments included varying coating thickness qualities, Random Forest is able to predict the values with a low deviation from the true values, including the regions with pronounced local variations, as shown in Fig. 9b. The green area in the graph represents the optimal coating thickness window, whereas the yellow areas indicate the upper and lower tolerance limits. Prediction within the red area correspond to critical coating thickness values and highlight operating conditions associated with increased process risk. The uncertainty GPR band shows narrower intervals in stable regions and pronounced widening around abrupt thickness changes, where the uncertainty can be associated with stronger nonlinearity or reduced data support. Since most of the test values lie within the approximate 95% interval, the model is considered well calibrated, but some regions of the prediction are to be treated with caution.
Fig. 9. Comparison of different algorithms for predicting the coating thickness.
4.2.2. Mean nickel ratio in coating [%]
For effective protection, the nickel mass fraction should reach 13-14% of the coating. When modelling the coating composition, the best results were achieved with the following input features:
- Current density [A∙dm−2]
- Zn concentration before the coating [g∙L−1]
- Ni concentration before the coating [g∙L−1]
Parameters such as temperature and coating time showed no effect on the model's predictions and were therefore not included.
Fig. 10 presents the modelling results for the mean nickel ratio and indicates a more complex prediction task than for coating thickness. Fig. 10a shows that nonlinear models clearly outperform linear regression, with the Random Forest achieving the best performance on the test set (R2 = 86% and lowest MAE = 0.53%), followed by the MLP and Gaussian Process models. The low performance of the Linear Regression suggests a nonlinear nature of nickel incorporation into the coating layer. As shown in Fig. 10b, the Random Forest prediction closely follows the overall trend of the experimental data and is able to capture most local variations, although larger deviations occur in regions with abrupt changes in nickel ratio. The GPR band (R2 = 78%) widens in these regions, reflecting that this particular model has lower performance and therefore increased uncertainty most likely due to stronger nonlinearity or data scarcity. The parity plot in Fig. 10c confirms good overall agreement between predicted and measured values, with some increased deviations at lower nickel ratios. Overall, the results demonstrate that nonlinear models provide reliable predictions for the nickel ratio, while the uncertainty information highlights regions where predictions should be interpreted with increased caution.
Fig. 10. Comparison of different algorithms for predicting the nickel ratio in the coating.
4.2.3. Binary coating quality [OK/NOK]
The coating quality is derived on the basis of defined specifications for the coating thickness and composition resulting in a class with a good coating quality (OK) or a poor coating quality (NOK). A Random Forest Classifier was applied using only temperature [°C] and current density [A∙dm−2] as model inputs. Zn and Ni concentrations were excluded from the final classifier because they did not improve classification performance in the tested feature combinations. Other classification models, including SVM with RBF kernel, logistic regression, Naive Bayes, and k-nearest-neighbors, were also evaluated. However, these approaches achieved accuracies of less than 75% and therefore performed lower than the Random Forest model. For this reason, only the Random Forest classifier is presented and discussed in detail.
Fig. 11a depicts the confusion matrix with the binary classes. The model has a high accuracy of 92%, meaning that it is able to mostly classify both classes correctly. As can be seen in the confusion matrix, the model only had false positives in three cases, leading to a precision of 86%. The ROC-Curve in Fig. 11b shows that the model is able to separate between an OK and NOK part, having a high true positive and a low false positive rate. To better understand the model decision making a decision space graph is illustrated in Fig. 11c. Based on the electrolyte manufacturer's guidelines, the optimal conditions for a good coating quality require a current density of 0.8 A dm−2 and a temperature of 30 °C. However, according to this graph, higher temperature does not have a negative impact on the coating quality. Whereas it is confirmed, that a lower current density leads to a thinner coating, resulting in a NOK part. Overall, the model shows promising results.
Fig. 11. Confusion matrix, ROC curve, and decision space of the Random Forest classifier for predicting binary coating quality.
4.3. Discussion of modelling in test environment
The following section discusses the modelling results of an alkaline Zn-Ni coating process at both the process and product-level. Table 3 shows some of the most important parameters influencing the electrolyte bath.
Table 3. Literature-based effects of selected bath and process parameters on electroplating behaviour (excerpt from (Gugua et al., 2024)).
| Parameter | Effects | 
| Metal ion concentration | Deposition rate; thickness of coating | 
| Temperature | Deposition rate | 
| Current density | Deposition rate; structure of deposited layer | 
| Agitation speed | Distribution of metal ions | 
The experimentally obtained data for the coating time, temperature, current density, and barrel speed (influences agitation speed), as well as the Zn and Ni concentrations before coating, were considered as input parameters.
1) Discussion of models at process level
At the process level, the metal concentrations of zinc and nickel in the electrolyte after coating were predicted. These concentrations were also determined experimentally, see “True Values” in Fig. 7, Fig. 8, and are used to verify the predicted concentrations and the prediction rate in the form of the criteria R2 and MAE. According to Table 3, the temperature, current density, and metal concentrations all have a directly proportional influence on the deposition rate. This means that the higher deposition rates lead to higher consumption of metal ions in the bath. The barrel speed affects the amount of zinc or nickel in the coating. Thus, the more of each element is incorporated into the coating, the greater the decrease in the concentration of that element in the electrolyte. The coating time is not listed in Table 3. However, one would expect that as the coating time increases, the layer thickness increases evenly and thus the metal concentrations in the electrolyte decrease linearly. When modelling with all the input factors mentioned, the predictions were initially inadequate. Through multiple modelling with a varying number and combination of input factors, it was determined that better results were achieved when the experiments with the coating time and barrel speed were omitted from the test dataset. This could be due to the fact that the available data is insufficient to model these relationships, which may be more complex than the empirical values. In the case of coating time, only 10 experiments with varying settings were carried out simultaneously with the barrel speed, and in the case of isolated barrel speed experiments, there were 9. Therefore, both parameters were not taken into account in the process-level modelling.
When predicting the Zn concentration after coating, the Random Forest Regressor (RFR) algorithm showed the best results with R2 = 87%, and MAE = 0.28. This indicates that changes in the input factors have a directly proportional effect on the Zn concentration after coating, as shown in Table 3, especially when the data with all parameter variations are included in the modelling in equal parts due to stratified sampling. When predicting the Ni concentration, the Linear Regression showed the best result with R2 = 91%, and MAE = 0.04. Here, too, a high prediction accuracy was achieved, but a linear correlation was not expected for various reasons: The zinc-nickel deposition is unusual, since zinc despite being less noble, tends to deposit more readily than nickel (anomalous Zn-Ni codeposition). This can be explained by the hydroxide suppression effect. As it happens, a secondary process of hydrogen evolution takes place at the same time during which the medium is alkalized. The increased pH of the electrolyte solution contributes to the formation of the adsorptive zinc hydroxide. Consequently, metallic zinc is reduced at the cathode due to the adsorbed hydroxide film that obstructs the transport of nickel to the electrode's surface. This leads to the suppression of both nickel and hydrogen reduction (Burliaev et al., 2021; Son et al., 2023). Additionally, the hydrogen generated as a by-product at the cathode (Hydrogen Evolution Reaction (HER)), along with the fact that this reaction is kinetically favoured over nickel deposition, adversely impacts the deposition of nickel. (Zhang et al., 2014). The consumption of protons during hydrogen formation at the cathode also leads to a significant increase in pH and an accumulation of OH− ions. Zinc ions can form stable hydroxo complexes with OH− ions that are highly soluble, allowing zinc to be deposited. In the case of nickel, however, increased concentrations of OH− lead to the formation of nickel hydroxide, which is poorly soluble and causes nickel to precipitate, making it unavailable for deposition. In summary, varying the input parameters in the case of nickel triggers many further effects that influence each other. However, since the data set consists mainly of data with variations in temperature and metal concentrations–both parameters that are directly proportional to Ni concentration, as well as variations in current density in the medium current density range, in which hydrogen evolution is not yet so pronounced, it is possible that a process window was investigated in which the relationships actually behave linearly. However, the predictive quality of the model outside this process window should be viewed with caution and validated by further experimental data, if possible, also using multi-parameter variations.
2) Discussion of models at product level
Modelling at the product level was based on the prediction of the layer thickness, the prediction of the nickel ratio in the coating, and the prediction of the binary coating quality based on the combination of both output factors. The input factors were the temperature, the current density, and the metal concentrations before coating. For the prediction of the coating thickness, good results were again achieved with the RFR algorithm and stratified sampling (R2 = 88%, MAE = 0.45). This corresponds well with the empirical observations described above.
A Random Forest classifier was used to predict the binary coating quality. With the input factors temperature and current density, a high accuracy of 92% was achieved, which means that the model is able to classify both classes (OK/NOK) largely correctly. As discussed above, both input factors have a directly proportional effect on the coating thickness and an indirectly proportional effect on the nickel content in the layer, which is directly proportional to the availability of Ni2+ in the electrolyte. Thus, there is also an indirect proportionality between the layer thickness and the nickel content in the layer, which further improves the prediction accuracy. The decision space graph also shows that significantly higher temperatures, above 40 °C instead of max. suggested 32 °C, can be set in wide current density ranges in order to still classify the coatings as “OK.” This result was not expected, as the nickel availability in the bath should decrease with increasing temperature and increasing current density, as discussed previously. The high accuracy of the model can perhaps be explained by the fact that, in the higher temperature range considered in the experiment, the effects on the nickel concentration in the bath are not yet so greatly increased and the current density range considered in the experiment was within the range specified by the manufacturer. Further tests would be needed to check whether an “OK” classification can still be achieved at 40 °C and a very high current density of 1.5 A dm−2, for example. It should be noted that no long-term corrosion tests were conducted in order to keep the testing effort low with respect to cost–benefit considerations. The majority of the tests were carried out with parameter variations within the parameter ranges specified in the product data sheet. For these, the electrolyte manufacturer has ensured corrosion stability while maintaining the coating composition and thickness. However, it is correct that corrosion tests would have been useful for temperature variations above 35 °C, but only to confirm the theory that these layers are also corrosion-stable while maintaining the layer composition and thickness. However, since this data was not collected for the entire data set, it could not have been taken into account in the modelling. On the other side, increasing temperatures, especially above 40 °C, have a significant influence on the resulting layer properties, including additive consumption, microstructure, nickel distribution, nickel content, etc., and thus also have a negative effect on corrosion resistance. In order to better highlight these differences, additional layer properties, e.g., long-term corrosion must be recorded in further studies.
A direct comparison with previous studies is limited because most studies are based on Hull cells, beaker experiments, fresh electrolytes, or proprietary laboratory formulations. In contrast, the present study used a 20 L test environment that was designed to replicate an industrial Zn-Ni process as closely as possible. Moreover, only routinely available process variables were used as inputs. This distinguishes the proposed approach from studies that rely on detailed additive concentrations or image-based quality descriptors. The results therefore support the applicability of black-box models under more realistic industrial constraints, while also showing that model outputs must be interpreted against electrochemical process knowledge.
These, in turn, are factors that are monitored online in practice, or at least at short intervals, and can therefore be used for process control. Furthermore, the cited studies were generally purely data science investigations. This means that algorithms were selected and tested, a performance evaluation was carried out, for example using the metrics XGBoost or F1 score, and the models were evaluated in terms of industrial suitability based on their robustness, interpretability, or even computing time. However, there was a general lack of industrial-technical discussion, meaning that only patterns in the datasets were examined, but it was not clarified whether these were plausible. With a black box model, there is a risk that correlations will be learned that are only coincidental and that the model will deliver incorrect decisions. In addition, the model should expand existing expertise as much as possible and not just provide numbers.
5. Knowledge transfer and industrial transferability
In a subsequent step, the knowledge derived from modelling the dataset in the test environment was transferred to the industrial context. In addition to replicating the industrial Zn-Ni process in the test environment, the industrial process was modelled using the same input parameters (features) and prediction targets as previously described. For comparison, two approaches were evaluated: in the first, the models were trained exclusively on the original industrial dataset (OID, n = 151), whereas in the second, the dataset from the test environment (n = 186) was incorporated into the industrial dataset as a form of augmented dataset (AD, n = 337).
5.1. Scenario 1b: modelling at process level in industrial environment
As shown in Table 4, the Zn and Ni models achieved high predictive performance when trained on the OID. This indicates that process level modelling can be successfully implemented in the industrial environment, particularly because the required data can be collected during regular production without interfering with day-to-day operations. In this setting, the industrial process itself provides the most relevant data basis for modelling bath composition.
Table 4. Overview of modelling results (Gaussian Process) with the original industrial dataset.
| Target variable | Original industrial dataset (OID) | Augmented dataset (test + industrial) (AD) | 
| Zn concentration | R2 = 92%; MSE = 0.15; MAE = 0.12 | Not feasible | 
| Ni concentration | R2 = 94%; MSE = 0.02; MAE = 0.01 | Not feasible | 
However, transferring process-level information from the test environment to the industrial environment proved infeasible. The main limitation arises from differences in operating conditions. In the industrial process, Zn anodes were immersed in the electrolyte during coating. However, this intervention – and in particular the resulting changes in zinc concentrations – was not recorded, so it was not possible to determine the actual zinc consumption in the electrolyte. In the test environment, however, the Zn concentration was adjusted to the same target concentration for all batches prior to coating by adding a metal salt solution, so that the Zn concentrations measured after coating always reflected the consumption of Zn in the electrolyte. Supplementing the industrial dataset with data from the test environment for process-level modelling was not suitable. Models trained on the AD showed poor prediction performance because industrial Zn and Ni concentrations often increased after coating, whereas the test-environment data reflected a different concentration trend. This indicates that the target at process level is directly coupled to the local mass balance of the industrial bath. In the test environment, the concentration change after coating is mainly determined by metal deposition and the predefined initial bath composition. In the industrial environment, however, the measured post-coating concentration is also influenced by zinc supplied during production. Since this zinc input was neither recorded as a feature nor represented in the test environment, the same input variables can lead to opposite concentration trends in both datasets. Therefore, the AD does not describe one consistent process relationship, but combines two different concentration mechanisms.
Therefore, cross-environment knowledge transfer could not be validated at process level in this study. The experimentally generated data were only suitable for product-level augmentation, where the target variables were less directly affected by unrecorded industrial bath interventions.
A possible solution to overcome the data gap in zinc immersion could be a combined evaluation of time-resolved zinc concentration measurements in the coating module and current-derived zinc dosage from the dissolution module. With this approach, regularly measured Zn2+ concentrations could be synchronized with production timestamps to assign concentration changes to individual barrels, while the module current could be recorded and converted into the zinc mass supplied using Faraday's law. The actual zinc consumption per barrel can then be calculated from the difference between the zinc supplied and the net change in bath concentration, allowing for electrochemical losses and possible overcompensation. Since the module current scales with the area of the immersed anode, a controlled and reproducible anode immersion depth could be used as an indirect control variable for zinc dosing, supporting bath stability and consistent alloy composition even without direct measurements of immersion depth. Finally, collecting data in an experimental environment offers the potential to generate a broader diversity of coating scenarios that are rarely available in industrial production due to the high associated costs. Such experimentally acquired data can serve as an effective form of data augmentation, enhancing model robustness and improving generalization to industrial applications.
5.2. Scenario 2b: modelling at product level in industrial environment
For product-level modelling Random Forest was selected because it showed the best performance for the considered target variables and was therefore trained for this task. As shown in Table 5, product-level models became more robust when trained on AD. Although the test environment dataset contains only one part geometry, whereas the industrial dataset includes 43 different part types, the models were still able to generalize effectively. This improvement can be attributed to the higher diversity of the test environment dataset, which includes different experiments and deliberately produced NOK parts. In contrast, in an industrial setting the objective is to avoid producing such parts.
Table 5. Comparison of modelling results (Random Forest) with the original industrial dataset and the augmented dataset by test environment dataset.
| Target variable | Original industrial dataset (OID) | Augmented dataset (test + industrial) (AD) | 
| Coating Thickness | R2 = 61%; MSE = 2.3; MAE = 1.2 | R2 = 74%; MSE = 1.2; MAE = 0.8 | 
| Nickel Ratio in Coating | R2 = 35%; MSE = 0.3; MAE = 0.45 | R2 = 74%; MSE = 0.5; MAE = 0.5 | 
| Coating Quality | Accuracy = 93%; ROC =0.75 | Accuracy = 82%; ROC = 0.95 | 
Especially in the coating quality model the ability to recognize NOK parts improves significantly from 75% to ROC = 95%.
In contrast to the process-level targets, the product-level targets integrate the cumulative effect of the coating process on the part. Despite containing one part geometry, the test dataset includes a broader range of coating outcomes due to systematic parameter variation. This is particularly relevant for the coating quality classifier, since industrial production data are biased towards OK parts. The test data therefore add information about the decision boundary between OK and NOK, which is underrepresented in regular production.
Although the coating quality model achieved an overall accuracy of 93% when trained exclusively on OID, this result is not reliable due to the severe class imbalance in the validation data. Specifically, the dataset contained only three non-OK (NOK) parts, which is insufficient to robustly evaluate the model's ability to detect defective cases. As a consequence, the model correctly classified only one NOK part, highlighting its limited sensitivity to the minority class. This indicates that the reported accuracy is dominated by the abundance of OK parts and therefore overestimates the true predictive performance (ROC = 75%).
5.3. Comparison of process-level and product-level transferability
The comparison of both modelling scenarios shows that transferability depends on the causal proximity between the target variable and unrecorded environment-specific process interventions. Product level targets, such as coating thickness, nickel ratio, and coating quality, benefited from augmentation with test-environment data because the experimental dataset increased the diversity of coating outcomes. In contrast, process-level targets were highly sensitive to the zinc dosing mechanism in the industrial setting. Since zinc anode immersion was not recorded and was not represented in the test environment, the concentration dynamics differed between both environments. Consequently, process-level modelling was successful within the industrial environment itself, but cross-environment augmentation was not feasible.
Table 6 summarizes the resulting transferability assessment. The decisive factor is not only the similarity of the experimental setup, but whether the relevant mechanism behind the target variable is represented in both environments. For product-level targets, the test environment captures relevant coating outcomes caused by parameter variation. For process-level targets, however, the industrial zinc dosing mechanism changes the bath concentration independently of the coating outcome and must therefore be recorded explicitly.
Table 6. Summary of industrial transferability for process-level and product-level modelling.
| Modelling level | Industrial-only modelling | Test-to-industrial augmentation | Explanation | 
| Process Level | Successful | Not feasible | Unrecorded zinc dosing changes concentration dynamics | 
| Product Level | Partly successful | High potential | Test data add broader coating outcomes and NOK cases | 
6. Conclusion and outlook
In this work, a CPPS-based data-driven modelling approach for an alkaline Zn-Ni barrel electroplating process was presented. The approach links a controlled test environment with an industrial production environment and proposes two modelling scenarios: process-level modelling of Zn and Ni concentrations in the electrolyte after coating and product-level modelling of coating thickness, nickel ratio in the coating and binary coating quality.
The results show that relevant targets in the electroplating process can be modelled with high prediction performance using only routinely available industrial process data. In the test environment, both modelling scenarios achieved good results despite the limited amount of data and the high process variability. This indicates that standard process parameters and bath concentrations are suitable input features for data-driven monitoring, even without additional sensor systems or detailed knowledge of proprietary additives.
The transfer to the industrial environment showed different results depending on the modelling scenario. At process level, modelling with the original industrial dataset was successful. However, augmentation with data from the test environment was not feasible, mainly because the industrial process includes zinc dosing by immersed Zn anodes during coating, which was not recorded in the dataset. At product level, the augmented dataset improved model robustness, especially for the binary coating quality model, since the test environment included deliberately generated NOK parts that are rarely available in industrial production.
Therefore, the main finding of this study is that knowledge transfer from test to industrial environment depends strongly on the modelling target. Modelling at product level can be beneficial with an experimental data augmentation, whereas process-level modelling requires a more complete recording of bath maintenance and dosing actions. Thus, the suitability of knowledge transfer depends on the available data and on whether the relevant process mechanisms are represented in both environments.
Future work should focus on making more extensive use of transfer learning models in practice in order to apply the acquired knowledge in a more generalized manner. To achieve this in the context of the described Zn-Ni process, changes in Zn concentrations must be monitored more closely, for example by synchronizing Zn2+ concentration measurements with current signals from the zinc dissolution module to improve process alignment across different scales. Furthermore, more general modelling objectives, such as the deviation from the target coating thickness rather than the absolute coating thickness, could be investigated to improve the transferability to different component geometries.

records.summary: This 1994 article reports an experimental study of how the monovalent cations NH4+, Li+, Na+, and K+ affect plating rate, bath stability, and deposit properties in a lactate-acetate electroless nickel (EN) bath. The authors prepared 0, 3, and 6 metal-turnover (MTO) baths by neutralizing sulfuric and phosphorous acids with the corresponding hydroxide or ammonia, then plated at 87 ± 2 °C and pH 4.6, measuring rate, phosphorus content, intrinsic stress, deposition potential, and crystal structure. Plating rates fell about 30 percent after three turnovers for all baths; the lithium bath gave the fastest initial rate but precipitated after a few turnovers, while the ammonium bath was slowest but was the only one to reach six MTOs without precipitation. The authors attribute the ammonium behavior to nickel complexing by ammonia and higher sulfate solubility, and propose that the low solubility of Li2HPO3 could be exploited to remove phosphite by hot filtration during plating. Reported filtration of a simulated 1.75-MTO lithium bath at 95 °C reduced phosphite from 39 to 30 g/L and raised the rate from 16.3 to 17.5 µm/hr (units as printed).
records.why_it_matters: The results indicate that cation choice in an EN bath trades plating rate against bath life, and that lithium's low phosphite solubility may offer a filtration-based route to extend bath life beyond the typical 3–6 MTO limit, though this remains a proposed rather than demonstrated process.

records.body_text:
We investigated the effect of increasing concentrations of NH4+, Li+, Na+, and K+ on plating rate and bath stability in a lactate-acetate EN plating solution.
The relationship between sulfate and phosphite salt solubilities and metal turnovers was studied. We also determined deposition potentials, microstructures, and phosphorus contents.
Since its industrial development in the 1950s, electroless nickel (EN) has found increasing use on a wide variety of parts, primarily for functional engineering applications requiring corrosion and/or wear resistance. Although its growth has slowed in the last few years, the total value of EN coatings in the U.S. is estimated at $200 million.1
EN plating has three major disadvantages compared to electrolytic nickel plating:
- High chemical cost ($0.40 to 0.70/L)
- Limited plating bath life (3 to 6 MTO)
- Expensive spent bath treatment or disposal
Limited bath life results from the continuous accumulation of phosphite and sulfate salts as byproducts of the plating reaction. To maintain optimum pH, frequent alkali addition is necessary. The main reactions are:
(1) Reduction NiSO4 + 3MH2PO2 → Ni0 + 2MH2PO3 + MHSO4 + P + 1/2H2
(2) pH adjustment (4.5 to 6.0) 2MOH + MH2PO3 + MHSO4 → M2HPO3 + M2SO4 + 2H2O
Note: This article was published in 1994, and some financial data may not be adjusted.
Table 1 shows the rapid increase in salt concentration with each nickel turnover (MTO = 1, initial nickel concentration is replenished once) in a typical EN plating bath containing nickel sulfate, sodium hypophosphite, and sodium salts of organic acids, with potassium carbonate as the pH adjuster. Increased salt content increases the solution's density and viscosity, decreases the plating rate, and induces precipitation of nickel phosphite. The NiP deposit properties deteriorate, as evidenced by increasing porosity and tensile stress. Blistering on aluminum is common after three MTOs.

The solubilities of alkali phosphite and sulfate salts are shown in Tables 2 and 3. As expected, the ammonium salts are most soluble. The nickel and lithium phosphites have the lowest solubilities in water. Because a mixture of sodium and potassium sulfates is present in the used plating bath, the actual phosphite solubilities are lower than in water alone. The nickel phosphite solubility depends on the chelating acids used in the EN formulation, which control the “free nickel” ion concentration.2
Sodium and potassium sulfate often crystallize when the spent bath is stored below 5 C. The phosphite anion can precipitate as a calcium or magnesium salt; however, the plating solution will then contain calcium or magnesium cations that impair deposit properties.3 The use of lithium salts in an EN bath has not been previously reported. In an electroless copper bath, lithium hydroxide was superior to sodium and potassium hydroxide in improving the plating rate and the mechanical properties of the copper deposits.4 One early reference found a sodium glycolate bath to plate at 21 mm/hr at 97°C and an initial pH of 4.5, compared to a rate of 16 mm/hr for an ammonium glycolate bath.5
This investigation explores the effect of varying the monovalent alkali ions in an EN plating solution.
Experimental Procedure
For all plating experiments, 4L solutions were used. Because only the sodium salts of hypophosphorous acid are commercially available, the other alkali hypophosphites were prepared in situ from the acids by neutralization with the appropriate alkali or ammonium hydroxide. The initial and simulated three- and six-turnover generic formulation baths are as shown in Table 4.
We prepared the three- and six-MTO baths from MTO0 by adding the calculated amounts of sulfuric and phosphoric acids, then neutralizing with the appropriate alkali or ammonia to reach the desired salt concentrations. Plating was performed in thermostatically controlled 4L Pyrex beakers. The initial pH of all baths was 4.6. Plating was carried out at 87°C ±2 for 1 to 2 hr. Plating rates were determined by measurement of deposit thickness. Initial deposition potentials were measured against Ag/AgCl with a digital multimeter at 85°C. Deposit composition was obtained by foil analysis using an electron beam microprobe (EDS). Intrinsic stress measurements were made with a spiral contractometer. The MTO0 deposit crystal structures were examined on foils with an X-ray diffractometer. Plating solutions containing potassium salts, but no sulfate ions, were prepared and evaluated as listed in Table 5.
Fig. 1—Solubility of anhydrous phosphites; Fig. 2—Solubility of lithium phosphite; Fig. 3—Lithium phosphite removal.
Results and Discussion
The results of the initial experiments are shown in Table 6. The plating rates of all the baths decreased by about 30 percent after three metal turnovers. Surprisingly, the lithium bath showed the fastest initial plating rate and produced a deposit with relatively low potential and slightly higher phosphorus content.
The ammonium bath plated the slowest; however, it yielded six turnovers without precipitation. Both results can be attributed to the nickel complexing action of ammonia. Tensile stress increased considerably with turnovers in deposits from the ammonium and potassium baths. Comparison of X-ray diffraction diagrams of the MTO0 foils reveals no microstructural differences among the various cation deposits (Table 7).
In the absence of sulfate, the potassium plating bath initially plated at 12.5 mm/hr. After adding 68 M potassium phosphite (6 MTO), the plating rate decreased to 5 mm/hr. The deposition potential also decreased from 590 to 620 mV.
Because lithium phosphite has lower solubility than other monovalent cation phosphites (Figs. 1 and 2), we investigated the possibility of phosphite reduction in a used lithium plating bath. A 1.75 MTO solution was simulated with lithium acetate, sulfate, and hydroxide (Table 8). Filtration at 95°C through a 0.5 µm membrane reduced the phosphite content from 39 to 30 g/L. It increased the plating rate from 16.3 to 17.5 mm/hrmA/hmay be possible to remove part of the accumulating phosphite during plating by continuous filtration, as shown in the diagram of Fig. 3. The operating life of the lithium bath would thereby be extended, and the plating rate increased.
Summary
Electroless nickel plating solutions containing lactic and acetic acids as complexants and buffers were prepared with hypophosphorous acid and ammonium, lithium, sodium, or potassium hydroxide at 0, 3, and 6 metal turnovers. At 87°C and pH 4.6, the lithium bath had an appreciably faster initial plating rate, but it precipitated after a few metal turnovers. The ammonium bath had the slowest initial plating rate; however, it was the only solution that plated at six metal turnovers without precipitation. Further investigation is warranted into removing lithium phosphite by filtration during plating to extend the life of an EN plating bath.
Findings
The four monovalent cations investigated have diverse effects on the operation of an electroless nickel plating system. The low solubility of the accumulated potassium sulfate limits the potassium bath. Sodium ions have a similar effect on the process at greater MTOs, but for different reasons. In the all-sodium bath, nickel phosphite is the principal precipitate, at about three MTOs.
When ammonium ions are used, the amine group's complexing effect with nickel enhances nickel solubility at the expense of nickel phosphite precipitation. Also, ammonium ions increase the solubility of the sulfate anion relative to sodium and potassium sulfate. However, the deposition rate decreases with increased NH+ concentration.
Finally, the lithium ion has two positive effects on the EN plating system. First, the rate of deposition increases in the all-lithium bath. Second, and most importantly, the low solubility of dilithium phosphite (Li2HPO3) at 88°C can control the accumulation of orthophosphite in the EN plating bath to about one MTO.

evidence_meta.coverage: Extracted accessible page text; figures, supplementary files and paywalled content may be missing.

technical_points: Baths used nickel sulfate, lactic and acetic acids, hypophosphorous acid, and 0.5 ppm lead, with NH4+, Li+, Na+, or K+ hydroxide/ammonia for neutralization; plating at 87 ± 2 °C, initial pH 4.6, 4 L volumes.

Plating rates decreased by about 30 percent after three metal turnovers in all baths; the lithium bath had the fastest initial rate (19 µm/hr at MTO-0 in Table 6) but precipitated after a few turnovers.

The ammonium bath plated slowest (13 µm/hr at MTO-0) but was the only solution reaching six MTOs without precipitation, attributed to ammonia's nickel complexing and higher ammonium sulfate solubility.

Intrinsic tensile stress rose with turnovers in ammonium and potassium deposits (e.g., ammonium from 0.02 to 8.3 KSI by MTO-6); X-ray data showed no microstructural differences among MTO-0 deposits (d ≈ 2.01 Å).

Hot filtration (0.5 µm, 95 °C) of a simulated 1.75-MTO lithium bath reduced phosphite from 39 to 30 g/L and increased plating rate from 16.3 to 17.5 µm/hr, supporting a proposed continuous-filtration concept (Fig. 3).
limitations: The article is a 1994 trade-publication report; figures and some table entries are garbled or missing in the retrieved text, and units (e.g., 'mm/hr' vs 'µm/hr') are inconsistent.
The filtration result is from a simulated 1.75-MTO lithium bath, not a full-life plating trial; extending bath life via continuous filtration is proposed, not demonstrated.
No statistical analysis, replicate counts, or direct comparison to prior art beyond cited references is provided in the available text.

The solubilities of alkali phosphite and sulfate salts are shown in Tables 2 and 3. As expected, the ammonium salts are most soluble. The nickel and lithium phosphites have the lowest solubilities in water. Because a mixture of sodium and potassium sulfates is present in the used plating bath, the actual phosphite solubilities are lower than in water alone. The nickel phosphite solubility depends on the chelating acids used in the EN formulation, which control the “free nickel” ion concentration.2
Sodium and potassium sulfate often crystallize when the spent bath is stored below 5 C. The phosphite anion can precipitate as a calcium or magnesium salt; however, the plating solution will then contain calcium or magnesium cations that impair deposit properties.3 The use of lithium salts in an EN bath has not been previously reported. In an electroless copper bath, lithium hydroxide was superior to sodium and potassium hydroxide in improving the plating rate and the mechanical properties of the copper deposits.4 One early reference found a sodium glycolate bath to plate at 21 mm/hr at 97°C and an initial pH of 4.5, compared to a rate of 16 mm/hr for an ammonium glycolate bath.5
This investigation explores the effect of varying the monovalent alkali ions in an EN plating solution.
Experimental Procedure
For all plating experiments, 4L solutions were used. Because only the sodium salts of hypophosphorous acid are commercially available, the other alkali hypophosphites were prepared in situ from the acids by neutralization with the appropriate alkali or ammonium hydroxide. The initial and simulated three- and six-turnover generic formulation baths are as shown in Table 4.
We prepared the three- and six-MTO baths from MTO0 by adding the calculated amounts of sulfuric and phosphoric acids, then neutralizing with the appropriate alkali or ammonia to reach the desired salt concentrations. Plating was performed in thermostatically controlled 4L Pyrex beakers. The initial pH of all baths was 4.6. Plating was carried out at 87°C ±2 for 1 to 2 hr. Plating rates were determined by measurement of deposit thickness. Initial deposition potentials were measured against Ag/AgCl with a digital multimeter at 85°C. Deposit composition was obtained by foil analysis using an electron beam microprobe (EDS). Intrinsic stress measurements were made with a spiral contractometer. The MTO0 deposit crystal structures were examined on foils with an X-ray diffractometer. Plating solutions containing potassium salts, but no sulfate ions, were prepared and evaluated as listed in Table 5.
Fig. 1—Solubility of anhydrous phosphites; Fig. 2—Solubility of lithium phosphite; Fig. 3—Lithium phosphite removal.
Results and Discussion
The results of the initial experiments are shown in Table 6. The plating rates of all the baths decreased by about 30 percent after three metal turnovers. Surprisingly, the lithium bath showed the fastest initial plating rate and produced a deposit with relatively low potential and slightly higher phosphorus content.
The ammonium bath plated the slowest; however, it yielded six turnovers without precipitation. Both results can be attributed to the nickel complexing action of ammonia. Tensile stress increased considerably with turnovers in deposits from the ammonium and potassium baths. Comparison of X-ray diffraction diagrams of the MTO0 foils reveals no microstructural differences among the various cation deposits (Table 7).
In the absence of sulfate, the potassium plating bath initially plated at 12.5 mm/hr. After adding 68 M potassium phosphite (6 MTO), the plating rate decreased to 5 mm/hr. The deposition potential also decreased from 590 to 620 mV.
Because lithium phosphite has lower solubility than other monovalent cation phosphites (Figs. 1 and 2), we investigated the possibility of phosphite reduction in a used lithium plating bath. A 1.75 MTO solution was simulated with lithium acetate, sulfate, and hydroxide (Table 8). Filtration at 95°C through a 0.5 µm membrane reduced the phosphite content from 39 to 30 g/L. It increased the plating rate from 16.3 to 17.5 mm/hrmA/hmay be possible to remove part of the accumulating phosphite during plating by continuous filtration, as shown in the diagram of Fig. 3. The operating life of the lithium bath would thereby be extended, and the plating rate increased.
Summary
Electroless nickel plating solutions containing lactic and acetic acids as complexants and buffers were prepared with hypophosphorous acid and ammonium, lithium, sodium, or potassium hydroxide at 0, 3, and 6 metal turnovers. At 87°C and pH 4.6, the lithium bath had an appreciably faster initial plating rate, but it precipitated after a few metal turnovers. The ammonium bath had the slowest initial plating rate; however, it was the only solution that plated at six metal turnovers without precipitation. Further investigation is warranted into removing lithium phosphite by filtration during plating to extend the life of an EN plating bath.
Findings
The four monovalent cations investigated have diverse effects on the operation of an electroless nickel plating system. The low solubility of the accumulated potassium sulfate limits the potassium bath. Sodium ions have a similar effect on the process at greater MTOs, but for different reasons. In the all-sodium bath, nickel phosphite is the principal precipitate, at about three MTOs.
When ammonium ions are used, the amine group's complexing effect with nickel enhances nickel solubility at the expense of nickel phosphite precipitation. Also, ammonium ions increase the solubility of the sulfate anion relative to sodium and potassium sulfate. However, the deposition rate decreases with increased NH+ concentration.
Finally, the lithium ion has two positive effects on the EN plating system. First, the rate of deposition increases in the all-lithium bath. Second, and most importantly, the low solubility of dilithium phosphite (Li2HPO3) at 88°C can control the accumulation of orthophosphite in the EN plating bath to about one MTO.
References

- O. Mallory, Plating, 61, 1005 (Nov., 1974).
- Parker, Plat. and Surf. Fin., 67, 48 (Mar., 1980).
- Matsuoka et al., Chemistry Express, 7(3), 181 (1992)
- Bosdorf and K. Muller. Metalloberfläche 12(5), 150 (1958).
About the Authors
Glenn O. Mallory is a founder of Electroless Technologies Corp. (ETC), 3860 Cloverdale Ave., Los Angeles, CA 90008. He specializes in electroless deposition and has more than 30 years’ experience in the surface finishing industry. He is a former vice president of R&D for electroless nickel development at Allied-Kelite Div. of Witco Chemical Corp. He holds a BS from UCLA and an MS from California State University, Los Angeles.
Konrad Parker is a specialist in electroless nickel plating. An MS graduate of the Illinois Institute of Technology, he holds many patents. He has authored numerous papers, including “The Formulation of Electroless Nickel-Phosphorus Plating Baths,” for which he received the AESF Gold Medal in 1988.

RI Regulators Cite Electrolizing Over Hazardous Waste Issues at Chrome Plating Facility
Rhode Island environmental regulators have issued a “Notice of Intent to Enforce” against Electrolizing Inc. following an inspection of the company's Providence chrome plating facility.
The report identified a series of alleged hazardous waste violations involving chromic acid, containment pits and waste-management practices.
The Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management (RIDEM) issued the notice Sept. 25 to Billy Brauer, general manager of Electrolizing Inc. The agency said it has reasonable grounds to believe Electrolizing and property owner B&J Properties violated statutes or regulations under RIDEM's jurisdiction.
The enforcement action provides a detailed look at hazardous waste management challenges at a working chrome plating operation. It could offer lessons for other finishing companies that generate and manage hazardous waste.
Complaints Lead to RIDEM Inspection
The investigation began after RIDEM received two anonymous complaints on Aug. 25 alleging problems with chemical containment at the facility. One alleged that a containment area holding liquids that included chromium compounds, water, alkaline materials, and acids could be leaking into the ground. Another raised concerns about changing liquid levels in a containment area.
RIDEM inspected the facility the following day. According to the agency's enforcement notice, Brauer told inspectors that in July, Tank No. 10 on an aluminum processing line had leaked approximately 100 to 200 gallons of chromic acid into a containment pit beneath the line. The company subsequently took the tank out of service while it awaited a replacement.
The document says Brauer told RIDEM that the liquid level in the containment pit had increased significantly since the tank leak. He believed chromic acid in the pit was mixing with water from sources including condensation, steam leaks, and groundwater entering the pit.
Inspectors reported observing substantial amounts of liquid waste in containment pits underneath several processing areas. In one area, the agency says Billy Brauer indicated that the employee responsible for maintaining liquid accumulation levels had resigned and that monitoring logs could not be found. According to the notice, liquid levels were measured with a stick marked in 6-inch increments.
Tests Find Chromium and Cadmium
Laboratory testing became another significant part of RIDEM's case. According to the notice, Electrolizing Inc. provided RIDEM with an Aug. 17 analytical report from Phoenix Environmental containing results for waste-liquid mixtures sampled from three containment pits underneath separate plating lines. The samples underwent Toxicity Characteristic Leaching Procedure testing.
RIDEM said the sample from the containment pit serving Tanks Nos. 1-6 exceeded the RCRA toxicity thresholds for cadmium, with a reported result of 12.7 mg/L, and chromium, reported at 546,000 mg/L. The pit serving Tanks Nos. 7-9 had reported results of 2.11 mg/L for cadmium and 25,000 mg/L for chromium, also exceeding the applicable toxicity thresholds cited by the agency.
The sample from the containment pit serving Tanks Nos. 10 and 11 exceeded the chromium toxicity threshold with a reported result of 1,070 mg/L and had a reported pH of 2, placing it at the corrosivity regulatory level cited by RIDEM.
Scrubber Leaks and Chromic Acid Also Cited
RIDEM's inspection extended beyond the containment pits. On the facility's mezzanine, inspectors observed an air scrubber connected to Chromic Acid Plating Tanks Nos. 1, 2 and 3. According to the enforcement notice, Brauer said the unit had experienced leaks over the years because of its age. Inspectors observed drip pans, containment trays, cardboard, and absorbent pads beneath the unit.
RIDEM also reported observing chromic acid on the mezzanine floor and alleged there had been no apparent effort to clean up or contain that particular release. Inspectors additionally reported finding two drip pans containing waste chromic acid that were uncovered, unlabeled, and lacked accumulation start dates.
The enforcement notice says Brauer suggested that previous leaks from the scrubber may have allowed chromic acid to enter hollow concrete blocks before eventually migrating through the wall. RIDEM directed the company to conduct analytical soil testing outside the building to determine whether hazardous materials may have reached the environment. ￼
RIDEM further alleged that Electrolizing Inc. failed to report chromic acid spills that accumulated below the scrubber and seeped through the building wall.
Waste-Management Procedures Under Scrutiny
The enforcement action also focuses heavily on the facility's hazardous waste management systems.
On Sept. 1, Brauer told RIDEM that Electrolizing Inc. did not have a procedure in place to pump out containment pits after hazardous waste was released or spilled into them, according to the notice.
RIDEM subsequently reviewed the company's hazardous waste contingency plan and personnel training program. The agency said its review found that both documents lacked required elements and did not satisfy Rhode Island's hazardous waste rules.
The state also alleged issues involving waste labeling, accumulation dates and spill records. A separate ecoRI News report says the notice identified 13 hazardous waste regulatory violations, including allegations involving labeling, recordkeeping, waste storage, and spill reporting.
Company Required to Respond
The Sept. 25 letter requires Electrolizing Inc. to submit a written response within 10 days stating its intentions to comply with RIDEM's required actions within the specified timeframes.
Importantly, the document is a Notice of Intent to Enforce, representing RIDEM's initial enforcement response to the alleged violations rather than a final adjudication of those allegations.
RIDEM also notified the company that it intends to assess administrative monetary penalties and said noncompliance in these matters could carry maximum penalties of up to $25,000 per violation, per day. The agency said the notice does not prevent it from subsequently issuing a Notice of Violation assessing administrative penalties.
Electrolizing Inc., an Armoloy company, specializes in precision surface treatments and offers processes including thin dense chrome, biocompatible chromium and several nickel coatings. Its company website says the Providence operation traces its work in surface treatment to 1945.

Lubrication Engineers Acquires BioBlend Renewable Resources
Lubrication Engineers, Inc. (LE) has acquired BioBlend Renewable Resources, LLC, expanding its portfolio of bio-based and specialty industrial lubricants. The Wichita, Kansas-based company announced the acquisition on October 19, 2026. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed.
Founded in 2007, BioBlend develops and manufactures high-performance bio-based and hybrid lubricants for the mining, marine, drilling, food-grade, and industrial markets. Operating from its manufacturing facility in Grundy Center, Iowa, the company has developed proprietary formulations used in demanding applications, including underground mining, dredging, and fire-resistant hydraulic systems. Its hybrid and fully biodegradable lubricants are designed to match or exceed the performance of conventional petroleum-based products while helping customers reduce environmental impact and meet regulatory requirements in environmentally sensitive applications.
“BioBlend has built an impressive portfolio of high-performance, bio-based products backed by deep application expertise and a loyal customer base,” said Paul Vallis, CEO of Lubrication Engineers. “Together with the talented BioBlend team, we are committed to expanding access to sustainable, high-performing lubrication solutions for customers across the industries we serve.”
Jeff Hart, CEO of BioBlend, said the acquisition provides a platform for the company's continued growth. “For 20 years, BioBlend has been built by dedicated employees, supportive investors and loyal customers, and I'm grateful to every one of them. After careful consideration, we know that LE is the ideal home for our people, our customers and the future of BioBlend,” Hart said. “With LE's long-standing leadership in industrial lubrication and its focus on performance and quality, our team and our renewable products now have the platform to grow and make an even bigger difference.”
The transaction marks LE's fourth acquisition since partnering with private equity firm Aurora Capital Partners in September 2023, following its acquisitions of Royal Purple Industrial, SWEPCO, and RSC Bio Solutions. Through these acquisitions, LE has expanded its industrial lubrication expertise and broadened its portfolio of synthetic, specialty, and sustainable lubricant products. The addition of BioBlend further extends its offerings in bio-based lubrication technologies and environmentally oriented industrial applications.
Founded in 1951, Lubrication Engineers manufactures premium industrial greases, gear oils, and other lubricants, along with related asset reliability products. The company serves customers in more than 60 countries from its 150,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Wichita, Kansas. Aurora Capital Partners, headquartered in Los Angeles, is a middle-market private equity firm with approximately $6 billion in assets under management.
About BioBlend Renewable Resources
Founded in 2007, BioBlend Renewable Resources, LLC develops and manufactures high-performance, bio-based lubricants for the mining, marine, drilling, food grade, and industrial markets. BioBlend’s proprietary hybrid and fully biodegradable formulations are engineered to match or exceed the performance of conventional petroleum-based products, giving customers a viable path to reduce environmental impact across demanding applications. The company operates from its manufacturing facility in Grundy Center, Iowa. For more information about BioBlend, visit: www.bioblend.com.
About Lubrication Engineers
A leader in lubricants since 1951, Lubrication Engineers develops, manufactures and sells premium industrial greases, gear oils and other lubricants, and markets related asset reliability products. LE’s highly engineered products directly lower its customers’ total cost of ownership through reduced energy consumption, reduced maintenance and improved equipment longevity. LE serves customers in more than 60 countries from its flagship 150,000 square-foot manufacturing plant in Wichita, Kansas. For more information about LE, visit: www.LElubricants.com.
About Aurora Capital Partners
Aurora Capital Partners is a leading Los Angeles-based private equity firm with $6 billion in assets under management. Founded in 1991, the firm invests in middle-market companies with leading market positions, stable industry dynamics, attractive business model characteristics and actionable opportunities for growth in partnership with management. For more information about Aurora Capital Partners, visit: www.auroracap.com.

U.S. Lubricants Names Adam Puzach President as Pack Logix Integration Advances
U.S. Lubricants has named Adam Puzach president as the company continues integrating Pack Logix, the blending and packaging business acquired by parent company U.S. Venture earlier this year.
Puzach had served as president and CEO of Pack Logix before the April acquisition. Following the transaction, he became vice president and general manager of packaging and operations for U.S. Lubricants. His move into the president’s role places him at the center of a broader effort to combine lubricant distribution with blending, packaging, custom formulation and private-label manufacturing.
James Williams, who had been president of U.S. Lubricants, will continue to lead the division’s national sales strategy as vice president of sales, according to the company.
“The acquisition of Pack Logix has poised U.S. Lubricants uniquely in the marketplace as a fully integrated platform, providing its partners a single point of contact for all of their lubricant needs,” Puzach said in announcing his appointment.
U.S. Lubricants distributes automotive, commercial and industrial lubricants and fluids, including major branded products, while also manufacturing its proprietary THRIVE lubricant line. The addition of Pack Logix brought in-house blending and packaging, toll-blending, custom formulation and private-label capabilities.
The company says it moves nearly 14 million gallons of lubricants annually through its regional and national network.
More Than a Packaging Acquisition
When U.S. Venture announced the Pack Logix acquisition on April 16, it described the transaction as more than an expansion of packaging capacity. The combination was expected to provide greater toll-blending capacity, broader packaging options and a more integrated supply chain.
Pack Logix brought 36 employees into the organization, along with experience in custom formulations, private-label programs and specialty packaging. U.S. Lubricants said at the time that the business would be systematically integrated over the following year.
Puzach’s appointment suggests that integration is becoming an increasingly important part of the company’s strategy.
For lubricant distributors, the traditional model has centered largely on representing major brands and moving finished products from suppliers to customers. U.S. Lubricants is expanding that model by adding capabilities farther upstream in the value chain, including formulation, blending, packaging and contract manufacturing.
That can provide greater control over product availability, packaging formats, private-label programs and supply-chain response—capabilities that have taken on added significance during a year marked by substantial base-oil and finished-lubricant supply disruptions.
U.S. Lubricants said earlier this year that its growth had enabled it to secure higher contracted volumes with base-oil and additive suppliers. The company also said the Pack Logix acquisition was attracting additional supplier interest, although it remained exposed to the same market-driven price increases affecting the broader industry.
Puzach said his priorities as president will include maintaining the company’s growth, strengthening customer relationships and positioning the business for long-term success.
“We’ve built strong momentum, and I’m focused on continuing that growth, deepening our customer relationships, and positioning this team for long-term success,” he said.
Eric Kessenich, CEO of U.S. Venture, said Puzach’s experience fits what the company sees as the next stage for the lubricant division and pointed specifically to the continuing integration of Pack Logix.
The broader question now is how far U.S. Lubricants intends to take the integrated model. The combination of distribution, proprietary lubricants, blending, packaging and private-label manufacturing gives the company a broader platform than it had before the acquisition.
Whether that ultimately leads to deeper penetration in existing markets, broader geographic expansion, additional acquisitions or further growth in contract manufacturing remains to be seen.
For now, Puzach’s appointment makes clear that Pack Logix is becoming an important part of the direction of U.S. Lubricants, rather than simply operating as an acquired packaging business.
About U.S. Lubricants
U.S. Lubricants brings 50 years of experience delivering automotive, commercial and industrial fluids. The company combines authorized distribution of top-tier brands with the manufacturing of its proprietary THRIVE® lubricants, supported by in-house blending and packaging capabilities. Moving nearly 14 million gallons annually through an integrated regional and national network, U.S. Lubricants helps customers maximize performance, efficiency and supply continuity. Headquartered in Appleton, Wisconsin, U.S. Lubricants is a U.S. Venture company.
About U.S. Venture, Inc.
For more than 75 years, U.S. Venture, Inc. has been active in the distribution of renewable and traditional energy products, lubricants, tires and parts, as well as data-driven energy and logistics solutions. Its family of brands includes U.S. Energy®, U.S. AutoForce, Breakthrough®, U.S. Lubricants and IGEN®.

In Memoriam: Carol Lee Poole
In Memoriam: Carol Lee Poole
ILMA mourns the passing of Carol Lee Poole, a dedicated health and safety professional whose expertise and commitment made a lasting contribution to the lubricants industry and the Association.
As a Health and Safety Specialist at Quaker Chemical Corp. in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania, Poole worked closely with John Howell, Ike Tripp of Etna Products, and others to develop an important best practices document to minimize or prevent occurrences of occupational dermatitis sometimes associated with metal removal fluids. That document is now an ASTM standard, E2693-26, “Standard Practice for Prevention of Dermatitis in the Wet Metal Removal Environment.”
Poole’s outstanding service to ILMA was recognized in 2007 when she received the Association’s Distinguished Service Award, now known as the Bellanti Award.
In 2014, Poole joined GHS Resources Inc., where she continued sharing her extensive occupational health and safety expertise, helping organizations develop training and compliance programs under OSHA’s Globally Harmonized System (GHS) requirements.
“Carol provided our industry with clarity on subjects that were problematic,” remembered Cathy Novak, formerly of Cadillac Oil Co. and a fellow Bellanti Award recipient. “She was able to communicate, in laymen’s terms, the issues and solutions. Her superpower was her ability to stay focused on the problems, find the root cause and find a solution. Her gift to all of us was providing a safe work environment and teaching others how to achieve that.”
Poole’s dedication to workplace safety, her generous sharing of knowledge, and her service to ILMA leave a meaningful legacy. We extend our heartfelt condolences to her family, friends and colleagues. She will be remembered with gratitude and respect.
Celebration of Life
A celebration of Poole’s life will be held on Sunday, October 11, 2026, from 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. at James J. Terry Funeral Home, 736 E. Lancaster Avenue, Downingtown, Pennsylvania.
Memorial Donations
In lieu of flowers, Carol’s family requests that memorial donations be made to Oceana.

CASSIDA FM GEAR OIL TLS 150
Specialty gear fluid for use in food manufacturing equipment
Description
CASSIDA FM GEAR OIL TLS 150 is a specialty anti-wear gear fluid which is specifically designed for use in the food and beverage canning industry.
This product is based on careful blend of fluids and selected additives chosen for their ability to meet the stringent requirements of food and beverage industry.
Certified by NSF for ISO 21469 and registered by NSF (Class H1) for use where there is potential for incidental food contact. This product is produced according to FUCHS quality standards, in facilities where HACCP audit and Good Manufacturing Practice have been implemented and form part of the quality and hygiene management systems ISO 9001 and ISO 21469.
Certifications and Specifications
- NSF H1
- NSF ISO 21469
- Kosher
- Halal
- DIN 51517 CLP
Performance Features
- The base fluid has been selected for its ability to provide superior lubrication under variety of applications
- Specially formulated to provide good lubrication even when operating in locations where it is subject to contamination with water, juice and food, which is held in suspension, thus protecting metal surfaces from wear and corrosion.
- Neutral odor and taste
- Good anti-oxidant properties. Resists the formation of deposits and sludge even at elevated temperatures, resulting in long equipment life
Applications
- Lubrication of rotary can seaming machines equipped with total loss systems
- Circulating and bearing oil systems where contamination with water or food juice can occur, such as citrus juice extraction machines
- Can be used on drives and transport chains in the food Industry. Easily applied by either brush, through baths or by automatic lubrication system.
Seal and paint compatibility
Compatible with the elastomers, gaskets, seals and paints such as poly-urethane and two part epoxy resin paints, frequently used on machinery and in lubrication systems employed in the food processing industry.
Handling and storage
All food grade lubricants should be stored separately from other lubricants, chemical substances and foodstuffs and out of direct sunlight or other heat sources. Store between 32 °F and 100 °F. Provided that the product has been stored under these conditions we recommend that the product be used within 5 years from the date of manufacture. Upon opening a pack, the product must be used within 2 years (or within 5 years of the date of manufacture, whichever is sooner).
Industries
- Food
Note
The information shown on this side is based on the experience and expertise of the FUCHS Group in the development and manufacture of lubricants and represents the current state of the art. The performance of our products can be influenced by a series of factors, especially the specific use, the method of application, the operational environment, component pretreatment, possible external contamination, etc. For this reason, universally valid statements about the function of our products are not possible. We therefore recommend that you consult a FUCHS Group application engineer to discuss application conditions and the performance criteria of the products before the products are used. It is the responsibility of the user to test the functional suitability of the products and to use them with the corresponding care. Our products are subject to continuous further development. We therefore retain the right to change our product range, the products, and their manufacturing processes as well as all details on this side at any time and without warning, provided that no customer-specific agreements exist that require otherwise.

Metal Forming Lubricants
The metal forming industry is undergoing rapid transformation driven by the use of lighter and stronger materials, increasingly complex production processes, and stricter environmental regulations.
In this context, metal forming lubricants play a critical role in ensuring process efficiency, part quality, and tool protection across industrial applications.
Manufacturers are increasingly working with advanced materials such as high-strength steels (AHSS), aluminium, and lightweight alloys, particularly in sectors such as automotive and industrial manufacturing. While these materials offer clear advantages in terms of weight reduction and performance, they also introduce new challenges in metal forming processes. These include increased tool wear, a higher risk of edge cracking, springback effects, and overall greater process complexity. To successfully address these challenges, it is essential to use high-performance metal forming lubricants that ensure process stability, part quality, and operational efficiency.
Modern metal forming lubricants must meet multiple technical and operational requirements:
Material compatibility: Today’s processes involve a wide range of metals, including ferrous materials, aluminum, and coated substrates, requiring versatile lubrication solutions.
Performance under demanding conditions: Lubricants must deliver excellent friction reduction and tool protection in operations such as deep drawing, stamping, and in-die tapping.
Post-process compatibility: Residues must be compatible with cleaning, painting, or assembly processes to ensure seamless production flow.
Health, safety, and sustainability: There is growing demand for chlorine-free lubricants and environmentally friendly solutions that reduce impact on operators and the environment.
FUCHS offers a comprehensive portfolio of metalworking lubricants designed to optimize forming processes:
Chlorine-free lubricants: Efficient alternatives to traditional oils, delivering high performance while reducing environmental impact.
Synthetic lubricants: Ideal for demanding applications, providing enhanced tool protection and reducing or eliminating cleaning requirements.
Water-miscible lubricants and neat oils: Versatile solutions suitable for a wide range of forming operations, offering excellent lubrication and corrosion protection.
Choosing the right metal forming lubricant delivers key operational advantages:
- Extended tool and die life
- Reduced maintenance and operating costs
- Improved part quality
- Enhanced process stability and efficiency
- Compliance with environmental and safety regulations
