records.abstract: SantoLubes manufactures PPE-based synthetic lubricants—including SantoVac, SantoTrac, and SantoLight—for extreme temperature and vacuum applications.
records.summary: This is a company product page from SantoLubes describing a family of polyphenyl ether (PPE)-based synthetic lubricants and specialty fluids. The page states that all product families share PPE base chemistry, which the company says provides thermal stability up to 450°C (840°F), vacuum performance down to 5×10⁻¹⁰ torr, and chemical and radiation resistance beyond conventional mineral and PAO fluids. Named product lines include SantoVac high-vacuum pump fluids, SantoTrac traction drive fluids, ultEbase synthetic base oils, ACCL anticorrosion connector lubricants, SantoLight optical-grade fluids, and SantoRad radiation-resistant fluids. The company says products are formulated and manufactured under ISO 9001:2015 quality management at its Spartanburg, South Carolina facility and that the line has been in service for more than 30 years. The claims are company statements; no independent test data or peer-reviewed results are provided in the source text.

Products
Seven PPE-based product families engineered for the operating conditions where conventional mineral and PAO lubricants fail — extreme temperature, ultra-high vacuum, radiation exposure, and demanding traction environments.
Engineered for Extreme Conditions
Custom Formulated Solutions
ISO 9001:2015 Certified
Every SantoLubes product family shares a common foundation: advanced polyphenyl ether base chemistry, formulated and manufactured under ISO 9001:2015 quality management at our Spartanburg, South Carolina facility. That chemistry is what delivers thermal stability to 450°C (840°F), vacuum performance down to 5×10-10 torr, and chemical and radiation resistance that conventional fluids can’t match.
Each product family below is engineered for a distinct performance requirement — vacuum, traction, base oil viscosity, connector protection, optical clarity, radiation resistance, or PFAS-free compliance. Not sure which fits your application? Our applications engineers will review your operating conditions and recommend the right grade at no obligation.
Expert guidance and resources to help you find the right solution.

Each is engineered for a distinct performance requirement where conventional mineral and PAO lubricants fail.
Every SantoLubes product is built on advanced polyphenyl ether (PPE) base chemistry. This shared foundation delivers thermal stability up to 450°C (840°F), vacuum performance down to 5×10⁻¹⁰ torr, and chemical and radiation resistance beyond the reach of conventional fluids. All products are formulated and manufactured under ISO 9001:2015 quality management at the company's Spartanburg, South Carolina facility.
SantoLubes fluids are engineered for conditions where conventional lubricants fail — from vacuum pumps in orbit to gearboxes underground. Their PPE-based chemistry delivers resistance to extreme temperatures, high loads, radiation, corrosion, and chemical exposure, which is why OEMs and operators specify them for the most demanding applications. The product line has been in service for more than 30 years.

records.title: Analytical and Experimental Assessment of the Effect of Current Harmonics on the Heating of a Flat Rectangular Busbar
records.abstract: Higher harmonics can increase conductor temperature even when the total current root mean square (RMS) value remains unchanged, because Joule losses depend on frequency and the spatial distribution of current density. This study develops a compact analytical model of the heating of an isolated, flat rectangular copper busbar and assesses its predictions against laboratory measurements. A one-dimensional solution of the electromagnetic field and heat conduction equation yields a dimensionless heating coefficient for each harmonic and a weighted superposition rule for an arbitrary spectrum. The experimental assessment was limited to a copper busbar with a cross-section of 40 mm × 10 mm at a current of approximately 400 A with temperature rise predictions referenced to the 50 Hz experiment. Eight measurement tests covered four spectra with a fundamental frequency of 50 Hz and single-frequency excitations from 100 to 250 Hz. Nine temperature channels and the actual current spectra were recorded. For the controlled mixed spectra, the relative error of the analytical prediction with respect to the measured relative temperature rise ranged from −3.1% to +0.4%. Under excitation at 100–250 Hz, the analytical model underestimated the measured rise by 3.4–8.8%. The model can be useful for rapidly assessing the effect of harmonic spectra on the ampacity of strip conductors.
records.summary: The study addresses the problem that higher current harmonics can raise the temperature of a conductor even when the total RMS current is unchanged, because Joule losses depend on frequency and on the spatial distribution of current density. The authors develop a compact analytical model of heating for an isolated flat rectangular copper busbar, using a one-dimensional solution of the electromagnetic field and heat conduction equations to derive a dimensionless heating coefficient per harmonic and a weighted superposition rule for arbitrary spectra. They assess the model against laboratory measurements on a 40 mm × 10 mm copper busbar at approximately 400 A, with temperature-rise predictions referenced to a 50 Hz experiment. Eight measurement tests covered four spectra with a 50 Hz fundamental plus single-frequency excitations from 100 to 250 Hz, using nine temperature channels and recorded current spectra. For controlled mixed spectra, the relative error of the analytical prediction versus measured relative temperature rise ranged from −3.1% to +0.4%; under 100–250 Hz excitation the model underestimated the measured rise by 3.4–8.8%. This summary is based on the abstract only, since the full text could not be retrieved.

records.abstract: Celestica DS6005: 102.4-Tbit/s Switch with Co-Packaged Optics and Full Liquid Cooling igor´sLAB
records.summary: The article reports on Celestica's DS6005, a data-center switch announced October 12, 2026, aimed at AI accelerator clusters. It combines a Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson switch ASIC with Co-Packaged Optics (CPO), where optical engines sit directly next to the ASIC instead of using front-panel pluggable transceivers, shortening high-speed electrical traces. Celestica states the system provides 102.4 Tbit/s of switching capacity via 64 optical Ethernet ports at 1.6 Tbit/s each, in a 1.5 Open Unit form factor for OCP Open Rack V3 with full liquid cooling and SONiC support. External, replaceable laser modules are used to keep part of the optical infrastructure serviceable. The article notes that no independent measurements of power, latency, or efficiency advantages have been published, so the claimed benefits remain manufacturer statements.

records.body_text:
For network hardware used in AI clusters, simply adding more ports is no longer enough. Bandwidth, power consumption, cooling, and electrical signal paths are so closely interrelated that conventional switch architectures are increasingly reaching their technical limits. Celestica therefore introduced the DS6005 on October 12, 2026. The system combines the Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson with Co-Packaged Optics, full liquid cooling, and a form factor designed for OCP Open Rack V3. According to the manufacturer, the DS6005 delivers 102,4 Tbit/s of switching capacity and provides 64 optical ports, each with a bandwidth of 1,6 Tbit/s. The platform is intended for AI data centers in which large accelerator clusters must communicate with high bandwidth and the lowest possible latency. Unlike conventional switches, the optical components are integrated directly next to the network chip.
The key difference lies in the optical architecture. Conventional network switches often use replaceable transceivers on the front of the device. Electrical signals must therefore travel from the switch ASIC along circuit-board traces to the corresponding modules. As data rates increase, this transmission path becomes increasingly demanding. Signal loss, electrical interference, and the signal conditioning required can increase power consumption. For the DS6005, Celestica uses Co-Packaged Optics, or CPO. The optical engines are located directly next to the switch ASIC. This shortens the electrical connection, while optical links carry signals over longer distances.
The manufacturer associates this architecture with higher bandwidth density, lower latency, and improved energy efficiency. No concrete independent measurements of the actual advantage over conventional 102,4-Tbit/s switches have been published to date. Celestica uses the Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson as the central network chip. The switch provides 64 optical Ethernet ports, each with a bandwidth of 1,6 Tbit/s. This results in an aggregate interface capacity of 102,4 Tbit/s.
| Feature | Celestica DS6005 |
|---|---|
| Switch ASIC | Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson |
| Switching capacity | 102,4 Tbit/s |
| Optical ports | 64 × 1,6 TbE |
| Optical architecture | Co-Packaged Optics |
| Form factor | 1,5 OU |
| Rack standard | OCP Open Rack V3 |
| Cooling | Full liquid cooling |
| Network software | SONiC support |
| Laser modules | External and replaceable |
| Applications | AI data centers and AI fabrics |
| Power consumption | Not disclosed |
However, optical integration introduces new requirements for packaging, cooling, and maintenance. While conventional transceivers can be replaced individually, integrated optical engines are more closely coupled to the network hardware itself. Celestica therefore uses external, replaceable laser modules. This is intended to keep at least part of the optical infrastructure serviceable. The system also supports software management tailored to the CPO architecture.
The DS6005 is fully liquid-cooled and was developed for the Open Compute Project’s Open Rack V3 concept. Its height is just 1,5 Open Units. This compact design is notable because the switch must accommodate both a high-performance network chip and numerous optical components. The resulting heat is intended to be removed by liquid cooling, enabling high rack density. Thermal integration is particularly important with Co-Packaged Optics. Optical engines and electronic circuits have different temperature requirements, so the cooling architecture must be designed accordingly.
Celestica has not yet disclosed either the total power consumption or the required coolant volume. As a result, the system’s energy efficiency cannot currently be compared independently with that of other high-performance switches. On the software side, the DS6005 supports the open network operating system SONiC. This is already used in large data centers and enables standardized management of different network platforms. This is an important consideration for operators, since new hardware should not necessarily require a completely new management system. Automated configuration, monitoring, and integration into existing workflows are just as relevant in large AI clusters as transmission speed itself.

original_evidence.body_text:
For network hardware used in AI clusters, simply adding more ports is no longer enough. Bandwidth, power consumption, cooling, and electrical signal paths are so closely interrelated that conventional switch architectures are increasingly reaching their technical limits. Celestica therefore introduced the DS6005 on October 12, 2026. The system combines the Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson with Co-Packaged Optics, full liquid cooling, and a form factor designed for OCP Open Rack V3. According to the manufacturer, the DS6005 delivers 102,4 Tbit/s of switching capacity and provides 64 optical ports, each with a bandwidth of 1,6 Tbit/s. The platform is intended for AI data centers in which large accelerator clusters must communicate with high bandwidth and the lowest possible latency. Unlike conventional switches, the optical components are integrated directly next to the network chip.
The key difference lies in the optical architecture. Conventional network switches often use replaceable transceivers on the front of the device. Electrical signals must therefore travel from the switch ASIC along circuit-board traces to the corresponding modules. As data rates increase, this transmission path becomes increasingly demanding. Signal loss, electrical interference, and the signal conditioning required can increase power consumption. For the DS6005, Celestica uses Co-Packaged Optics, or CPO. The optical engines are located directly next to the switch ASIC. This shortens the electrical connection, while optical links carry signals over longer distances.
The manufacturer associates this architecture with higher bandwidth density, lower latency, and improved energy efficiency. No concrete independent measurements of the actual advantage over conventional 102,4-Tbit/s switches have been published to date. Celestica uses the Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson as the central network chip. The switch provides 64 optical Ethernet ports, each with a bandwidth of 1,6 Tbit/s. This results in an aggregate interface capacity of 102,4 Tbit/s.

|---|---|
| Switch ASIC | Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson | 
| Switching capacity | 102,4 Tbit/s |

| Rack standard | OCP Open Rack V3 | 
| Cooling | Full liquid cooling | 
| Network software | SONiC support | 
| Laser modules | External and replaceable | 
| Applications | AI data centers and AI fabrics | 
| Power consumption | Not disclosed | 
However, optical integration introduces new requirements for packaging, cooling, and maintenance. While conventional transceivers can be replaced individually, integrated optical engines are more closely coupled to the network hardware itself. Celestica therefore uses external, replaceable laser modules. This is intended to keep at least part of the optical infrastructure serviceable. The system also supports software management tailored to the CPO architecture.
The DS6005 is fully liquid-cooled and was developed for the Open Compute Project’s Open Rack V3 concept. Its height is just 1,5 Open Units. This compact design is notable because the switch must accommodate both a high-performance network chip and numerous optical components. The resulting heat is intended to be removed by liquid cooling, enabling high rack density. Thermal integration is particularly important with Co-Packaged Optics. Optical engines and electronic circuits have different temperature requirements, so the cooling architecture must be designed accordingly.
Celestica has not yet disclosed either the total power consumption or the required coolant volume. As a result, the system’s energy efficiency cannot currently be compared independently with that of other high-performance switches. On the software side, the DS6005 supports the open network operating system SONiC. This is already used in large data centers and enables standardized management of different network platforms. records.body_text:
Lubrication Engineers Acquires BioBlend Renewable Resources
WICHITA, Kan. (October 19, 2026) – Lubrication Engineers, Inc. (“LE”), a leading developer and manufacturer of high-performance industrial lubricants and asset reliability solutions, today announced that it has acquired BioBlend Renewable Resources, LLC (“BioBlend”), an innovator of high-performance, bio-based lubricants.
BioBlend, with its comprehensive portfolio of bio-based and hybrid lubricants, helps its mining, marine, drilling and industrial customers reduce environmental impact without compromising performance. Its proprietary formulations, developed over nearly two decades, are used in demanding applications ranging from underground mining and dredging to fire-resistant hydraulic systems, and are trusted by customers who require reliability and regulatory compliance in sensitive operating environments.
This is LE’s fourth acquisition since partnering with Aurora Capital Partners in September 2023, following its acquisitions of Royal Purple Industrial, SWEPCO and RSC Bio Solutions. During this time, LE has significantly expanded its lubrication expertise with powerful new synthetic and sustainable product offerings. Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed.
About BioBlend Renewable Resources
Founded in 2007, BioBlend Renewable Resources, LLC develops and manufactures high-performance, bio-based lubricants for the mining, marine, drilling, food grade, and industrial markets. BioBlend’s proprietary hybrid and fully biodegradable formulations are engineered to match or exceed the performance of conventional petroleum-based products, giving customers a viable path to reduce environmental impact across demanding applications. The company operates from its manufacturing facility in Grundy Center, Iowa. For more information about BioBlend, visit: www.bioblend.com.

records.body_text:
Lithium Battery Pack Busbar Design and Current Density Limits
When a customer asks me to push more current through a lithium battery pack, the cells are rarely the bottleneck. In my fifteen years designing packs at Horizon Power, the component that quietly decides whether a 100 A or 200 A rating is realistic is the busbar. A busbar is the solid metal strip that links cells or modules together, and its cross-section, material, and connection method set a hard ceiling on current density. Get it wrong and you get hot spots, voltage sag, and in the worst case a thermal event that no amount of cell-level protection can fix.
In this guide I will walk through how we size busbars for lithium battery packs, the current density limits we use in production, and the safety margins that keep a pack within UN38.3 and IEC 62133 expectations.
Why Busbar Design Defines Pack Current Capability
A lithium battery pack is only as strong as its weakest series link. The busbar carries the full pack current between parallel groups, so every amp that leaves the pack also crosses every busbar joint. Unlike a wire, a busbar is a fixed geometry: its resistance is set the moment you choose the material, thickness, and width. We model it early in the mechanical layout because changing it later means re-tooling the cell holder and the laser-welding fixture.
The first number I look at is not capacity but continuous current divided by busbar cross-section. That ratio, current density, tells me whether the strip will stay cool or slowly cook the pack. A drone battery that draws 60 A peak through a 2 mm thick, 10 mm wide nickel strip is already running near the edge, which is why high-rate packs move to copper or nickel-plated copper busbars.
Current Density Limits for Lithium Battery Busbars
For nickel-plated steel busbars, which are common in cylindrical cell holders, we hold continuous current density to about 4 A per square millimeter and peak, sixty second, to about 8 A per square millimeter. Pure nickel is better at roughly 6 A per square millimeter continuous. Copper busbars, with conductivity near 58 megasiemens per meter, comfortably carry 8 to 10 A per square millimeter continuous and 15 to 20 A per square millimeter for short pulses. Aluminum sits between, around 5 to 6 A per square millimeter continuous, but it needs careful surface treatment to stop oxidation at the joint.
These are not arbitrary numbers. They come from balancing temperature rise against the pack enclosure’s ability to shed heat. Inside a sealed case with still air, a strip running at 10 A per square millimeter in copper still climbs several degrees per minute, so we derate for duty cycle. A custom battery solution that runs a thirty percent duty cycle can use a higher density than one running flat out for an hour.
Material Choices: Copper, Aluminum, and Nickel-Plated Steel
Copper is the default for high-current lithium battery packs. It is expensive and heavy, but its low resistance means thin bars can carry serious current. We use tin or nickel plating on copper to stop verdigris and to make ultrasonic or laser welding consistent.
Nickel-plated steel is the workhorse of consumer 18650 and 21700 packs because spot welding nickel to the cell cap is fast and reliable. The trade-off is higher resistance, so you need more cross-section for the same current. Aluminum is lighter and cheaper than copper but demands ferrite or laser cleaning at the joint; a dirty aluminum interface can double contact resistance overnight.
For an LFP battery used in stationary storage, weight matters less than cost, so we often choose thick tinned copper. For a NCM battery in a mobile device where every gram counts, aluminum busbars with plated joints earn their place.
Cross-Section Sizing and the 4 A per Square Millimeter Rule
The quick field rule I teach new engineers is 4 A per square millimeter of busbar cross-section for nickel-based strip under continuous load. A 2 mm by 10 mm strip gives 20 square millimeters, so it is good for about 80 A continuous. If the application is a 12v lithium battery in a trolling motor pulling 50 A, that strip has comfortable margin. If it is a 120 A power pack, we double the section or switch to copper.
Sizing is not just area. Width spreads heat better than thickness because more surface faces the air. We prefer wide, thin bars over narrow, thick ones when space allows. The section must also survive the weld: a 0.2 mm foil welds cleanly, while a 3 mm bar needs a pre-weld and a penetration check.
Connection Methods: Welding, Bolting, and Busbar Rivets
How the busbar meets the cell decides whether your calculated resistance is real. Laser welding gives the lowest, most repeatable resistance on prismatic terminals and is our choice for automotive-grade lithium ion battery modules. Ultrasonic welding suits foil-to-busbar tabs and leaves no heat-affected zone in the cell. Resistance spot welding is cheap for nickel strip on cylindrical cans but drifts with electrode wear, so we audit weld strength weekly.
Bolted joints are serviceable and let you open the pack, but every bolt is a resistance point. We specify spring washers and a torque window, then verify with a milliohm test. Busbar rivets are a middle path for modular packs that must be field-repairable without special welders.
Busbar Layout: Series, Parallel, and Hybrid Topologies
The geometry of the busbar matters as much as its material. In a series layout the same current runs through every link, so each busbar must carry the full pack current and the section is uniform. In a parallel group the current splits, so the busbar that collects the group current is the thick one while the intra-group links carry only a share. I have seen packs where the parallel busbar was sized for the cell current and then used as the series link by mistake, overheating on the first full discharge.
Hybrid topologies, common in a high-voltage lithium ion battery module, use wide copper bars to gather many parallel strings and thin nickel links between series groups. The rule is simple: draw the current path, find the highest current any one bar carries, and size that bar first. We color-code the current path in the CAD model so a reviewer can see the peak at a glance before the first prototype is cut.
Thermal Rise, Voltage Drop, and Safety Margins
Two numbers close the loop. First, voltage drop: I equals V over R, and a busbar at 1 milliohm dropping 0.1 V at 100 A is wasting 10 W as heat. Second, temperature rise: we simulate the strip in still air and derate until the steady-state surface stays below 60 degrees Celsius inside the case. That 60 degree figure protects the cell seals and the surrounding polymer parts.
We also watch the joint, not just the bar. A perfect copper bar with a poor weld can carry half its rated current before the joint glows. Our production test is a four-wire milliohm measurement across every series busbar after welding; any joint above the design limit is cut and reworked. This step is cheap insurance against field failures that no battery management system can see until it is too late.
Safety margins are where experience shows. We never run a busbar at its calculated limit. A thirty percent margin on current density covers plating variation, dust on contacts, and the day the cooling fan fails. This discipline is what lets a pack pass IEC 62619 and UL 1973 abuse tests without the busbar becoming the failure point.
Frequently Asked Questions
What current density is safe for a lithium battery busbar?
For nickel-plated steel we hold about 4 A per square millimeter continuous and 8 A per square millimeter peak. Copper busbars are safe near 8 to 10 A per square millimeter continuous. Always derate for duty cycle and enclosure heat.
How do I size a busbar for a 100 A lithium battery pack?
Plan for at least 25 square millimeters of cross-section in copper, or about 50 square millimeters in nickel strip, then verify with a temperature-rise test in the real enclosure. The 4 A per square millimeter rule gives a 120 A rating on a 30 square millimeter nickel bar, leaving margin.
Is copper or aluminum better for battery busbars?
Copper carries more current per gram and per millimeter, welds cleanly, and resists corrosion with plating. Aluminum is lighter and cheaper but needs surface preparation at joints. Choose copper for high-rate packs and aluminum when weight and cost dominate.
Can busbar current limits affect UN38.3 or IEC 62133 compliance?
Yes. A busbar that overheats or develops a high-resistance joint can trigger the thermal and short-circuit tests in UN38.3 and the safety requirements in IEC 62133. Proper sizing and welding are part of passing those standards.
How does busbar resistance impact pack runtime?
Every milliohm in the busbar wastes energy as heat instead of reaching the load. A pack with 2 milliohm of busbar loss at 100 A sheds 20 W, which shortens runtime and heats the case. Lower-resistance copper busbars recover that capacity.

records.body_text:
Battery Temperature Monitoring in BESS: From Sensing Points to System Protection
2026-10-20
Temperature monitoring is a basic function in a battery energy storage system, but the value of the measurement depends heavily on where the temperature is measured and how the data is used.
In a BESS, heat does not come from the battery cells alone. Current-carrying connections, busbars, contactors, fuses, cables and other electrical components can also become local heat sources. A temperature value taken from one location may therefore tell only part of the story.
For battery racks and high-voltage electrical systems, temperature monitoring needs to be considered as part of the wider monitoring and protection architecture.
Where Should Temperature Be Measured?
There is no single temperature point that can represent the condition of an entire battery rack.
Different parts of the system can experience different thermal conditions.
At the battery level, temperature monitoring may focus on cells or modules because battery temperature affects charging, discharging and overall operating conditions.
At the electrical level, other locations can also deserve attention:
Busbar connections
Cable terminals
High-current connection points
DC contactors
Fuse installation points
Other components inside the battery rack or electrical enclosure
These locations do not necessarily have the same thermal behavior as the battery cells.
A rack can therefore have a normal average temperature while a particular connection point is running significantly hotter than the surrounding area.
This is one reason why sensor placement matters as much as the sensor itself.
A Hotspot Can Be More Important Than Average Temperature
Battery thermal monitoring is sometimes viewed mainly as a way to detect an overall rise in temperature.
For system protection, however, the location of the temperature rise can be just as important.
A localized increase may be associated with:
Increased contact resistance
A loose or degraded connection
High current concentration
Poor heat dissipation
Abnormal loading
Component aging
A temperature sensor installed at an appropriate electrical connection can therefore provide information that would not be visible from a general ambient-temperature measurement.
This is particularly relevant in compact BESS designs where high-current components are installed close together.
The objective is not to place sensors everywhere. It is to identify the points where temperature data can provide useful information about battery and electrical-system conditions.
Battery Temperature and Electrical Temperature Are Different Measurements
Battery temperature and electrical-component temperature should not automatically be treated as the same thing.
A battery cell may be operating within its expected temperature range while a cable terminal or busbar connection is experiencing abnormal local heating.
The reverse can also occur. A battery module may experience a temperature increase because of its operating condition while the surrounding electrical connections remain within their normal range.
This distinction matters when temperature data is used for protection decisions.
The monitoring system needs to know what each measurement represents rather than treating all temperature values as interchangeable.
For this reason, the physical location of each sensing point should be considered when defining the monitoring architecture.
From Sensor Data to BMS Decisions
Temperature measurement becomes more useful when it is connected to the BMS and the wider control system.
A BMS can use temperature information together with other battery parameters such as cell voltage, pack voltage and charge/discharge current to determine whether the battery is operating within its defined limits.
Temperature can affect several decisions, including:
Whether charging or discharging should continue
Whether current should be limited
Whether an abnormal condition should trigger an alarm
Whether a protection threshold has been reached
Whether the battery needs to enter a different operating state
The important point is that the sensor does not make the protection decision by itself.
The sensor provides the measurement. The BMS interprets the data according to the configured protection and control logic.
This distinction becomes increasingly important as battery systems use more monitoring points and more detailed operating information.
Temperature Difference Can Also Carry Useful Information
Absolute temperature is not always the only useful value.
The difference between sensing points can provide additional information about the condition of the battery system.
For example, if several comparable battery sections operate under similar conditions but one location shows a persistent temperature difference, that variation may deserve further investigation.
The same principle can apply to electrical connection points.
A single temperature value may appear acceptable when viewed on its own, while a comparison between multiple points can reveal an abnormal pattern.
This makes multi-point temperature monitoring useful not only for protection, but also for condition monitoring and maintenance.
The quality of the monitoring architecture therefore depends on both the sensor performance and the way the collected data is interpreted.
Wired and Wireless Temperature Monitoring
The choice between wired and wireless sensing depends on the physical structure of the system.
Wired sensors can provide a straightforward connection to the monitoring system, but a larger number of sensing points can increase wiring requirements.
In a battery rack with many modules and multiple monitoring locations, cable routing can become a practical design consideration.
Wireless temperature monitoring can reduce the amount of signal wiring required between sensing points and the data collection system. This can be useful where installation space is limited or where monitoring points are distributed across a larger electrical structure.
Wireless sensing can also be relevant when monitoring is required at locations such as busbars, cable connections or other electrical interfaces where adding additional wiring is inconvenient.
The choice should still be based on the complete system requirements, including communication method, installation environment, measurement accuracy, power supply and maintenance requirements.
Temperature Monitoring Beyond the Battery Cell
As BESS electrical architectures become more compact, temperature monitoring does not necessarily stop at the battery module.
The electrical path around the battery can also contain important thermal information.
For example, a high-current connection may experience additional heating because of contact resistance. A fuse may operate in an enclosure where the local temperature is considerably different from the external ambient temperature. A contactor may also experience its own thermal conditions depending on continuous current and installation environment.
These measurements can help engineers distinguish between a battery-related thermal issue and a problem associated with the electrical path.
This is also why temperature monitoring and component selection should not be treated as completely separate design tasks.
The thermal environment around a protection or switching component can affect its operating margin, while the component itself can contribute to the local thermal environment.
Sensor Placement Should Follow the Electrical and Thermal Architecture
Sensor placement is best considered together with the physical layout of the BESS.
A useful approach is to identify:
Where heat is generated → where heat can accumulate → where temperature changes can indicate an abnormal condition
This may lead to different sensing priorities in different parts of the system.
Battery modules may require temperature monitoring for battery operating limits.
Busbars and terminals may require monitoring because they carry high current.
Connection points may deserve attention because local resistance can create concentrated heat.
Other components may need monitoring when their operating temperature has a direct relationship with reliability or protection requirements.
This approach is more useful than simply increasing the number of sensors.
More data does not automatically mean better monitoring. The sensing points need to provide information that can be acted upon.
Temperature Monitoring and BESS Protection Work Together
Temperature monitoring is one layer of a larger protection system.
In a BESS, electrical protection may involve fuses, DC contactors, insulation monitoring, current measurement and BMS protection functions.
Temperature monitoring provides another source of information that can help identify abnormal operating conditions.
These functions have different roles.
A temperature sensor detects a physical condition.
The BMS evaluates that condition together with other battery information.
A control system can then determine the appropriate response.
A fuse or contactor, depending on the system architecture and fault condition, may provide the physical isolation or interruption function.
Keeping these roles clear is important when designing the complete protection strategy.
It also prevents a common design mistake: expecting one monitoring device or one protection component to solve a system-level problem on its own.
Temperature Data Becomes More Valuable Over Time
A temperature measurement is useful at the moment it is taken, but recorded temperature data can provide additional value.
Continuous monitoring can show how a particular point behaves under different charging and discharging conditions.
Over time, engineers may be able to identify:
Repeated temperature rises at the same location
Differences between battery sections
Changes in thermal behavior under similar loads
Abnormal temperature patterns
Conditions that occur before a fault or maintenance event
This moves temperature monitoring beyond simple alarm generation.
It can also support maintenance decisions by helping engineers identify locations that require closer inspection.
For larger or more complex battery systems, this historical information can become increasingly useful because the operating condition of the system changes over its service life.
Designing the Monitoring Layer Alongside the Battery Rack
Temperature monitoring works best when it is considered during the battery rack design rather than added after the electrical architecture has already been fixed.
The battery modules, busbars, high-current connections, protection components, cooling system and sensing points occupy the same physical space and interact thermally.
The monitoring architecture therefore needs to reflect the actual rack structure.
This is consistent with the broader approach to high-voltage battery rack design: battery monitoring, thermal management, protection and electrical integration need to work together rather than being treated as separate tasks.
For BESS developers, the practical question is not simply how many temperature sensors are required. It is which locations need to be monitored, what information each point provides, and how that information will be used by the BMS or system controller.
That is where temperature sensing becomes part of the system design rather than just another component installed inside the rack.

original_evidence.body_text:
\# Battery Temperature Monitoring in BESS\: From Sensing Points to System Protection

2026\-10\-20

Temperature monitoring is a basic function in a battery energy storage system\, but the value of the measurement depends heavily on where the temperature is measured and how the data is used\.

In a BESS\, heat does not come from the battery cells alone\. Current\-carrying connections\, busbars\, contactors\, fuses\, cables and other electrical components can also become local heat sources\. A temperature value taken from one location may therefore tell only part of the story\.

For battery racks and high\-voltage electrical systems\, temperature monitoring needs to be considered as part of the wider monitoring and protection architecture\.

\#\# Where Should Temperature Be Measured\?

There is no single temperature point that can represent the condition of an entire battery rack\.

Different parts of the system can experience different thermal conditions\.

At the battery level\, temperature monitoring may focus on cells or modules because battery temperature affects charging\, discharging and overall operating conditions\.

At the electrical level\, other locations can also deserve attention\:

Busbar connections

Cable terminals

High\-current connection points

DC contactors

Fuse installation points

Other components inside the battery rack or electrical enclosure

These locations do not necessarily have the same thermal behavior as the battery cells\.

A rack can therefore have a normal average temperature while a particular connection point is running significantly hotter than the surrounding area\.

This is one reason why sensor placement matters as much as the sensor itself\.

\#\# A Hotspot Can Be More Important Than Average Temperature

Battery thermal monitoring is sometimes viewed mainly as a way to detect an overall rise in temperature\.

For system protection\, however\, the location of the temperature rise can be just as important\.

A localized increase may be associated with\:

Increased contact resistance

A loose or degraded connection

High current concentration

Poor heat dissipation

Abnormal loading

Component aging

A temperature sensor installed at an appropriate electrical connection can therefore provide information that would not be visible from a general ambient\-temperature measurement\.

This is particularly relevant in compact BESS designs where high\-current components are installed close together\.

The objective is not to place sensors everywhere\. It is to identify the points where temperature data can provide useful information about battery and electrical\-system conditions\.

\#\# Battery Temperature and Electrical Temperature Are Different Measurements

Battery temperature and electrical\-component temperature should not automatically be treated as the same thing\.

A battery cell may be operating within its expected temperature range while a cable terminal or busbar connection is experiencing abnormal local heating\.

The reverse can also occur\. A battery module may experience a temperature increase because of its operating condition while the surrounding electrical connections remain within their normal range\.

This distinction matters when temperature data is used for protection decisions\.

The monitoring system needs to know what each measurement represents rather than treating all temperature values as interchangeable\.

For this reason\, the physical location of each sensing point should be considered when defining the monitoring architecture\.

\#\# From Sensor Data to BMS Decisions

Temperature measurement becomes more useful when it is connected to the BMS and the wider control system\.

A BMS can use temperature information together with other battery parameters such as cell voltage\, pack voltage and charge\/discharge current to determine whether the battery is operating within its defined limits\.

Temperature can affect several decisions\, including\:

Whether charging or discharging should continue

Whether current should be limited

Whether an abnormal condition should trigger an alarm

Whether a protection threshold has been reached

Whether the battery needs to enter a different operating state

The important point is that the sensor does not make the protection decision by itself\.

The sensor provides the measurement\. The BMS interprets the data according to the configured protection and control logic\.

This distinction becomes increasingly important as battery systems use more monitoring points and more detailed operating information\.

\#\# Temperature Difference Can Also Carry Useful Information

Absolute temperature is not always the only useful value\.

The difference between sensing points can provide additional information about the condition of the battery system\.

For example\, if several comparable battery sections operate under similar conditions but one location shows a persistent temperature difference\, that variation may deserve further investigation\.

The same principle can apply to electrical connection points\.

A single temperature value may appear acceptable when viewed on its own\, while a comparison between multiple points can reveal an abnormal pattern\.

This makes multi\-point temperature monitoring useful not only for protection\, but also for condition monitoring and maintenance\.

The quality of the monitoring architecture therefore depends on both the sensor performance and the way the collected data is interpreted\.

\#\# Wired and Wireless Temperature Monitoring

The choice between wired and wireless sensing depends on the physical structure of the system\.

Wired sensors can provide a straightforward connection to the monitoring system\, but a larger number of sensing points can increase wiring requirements\.

In a battery rack with many modules and multiple monitoring locations\, cable routing can become a practical design consideration\.

Wireless temperature monitoring can reduce the amount of signal wiring required between sensing points and the data collection system\. This can be useful where installation space is limited or where monitoring points are distributed across a larger electrical structure\.

Wireless sensing can also be relevant when monitoring is required at locations such as busbars\, cable connections or other electrical interfaces where adding additional wiring is inconvenient\.

The choice should still be based on the complete system requirements\, including communication method\, installation environment\, measurement accuracy\, power supply and maintenance requirements\.

\#\# Temperature Monitoring Beyond the Battery Cell

As BESS electrical architectures become more compact\, temperature monitoring does not necessarily stop at the battery module\.

The electrical path around the battery can also contain important thermal information\.

For example\, a high\-current connection may experience additional heating because of contact resistance\. A fuse may operate in an enclosure where the local temperature is considerably different from the external ambient temperature\. A contactor may also experience its own thermal conditions depending on continuous current and installation environment\.

These measurements can help engineers distinguish between a battery\-related thermal issue and a problem associated with the electrical path\.

This is also why temperature monitoring and component selection should not be treated as completely separate design tasks\.

The thermal environment around a protection or switching component can affect its operating margin\, while the component itself can contribute to the local thermal environment\.

\#\# Sensor Placement Should Follow the Electrical and Thermal Architecture

Sensor placement is best considered together with the physical layout of the BESS\.

A useful approach is to identify\:

Where heat is generated → where heat can accumulate → where temperature changes can indicate an abnormal condition

This may lead to different sensing priorities in different parts of the system\.

Battery modules may require temperature monitoring for battery operating limits\.

Busbars and terminals may require monitoring because they carry high current\.

Connection points may deserve attention because local resistance can create concentrated heat\.

Other components may need monitoring when their operating temperature has a direct relationship with reliability or protection requirements\.

This approach is more useful than simply increasing the number of sensors\.

More data does not automatically mean better monitoring\. The sensing points need to provide information that can be acted upon\.

\#\# Temperature Monitoring and BESS Protection Work Together

Temperature monitoring is one layer of a larger protection system\.

In a BESS\, electrical protection may involve fuses\, DC contactors\, insulation monitoring\, current measurement and BMS protection functions\.
Temperature monitoring provides another source of information that can help identify abnormal operating conditions\.

These functions have different roles\.

A temperature sensor detects a physical condition\.

The BMS evaluates that condition together with other battery information\.

A control system can then determine the appropriate response\.

A fuse or contactor\, depending on the system architecture and fault condition\, may provide the physical isolation or interruption function\.

Keeping these roles clear is important when designing the complete protection strategy\.

It also prevents a common design mistake\: expecting one monitoring device or one protection component to solve a system\-level problem on its own\.

\#\# Temperature Data Becomes More Valuable Over Time

A temperature measurement is useful at the moment it is taken\, but recorded temperature data can provide additional value\.

Continuous monitoring can show how a particular point behaves under different charging and discharging conditions\.

Over time\, engineers may be able to identify\:

Repeated temperature rises at the same location

Differences between battery sections

Changes in thermal behavior under similar loads

Abnormal temperature patterns

Conditions that occur before a fault or maintenance event

This moves temperature monitoring beyond simple alarm generation\.

It can also support maintenance decisions by helping engineers identify locations that require closer inspection\.

For larger or more complex battery systems\, this historical information can become increasingly useful because the operating condition of the system changes over its service life\.

\#\# Designing the Monitoring Layer Alongside the Battery Rack

Temperature monitoring works best when it is considered during the battery rack design rather than added after the electrical architecture has already been fixed\.

The battery modules\, busbars\, high\-current connections\, protection components\, cooling system and sensing points occupy the same physical space and interact thermally\.

The monitoring architecture therefore needs to reflect the actual rack structure\.

This is consistent with the broader approach to high\-voltage battery rack design\: battery monitoring\, thermal management\, protection and electrical integration need to work together rather than being treated as separate tasks\.

For BESS developers\, the practical question is not simply how many temperature sensors are required\. It is which locations need to be monitored\, what information each point provides\, and how that information will be used by the BMS or system controller\.

That is where temperature sensing becomes part of the system design rather than just another component installed inside the rack\.

records.title: Renault Issues Fire Risk Recall for Captur and Symbioz Hybrid Vehicles
records.abstract: A small number of Captur and Symbioz crossovers are being recalled in Europe because of a potentially compromised busbar-to-relay connection inside the traction battery. ... Regarding the problem per se, the busbar is the conductive bar that carries current within the battery. A relay creates resistance at the joint, and resistance turns current into heat. Too much of it...
records.summary: This autoevolution news article reports a European recall of Renault Captur and Symbioz hybrid crossovers built between December 1, 2025, and February 6, 2026, identified by campaign code 0FDZ and listed through the European Commission's Safety Gate rapid alert system. The reported defect is a potentially compromised busbar-to-relay connection inside the traction battery: the busbar carries current within the battery, and resistance at the relay joint converts current into heat, which the Safety Gate description says could cause abnormal heating of the connection and battery cells and result in a fire. The article states that no such fires have been reported in Europe and that Renault's local subsidiaries will send registered letters asking owners to book a service appointment. Both models are built on the CMF-B platform at the Valladolid plant in Spain. The piece is publisher reporting on a regulatory alert and does not present independent testing or a detailed technical failure analysis.
records.why_it_matters: The case highlights that joint resistance at a busbar-to-relay connection inside a traction battery is a heat-generation failure mode that can escalate to fire risk, making connection quality and joint-level thermal monitoring relevant design and manufacturing controls for hybrid battery packs.

This directly touches the battery interconnect/joining failure mode, but the text gives no joint design, materials, torque/contact-resistance data, or corrective action, and no fires were reported. Much of the body is pricing and sales context, lowering evidence quality.

records.body_text:
Per the European Commission's Safety Gate rapid alert system for dangerous non-food products, the recall covers Captur and Symbioz hybrids produced between December 1, 2025, and February 6, 2026. The French automaker uses 0FDZ to identify said campaign.
The vehicles in question are based on the CMF-B platform, with both the Captur and Symbioz hailing from the Valladolid plant in Spain. Although they are identical in many respects, the Captur is a bit shorter than its brother. Featuring an extended overhang, the wagon-like Symbioz offers a bit more luggage space while retaining the Captur's wheelbase.
Regarding the problem per se, the busbar is the conductive bar that carries current within the battery. A relay creates resistance at the joint, and resistance turns current into heat. Too much of it, and the lithium-ion battery could very well sign off in a ball of fire.
The Safety Gate description of the problem reads that abnormal heating of the connection and battery cells may result in a fire, but no such fires have been reported thus far in the European space. Renault's local subsidiaries will send owners registered letters asking them to book a service appointment.
Instead of 29,990 euros for the Eco-G with the manual box, the full-hybrid model retails at 34,400 euros. The Captur sits below it, with prices kicking off at 26,800 euros for the Eco-G and 27,300 euros for the TCe. Upgrading to the noticeably more frugal hybrid means 30,500 euros from the outset.
Competing against the Peugeot 2008, Toyota Yaris Cross, and the Volkswagen T-Roc, the Captur is one of the best-selling crossovers in France. It and the Symbioz maintain consistent placement in the country's top 20 best sellers, with Renault being the leading automotive brand in France.
The group as a whole experienced a successful year in 2025, driven by strong demand for electrified vehicles in the core brand's home market. Renault alone sold more than a million vehicles across the continent, ranking second overall, while French registrations totaled nearly 285,600 vehicles in 2025. When it comes to best-selling passenger vehicle overall in France, the Renault Clio made easy work of second-placed Peugeot 208 and third-placed Dacia Sandero.

records.summary: The paper reports a sulfonate-oleylammonium ionic covalent organic framework (soa-TADA) designed as a lubricant additive for precision lubrication. The concept addresses the trade-off between physically adsorbed films, which lack anchoring strength, and tribochemical films, which grow uncontrollably and deplete. In soa-TADA, immobilized sulfonate anions provide electrostatic anchoring to metal surfaces, oleylammonium cations aid oil dispersibility, and the rigid covalent skeleton supplies mechanical robustness, enabling self-limiting assembly of a compact physical adsorption film. The authors report that in 500 SN base oil, soa-TADA reduced friction by 64% and wear volume by 89.5% at 200 N, reached a load-carrying capacity of 400 N, and maintained lubrication under varying speeds and prolonged operation, whereas 500 SN alone and a non-ionic analogue failed. Combined tribological testing, interfacial characterization, and DFT calculations were used to support an 'electrostatically anchored, reinforced physical adsorption' mechanism involving lower electron-transfer barriers, p-d orbital hybridization via sulfonate groups, and hard acid-hard base interactions.
records.why_it_matters: The design suggests a molecular-engineering route to lubricant additives that combine electrostatic surface anchoring with a rigid framework, potentially avoiding the uncontrolled growth and depletion associated with tribochemical films while improving on weak physical adsorption.

records.body_text:
Published by: Elsevier
Published by
Highlights
- •Ionic covalent organic frameworks (iCOFs) are designed as lubricant additives.
- •Sulfonate anchors enable robust physical adsorption on metal surfaces.
- •Friction and wear volume decrease by 64% and 89.5% at 200 N.
- •DFT reveals strong p-d hybridization and hard acid-hard base interactions.
Abstract
Precision lubrication demands interfacial films with strong adhesion, high load-bearing capacity, and long-term durability. However, conventional physically adsorbed films lack anchoring strength, while tribochemical films suffer from uncontrollable growth and consumption. Here, we revealed that ionic covalent organic framework (iCOF) could enable an electrostatically anchored, robust physical adsorption film to overcome shortcomings. A sulfonate-oleylammonium iCOF additive (soa-TADA) is designed, in which immobilized sulfonate anions provide instantaneous electrostatic anchoring to metal surfaces, oleylammonium cations ensure oil dispersibility, and the rigid covalent skeleton delivers mechanical robustness. The electrostatic manipulation drives self-limiting assembly into a compact, robust and cohesive physical adsorption film, where covalent skeleton imparts high load-bearing strength and ionic moieties facilitate inter-sheet shear. Consequently, soa-TADA reduces friction by 64% and wear volume by 89.5% at 200 N, also achieves load-carrying capacity of 400 N and maintains unchanged lubrication under varying speeds and prolonged operation, where both 500 SN and non-ionic analogue fail. Combined experimental and DFT calculations elucidate an “electrostatically anchored, reinforced physical adsorption” mechanism. The lower electron-transfer barrier, stronger p-d orbital hybridization via sulfonate groups, and favorable hard acid-hard base interactions ensure rapid formation and exceptional durability. This iCOF-enabled strategy provides a molecular engineering route for precision lubrication where both surface integrity and interfacial stability are paramount.
Graphical abstract
Keywords
Ionic covalent organic frameworks
;
Electrostatic anchoring
;
Precision lubrication
;
Physical adsorption film
Introduction
Under harsh boundary lubrication regimes, the ability to construct an interfacial film with superior mechanical strength, persistent adhesion stability and adaptability to varying operational conditions at the contact interfaces of moving components dictates the systemic efficiency, lifespan and reliability of machinery [1], [2], [3]. Ideally, such interfacial film not only possesses low shear strength to effectively reduce friction, but also exhibits high load-bearing capacity, strong film-substrate adhesion and excellent shear durability to maintain structural integrity and functional continuity under the synergistic impact of extreme pressure, cyclic shear and triboheat. As aerospace, precision manufacturing or machining and new micro/nano-device systems advance toward high-speed, heavy-load, extreme-precision, and long-term stable operation conditions, traditional lubrication systems containing organic modifiers and anti-wear additives face profoundly limitations, because these systems predominantly rely on molecular physical adsorption or tribochemical reactions to form interfacial films [4], [5]. The adsorption film fed by the former (organic modifiers) presents weak bonding forces that are prone to desorption under higher loads or temperatures, while the tribofilm created by the latter (anti-wear additives) requires a high activation energy, often grows uncontrollable film configuration and consumes continuously active components. The intense operational dependence, unpredictability and unsustainable supply in lubricating performance render their unavailability to meet the urgent demands of modern equipment for the stability, predictability and low environmental dependence of lubrication interface.
Over the past two decades, ionic liquids (ILs) have been emerging as versatile lubricants that spontaneously adsorb via electrostatic interactions, yet while film formation proceeds through tribochemical pathways. Thus, ILs inherit the typical drawbacks of reaction-based films: uncontrollable growth, potential corrosion, and progressive depletion (Scheme 1) [6], [7]. Meanwhile, two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have drawn attention as “pre-designable” solid lubricants due to their layered structures, tunable interlayer interactions, and exceptional mechanical strength [8], [9]. However, their lubrication films are assembled predominantly through weak van der Waals, ion-π, or coordination forces, resulting in critically insufficient adhesion to the substrate. Under high loads or variable frequencies, these films are prone to slippage or delamination, preventing their intrinsic mechanical properties from translating into effective interfacial protection (Scheme 1) [10], [11], [12]. Therefore, a fundamental contradiction persists: physical adsorption films lack sufficient anchoring strength, while tribochemical films suffer from poor controllability and consumptive nature, which presents the limitation of strategies relying solely on structural mechanical enhancement while neglecting interfacial force engineering.
To resolve this contradiction, herein, we propose a molecular interfacial engineering strategy that integrates the strong interfacial anchoring capability of immobilized ionic groups with the robust mechanical framework of COFs. A sulfonate-oleylammonium ionic pair-functionalized COF (soa-TADA) was rationally designed and fabricated, wherein the fixed sulfonate anions serve as powerful electrostatic anchors that bind instantly to positively charged metal surfaces, while the rigid covalent skeleton provides structural support and prevents the migration and depletion typical of liquid-phase ions. This synergy enables the formation of a “reinforced physical adsorption film” with excellent adhesion, structural integrity, and shear/compressive resistance. When applied in 500 SN base oil, soa-TADA reduces the coefficient of friction by 64% and wear volume by 89.5%, and boosts the load-carrying capacity to 400 N, far surpassing the non-ionic analogue TADA (150 N). The film also exhibits exceptional adaptability under variable frequencies, elevated temperatures, and prolonged operation. Combined with systematic tribological tests, multi-scale interfacial characterizations, and DFT quantum chemical calculations, the structure–performance correlation and electronic-level reinforcement mechanism of electrostatically anchored lubrication are thoroughly uncovered. This work not only provides a high-efficiency and multi-environment adaptive lubricant additive for precision lubrication, but also offers a universal molecular design principle for developing advanced functional COF materials toward interfacial friction regulation.

FUCHS LUBRICANTS SOUTH AFRICA Achieves GBCSA Net Zero Carbon Level 2 Certification
20.10.2026 - 10:00
As businesses face increasing pressure to reduce their environmental impact, FUCHS LUBRICANTS SOUTH AFRICA is demonstrating what sustainable industrial development can look like in practice. The company's headquarters in Isando has been rated Net Zero Carbon Level 2 certification by the Green Building Council South Africa (GBCSA), placing it among a select group of buildings recognised for their commitment to low-carbon operations and sustainable design.
The achievement was recently commemorated through a plaque handover ceremony, recognising FUCHS' ongoing efforts to reduce emissions while creating a high-performance workplace aligned with its long-term sustainability ambitions.
Developed as part of the FUCHS Net-Zero Carbon Strategy, the headquarters was designed to maximise energy efficiency while enhancing employee comfort and wellbeing. Key sustainability features include high-performance double glazing, passive design principles that reduce reliance on mechanical cooling, intelligent fresh-air ventilation systems, comprehensive energy monitoring and a 100% electrification approach that creates opportunity for renewable energy use through our solar PV system.
Together, these measures help reduce the building's carbon footprint while supporting more efficient and resilient operations.
The certification was achieved with support from sustainability consultancy Solid Green Consulting, which served as the Accredited Professional on the project, and Brundtland Consulting, which provided carbon credit specialist expertise.
According to Esther Seabi, Sustainability Director at FUCHS LUBRICANTS SOUTH AFRICA, the recognition reflects the company's long-term commitment to responsible business practices. “This certification demonstrates how sustainability can be integrated into everyday business operations and infrastructure decisions. As a company, we continue to pursue practical solutions that reduce environmental impact while supporting operational excellence and long-term resilience.”
The GBCSA Net Zero Carbon certification recognises projects that achieve highly energy-efficient operations while balancing or eliminating carbon emissions associated with building performance. Level 2 certification extends beyond base building emissions to include occupant operational energy use, reflecting a broader and more comprehensive sustainability approach.
Managing Director Paul Deppe said the recognition aligns with the wider sustainability objectives of both the local business and the global FUCHS Group. “Sustainability is becoming increasingly important across every sector we serve. This certification demonstrates that meaningful progress is possible when environmental considerations are integrated into strategic planning from the outset. It is an achievement that reflects the commitment of our teams and partners, while supporting our broader journey towards a lower-carbon future.”
The headquarters forms part of FUCHS LUBRICANTS SOUTH AFRICA’s broader sustainability roadmap, which includes ongoing investments in renewable energy, energy efficiency and emissions reduction initiatives across its operations.

High Diesel Margins and Rising Freight Costs Compound Lubricant Industry Challenges
Global petroleum markets continue to face unusual pressures as tight diesel supplies support exceptionally high refining margins in some regions, while sharply higher shipping and insurance costs are undermining refinery economics elsewhere. The contrasting conditions underscore the challenges facing refiners and raise questions about potential implications for base-oil supply and pricing.
According to an October 16 report in The Wall Street Journal, diesel refining margins in New York Harbor have exceeded $100 per barrel, reflecting tight distillate supplies and continuing disruptions to global petroleum markets. Low inventories, interruptions to Russian refinery operations, and shipping constraints in the Middle East have contributed to the pressure on diesel availability.
Meanwhile, an October 19 Reuters analysis reports that Asian refiners are confronting exceptionally high transportation and insurance costs, even as crude oil exports from the Middle East show signs of recovery. Freight expenses can account for as much as 30% of the delivered cost of crude oil on certain routes, compared with a more typical 3% to 7%. Reuters reported that these additional expenses are substantially reducing refining margins and contributing to decisions by some refiners to limit crude processing or draw on inventories.
The developments are also relevant to the lubricant industry. Strong diesel margins can influence refinery production economics, while higher transportation costs and changes in refinery operating rates can affect the economics of base-oil production and international trade. However, the extent to which these conditions will affect base-oil availability or finished-lubricant prices remains uncertain and will depend on individual refinery operations, supply arrangements, and regional market conditions.
For lubricant manufacturers, blenders, and distributors, these developments add to the challenges of managing costs and maintaining profitability in an already strained market. Changes in feedstock costs, transportation expenses, and product replacement costs do not always move in step with selling prices. JobbersWorld has heard from blenders and distributors who say that competitive pressures are making it increasingly difficult to pass along higher costs to customers. According to these industry participants, margins are coming under increasing pressure, forcing companies to balance the need to remain competitive with the need to protect profitability.

records.body_text:
How to Diagnose and Address BMW B38 Boost Control Connector Corrosion
Corrosion at a boost-control electrical connector can interrupt the signal or power that the engine management system needs to regulate turbocharger boost.
This guide explains how to identify the likely connector, inspect it safely, clean minor contamination, and decide when a damaged terminal or separate boost-control fault needs professional diagnosis.
What the boost-control connector does
The BMW B38 is a turbocharged three-cylinder engine used in several BMW and MINI models.
Depending on the exact vehicle, model year, and engine configuration, boost control may involve an electronically controlled actuator or a solenoid, along with pressure sensors and related wiring.
The connector at one of these components carries electrical power or control signals; it does not itself control boost mechanically.
A loose, wet, corroded, or poorly repaired connection can cause an intermittent electrical circuit.
Possible symptoms include a warning light, reduced engine power, uneven acceleration, or a fault code referring to a boost-control circuit or actuator.
These symptoms are not proof of connector corrosion.
A split charge pipe, vacuum or pressure leak, faulty sensor, damaged wire, actuator problem, or software issue can produce overlapping complaints.
BMW uses different engine and wiring configurations across vehicles.
Identify the component using the VIN-specific wiring diagram or a reliable repair manual before unplugging anything.
Do not assume that a connector shown for one B38-equipped car is in the same location or has the same pinout on another.
Signs that justify an inspection
Look for a pattern that changes with rain, washing, temperature, or vibration, such as an intermittent warning or power loss.
A stored diagnostic trouble code can help identify the affected circuit, but a code is a starting point, not a parts-replacement instruction.
Check for these visible clues:
- Green, blue, white, or powdery deposits on exposed metal contacts.
- Moisture, dirt, or oily residue inside the connector shell.
- A cracked housing, broken lock, bent pin, or terminal pushed backward into the connector.
- Chafed, stretched, brittle, or previously spliced wiring near the plug.
- A connector that does not latch firmly or separates with very little force.
Corrosion may be hidden inside a sealed connector or under insulation.
Conversely, a dirty exterior does not prove that the electrical contacts are corroded.
Avoid disturbing wiring just to look for a problem if there are no symptoms or relevant codes.
Gather tools and make the car safe
You will need the vehicle-specific service information, a scan tool that can read BMW-relevant engine codes, a flashlight, eye protection, and suitable electrical contact cleaner.
A small nylon detailing brush can help with light surface contamination.
If terminal repair is needed, use the correct terminal release tool and replacement contacts specified for the connector; improvised picks can spread or break the locking features.
Before working:
- Park on a level surface, select Park or a gear, apply the parking brake, and let the engine and nearby exhaust parts cool.
- Switch off the ignition and remove the key or keep the key away from the vehicle. Follow the model-specific procedure for disconnecting the battery if the repair information requires it. Some electrical systems require a waiting period before service.
- Keep metal tools, liquids, and loose hardware away from belts, fans, and other moving parts. Electric cooling fans can start unexpectedly on some vehicles, even after shutdown.
- Confirm the connector identity from service information. Do not probe terminals or unplug an unknown sensor based only on location or wire color.
If you are uncertain about battery isolation, airbag-adjacent wiring, or how to access the component, stop and consult a qualified technician.
Avoid working on orange high-voltage cables in hybrid or electric vehicles; those are outside this repair procedure.
Inspect the connector without damaging it
Photograph the connector and wire routing before disconnecting it.
This gives you a reference for reassembly and helps document the condition if the repair needs to be escalated.
Release the connector by its locking tab or secondary lock as designed.
Pull on the connector body, not the wires.
If it will not release, check for a secondary latch and use the specified tool rather than levering against the housing.
Once apart, inspect both halves under good light.
Look for corrosion on the metal contact surfaces, but also check the plastic shell, seals, and wire entry points.
A swollen seal, missing weather seal, cracked housing, or damaged lock can let contamination return.
Gently compare the terminals: they should sit at a similar depth and should not look spread, bent, blackened, or loose.
Do not scrape contacts with a knife, sandpaper, or steel brush; removing plating can make future corrosion and poor contact more likely.
If the connector is wet, identify how water could enter.
Nearby damaged covers, an incorrectly routed harness, a missing seal, or a prior repair may be the underlying cause.
Cleaning without correcting water entry often provides only temporary improvement.
Clean light corrosion and reassemble
Only attempt cleaning when the contamination is minor and the terminals, seals, and housing remain intact.
Use an electronics-safe contact cleaner labeled for automotive electrical connectors, and follow its product directions.
Avoid household acids, vinegar, baking soda mixtures, carburetor cleaner, brake cleaner, and general-purpose lubricants.
They may attack plastics, seals, coatings, or leave residue.
- Keep the connector disconnected and protect nearby painted or sensitive surfaces from overspray.
- Apply a small amount of contact cleaner to the affected contacts. Do not flood the harness or force liquid deep into a sealed assembly.
- If needed, use a clean, soft nylon brush on accessible light deposits. Do not bend terminals or insert anything that can widen the female contact.
- Allow the connector to dry completely for the time stated on the cleaner label. Do not use a flame, heat gun, or compressed air at excessive pressure.
- Inspect again. If deposits remain, contact surfaces are pitted, or a terminal has lost tension, stop cleaning and arrange terminal or connector replacement.
- Reconnect the plug squarely until its primary and secondary locks engage. Check that the harness is routed as before and is not under tension or rubbing on adjacent parts.
Use dielectric grease only if the vehicle repair instructions or connector manufacturer specifies it, and only in the manner directed.
It is generally applied to seals or used as specified for connector protection; it should not be packed onto contact surfaces as a substitute for clean, correctly tensioned terminals.
Never use grease to conceal a loose or damaged connection.
Connector condition | Suitable next step
---|---
Dry, clean, secure, no visible damage | Reconnect and continue diagnosis based on codes and symptoms
Minor removable surface contamination; sound pins and seals | Clean with suitable contact cleaner, dry, and reassemble
Pitted, loose, bent, or heat-discolored terminal | Replace the affected terminal or connector using the correct repair parts
Cracked housing, failed seal, water entry, or damaged wire | Repair the cause and replace compromised components
Troubleshoot after the repair
Clear a stored code only after recording it and its freeze-frame information, if available.
The code can help show when and under what conditions the fault occurred.
Then follow the vehicle’s service procedure to confirm that the connector is seated and that any repair is recognized by the engine control system.
If you have a capable scan tool, review live data and relevant fault status while following the manufacturer’s diagnostic procedure.
Do not run the engine with hands, tools, or loose clothing near moving components.
A basic code reader may show a generic description but may not provide BMW-specific details or guided tests.
If the same fault returns, work through the circuit instead of repeatedly cleaning the plug:
- Check the harness: Look for abrasion, a broken conductor near the connector, tension, or a poor prior splice. A wire can break internally while its insulation still looks normal.
- Verify electrical supply and ground: Use the correct wiring diagram and specified test points. Back-probing or probing the wrong terminal can damage a seal or short a circuit. Avoid applying battery voltage to control wires.
- Check the actuator or solenoid: A connector fault and a failed component can produce similar codes. Use model-specific resistance, output, or functional tests rather than guessing from a generic code description.
- Check boost plumbing and pressure readings: A boost leak or implausible sensor reading may cause underboost or reduced power even when the electrical connector is sound.
- Consider intermittent faults: If the symptom comes and goes with movement or moisture, a technician may need to monitor the circuit during a controlled harness movement test. Do not tug on the harness with the engine running.
Do not replace a turbocharger, actuator, sensor, or engine computer solely because a warning mentions boost.
Diagnose the circuit and mechanical system in the order specified for the exact vehicle.
When connector repair is not a DIY cleaning job
Cleaning is not enough if a terminal is loose, deeply pitted, overheated, bent, or partially withdrawn.
Replace the affected terminal with the correct part and crimp tool, or replace the connector repair lead or housing as the manufacturer specifies.
A poor crimp or mismatched terminal can create resistance and heat, leading to another failure.
Seek professional help when the connector is inaccessible, several wires are damaged, water has entered a control module, the wiring diagram is unavailable, or the fault persists after a careful inspection.
A BMW specialist can use the VIN to identify the correct circuit and repair procedure, test the actuator and wiring, and determine whether programming or adaptation is required after component replacement.
Avoid driving if the vehicle has severe power loss, repeated stalling, a flashing engine warning, burning electrical odor, visible smoke, or signs of overheating.
Arrange recovery or prompt inspection.
For a mild intermittent warning, follow the vehicle’s manual and avoid hard acceleration or sustained boost until the fault is diagnosed; reduced power can make merging or passing unsafe.
Preventing repeat corrosion
After a successful repair, keep the connector and its seals intact.
Make sure any covers, clips, and splash shields removed for access are refitted, and route the harness through its original supports.
Do not direct a pressure washer at engine-bay connectors.
During routine service, look for chafing, cracked protective covering, or a harness pulled tight after other work.
If the connector repeatedly becomes wet, trace the water path and repair the source rather than applying more cleaner or grease.
Record the fault codes, the connector condition, and the repair performed.
That history helps a technician distinguish a recurring moisture problem from a separate boost-control fault.
