records.summary: This is a market-research report page from Knowledge Sourcing Intelligence LLP forecasting the co-packaged optics (CPO) and optical-engine market for AI data centers at an 85.0% CAGR, from USD 85.0 million in 2026 to USD 3,400.0 million in 2032. The report frames CPO as a response to rising high-speed electrical channel loss and retimer power as switch bandwidth and link counts grow, moving optical-electrical conversion closer to the switch ASIC so the longest signal path is optical. It cites vendor and foundry announcements—NVIDIA's Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics entering production (May 2026), Broadcom's 102.4 Tb/s CPO-enabled switching shipments, TSMC's 2026 COUPE-on-substrate production, and Coherent's demonstrated 6.4 Tb/s socketed CPO engine with an external laser—as commercialization signals. It also stresses that serviceable external lasers, detachable fiber arrays and package-level testing are qualification requirements, and that CPO competes with improving 800G/1.6T pluggables rather than replacing all data-center optics. Home/ICT/Data Centers/Co-Packaged Optics and Optical Engines for AI Data Centers Market
The Co-Packaged Optics and Optical Engines for AI Data Centers Market is forecast to grow at a CAGR of 85.0%, reaching USD 3,400.0 million in 2032 from USD 85.0 million in 2026.
Highlights:
- 1NVIDIA reports that Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics entered production in May 2026, while Broadcom disclosed shipments of 102.4 Tb/s CPO-enabled switching technology.
- 2High-speed electrical channel loss and retimer power make photonic integration more attractive as switch bandwidth and the number of links rise.
- 3TSMC is beginning production of COUPE-on-substrate technology in 2026, creating a repeatable foundry and packaging route for integrated photonics.
- 4Serviceable external lasers, removable fiber interfaces and package-level testing remain commercial qualification requirements, not secondary engineering details.
- 5Scale-out switches provide the initial installed base, while photonic I/O for custom accelerators and multi-rack scale-up domains represents a later adoption path.
- 6CPO competes with continuously improving 800G, 1.6T and higher-speed pluggable technologies and therefore does not replace all data-center optical connections.
Market Overview
At high electrical lane rates, sending signals across a circuit board and through faceplate connectors creates insertion loss, equalization, and retiming requirements. The penalties rise with lane rate, physical distance, and switch radix. CPO moves the optical-electrical conversion closer to the ASIC so the longest path is optical. The resulting power saving is especially valuable when every additional kilowatt devoted to networking competes with accelerator capacity inside a constrained AI factory.
NVIDIA states that Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics provides materially better power efficiency than conventional transceiver-based designs. Broadcom is commercializing its own high-radix CPO-enabled Ethernet switching platforms. The platforms differ in optical bandwidth, engine configuration, port reach, topology, and field-service requirements. Operators therefore evaluate the entire network power budget, network topology and operational risks rather than purchase optics against a nominal cost per terabit alone.
The packaging transition changes supplier bargaining power. Photonic engines must align with electrical SerDes, laser wavelengths, fiber arrays, thermal performance, and high-yield package assembly. TSMC has identified 2026 production for COUPE on substrate; Coherent has demonstrated a socketed 6.4 Tb/s CPO engine paired with an external laser. The socketed design adds a serviceability option, while volume production will depend on package yield, component reliability, and customer qualification.
The next adoption decision concerns optical connections associated with accelerators rather than network switches alone. Ayar Labs, Lightmatter and other developers are integrating optical I/O with system or accelerator packaging, with production volumes dependent on system-level qualification and design wins. Commercial adoption will depend on optical-link reliability, fabric compatibility and the economics of replacing copper. Customer production schedules will determine the timing of volume ramps.
Market Drivers
Increasing Cost of Electrical Reach
The decisive constraint is the shortening usable reach of high-speed electrical links, not optical speed in isolation. Additional retiming can preserve a front-panel architecture, but it adds power, board area, heat, and component count. Moving optical conversion closer to the switch silicon changes the design trade-off: the system accepts more difficult package assembly to reduce recurring network electricity and board-level signal conditioning. This improves CPO economics first in the largest and most heavily utilized AI fabrics.
AI Fabric Bandwidth and Accelerator Utilization
Large AI training domains demand synchronized communication and predictable throughput across many network hops. Congestion and electrical link constraints can lower the useful compute delivered by expensive accelerators. CPO supports higher optical bandwidth density, while procurement decisions increasingly depend on sustained network performance and energy per delivered bit rather than peak interface throughput alone. Buyers may retain pluggables wherever replacement access, price competition and incremental installation are more valuable.
Packaging and External Laser Supply
As optical engines move inside the system, manufacturing yield and external laser supply become procurement risks. A photonic defect at final assembly may affect an expensive system package, while a hard-to-service laser could raise lifecycle costs. Socketed engines, external light sources and detachable fiber arrays preserve serviceability, creating opportunities for specialized optics and connector suppliers. Capacity investments by NVIDIA, Coherent and Corning reflect increasing demand for a reliable, qualified photonics supply chain.
Market Restraints
Yield, Qualification and Repair Economics
CPO raises the cost of incomplete optical testing. Yield losses can multiply when photonics, packaging and high-value switch electronics are integrated before defects are detected. Operators also require clear repair procedures because an optical fault may take an entire switch out of service rather than a single transceiver port. Test-at-source, detachable fiber interfaces and field-replaceable lasers directly influence procurement acceptance and supplier margins.
Strong Pluggable Optics Competition
Transceiver suppliers are improving density and power efficiency at 800G and 1.6T, with higher-speed roadmaps continuing. Pluggables provide multivendor flexibility, straightforward field replacement and incremental port deployment. CPO is therefore more likely to gain penetration in high-port-count configurations with sustained bandwidth use than in small AI pods or enterprise networks where operational simplicity has greater value.
Segment Analysis
By Integration Target
Switch-ASIC CPO constitutes the initial commercial installation base because Ethernet and InfiniBand switching platforms already have identified products and production programs. It concentrates optical subsystems next to a high-radix switch ASIC and requires careful integration of thermal control, laser distribution, and fiber routing. Accelerator/XPU optical I/O is an emerging adjacent opportunity, with a wider set of possible architectures from directly co-packaged optical chiplets to near-package systems. Its commercial growth depends on accelerator and fabric qualification, not simply the number of AI GPUs sold.
By Component
Photonic engines and optical control electronics account for the main subsystem content, while external light sources are critical to lifetime reliability and serviceability. Fiber-array units, connector systems and assembly/test providers influence manufacturability and cost even when their individually invoiced value is smaller. Greater integration can simplify procurement while concentrating component-sourcing and manufacturing risk at the optical-engine supplier.
By Network Role and Customer
Scale-out switching is the near-term deployment center, led by hyperscalers and major AI-platform vendors. Scale-up optical interconnects potentially extend photonics across accelerator trays and racks, but face strict latency, power, error-rate and fabric-control requirements. System OEMs often make integration and qualification decisions, while cloud operators influence architectures and purchasing terms. Consequently, equipment specifications are often set jointly by cloud buyers and system vendors, while component purchasing is concentrated among platform integrators.
Regional Analysis
North America
North America leads architectural decisions through NVIDIA, Broadcom, hyperscale AI operators, photonic-engine specialists and large network-equipment programs. The commercial opportunity is shaped by demand for high-bandwidth AI fabrics and by access to supply chains in Taiwan and other Asian electronics hubs. Taiwan remains essential to foundry, packaging and system assembly even where AI systems are ultimately deployed in the United States. Consequently, manufacturing investment in Asian supply chains can expand even when North America remains the principal end market.
Near-term investment includes suppliers of laser sources, photonics, fiber handling and system test. NVIDIA announced a multiyear optics agreement with Coherent and separately expanded its optical-connectivity partnership with Corning. These partnerships strengthen access to optical components and manufacturing capacity as AI networking platforms adopt higher-bandwidth architectures.
Competitive and Technology Landscape
NVIDIA and Broadcom lead identifiable switch-level CPO commercialization. Marvell supplies optical and custom-compute semiconductor capabilities; Coherent, Lumentum and Ayar Labs focus on active optical engines or light-source technology; Lightmatter and Intel participate in optical I/O architectures. TSMC is a foundry and packaging enabler, while Corning, SENKO and Sumitomo Electric serve fiber attachment and connector requirements. Competition therefore differs across integrated switching systems, photonic-engine development, advanced packaging and passive optical connectivity.
The wider CPO supply chain also depends on network-equipment design, advanced assembly and high-volume manufacturing. Arista, Cisco, Celestica, Foxconn Interconnect Technology, Fabrinet and others remain relevant ecosystem participants where they qualify integrated hardware or contribute packaging, assembly and supply capacity.
Recent Developments
September 2026: Ayar Labs disclosed additional funding to expand manufacturing capability and advance customer qualification of optical-I/O technology.
May 2026: NVIDIA stated that Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics had entered production with Vera Rubin systems.
April 2026: TSMC announced 2026 production for COUPE on substrate, a photonic engine integrated within advanced packages.
March 2026: Coherent demonstrated a 6.4 Tb/s socketed CPO optical engine with an external laser source and a separate 400G-lane technology path.
March 2026: Broadcom confirmed production shipments of the 102.4 Tb/s Tomahawk 6 family; its CPO-enabled Davisson configuration was announced separately.
March 2026: NVIDIA and Coherent announced a multi-year optics partnership that includes purchase commitments and manufacturing investment.

records.body_text:
Co-Packaged Optics Clears System-Level Proof: Wiwynn Runs Live AI Rack at OCP Summit
Ayar Labs Optical Chiplets Stream Live Rack Telemetry at OCP Summit, Crossing Hyperscale Proof Gate
Co-packaged optics has crossed the milestone hyperscale data center operators have been waiting for. At the OCP Global Summit in San Jose this past week, Wiwynn, Ayar Labs, and Global Unichip Corp. (GUC) jointly ran the most complete live demonstration of a co-packaged optics (CPO) rack system to date — a working compute platform with a GUC ASIC, Ayar Labs TeraPHY optical engines, and SuperNova external laser sources transmitting real-time health telemetry in an Open Rack V3 (ORV3) enclosure. The demo, staged at the San Jose Convention Center during the summit's October 12–15 run, marked what the three companies described as CPO's transition from "architectural validation to system-level functional proof" — the specific engineering gate that separates lab credibility from procurement relevance.
Why System-Level Proof Is the Hyperscale Gate
To understand why that phrase carries weight, it helps to know what the earlier milestones were not. Optical components functioning correctly in a lab, or in a purpose-built testbed, demonstrate physics. A running system — with a real ASIC, a real rack form factor, open-standard die-to-die interfaces, and a multi-vendor fiber plant — demonstrates deployment feasibility. These are different claims, and hyperscalers wait for the second kind before committing qualification resources.
Three features of the OCP demonstration make it the second kind. First, the GUC XPU multi-chip package (MCP) uses UCIe-S chiplet links (Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express Standard) at 64 Gbps per lane to connect Ayar Labs' TeraPHY optical engines to I/O chiplets, and UCIe-A (Advanced) at 64 Gbps per lane via LSI bridges to connect I/O chiplets to the main AI compute die. UCIe is an open standard; using it rather than a proprietary interface lets a hyperscaler add multiple chiplet suppliers to the same platform without renegotiating license terms.
Second, the rack platform is built to ORV3, the OCP open rack standard already deployed in major hyperscaler facilities. Third, the fiber and connector partners in the demonstration—Corning and Senko at OCP, plus Browave, FOCI, Molex, and TE Connectivity at Computex in May—represent the kind of multi-vendor supply chain hyperscalers require before committing to a new interconnect architecture.
OCP Summit 2026 dedicated a full technical track — "Short Reach Optical Interconnect" — to CPO standardization across 22 total summit tracks, signaling that the open-standards consortium is treating CPO as an active priority, not a roadmap aspiration.
From Blueprint to Running System
The OCP demonstration was the third public proof point in a nine-month progression.
Ayar Labs and Wiwynn announced their strategic partnership in March 2026 at the Optical Fiber Communication Conference (OFC) in Los Angeles, where they presented a joint architecture targeting an HVDC (High Voltage Direct Current)-enabled rack-level system designed to scale to 1,024 accelerators with more than 100 Tbps of optical connectivity per XPU package. That announcement was a design commitment — a shared vision for what the architecture should look like.
By May, at Computex 2026 in Taipei, Wiwynn expanded the demonstration to a broader fiber and connectivity ecosystem, bringing in Browave, Corning, FOCI, Molex, Senko, and TE Connectivity alongside Ayar Labs and GUC. The wider supplier roster reflected the practical engineering complexity of routing fiber at rack scale: CPO is not merely a chip-level problem, but a full-stack infrastructure challenge.
At OCP in October, the goal shifted from integration design to operational proof. For the first time, the three companies demonstrated a live Wiwynn compute system with a GUC ASIC, Ayar Labs TeraPHY optical engines, and SuperNova light sources, transmitting health telemetry data in real time.
Inside TeraPHY: Why Shortening the Electrical Path Changes the Economics
Co-packaged optics integrates photonic integrated circuits (PICs) with electronic integrated circuits (EICs) inside the same package, positioning the optical modulator within millimeters (roughly 0.2 inches) of the ASIC rather than at the end of the 15–30 centimeter (5.9–11.8 inch) electrical trace that runs from a switch chip to a faceplate pluggable transceiver. At 1.6 terabit-per-second data rates and above, every centimeter of that electrical trace requires signal amplification; the DSP retimer chip responsible for that amplification in a pluggable module alone consumes 10–15 watts per port.
Ayar Labs' TeraPHY optical engine uses CW-WDM (Continuous Wave Wavelength Division Multiplexing) across 8 wavelengths in the O-band (around 1310 nm), each carrying 256 Gbps, for 2 Tbps per direction and 4 Tbps total bidirectional bandwidth per chiplet, across 8 ports. The continuous-wave laser light is provided by a separate component — the SuperNova external laser source — in the ELSFP (External Laser Small Form Factor Pluggable) form factor. Separating the heat-intensive laser from the heat-sensitive photonic modulator addresses one of CPO's most persistent engineering challenges: photonic components are far more temperature-sensitive than digital CMOS, and co-locating a laser with a high-power AI accelerator creates thermal management complications. Wiwynn developed custom liquid-cooling infrastructure for SuperNova as part of the system design.
The aggregate target for the GUC XPU multi-chip package is more than 100 Tbps bandwidth of full-duplex optical bandwidth per package — a figure that is physically impossible to achieve with copper at this board geometry.
The power economics are straightforward. A conventional pluggable transceiver at 1.6T draws approximately 30 watts per port; the equivalent CPO path draws approximately 9 watts per port, a roughly 70% reduction. At the scale of a 100,000-GPU AI training cluster — where each accelerator needs an optical port — that 21-watt-per-port difference sums to approximately 2.1 megawatts of interconnect power that CPO eliminates, representing millions of dollars annually in direct operating cost savings at commercial power rates.
That arithmetic explains the urgency behind the $650 million in primary capital Ayar Labs raised in 2026 alone — by far the largest annual fundraising in the company's history — reflecting investor conviction that CPO is approaching a commercial inflection point, not a longer-horizon research bet.
What Was Shown
The OCP demo covered three interlocking layers: rack-level fiber routing, patch panel integration, and multi-vendor fiber management, along with a live optical engine telemetry demonstration.
The fiber-handling side of the demonstration is notable in its own right. AI scale-up clusters require dozens — potentially hundreds — of fiber runs per rack, and the mechanical problem of routing, connecting, and managing that optical infrastructure alongside high-density liquid cooling is one of the unsolved engineering challenges that has slowed CPO's path from lab to data center floor. The OCP demo brought fiber routing and patch panel integration into the same room as the live optical telemetry, signaling that the team is treating the full system stack — not just chip-level optics — as the deliverable.
A detachable FAU (Fiber Array Unit) in the system enables standard MPO connector compatibility, allowing fiber-to-chip coupling with field-serviceable interfaces rather than requiring module replacement for routine maintenance.
Summit engineering workshops co-presented by Wiwynn and Ayar Labs engineers covered rack-ready high-power ELSFPs developed to support CPO deployment in AI scale-up and scale-out data centers, and open rack-scale optical infrastructure design.
"The bar is no longer whether it works; it's whether it can be deployed and managed at scale," Mark Wade said in the companies' joint announcement. GUC President Sean Tai said that integrating TeraPHY optical engines is "critical to shortening the development cycle for the next generation of XPU compute systems."
Why CPO, and Why Now
The urgency behind CPO's commercialization tracks directly to a data center power crisis that shows no signs of abating. Gartner's 40% shortage projection established that 40% of AI data centers will face power constraints by 2027, driven by AI workloads consuming an increasingly large share of data center capacity. Within those facilities, approximately 60% of energy spent on data movement rather than computation — making the interconnect layer the most logical target for efficiency intervention.
CPO's case to that market rests on the bandwidth ceiling, not just the power problem. Conventional pluggable transceivers face hard physical limits at 3.2 terabit-per-second data rates; beyond that point, the electrical interface between switch ASIC and pluggable becomes the bottleneck. IDTechEx's co-packaged optics forecast projects the global co-packaged optics market will exceed $20 billion by 2036, growing at a compound annual rate of 37% from 2026, driven primarily by scale-up AI applications. CPO port shipments projected to surpass 10 million units annually by 2029.
William Lin said at OFC that co-packaged optics is "a foundational technology for the next generation of AI and cloud data centers," with the collaboration offering "a clear path to new architectures that reduce the power and complexity limits of copper interconnects."
Strategic Investment and Ecosystem Depth
The OCP demonstration reflects a financial commitment that goes beyond joint engineering. Ayar Labs disclosed in September 2026 that Wiwynn had made a strategic investment earlier in the year, joining a roster of strategic backers that includes Alchip, AMD, Intel, MediaTek, and NVIDIA. That disclosure came alongside Ayar Labs announcing $650 million in total 2026 primary capital — a fundraising trajectory that positions the company to invest in the manufacturing scale-up required for volume deployment.
For Wiwynn, the investment positions the company not merely as a system integrator purchasing components from CPO vendors, but as a stakeholder in the broader transition of the technology toward high-volume manufacturing — giving it an unusually close seat at the table as CPO specifications evolve toward productization.
Vera Rubin and AMD Helios: Wiwynn's Full AI Infrastructure Portfolio
The CPO demonstration did not occur in isolation at OCP. Wiwynn simultaneously revealed that it is among NVIDIA's first Pilot Build Partners for the Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, a distinction it shares with Wistron. The NVL72 combines 72 Rubin GPUs with 36 Vera CPUs connected via sixth-generation NVLink, with each Rubin GPU carrying 288 GB of HBM4 memory — representing the current frontier of rack-scale AI compute density.
Wiwynn also unveiled an AMD Helios rack-scale platform at OCP, built on AMD Instinct MI450 Series GPUs, sixth-generation AMD EPYC server CPUs, AMD Pensando advanced networking, and the AMD ROCm open software stack, constructed on the Open Rack Wide (ORW) standard for large-scale AI training and inference.
The combination of NVL72 readiness with a live CPO demonstration is thematically coherent: next-generation AI racks at Vera Rubin scale generate data movement requirements that are increasingly difficult to satisfy with conventional copper and pluggable optics, making optical interconnect a near-term architectural necessity rather than a distant aspiration.
What Stands Between CPO and Volume Deployment?
The companies were careful to frame the OCP demonstration as a milestone, not a product launch. The three companies' joint statement described it as establishing "a solid foundation for hyperscale adoption," with the three companies committed to continuing to drive CPO from validation toward high-volume deployment.
The distinction matters. Real-world CPO deployment at hyperscale requires not just a functioning system but repeatable manufacturing yield — and CPO's yield challenge is structural. In a co-packaged assembly, the optical engine is bonded to the ASIC die; a defective optical engine cannot be individually replaced without risking damage to the entire package, unlike a pluggable transceiver that can be swapped in the field. At high-volume production, this assembly-level yield constraint historically increases per-unit cost relative to what individual component yields would suggest.
Fiber density is the complementary infrastructure challenge. A rack serving 32 AI accelerators with CPO-scale per-accelerator bandwidth requires routing many dozens of fiber ribbons alongside liquid cooling — a mechanical problem that the Computex and OCP demonstrations addressed with fiber management partners, but that remains a non-trivial data center operations burden.
Standards maturity is the third barrier. CW-WDM MSA, UCIe, and ELSFP are relatively new specifications; vendor interoperability testing infrastructure is still being built out. The OCP Short Reach Optical Interconnect technical track is directly addressing this, and the GUC XPU design's use of UCIe open interfaces rather than proprietary chiplet connections signals an intent to build an ecosystem rather than a closed platform.
That said, the nine-month arc from OFC in March to Computex in May to OCP in October reflects an integration pace data center architects are watching closely. If the ecosystem sustains that trajectory through 2027, the preconditions for hyperscale qualification — standards alignment, multi-vendor supply chain, open rack form factor, live system demonstration — are already in place.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is co-packaged optics, and how is it different from the transceiver modules data centers use today?
A conventional pluggable transceiver is an optical module attached to the faceplate of a switch or server, connected to the chip inside via a 15–30 centimeter (5.9–11.8 inch) electrical trace that requires a DSP retimer chip for signal amplification. Co-packaged optics moves the optical engine — the photodetectors and modulators — into the same package as the ASIC, shortening that electrical path to roughly 5 millimeters (0.2 inches). As a result, the retimer stage is eliminated, reducing power consumption from about 30 watts per 1.6 terabit-per-second port (pluggable) to about 9 watts per port—a reduction of roughly 70%—while enabling bandwidth densities that copper-based pluggables cannot physically achieve at 3.2 terabits per second and beyond. The tradeoff is replaceability: a pluggable transceiver can be swapped in the field in minutes; a co-packaged optical engine is bonded to the chip and cannot be individually field-replaced.
Why does the OCP Summit demonstration specifically matter — hasn't CPO been demonstrated in labs for years?
Component-level demonstrations prove that the physics work. A system-level demonstration—a live compute rack with a real production-style ASIC, UCIe open-standard die-to-die interfaces, a multi-vendor fiber plant, and OCP-standard rack infrastructure transmitting real telemetry—proves the full deployment stack works together. Hyperscale data center operators do not begin qualification processes based on chip-level results; they begin qualification when a technology has been demonstrated in the form factor, with the supply chain, and to the standards their facilities already use. The OCP Summit demonstration, built on UCIe, ORV3, CW-WDM MSA, and ELSFP open standards, checked all of those boxes for the first time at OCP 2026.
What are the biggest remaining obstacles before co-packaged optics reaches production AI data centers?
Three barriers stand out. First, manufacturing yield: because the optical engine is bonded to the ASIC die, a defect in either component during assembly typically renders the entire package unusable, increasing effective per-unit cost at production volume. Second, fiber infrastructure: AI-scale CPO deployments require routing many dozens of fiber ribbons per rack alongside liquid cooling, a mechanical challenge that fiber-management partners in the Wiwynn/Ayar Labs/GUC ecosystem are actively addressing but have not yet validated at full production density. Third, standards maturity: UCIe, CW-WDM MSA, and ELSFP are new enough that cross-vendor interoperability testing infrastructure is still being built. The OCP Summit's dedicated Short Reach Optical Interconnect technical track is directly advancing the standards work.
What is TeraPHY, and why does it use an external laser instead of a built-in one?
TeraPHY is Ayar Labs' silicon photonics optical I/O chiplet. It delivers 4 terabits per second of total bidirectional bandwidth from a single chiplet, across 8 ports each carrying 256 Gbps, using CW-WDM (Continuous Wave Wavelength Division Multiplexing) with 8 wavelengths in the O-band. The reason for the external laser — delivered by Ayar Labs' SuperNova module in the ELSFP form factor — is thermal: lasers generate significant heat, and photonic modulators are highly temperature-sensitive. Placing the laser inside the ASIC package alongside a high-power AI accelerator would create a thermal management challenge that could degrade modulator performance. The external laser architecture separates heat-generating and heat-sensitive components, enabling better thermal stability for the optical path and allowing the SuperNova module to be independently cooled — in Wiwynn's system, with dedicated liquid cooling.

That arithmetic explains the urgency behind the \$650 million in primary capital Ayar Labs raised in 2026 alone — by far the largest annual fundraising in the company\'s history — reflecting investor conviction that CPO is approaching a commercial inflection point\, not a longer\-horizon research bet\.

\#\#\# What Was Shown

The OCP demo covered three interlocking layers\: rack\-level fiber routing\, patch panel integration\, and multi\-vendor fiber management\, along with a live optical engine telemetry demonstration\.

The fiber\-handling side of the demonstration is notable in its own right\. AI scale\-up clusters require dozens — potentially hundreds — of fiber runs per rack\, and the mechanical problem of routing\, connecting\, and managing that optical infrastructure alongside high\-density liquid cooling is one of the unsolved engineering challenges that has slowed CPO\'s path from lab to data center floor\. The OCP demo brought fiber routing and patch panel integration into the same room as the live optical telemetry\, signaling that the team is treating the full system stack — not just chip\-level optics — as the deliverable\.

A detachable FAU \(Fiber Array Unit\) in the system enables standard MPO connector compatibility\, allowing fiber\-to\-chip coupling with field\-serviceable interfaces rather than requiring module replacement for routine maintenance\.

Summit engineering workshops co\-presented by Wiwynn and Ayar Labs engineers covered rack\-ready high\-power ELSFPs developed to support CPO deployment in AI scale\-up and scale\-out data centers\, and open rack\-scale optical infrastructure design\.

\"The bar is no longer whether it works\; it\'s whether it can be deployed and managed at scale\,\" Mark Wade said in the companies\' joint announcement\. GUC President Sean Tai said that integrating TeraPHY optical engines is \"critical to shortening the development cycle for the next generation of XPU compute systems\.\"

\#\#\# Why CPO\, and Why Now

The urgency behind CPO\'s commercialization tracks directly to a data center power crisis that shows no signs of abating\. Gartner\'s 40\% shortage projection established that 40\% of AI data centers will face power constraints by 2027\, driven by AI workloads consuming an increasingly large share of data center capacity\. Within those facilities\, approximately 60\% of energy spent on data movement rather than computation — making the interconnect layer the most logical target for efficiency intervention\.

CPO\'s case to that market rests on the bandwidth ceiling\, not just the power problem\. Conventional pluggable transceivers face hard physical limits at 3\.2 terabit\-per\-second data rates\; beyond that point\, the electrical interface between switch ASIC and pluggable becomes the bottleneck\. IDTechEx\'s co\-packaged optics forecast projects the global co\-packaged optics market will exceed \$20 billion by 2036\, growing at a compound annual rate of 37\% from 2026\, driven primarily by scale\-up AI applications\. CPO port shipments projected to surpass 10 million units annually by 2029\.

William Lin said at OFC that co\-packaged optics is \"a foundational technology for the next generation of AI and cloud data centers\,\" with the collaboration offering \"a clear path to new architectures that reduce the power and complexity limits of copper interconnects\.\"

\#\#\# Strategic Investment and Ecosystem Depth

The OCP demonstration reflects a financial commitment that goes beyond joint engineering\. Ayar Labs disclosed in September 2026 that Wiwynn had made a strategic investment earlier in the year\, joining a roster of strategic backers that includes Alchip\, AMD\, Intel\, MediaTek\, and NVIDIA\. That disclosure came alongside Ayar Labs announcing \$650 million in total 2026 primary capital — a fundraising trajectory that positions the company to invest in the manufacturing scale\-up required for volume deployment\.

For Wiwynn\, the investment positions the company not merely as a system integrator purchasing components from CPO vendors\, but as a stakeholder in the broader transition of the technology toward high\-volume manufacturing — giving it an unusually close seat at the table as CPO specifications evolve toward productization\.

\#\#\# Vera Rubin and AMD Helios\: Wiwynn\'s Full AI Infrastructure Portfolio

The CPO demonstration did not occur in isolation at OCP\. Wiwynn simultaneously revealed that it is among NVIDIA\'s first Pilot Build Partners for the Vera Rubin NVL72 rack\, a distinction it shares with Wistron\. The NVL72 combines 72 Rubin GPUs with 36 Vera CPUs connected via sixth\-generation NVLink\, with each Rubin GPU carrying 288 GB of HBM4 memory — representing the current frontier of rack\-scale AI compute density\.

Wiwynn also unveiled an AMD Helios rack\-scale platform at OCP\, built on AMD Instinct MI450 Series GPUs\, sixth\-generation AMD EPYC server CPUs\, AMD Pensando advanced networking\, and the AMD ROCm open software stack\, constructed on the Open Rack Wide \(ORW\) standard for large\-scale AI training and inference\.

The combination of NVL72 readiness with a live CPO demonstration is thematically coherent\: next\-generation AI racks at Vera Rubin scale generate data movement requirements that are increasingly difficult to satisfy with conventional copper and pluggable optics\, making optical interconnect a near\-term architectural necessity rather than a distant aspiration\.

\#\#\# What Stands Between CPO and Volume Deployment\?

The companies were careful to frame the OCP demonstration as a milestone\, not a product launch\. The three companies\' joint statement described it as establishing \"a solid foundation for hyperscale adoption\,\" with the three companies committed to continuing to drive CPO from validation toward high\-volume deployment\.

The distinction matters\. Real\-world CPO deployment at hyperscale requires not just a functioning system but repeatable manufacturing yield — and CPO\'s yield challenge is structural\. In a co\-packaged assembly\, the optical engine is bonded to the ASIC die\; a defective optical engine cannot be individually replaced without risking damage to the entire package\, unlike a pluggable transceiver that can be swapped in the field\. At high\-volume production\, this assembly\-level yield constraint historically increases per\-unit cost relative to what individual component yields would suggest\.

Fiber density is the complementary infrastructure challenge\. A rack serving 32 AI accelerators with CPO\-scale per\-accelerator bandwidth requires routing many dozens of fiber ribbons alongside liquid cooling — a mechanical problem that the Computex and OCP demonstrations addressed with fiber management partners\, but that remains a non\-trivial data center operations burden\.

Standards maturity is the third barrier\. CW\-WDM MSA\, UCIe\, and ELSFP are relatively new specifications\; vendor interoperability testing infrastructure is still being built out\. The OCP Short Reach Optical Interconnect technical track is directly addressing this\, and the GUC XPU design\'s use of UCIe open interfaces rather than proprietary chiplet connections signals an intent to build an ecosystem rather than a closed platform\.

That said\, the nine\-month arc from OFC in March to Computex in May to OCP in October reflects an integration pace data center architects are watching closely\. If the ecosystem sustains that trajectory through 2027\, the preconditions for hyperscale qualification — standards alignment\, multi\-vendor supply chain\, open rack form factor\, live system demonstration — are already in place\.

\#\# Frequently Asked Questions

\#\#\# What is co\-packaged optics\, and how is it different from the transceiver modules data centers use today\?

A conventional pluggable transceiver is an optical module attached to the faceplate of a switch or server\, connected to the chip inside via a 15–30 centimeter \(5\.9–11\.8 inch\) electrical trace that requires a DSP retimer chip for signal amplification\. Co\-packaged optics moves the optical engine — the photodetectors and modulators — into the same package as the ASIC\, shortening that electrical path to roughly 5 millimeters \(0\.2 inches\)\. As a result\, the retimer stage is eliminated\, reducing power consumption from about 30 watts per 1\.6 terabit\-per\-second port \(pluggable\) to about 9 watts per port—a reduction of roughly 70\%—while enabling bandwidth densities that copper\-based pluggables cannot physically achieve at 3\.2 terabits per second and beyond\. The tradeoff is replaceability\: a pluggable transceiver can be swapped in the field in minutes\; a co\-packaged optical engine is bonded to the chip and cannot be individually field\-replaced\.

\#\#\# Why does the OCP Summit demonstration specifically matter — hasn\'t CPO been demonstrated in labs for years\?

Component\-level demonstrations prove that the physics work\. A system\-level demonstration—a live compute rack with a real production\-style ASIC\, UCIe open\-standard die\-to\-die interfaces\, a multi\-vendor fiber plant\, and OCP\-standard rack infrastructure transmitting real telemetry—proves the full deployment stack works together\. Hyperscale data center operators do not begin qualification processes based on chip\-level results\; they begin qualification when a technology has been demonstrated in the form factor\, with the supply chain\, and to the standards their facilities already use\. The OCP Summit demonstration\, built on UCIe\, ORV3\, CW\-WDM MSA\, and ELSFP open standards\, checked all of those boxes for the first time at OCP 2026\.

\#\#\# What are the biggest remaining obstacles before co\-packaged optics reaches production AI data centers\?

Three barriers stand out\. First\, manufacturing yield\: because the optical engine is bonded to the ASIC die\, a defect in either component during assembly typically renders the entire package unusable\, increasing effective per\-unit cost at production volume\. Second\, fiber infrastructure\: AI\-scale CPO deployments require routing many dozens of fiber ribbons per rack alongside liquid cooling\, a mechanical challenge that fiber\-management partners in the Wiwynn\/Ayar Labs\/GUC ecosystem are actively addressing but have not yet validated at full production density\. Third\, standards maturity\: UCIe\, CW\-WDM MSA\, and ELSFP are new enough that cross\-vendor interoperability testing infrastructure is still being built\. The OCP Summit\'s dedicated Short Reach Optical Interconnect technical track is directly advancing the standards work\.

\#\#\# What is TeraPHY\, and why does it use an external laser instead of a built\-in one\?

TeraPHY is Ayar Labs\' silicon photonics optical I\/O chiplet\. It delivers 4 terabits per second of total bidirectional bandwidth from a single chiplet\, across 8 ports each carrying 256 Gbps\, using CW\-WDM \(Continuous Wave Wavelength Division Multiplexing\) with 8 wavelengths in the O\-band\. The reason for the external laser — delivered by Ayar Labs\' SuperNova module in the ELSFP form factor — is thermal\: lasers generate significant heat\, and photonic modulators are highly temperature\-sensitive\. Placing the laser inside the ASIC package alongside a high\-power AI accelerator would create a thermal management challenge that could degrade modulator performance\. The external laser architecture separates heat\-generating and heat\-sensitive components\, enabling better thermal stability for the optical path and allowing the SuperNova module to be independently cooled — in Wiwynn\'s system\, with dedicated liquid cooling\.

records.summary: This Fiber-Mart.com vendor guide describes Near-Packaged Optics (NPO) as an intermediate architecture between front-panel pluggable modules and Co-Packaged Optics (CPO). In NPO, an independent, socketable optical engine sits on the motherboard near the ASIC/GPU package and is linked by short centimeter-level copper traces (the article cites ≤150 mm per OIF), converting electrical signals to optical for transmission over a fiber array. The stated goals are reduced high-frequency loss and crosstalk, possible DSP elimination via linear drive, lower power per bit, and freed front-panel space. The article tabulates approximate power figures (NPO ~8–10 pJ/bit, CPO ~5–6 pJ/bit, ~10 ns NPO link latency) and lists vendor examples including Coherent's 1.6T VCSEL engine, Broadcom's 3.2T VCSEL engine at 128 Gbps per channel, Lightmatter's Passage L20, and Corning's GlassBridge passive coupling components. These are vendor/editorial descriptions, not independently verified measurements.
records.why_it_matters: NPO offers a maintainable path to short-reach, low-power chip-to-optics links by keeping the optical engine as a separately replaceable socketed package rather than sharing the ASIC substrate, trading some bandwidth density for field serviceability.

records.body_text:
Near-Packaged Optics NPO: A Comprehensive Guide
The demand for bandwidth in AI computing clusters is surging, driving the large-scale deployment of 800G, 1.6T, and even higher-speed interconnects. In traditional setups, pluggable optical modules are positioned on the front panels of switches or servers; this requires high-speed electrical signals—output by ASICs or GPUs—to travel across long copper traces on the PCB to reach the optical modules.
These long copper traces create three primary bottlenecks: significant high-speed signal attenuation, crosstalk, and degraded signal integrity. To compensate for these losses, the link must incorporate a Digital Signal Processor (DSP), which keeps power consumption high. Furthermore, the limited physical space on the front panel constrains port density and hinders effective airflow for cooling. While LPO (Linear-Drive Pluggable Optics) simplifies the internal DSP, it fails to eliminate the signal loss inherent in the long electrical path from the chip to the front panel. Against this backdrop, NPO (Near-Package Optics) has emerged as an intermediate solution that balances performance, maintainability, and implementation feasibility. By relocating the optoelectronic conversion unit closer to the chip package, NPO effectively resolves the high-speed interconnect bottlenecks caused by long copper traces on the front panel.
What exactly is an NPO?
Definition
NPO stands for "Near-Packaged Optics." In an NPO configuration, the optical engine is placed on the motherboard in the vicinity of the ASIC/GPU chip package. The optical engine remains a separate, independent package—distinct from the chip’s own package substrate—and is connected to the chip via short-reach, high-speed electrical interconnects. In this setup, optical fibers emerge from the optical engine rather than from the device's front panel.
Working principle
Concept: Minimize the transmission distance of high-speed electrical signals.
High-speed electrical signals output by switching or computing chips travel only a few centimeters—via short PCB traces—to an adjacent NPO (Near-Packaged Optics) light engine. Within the light engine, electrical-to-optical and optical-to-electrical conversions take place; the signals are then transmitted externally via an optical fiber array. This significantly reduces losses in the short electrical link, potentially eliminating the need for a DSP (Digital Signal Processor) in certain scenarios by utilizing linear drive instead, thereby lowering interconnect power consumption. The light engine is designed as an independent, detachable unit, allowing for individual replacement in the event of a failure without requiring the replacement of the entire motherboard or the main chip.
The problem to be solved
● Significantly shorten the copper trace length between the chip and the optoelectronic conversion unit, reducing high-frequency signal loss and crosstalk, while improving signal integrity;
● Reduce or eliminate the need for a DSP, thereby lowering power consumption per bit transmitted;
● Free up space on the device's front panel, increasing the port bandwidth density of the entire system;
● Provide an engineering compromise between the high integration complexity of CPO (Co-Packaged Optics) and the high power consumption of traditional pluggable modules, balancing performance with operational and maintenance requirements.
What constitutes the system: Hardware overview
A complete NPO system mainly includes the following hardware components, with the signal flow as follows: ASIC/GPU chip → board-level high-speed electrical interconnect → NPO optical engine → fiber optic array → peer optical interconnect device.
● ASIC/GPU main chip : computing/switching core, outputting high-speed serial electrical signals;
● Onboard high-speed interconnect substrate/socket : connects the main chip and NPO optical engine, provides a short-distance high-speed electrical interface, and supports optical engine installation and removal;
● NPO optical engine (core unit) : integrates light emission, light reception, driving, and TIA components to complete electro-optical/photoelectric conversion;
● Fiber Array (FAU) : High-density fiber optic cabling, drawn from the optical engine, responsible for optical signal transmission;
● Supporting passive components : fiber optic connectors, alignment structures, heat dissipation components, and shielding structures;
● System motherboard PCB : contains chips, NPO optical engine, power supply and control circuitry.
Signal Path
The chip generates a high-speed electrical signal, which is sent to the NPO optical engine via a short-distance onboard power-on link; the optical engine modulates the electrical signal into an optical signal, which is then transmitted to the NPO engine at the other end via an optical fiber array; the receiving optical engine restores the optical signal into an electrical signal and sends it back to the receiving chip.
Product Type and Category Differentiation
NPO products can be classified according to light source solution, optical technology architecture, and bandwidth specifications.
Classified by light source/light technology
● CW continuous wave light source solution : external continuous laser, the optical engine is only responsible for modulation and reception; the light source is centrally deployed, which facilitates heat dissipation and wavelength management, and is suitable for high-density large-scale clusters;
● Integrated light source type optical engine : The laser is integrated inside the optical engine, resulting in higher overall integration, but the optical engine generates more heat and the thermal management becomes more difficult.
Classified by bandwidth specifications
Mainstream options are 800G, 1.6T, and 3.2T single-engine bandwidth, and specifications are divided into 100G/lane, 200G/lane, etc., based on channel rate.
Classification by installation method
● Plug-in NPO optical engine: can be individually disassembled and replaced on site, is maintenance-friendly, and is the current mainstream commercial form;
● Surface mount NPO light engine: directly mounted on the motherboard, with higher integration density, but increased maintenance difficulty.
Mainstream NPO-Related Vendors and Products
Corning: GlassBridge™ Glass-Based Optical Interconnect Components
Corning does not manufacture NPO optical engines directly; instead, it provides passive coupling components for NPO architectures that connect Photonic Integrated Circuits (PICs) to fiber arrays. Utilizing glass optical waveguides for passive alignment, these components offer low coupling loss and support high-density parallel channels. They simplify the micron-level optical assembly of optical engines and serve as an essential interconnect solution for NPO systems from various vendors.
Coherent: 1.6T VCSEL NPO Optical Engine
A socketable, pluggable optical engine based on VCSEL technology with an integrated laser source. It supports linear, DSP-free links. Designed for ease of deployment—eliminating the need for external light-source cabinets—it is targeted at AI supernodes and short-reach intra-rack interconnects, with a clear upgrade path to higher-bandwidth optical engine platforms.
Broadcom: 3.2T VCSEL NPO Optical Engine
Featuring a VCSEL-based architecture, this ultra-low-power, socketable optical engine can be arranged in arrays around a switching ASIC. With a per-channel data rate of 128 Gbps, it leverages the native NPO electrical interfaces of Broadcom’s Tomahawk switching chips. It is intended for next-generation AI leaf-spine switches and is currently a key solution under evaluation by major overseas cloud service providers.
Lightmatter: Passage L20 Optical Engine
A silicon photonics-based solution compatible with both NPO and CPO architectures, utilizing an external continuous-wave (CW) light source. By relocating the heat source externally, it reduces thermal stress around the chip. It supports bandwidths ranging from 800G to 6.4T and features a detachable socket, making it well-suited for high-speed interconnects within AI GPU supernodes.
Horizontal Comparison: Pluggable / LPO / NPO / CPO
Comparison Dimensions
Traditional Pluggable Optical Modules
LPO Linear Pluggable Module
NPO Near-packaged Optics
CPO Co-packaged Optics
---|---|---|---|---
Light Engine Installation Location
Switch front panel
Switch front panel
Motherboard, proximity switch chip
Shared substrate packaging with switching chip
Electrical Signal Trace Length
15–30cm
15–30cm
Centimeter level, ≤150mm (OIF)
millimeter level
Does It Have A Dedicated DSP?
yes
no
No (Linear direct drive or DSP integrated into the chip)
no
Power Consumption Level
High (800g, approximately 150kW/piece)
medium to low
Low (approximately 8–10 pJ/bit)
Minimum (approximately 5–6 pJ/bit)
Link Latency
On the order of approximately 100 ns
Lower than traditional pluggable
On the order of approximately 10 ns
nanosecond level
Maintenance Method
Front panel can be replaced directly
Front panel can be replaced directly
Socket plug-in replacement, single slot fault isolation

Commercialization Status
Mature technology, largest existing stock
Starting with bulk shipments
Large-scale commercial use starting in 2026
Mass production ramp-up, yield and standards continuously improved
In short: Traditional pluggable and LPO are panel-side solutions ; NPO is a board-level near-chip compromise solution ; CPO is a chip-substrate level deep integration solution . The greatest value of NPO is that it can achieve the low power consumption and high density benefits of short power links without incurring the extremely high packaging and yield costs of CPO, while retaining the maintainability of the optical engine.
NPO One-Step Solution: Select Scenario, Assemble Architecture, Run Links
Typical application scenarios
● AI Intelligent Computing Super Node Cluster (Core) : GPU pooling and high-bandwidth interconnection within the switch reduce overall power consumption and increase computing power density.
● High-density data center switches : The optical engine is moved next to the ASIC, freeing up front panel space to support high-density interconnects in a leaf-ridge architecture.
● In-rack short-distance interconnect : Point-to-point high-speed interconnect between servers in the same rack, reducing DSP power consumption.
● High-performance computing (HPC) clusters : reduce interconnection latency between nodes.
Deployment Architecture
● Point-to-point paired deployment : NPOs must be used in pairs – transmitting optical engine + fiber array + receiving optical engine, with one end converting electrical to optical and the other end converting optical to electrical, for direct connection between GPU-GPU and ASIC-ASIC devices.
● Parallel multi-engine array : Multiple NPO optical engines are arranged around the switching/computing chip, enabling high-speed external transmission through multiple ports in parallel, supporting the high bandwidth of the entire switch.
● Light source selection : centralized light source (external CW laser, good heat dissipation, suitable for large-scale) or built-in light source (simple deployment, suitable for small and medium-sized scale).
Usage process
Step 1: Prepare a complete set of link units. An NPO link consists of a pair of transmit/receive optical engines, a fiber optic array (FAU), and a light source. First, select and prepare the necessary components as needed.
Step 2: Complete the assembly by inserting the light engine into the dedicated socket on the motherboard. The engine is an independent, pluggable unit that does not share a package with the main chip and can be replaced separately later.
Step 3: Establishing Fiber Optic Connections: The fiber optic array is led out from the optical engine, and the cabling is completed inside the chassis and connected to the NPO optical engine at the other end. The two ends are paired for transmitting and receiving.
Step 4: Power-on Link Establishment: The high-speed interface (SerDes) of the chip directly drives the optical engine. In most scenarios, linear drive is used, eliminating the need for a DSP. High-speed interconnection is established upon power-on, replacing the front panel optical module.
Precautions
● Significant architectural changes: The motherboard and structural components need to be redeveloped, resulting in a long verification cycle.
● Stringent thermal management: Optical devices are sensitive to heat and require thermal isolation to prevent wavelength drift.
● Increased maintenance difficulty: The fiber optic cable is inside the chassis, making troubleshooting and replacement more complex than with panel modules.
● Process and Standards: Micron-level coupling precision affects mass production yield, and cross-vendor interface standards need to be unified.
● Complex troubleshooting and debugging: The optoelectronic system requires joint debugging and testing, and there are many steps involved in fault location.
Conclusion
Near-Package Optics (NPO) achieves an engineering balance among power consumption, bandwidth density, and maintainability by positioning the optical engine close to the chip package, thereby shortening the copper traces used for high-speed electrical signals. Far from being a mere transitional solution, NPO is a practical, viable technology roadmap designed for AI super-node interconnects. Situated between traditional pluggable optical modules and Co-Packaged Optics (CPO), it avoids the high manufacturing risks associated with CPO while resolving the bottlenecks caused by high-speed traces on the front panel. Consequently, NPO stands as a core optical interconnect choice for high-density computing networks in the coming years.
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
What is the core difference between NPO and CPO?
CPO optical devices and ASICs are on the same package substrate; NPO optical engines are independent and placed on the motherboard next to the chip, with a removable socket, and the optoelectronics do not share the same substrate.
Does NPO necessarily not need DSP?
Not absolutely. In short-link scenarios, the DSP can be removed and a linear drive LPO architecture can be adopted; in some longer on-board link scenarios, a lightweight DSP is still retained.
Can NPO only be used for AI switches?
It is mainly used for interconnection between intelligent computing switches and super node servers. It can also be used for high-density data center switches. In ordinary cloud data center traditional rack scenarios, pluggable modules are preferred.
The NPO light engine is broken. Do I need to replace the entire motherboard?
No. The standard NPO uses a socket-type structure, with the light engine as an independent unit that can be individually plugged in and replaced. The motherboard and main chip are retained.
Where does the NPO fiber optic cable originate?
The optical fiber is led out from the NPO optical engine on the motherboard inside the chassis, and no longer goes through the optical port on the front panel of the device. Dedicated optical fiber cabling management is required inside the chassis.

original_evidence.body_text:
\#\# Near\-Packaged Optics NPO\: A Comprehensive Guide

The demand for bandwidth in AI computing clusters is surging\, driving the large\-scale deployment of 800G\, 1\.6T\, and even higher\-speed interconnects\. In traditional setups\, pluggable optical modules are positioned on the front panels of switches or servers\; this requires high\-speed electrical signals—output by ASICs or GPUs—to travel across long copper traces on the PCB to reach the optical modules\.

These long copper traces create three primary bottlenecks\: significant high\-speed signal attenuation\, crosstalk\, and degraded signal integrity\. To compensate for these losses\, the link must incorporate a Digital Signal Processor \(DSP\)\, which keeps power consumption high\. Furthermore\, the limited physical space on the front panel constrains port density and hinders effective airflow for cooling\. While LPO \(Linear\-Drive Pluggable Optics\) simplifies the internal DSP\, it fails to eliminate the signal loss inherent in the long electrical path from the chip to the front panel\. Against this backdrop\, NPO \(Near\-Package Optics\) has emerged as an intermediate solution that balances performance\, maintainability\, and implementation feasibility\. By relocating the optoelectronic conversion unit closer to the chip package\, NPO effectively resolves the high\-speed interconnect bottlenecks caused by long copper traces on the front panel\.

\#\# What exactly is an NPO\?

\#\# Definition

NPO stands for \"Near\-Packaged Optics\.\" In an NPO configuration\, the optical engine is placed on the motherboard in the vicinity of the ASIC\/GPU chip package\. The optical engine remains a separate\, independent package—distinct from the chip’s own package substrate—and is connected to the chip via short\-reach\, high\-speed electrical interconnects\. In this setup\, optical fibers emerge from the optical engine rather than from the device\'s front panel\.

\#\# Working principle

Concept\: Minimize the transmission distance of high\-speed electrical signals\.

High\-speed electrical signals output by switching or computing chips travel only a few centimeters—via short PCB traces—to an adjacent NPO \(Near\-Packaged Optics\) light engine\. Within the light engine\, electrical\-to\-optical and optical\-to\-electrical conversions take place\; the signals are then transmitted externally via an optical fiber array\. This significantly reduces losses in the short electrical link\, potentially eliminating the need for a DSP \(Digital Signal Processor\) in certain scenarios by utilizing linear drive instead\, thereby lowering interconnect power consumption\. The light engine is designed as an independent\, detachable unit\, allowing for individual replacement in the event of a failure without requiring the replacement of the entire motherboard or the main chip\.

\#\# The problem to be solved

● Significantly shorten the copper trace length between the chip and the optoelectronic conversion unit\, reducing high\-frequency signal loss and crosstalk\, while improving signal integrity\;

● Reduce or eliminate the need for a DSP\, thereby lowering power consumption per bit transmitted\;

● Free up space on the device\'s front panel\, increasing the port bandwidth density of the entire system\;

● Provide an engineering compromise between the high integration complexity of CPO \(Co\-Packaged Optics\) and the high power consumption of traditional pluggable modules\, balancing performance with operational and maintenance requirements\.

\#\# What constitutes the system\: Hardware overview

A complete NPO system mainly includes the following hardware components\, with the signal flow as follows\: ASIC\/GPU chip → board\-level high\-speed electrical interconnect → NPO optical engine → fiber optic array → peer optical interconnect device\.

● ASIC\/GPU main chip \: computing\/switching core\, outputting high\-speed serial electrical signals\;

● Onboard high\-speed interconnect substrate\/socket \: connects the main chip and NPO optical engine\, provides a short\-distance high\-speed electrical interface\, and supports optical engine installation and removal\;

● NPO optical engine \(core unit\) \: integrates light emission\, light reception\, driving\, and TIA components to complete electro\-optical\/photoelectric conversion\;

● Fiber Array \(FAU\) \: High\-density fiber optic cabling\, drawn from the optical engine\, responsible for optical signal transmission\;

● Supporting passive components \: fiber optic connectors\, alignment structures\, heat dissipation components\, and shielding structures\;

● System motherboard PCB \: contains chips\, NPO optical engine\, power supply and control circuitry\.

\#\# Signal Path

The chip generates a high\-speed electrical signal\, which is sent to the NPO optical engine via a short\-distance onboard power\-on link\; the optical engine modulates the electrical signal into an optical signal\, which is then transmitted to the NPO engine at the other end via an optical fiber array\; the receiving optical engine restores the optical signal into an electrical signal and sends it back to the receiving chip\.

\#\# Product Type and Category Differentiation

NPO products can be classified according to light source solution\, optical technology architecture\, and bandwidth specifications\.

\#\# Classified by light source\/light technology

● CW continuous wave light source solution \: external continuous laser\, the optical engine is only responsible for modulation and reception\; the light source is centrally deployed\, which facilitates heat dissipation and wavelength management\, and is suitable for high\-density large\-scale clusters\;

● Integrated light source type optical engine \: The laser is integrated inside the optical engine\, resulting in higher overall integration\, but the optical engine generates more heat and the thermal management becomes more difficult\.

\#\# Classified by bandwidth specifications

Mainstream options are 800G\, 1\.6T\, and 3\.2T single\-engine bandwidth\, and specifications are divided into 100G\/lane\, 200G\/lane\, etc\.\, based on channel rate\.

\#\# Classification by installation method

● Plug\-in NPO optical engine\: can be individually disassembled and replaced on site\, is maintenance\-friendly\, and is the current mainstream commercial form\;

● Surface mount NPO light engine\: directly mounted on the motherboard\, with higher integration density\, but increased maintenance difficulty\.

\#\# Mainstream NPO\-Related Vendors and Products

\#\# Corning\: GlassBridge™ Glass\-Based Optical Interconnect Components

Corning does not manufacture NPO optical engines directly\; instead\, it provides passive coupling components for NPO architectures that connect Photonic Integrated Circuits \(PICs\) to fiber arrays\. Utilizing glass optical waveguides for passive alignment\, these components offer low coupling loss and support high\-density parallel channels\. They simplify the micron\-level optical assembly of optical engines and serve as an essential interconnect solution for NPO systems from various vendors\.

\#\# Coherent\: 1\.6T VCSEL NPO Optical Engine

A socketable\, pluggable optical engine based on VCSEL technology with an integrated laser source\. It supports linear\, DSP\-free links\. Designed for ease of deployment—eliminating the need for external light\-source cabinets—it is targeted at AI supernodes and short\-reach intra\-rack interconnects\, with a clear upgrade path to higher\-bandwidth optical engine platforms\.

\#\# Broadcom\: 3\.2T VCSEL NPO Optical Engine

Featuring a VCSEL\-based architecture\, this ultra\-low\-power\, socketable optical engine can be arranged in arrays around a switching ASIC\. With a per\-channel data rate of 128 Gbps\, it leverages the native NPO electrical interfaces of Broadcom’s Tomahawk switching chips\. It is intended for next\-generation AI leaf\-spine switches and is currently a key solution under evaluation by major overseas cloud service providers\.

\#\# Lightmatter\: Passage L20 Optical Engine

A silicon photonics\-based solution compatible with both NPO and CPO architectures\, utilizing an external continuous\-wave \(CW\) light source\. By relocating the heat source externally\, it reduces thermal stress around the chip\. It supports bandwidths ranging from 800G to 6\.4T and features a detachable socket\, making it well\-suited for high\-speed interconnects within AI GPU supernodes\.

\#\# Horizontal Comparison\: Pluggable \/ LPO \/ NPO \/ CPO

In short\: Traditional pluggable and LPO are panel\-side solutions \; NPO is a board\-level near\-chip compromise solution \; CPO is a chip\-substrate level deep integration solution \. The greatest value of NPO is that it can achieve the low power consumption and high density benefits of short power links without incurring the extremely high packaging and yield costs of CPO\, while retaining the maintainability of the optical engine\.

\#\# NPO One\-Step Solution\: Select Scenario\, Assemble Architecture\, Run Links

\#\# Typical application scenarios

● AI Intelligent Computing Super Node Cluster \(Core\) \: GPU pooling and high\-bandwidth interconnection within the switch reduce overall power consumption and increase computing power density\.

● High\-density data center switches \: The optical engine is moved next to the ASIC\, freeing up front panel space to support high\-density interconnects in a leaf\-ridge architecture\.

● In\-rack short\-distance interconnect \: Point\-to\-point high\-speed interconnect between servers in the same rack\, reducing DSP power consumption\.

● High\-performance computing \(HPC\) clusters \: reduce interconnection latency between nodes\.

\#\# Deployment Architecture

● Point\-to\-point paired deployment \: NPOs must be used in pairs – transmitting optical engine \+ fiber array \+ receiving optical engine\, with one end converting electrical to optical and the other end converting optical to electrical\, for direct connection between GPU\-GPU and ASIC\-ASIC devices\.

● Parallel multi\-engine array \: Multiple NPO optical engines are arranged around the switching\/computing chip\, enabling high\-speed external transmission through multiple ports in parallel\, supporting the high bandwidth of the entire switch\.

● Light source selection \: centralized light source \(external CW laser\, good heat dissipation\, suitable for large\-scale\) or built\-in light source \(simple deployment\, suitable for small and medium\-sized scale\)\.

\#\# Usage process

Step 1\: Prepare a complete set of link units\. An NPO link consists of a pair of transmit\/receive optical engines\, a fiber optic array \(FAU\)\, and a light source\. First\, select and prepare the necessary components as needed\.

Step 2\: Complete the assembly by inserting the light engine into the dedicated socket on the motherboard\. The engine is an independent\, pluggable unit that does not share a package with the main chip and can be replaced separately later\.

Step 3\: Establishing Fiber Optic Connections\: The fiber optic array is led out from the optical engine\, and the cabling is completed inside the chassis and connected to the NPO optical engine at the other end\. The two ends are paired for transmitting and receiving\.

Step 4\: Power\-on Link Establishment\: The high\-speed interface \(SerDes\) of the chip directly drives the optical engine\. In most scenarios\, linear drive is used\, eliminating the need for a DSP\. High\-speed interconnection is established upon power\-on\, replacing the front panel optical module\.

\#\# Precautions

● Significant architectural changes\: The motherboard and structural components need to be redeveloped\, resulting in a long verification cycle\.

● Stringent thermal management\: Optical devices are sensitive to heat and require thermal isolation to prevent wavelength drift\.

● Increased maintenance difficulty\: The fiber optic cable is inside the chassis\, making troubleshooting and replacement more complex than with panel modules\.

● Process and Standards\: Micron\-level coupling precision affects mass production yield\, and cross\-vendor interface standards need to be unified\.

● Complex troubleshooting and debugging\: The optoelectronic system requires joint debugging and testing\, and there are many steps involved in fault location\.

\#\# Conclusion

Near\-Package Optics \(NPO\) achieves an engineering balance among power consumption\, bandwidth density\, and maintainability by positioning the optical engine close to the chip package\, thereby shortening the copper traces used for high\-speed electrical signals\. Far from being a mere transitional solution\, NPO is a practical\, viable technology roadmap designed for AI super\-node interconnects\. Situated between traditional pluggable optical modules and Co\-Packaged Optics \(CPO\)\, it avoids the high manufacturing risks associated with CPO while resolving the bottlenecks caused by high\-speed traces on the front panel\. Consequently\, NPO stands as a core optical interconnect choice for high\-density computing networks in the coming years\.

\#\# Frequently Asked Questions \(FAQs\)

\#\# What is the core difference between NPO and CPO\?

CPO optical devices and ASICs are on the same package substrate\; NPO optical engines are independent and placed on the motherboard next to the chip\, with a removable socket\, and the optoelectronics do not share the same substrate\.

\#\# Does NPO necessarily not need DSP\?

Not absolutely\. In short\-link scenarios\, the DSP can be removed and a linear drive LPO architecture can be adopted\; in some longer on\-board link scenarios\, a lightweight DSP is still retained\.

\#\# Can NPO only be used for AI switches\?

It is mainly used for interconnection between intelligent computing switches and super node servers\. It can also be used for high\-density data center switches\. In ordinary cloud data center traditional rack scenarios\, pluggable modules are preferred\.

\#\# The NPO light engine is broken\. Do I need to replace the entire motherboard\?

No\. The standard NPO uses a socket\-type structure\, with the light engine as an independent unit that can be individually plugged in and replaced\. The motherboard and main chip are retained\.

\#\# Where does the NPO fiber optic cable originate\?

The optical fiber is led out from the NPO optical engine on the motherboard inside the chassis\, and no longer goes through the optical port on the front panel of the device\. Dedicated optical fiber cabling management is required inside the chassis\.

records.abstract: The system comprises a 2000W continuous wave (CW) fiber laser source integrated with a high-dexterity 6-axis collaborative arm. ... The 6-axis ... The deployment of the 6-axis collaborative welder in Antwerp has resulted in a 40% increase in production speed for copper busbar assemblies.
records.summary: This is a vendor-published engineering field report (PCL cutting and welding) describing a 2000W continuous-wave fiber laser integrated with a 6-axis collaborative robot arm at a maritime electrical facility in Antwerp, Belgium, for welding copper busbars and heat-exchange assemblies (C11000/C10100 grades). The report states the facility moved from manual TIG to automated welding to address copper's high thermal conductivity and reflectivity, using lead-through programming, a high-frequency beam wobble pattern, programmed power ramp-down, an Argon-Helium 70/30 shielding mix with a trailing gas lens, and floating toggle clamps to accommodate thermal expansion. Reported process parameters for 2mm copper sheet are a 1.5mm circular wobble at 180Hz, 12mm/s travel speed, and 85% duty cycle at 2000W. The report claims a 40% increase in production speed for copper busbar assemblies and near-elimination of rework, but these are the publisher's own field-report figures without independent verification or described measurement methodology. The laser is operated inside a Class 4 enclosure, so the 'collaborative' benefit is described as fast setup and teaching between cycles rather than side-by-side operation during welding.
records.why_it_matters: For engineers welding reflective, high-conductivity copper, the report's practical takeaway is that process stability depends on controlled beam oscillation, programmed power ramp-down, a slight push angle (5-10 degrees) to limit back-reflection into the fiber, and rigid-but-compliant fixturing, rather than on laser power alone.
