Engineering Review: 2000W 6-Axis Collaborative Welder – Antwerp, Belgium
Field Report: Deployment of 2000W 6-Axis Collaborative Welder for Copper Component Fabrication
1. Project Overview and Site Context
This report documents the technical deployment and process optimization of a 2000W 6-Axis Collaborative Welder at a specialized maritime electrical facility in Antwerp, Belgium. The facility focuses on the production of high-current busbars and heat exchange assemblies, where copper components welding has historically been a bottleneck due to the material’s high thermal conductivity and reflective properties. The objective was to transition from manual TIG processes to a fully Automated Welding workflow to improve throughput and reduce the high rate of thermal distortion common in manual copper fabrication.
2. Technical Specifications and System Integration
The system comprises a 2000W continuous wave (CW) fiber laser source integrated with a high-dexterity 6-axis collaborative arm. Unlike traditional industrial robots, this 6-axis collaborative welder allows for a “lead-through” programming approach, which is critical in the Antwerp workshop where batch sizes vary, and rapid re-tasking is required.
2.1. The Synergy of the 6-Axis Collaborative Welder and Automated Welding
The core advantage observed during this deployment is the synergy between the collaborative interface and the rigors of automated welding. In copper applications, the margin for error regarding the Tool Center Point (TCP) and travel speed is exceptionally narrow. A 6-axis system provides the necessary degrees of freedom to maintain a constant 90-degree torch angle (or a specific lead angle to manage back-reflection) across complex geometries. When we talk about automated welding in this context, we aren’t just discussing a “set and forget” machine; we are discussing a system that maintains a consistent energy density—critical for overcoming the latent heat of fusion in copper.
3. Challenges in Copper Components Welding
Copper (specifically C11000 and C10100 grades used on-site) presents a unique set of challenges for any 6-axis collaborative welder. With a thermal conductivity roughly ten times that of carbon steel, the “heat sink” effect is the primary enemy. At 2000W, the energy input must be concentrated and delivered with extreme precision.
3.1. Overcoming Reflectivity and Thermal Dissipation
Initial tests in the Antwerp facility showed that manual intervention struggled with the “start-stop” crater cracks caused by rapid cooling. By moving to automated welding, we implemented programmed ramp-down sequences for the laser power. The 6-axis arm allowed us to execute a “wobble” pattern—a high-frequency oscillation of the beam—which increases the effective width of the weld pool and helps in degassing the melt, significantly reducing porosity in the copper components welding process.
4. Process Optimization: The Antwerp Field Observations
4.1. Shielding Gas Dynamics
In the humid maritime environment of Antwerp, hydrogen embrittlement is a legitimate concern for copper welds. We transitioned from pure Argon to an Argon-Helium mix (70/30). While more expensive, the Helium component provides a hotter arc/plasma environment, assisting the 2000W laser in maintaining a stable keyhole. The 6-axis collaborative welder was programmed to maintain a specialized trailing gas lens, ensuring the copper remained shielded until it cooled below the oxidation threshold.
4.2. Jigging and Fixturing for Automated Welding
A lesson learned during the second week of deployment: automated welding is only as good as the fixturing. Copper expands significantly when heated. If the jigs are too rigid, the weld cracks during solidification; if too loose, the 6-axis path becomes misaligned. We developed “floating” toggle clamps that allow for lateral thermal expansion while maintaining vertical alignment. This is where the “collaborative” aspect of the welder shone—operators could safely adjust clamps in proximity to the arm without the need for extensive light-curtain resets.
5. Programming and Pathing Strategy
The 6-axis collaborative welder utilizes a software stack that allows for G-code interpolation. For the copper components welding, we utilized a “continuous path” strategy. Because copper dissipates heat so quickly, stopping the weld to reposition a 3-axis gantry would result in cold-lap at the join. The 6-axis range of motion allowed us to weld three sides of a busbar assembly in a single, uninterrupted movement, maintaining the thermal equilibrium of the workpiece.
5.1. Wobble Parameters and Frequency
We found the “sweet spot” for 2mm copper sheet to be a 1.5mm circular wobble at 180Hz, with a travel speed of 12mm/s. The 2000W power was utilized at an 85% duty cycle. This prevented the “burn-through” that occurs when the copper finally reaches its liquidus state and the reflectivity drops sharply.
6. Safety and Compliance in the Belgian Industrial Context
Operating a 2000W laser-based 6-axis collaborative welder in Antwerp requires strict adherence to CE standards and local Belgian safety regulations (revolving around the wellbeing of workers). Although the arm is “collaborative,” the laser radiation is not. We implemented a Class 4 enclosure with interlocked viewing windows. The “collaborative” benefit shifted from “working side-by-side during the weld” to “ultra-fast setup and teaching” between cycles.
7. Lessons Learned and Practical Recommendations
7.1. Thermal Management of the Laser Head
One unforeseen issue in the field was the back-reflection from the copper. Despite the 6-axis arm being able to tilt the head, high-angle reflections occasionally tripped the internal sensors of the 2000W laser source.
Lesson: Always program a 5-to-10 degree “push” angle when automated welding highly reflective copper to protect the optical fiber.
7.2. Surface Preparation is Non-Negotiable
In manual welding, an experienced welder can “burn through” slight oxidation. In automated welding, specifically with copper components welding, any surface oxide leads to immediate coupling inconsistencies. We integrated a pre-weld mechanical abrasion step into the workflow. The repeatability of the 6-axis collaborative welder means it expects the same material conditions every time; it cannot “feel” the puddle like a human can.
7.3. Power Stability
The power grid in the Antwerp industrial zone is generally stable, but we noticed fluctuations during peak hours (10:00 AM) that affected the 2000W output. We installed a dedicated voltage stabilizer to ensure the laser beam’s consistency. For copper, a 5% drop in power can be the difference between a full-penetration weld and a surface bead.
8. Conclusion and ROI Analysis
The deployment of the 6-axis collaborative welder in Antwerp has resulted in a 40% increase in production speed for copper busbar assemblies. The transition to automated welding has virtually eliminated the rework necessitated by the inconsistent thermal management of manual TIG.
Key to this success was recognizing that copper components welding requires more than just raw power; it requires the precise, multi-axis pathing and consistent speed that only a 6-axis system can provide. For future deployments, the focus should remain on perfecting the “wobble” geometries and ensuring that the collaborative interface is used to minimize downtime between different component runs. The technical synergy between the 2000W fiber source and the collaborative robotic arm represents the current “gold standard” for mid-tier copper fabrication in high-precision environments.

records.abstract: This paper provides a systematic review of research progress on lubricant additives ... focusing on two main categories: liquid and nanoparticle lubricant additives. Liquid lubricant additives are categorized into fatty alcohol ether-based, vegetable oil-based, and ionic liquid-based additives; nanoparticle-based additives include inorganic nanoparticles and organic–inorganic composite particles.
records.summary: This review article, published in Lubricants (MDPI, 2026), systematically surveys lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids used in coal-mine hydraulic support systems in China. It organizes additives into liquid types (fatty alcohol ether-based, vegetable oil-based, and ionic liquid-based) and nanoparticle types (inorganic nanoparticles and organic–inorganic composite particles), and analyzes molecular structure design strategies, lubrication mechanisms, and performance regulation pathways for each. The authors argue that additive development should move toward multifunctional integration and environmental friendliness to meet the demands of intelligent coal mining and green mine construction. They further propose that improved dilution-water quality and more mature cylinder anticorrosion technology would enable single-component or few-component hydraulic fluids, and call for deeper structure–performance understanding to support engineering application of high-performance, low-dose, degradable green additives. Only the abstract and page metadata were retrieved, so this summary reflects the review's stated scope rather than its detailed findings.
records.why_it_matters: For engineers specifying water-based hydraulic fluids for mine supports, the review frames additive selection as a trade-off across liquid and nanoparticle chemistries, and suggests that reducing additive count depends on upstream water quality and cylinder corrosion control rather than on additive design alone.

Abstract
Water-based hydraulic fluids serve as the power transmission medium for hydraulic support systems in coal mines, and the performance of their lubricant additives directly affects the stable operation of the supports. This paper provides a systematic review of research progress on lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids in China, focusing on two main categories: liquid and nanoparticle lubricant additives. Liquid lubricant additives are categorized into fatty alcohol ether-based, vegetable oil-based, and ionic liquid-based additives; nanoparticle-based additives include inorganic nanoparticles and organic–inorganic composite particles. This article analyzes the molecular structure design strategies, lubrication mechanisms, and performance regulation pathways of various additives. In response to the demands of intelligent coal mining and green mine construction, it is proposed that the development of lubricant additives for water-based hydraulic fluids should target multifunctional integration and environmental friendliness. Improvements in the quality of the dilution water and the maturity of cylinder anticorrosion technology will create favorable conditions for the development of single-component (or few-component) hydraulic fluids. In the future, research should deepen understanding of the structure–performance relationships of lubricant additives, so as to facilitate the engineering application of high-performance, low-dose, degradable green lubricant additives and provide technical support for intelligent coal mine construction and ecological protection in the Yellow River Basin.

AkzoNobel Powder Coatings Earns Double Recognition at Maxion Wheels Supplier Awards
The Green Wheel 2025 Award and the Supplier of the Year 2025 Americas honors sustainability ambitions, collaborative strength and consistent performance gains derived from AkzoNobel and its teams.
Share
Read Next
AkzoNobel Powder Coatings (Reading, Pennsylvania) has earned two supplier awards from Maxion Wheels (Northville, Michigan), recognizing its role in sustainable innovation and its collaboration with the wheel manufacturer. The company;s team in the Czech Republic received the Green Wheel 2025 Award, while its Brazil team was named Supplier of the Year 2025 Americas.
“AkzoNobel has been a reliable partner and an important contributor to our success over many years,” says Pia Schuetz, VP of global purchasing at Maxion Wheels. “Their contribution goes well beyond supplying high-quality coatings. The teams bring deep technical expertise, helping us optimize application processes, achieve consistently strong coating performance and develop practical solutions that improve efficiency and support our sustainability goals. Combined with responsive technical support and dependable day-to-day service, that makes this a true partnership, and one we value enormously.”
The Green Wheel 2025 Award recognizes suppliers that support Maxion Wheels’ sustainability ambitions. For AkzoNobel, the award reflects a long-term focus on reducing emissions, advancing responsible sourcing and developing coating solutions designed to help customers reduce their environmental impact.
The Supplier of the Year 2025 Americas award celebrates the collaboration between AkzoNobel’s team in Brazil and Maxion Wheels. The partnership combines high-performing coating technologies with local technical expertise and responsive support. AkzoNobel supplies a portfolio of powder and liquid primers, basecoats and clearcoats for aluminum wheels.

records.title: How thick should the gold plating on a pogo pin be? - Blog - Dongguan Xinteng
records.abstract: Humidity, skin oils and cleaning residues can affect exposed contacts. Gold helps maintain a conductive surface because it does not readily form an insulating oxide in air, but a thin gold layer may contain pores. The nickel beneath it and the quality of the plating process therefore matter alongside the stated gold thickness.
records.summary: This Dongguan Xinteng blog post explains that gold plating thickness on pogo pins is commonly specified in microinches (1 µin = 0.0254 µm), and that 1, 3, 5 and 10 µin correspond to roughly 0.0254, 0.0762, 0.127 and 0.254 µm. The author argues that thickness alone does not determine service life: gold type, nickel underplate, mating pad finish, contact force, sliding motion, humidity, skin oils and cleaning residues all matter, and thin gold layers may contain pores that expose the underplate. The article rejects universal thickness standards for consumer, industrial or medical products and states that 10 µin cannot be translated into a mating-cycle rating without testing. It recommends specifying whether the value is nominal or minimum, identifying the actual contact areas (tip, mating pad, plunger-to-barrel interface), and testing the complete contact pair for resistance before and after cycling. This is vendor guidance rather than peer-reviewed experimental data; no measured results are reported.
records.why_it_matters: Plating specifications should be written against the actual contact interface and validated by cycling the finished pin-pad pair, rather than by assigning a nominal gold thickness as a performance grade.

records.body_text:
Oct 19, 2026 View: 106 Leave a message
How thick should the gold plating on a pogo pin be?
Alice Smith
Alice is a senior R&D engineer at Dongguan Xinteng Electronics Co., Ltd. With over 8 years of experience in the field of Pogo Pin connectors, she specializes in the research of high - current and miniaturization scenarios. She has contributed to many of the company's patented products and more than 300 solutions.
Gold thickness is often written in microinches, shown as µin or µ". One microinch equals 0.0254 micrometers (µm), so the differences between 1 µin, 3 µin and 5 µin are extremely small. They still matter: a thin coating can wear through or develop pores sooner than a thicker one under the same conditions.
Thickness is only part of the specification. The type of gold deposit, nickel underplate, mating pad, contact force and movement during connection all affect service life. There is no reliable rule that assigns one gold thickness to all consumer products and another to all industrial or medical products.
What do 1, 3, 5 and 10 microinches mean?
Nominal gold thickness | Metric equivalent | How to assess it
---|---|---
1 µin | 0.0254 µm | A very thin finish. Consider it only after checking wear and corrosion requirements.
3 µin | 0.0762 µm | Still a thin finish. Its suitability depends on the mating design and expected use.
5 µin | 0.127 µm | Provides more gold than a 1 or 3 µin finish, but does not establish a cycle-life rating.
10 µin | 0.254 µm | May be considered when more coating thickness is needed at the contact area; testing remains necessary.
These figures describe thickness, not guaranteed performance grades. In particular, a 3 to 5 µin finish should not be described as a universal "industrial standard," and 10 µin cannot be translated into tens of thousands of mating cycles without test results for the specific connector.
Start with the way the contact is used
A pogo pin that touches a pad a few times during factory testing has a different duty from a charging contact used several times each day. Count both the expected connections and what happens during each one. A pin that lands squarely on a pad experiences different wear from one that slides across the pad as a device settles into a dock.
The environment changes the decision too. Humidity, skin oils and cleaning residues can affect exposed contacts. Gold helps maintain a conductive surface because it does not readily form an insulating oxide in air, but a thin gold layer may contain pores. The nickel beneath it and the quality of the plating process therefore matter alongside the stated gold thickness.
For a magnetic connector, attraction and alignment also need review. If the magnets pull the two halves together with sideways movement, the contacts may wipe across their pads on every connection. That motion can be useful for clearing minor surface contamination, but it also changes the wear pattern. The required plating should be chosen with the assembled connector in mind.
Specify the surface that actually makes contact
A drawing that says only "gold plated, 5 µin" leaves several questions unanswered. Is 5 µin a nominal value or the minimum permitted thickness? Is it required at the tip, on the mating pad or across the entire part? What nickel underplate is specified? Is the gold finish intended for repeated electrical contact?
These details affect both cost and inspection. Gold applied to areas that never make contact may add expense without improving performance. Conversely, a thickness measured on an accessible area of the part may not describe the coating at the point where the pin meets its pad. The internal plunger-to-barrel interface also deserves consideration because it can form part of the current path.
When a customer provides a drawing, we can review these contact areas together with the pin stroke, tip geometry and mating arrangement, then develop a pogo pin or magnetic connector solution for the intended application. Sample testing can help resolve the plating specification before it is applied to a production order.
Test the complete contact pair
The most useful comparison is between candidate finishes tested under the same conditions. Measure contact resistance at the intended working stroke, cycle the pin against the specified mating pad, then measure resistance again and inspect both surfaces. Where the product may encounter moisture or contaminants, add environmental testing that reflects its expected use.
A thicker gold deposit may be justified if the thinner candidate wears through or its resistance becomes unstable. If both candidates meet the requirement, the thinner finish may be a reasonable cost choice. The result belongs to that pin, pad and test setup; it should not be treated as a rating for every product with the same plating thickness.
FAQ
Is 1 µin of gold enough for a consumer product?
It may be enough for a particular low-use design, but the product category alone cannot answer the question. Check the mating frequency, contact motion, environment and test results before specifying such a thin finish.
Is 3 to 5 µin the standard for industrial or medical pogo pins?
No universal thickness applies to either category. The required finish follows the device's contact design, expected service life and applicable qualification requirements.
Will 10 µin of gold support tens of thousands of connections?
Thickness alone cannot guarantee that. Tip shape, spring force, alignment, mating pad finish and the type of gold deposit all affect wear. A cycle-life claim needs testing on the finished contact pair.
What should be included on a custom pogo pin drawing?
Identify the contact areas and state whether the specified gold thickness is nominal or minimum. Include the underplate, mating pad finish, working stroke, expected connection cycles and operating environment so the design can be sampled and checked against its intended use.

Alice is a senior R\&D engineer at Dongguan Xinteng Electronics Co\.\, Ltd\. With over 8 years of experience in the field of Pogo Pin connectors\, she specializes in the research of high \- current and miniaturization scenarios\. She has contributed to many of the company\'s patented products and more than 300 solutions\.

Gold thickness is often written in microinches\, shown as µin or µ\"\. One microinch equals 0\.0254 micrometers \(µm\)\, so the differences between 1 µin\, 3 µin and 5 µin are extremely small\. They still matter\: a thin coating can wear through or develop pores sooner than a thicker one under the same conditions\.

Thickness is only part of the specification\. The type of gold deposit\, nickel underplate\, mating pad\, contact force and movement during connection all affect service life\. There is no reliable rule that assigns one gold thickness to all consumer products and another to all industrial or medical products\.

\#\# What do 1\, 3\, 5 and 10 microinches mean\?

Nominal gold thickness \| Metric equivalent \| How to assess it 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
1 µin \| 0\.0254 µm \| A very thin finish\. Consider it only after checking wear and corrosion requirements\. 
3 µin \| 0\.0762 µm \| Still a thin finish\. Its suitability depends on the mating design and expected use\. 
5 µin \| 0\.127 µm \| Provides more gold than a 1 or 3 µin finish\, but does not establish a cycle\-life rating\. 
10 µin \| 0\.254 µm \| May be considered when more coating thickness is needed at the contact area\; testing remains necessary\. 

These figures describe thickness\, not guaranteed performance grades\. In particular\, a 3 to 5 µin finish should not be described as a universal \"industrial standard\,\" and 10 µin cannot be translated into tens of thousands of mating cycles without test results for the specific connector\.

\#\# Start with the way the contact is used

A pogo pin that touches a pad a few times during factory testing has a different duty from a charging contact used several times each day\. Count both the expected connections and what happens during each one\. A pin that lands squarely on a pad experiences different wear from one that slides across the pad as a device settles into a dock\.

The environment changes the decision too\. Humidity\, skin oils and cleaning residues can affect exposed contacts\. Gold helps maintain a conductive surface because it does not readily form an insulating oxide in air\, but a thin gold layer may contain pores\. The nickel beneath it and the quality of the plating process therefore matter alongside the stated gold thickness\.

For a magnetic connector\, attraction and alignment also need review\. If the magnets pull the two halves together with sideways movement\, the contacts may wipe across their pads on every connection\. That motion can be useful for clearing minor surface contamination\, but it also changes the wear pattern\. The required plating should be chosen with the assembled connector in mind\.

\#\# Specify the surface that actually makes contact

A drawing that says only \"gold plated\, 5 µin\" leaves several questions unanswered\. Is 5 µin a nominal value or the minimum permitted thickness\? Is it required at the tip\, on the mating pad or across the entire part\? What nickel underplate is specified\? Is the gold finish intended for repeated electrical contact\?

These details affect both cost and inspection\. Gold applied to areas that never make contact may add expense without improving performance\. Conversely\, a thickness measured on an accessible area of the part may not describe the coating at the point where the pin meets its pad\. The internal plunger\-to\-barrel interface also deserves consideration because it can form part of the current path\.

When a customer provides a drawing\, we can review these contact areas together with the pin stroke\, tip geometry and mating arrangement\, then develop a pogo pin or magnetic connector solution for the intended application\. Sample testing can help resolve the plating specification before it is applied to a production order\.

\#\# Test the complete contact pair

The most useful comparison is between candidate finishes tested under the same conditions\. Measure contact resistance at the intended working stroke\, cycle the pin against the specified mating pad\, then measure resistance again and inspect both surfaces\. Where the product may encounter moisture or contaminants\, add environmental testing that reflects its expected use\.

A thicker gold deposit may be justified if the thinner candidate wears through or its resistance becomes unstable\. If both candidates meet the requirement\, the thinner finish may be a reasonable cost choice\. The result belongs to that pin\, pad and test setup\; it should not be treated as a rating for every product with the same plating thickness\.

\#\# FAQ

\#\#\# Is 1 µin of gold enough for a consumer product\?

It may be enough for a particular low\-use design\, but the product category alone cannot answer the question\. Check the mating frequency\, contact motion\, environment and test results before specifying such a thin finish\.

\#\#\# Is 3 to 5 µin the standard for industrial or medical pogo pins\?

No universal thickness applies to either category\. The required finish follows the device\'s contact design\, expected service life and applicable qualification requirements\.

\#\#\# Will 10 µin of gold support tens of thousands of connections\?

Thickness alone cannot guarantee that\. Tip shape\, spring force\, alignment\, mating pad finish and the type of gold deposit all affect wear\. A cycle\-life claim needs testing on the finished contact pair\.

\#\#\# What should be included on a custom pogo pin drawing\?

Identify the contact areas and state whether the specified gold thickness is nominal or minimum\. Include the underplate\, mating pad finish\, working stroke\, expected connection cycles and operating environment so the design can be sampled and checked against its intended use\.

NovaEuris provides industrial equipment, instruments, food processing systems and green energy solutions for manufacturers and engineering companies across European markets.
Contact Info
- Gustav Mahlerplein 29, 1082 MA Amsterdam, Netherlands
- support@novaeuris.com
News
2026 Energy Storage PACK Busbar Selection Guide: Conductive Copper Components for Battery Packs
Energy storage systems are moving from pilot projects to gigawatt-scale deployment across Europe, and the battery pack remains the cost and safety center of gravity. Inside every PACK, copper busbars and conductive connecting components carry hundreds of amps between cells, modules and terminals. A busbar that is undersized, poorly plated or sourced from an unqualified supplier can drive contact resistance up, create hot spots and, in the worst case, contribute to thermal runaway. This guide sets out what procurement and engineering teams should evaluate in 2026 when selecting copper busbars for energy storage PACKs, from material specification through supplier vetting, compliance, logistics and in-service maintenance.
The market context matters. European buyers are balancing cost pressure from Chinese and Southeast Asian suppliers against the incoming requirements of the EU Batteries Regulation, which tightens documentation, carbon footprint disclosure and due diligence across the battery value chain. At the same time, PACK designs are converging on higher current densities, more compact module layouts and liquid-cooled architectures, all of which raise the demands on busbar geometry, insulation and joint quality. Buyers who treat busbars as a commodity item rather than an engineered component tend to discover the cost of that assumption during commissioning or, worse, in the field.
Use the table below as a starting checklist when building a technical specification or evaluating quotations from competing suppliers.
Selection Area | What to Specify | Procurement and Risk Notes
---|---|---
Copper material | T2 or TU1 oxygen-free copper; conductivity typically ≥ 99.9% IACS; hardness and temper stated on the drawing | Request mill certificates and conductivity test reports per lot; verify that the grade on the certificate matches the purchase order
Surface treatment | Nickel plating (typical 3–8 µm), tin plating, or bare copper with antioxidant treatment depending on joint design and environment | Plating thickness and adhesion should be measurable; thin or porous plating is a common cause of rising contact resistance in humid or coastal installations
Cross-section and current rating | Current-carrying capacity with defined temperature rise limit (for example ≤ 65 K above ambient), plus short-circuit withstand | Do not accept supplier ratings without test conditions; confirm the calculation basis and request thermal test data
Insulation and spacing | Heat-shrink or powder coating, dielectric strength, creepage and clearance distances for the system voltage class | Insulation must be compatible with the cooling method (air or liquid) and with the PACK's expected operating temperature range
Joint and connection design | Bolt size, torque values, contact surface flatness, use of Belleville washers, anti-seize or conductive paste | Define torque in the assembly work instruction and audit it at the supplier; loose joints are a leading field failure mode
Dimensional tolerances | Hole position, bend radius, flatness and twist limits tied to the module stack-up | Request first-article inspection reports and CMM data; tolerance stack-up errors cause assembly line stoppages
Compliance and documentation | RoHS and REACH declarations, material traceability, UL 1973 or IEC 62619 alignment at system level, IEC 61439 where applicable to assemblies | Keep declarations on file per shipment; EU Batteries Regulation due diligence expectations are increasing, so supplier documentation quality is a selection criterion
Supplier capability | In-house stamping, bending, plating and inspection; ISO 9001 and preferably IATF 16949 where automotive-grade discipline is required | Audit plating lines in person or by video; outsourced plating is a frequent weak point in the supply chain
Logistics and packaging | Anti-oxidation wrapping, moisture barrier bags, shock-resistant cartons, pallet configuration | Copper is a theft target and plating is sensitive to humidity; agree Incoterms, insurance and packaging standards in the contract
Maintenance and service life | Inspection intervals for torque and thermal imaging, spare parts availability, replacement part traceability | Build busbar inspection into the PACK maintenance schedule; require the supplier to hold spare capacity or stock for the contract term
On material selection, T2 and TU1 copper grades are the common baseline for energy storage busbars, with conductivity verified against the ≥ 99.9% IACS expectation. Buyers should insist on lot-level mill certificates and, for high-current joints, independent conductivity or resistance testing. Plating choice depends on the joint and environment: nickel plating offers good wear and corrosion resistance for bolted joints, tin plating supports solderability and lower contact resistance in some designs, and bare copper with antioxidant treatment can be acceptable in sealed, dry enclosures. The specification should state plating thickness with a tolerance band and a measurable adhesion test, because plating quality varies widely between suppliers and is difficult to assess from a datasheet alone.
Sizing is where many procurement errors originate. Suppliers frequently quote a current rating without stating the allowable temperature rise, ambient conditions, mounting orientation or cooling assumptions. A defensible specification defines the temperature rise limit, the short-circuit withstand current and duration, and the test method used to verify both. For liquid-cooled PACKs, the busbar and insulation must be qualified for direct or indirect contact with the coolant and for the operating temperature window. For high-voltage systems, creepage and clearance distances should be calculated for the system voltage class and confirmed against the relevant standards rather than copied from a previous project.
Joint design deserves the same rigor as the busbar itself. Bolt size, torque, contact surface flatness and the use of Belleville washers or conductive paste all influence long-term contact resistance. Procurement teams should require the supplier to document torque values and to demonstrate that assembly instructions are controlled and audited. Where possible, request joint resistance and thermal cycling test data, since a busbar that passes a static resistance test can still degrade under repeated thermal cycling in the field.
Supplier selection in 2026 should combine commercial and technical due diligence. Look for manufacturers with in-house stamping, bending and plating, because outsourced plating is one of the most common sources of quality escapes. ISO 9001 is the minimum; IATF 16949 certification signals automotive-grade process discipline that transfers well to energy storage. Ask for first-article inspection reports, CMM dimensional data, plating thickness measurements and references from comparable PACK projects. Where possible, audit the plating line and the final inspection station in person or by live video. Established connector and busbar specialists, as well as tier-one automotive suppliers expanding into storage, are worth shortlisting, but verify capability rather than relying on brand recognition alone.
Compliance documentation is now a selection criterion, not an afterthought. RoHS and REACH declarations should accompany every shipment, and material traceability should allow a finished busbar to be linked back to a copper mill lot. At system level, UL 1973 and IEC 62619 alignment is expected by many European customers, and IEC 61439 applies where busbars form part of an assembly. The EU Batteries Regulation is raising expectations for carbon footprint disclosure and supply chain due diligence, so suppliers who can provide consistent environmental and traceability documentation will be easier to onboard and less likely to create compliance gaps later.
Logistics and packaging protect both quality and margin. Copper is a theft target in transit, and plated surfaces are sensitive to humidity, so contracts should specify moisture-barrier packaging, anti-oxidation wrapping and shock-resistant cartons, along with Incoterms, insurance and inspection rights. For European buyers sourcing from Asia, build in incoming inspection for plating thickness, dimensions and conductivity on the first lots, and consider a pre-shipment inspection for high-value orders.
Finally, plan for maintenance. Busbar joints should be included in the PACK inspection schedule, with periodic torque checks and thermal imaging to detect rising resistance before it becomes a failure. Agree spare parts availability and replacement lead times in the supply contract, and keep replacement busbars traceable to the original specification. Teams that treat busbars as engineered, documented and maintained components rather than commodity hardware will see fewer commissioning delays, lower field failure rates and a cleaner compliance position as European requirements tighten through 2026 and beyond.

idw – Informationsdienst Wissenschaft
Nachrichten, Termine, Experten
Share on:
10/14/2026 13:30
Precision instead of immersion electroplating: New platform for selective surface modification
Dr. Simone Kondruweit Presse- und Öffentlichkeitsarbeit
Fraunhofer-Institut für Schicht- und Oberflächentechnik IST
With a comprehensive expansion of its research infrastructure, the Fraunhofer Institute for Surface Engineering and Thin Films IST is establishing a new platform for localized electrochemical surface processing. The combination of proven electroplating processes with innovative technologies such as Electrochemical Jet Processing (EJP) and intelligent robotics enables precise, resource-efficient processing of complex workpieces. In doing so, the institute is creating new opportunities for industry in fields such as electronics, energy technology, medical engineering, and aerospace.
Electroplated coatings play a central role in numerous future-oriented industries. They impart specific functional properties to components, improve their durability and performance, and extend the service life of products, thereby contributing to resource conservation and the reduction of CO₂ emissions over the entire life cycle. In this context, Fraunhofer IST is specifically advancing electrochemical manufacturing technologies and combining established electroplating processes with selective approaches to surface treatment.
Expansion for the next generation of electrochemical manufacturing
At the heart of the facility expansion is the new Electrochemical Jet Processing (EJP) platform, which combines various selective electrochemical processes for the localized processing and functionalization of surfaces. These include Electrochemical Jet Machining (EJM) for non-contact, micrometer-precise material machining, as well as Electrochemical Jet Deposition (EJD) for the localized deposition of functional layers. This allows surfaces to be selectively structured, smoothed, repaired, or coated.
In contrast to conventional electroplating processes, in which entire components are treated in process baths, the EJP platform uses a movable electrochemical jet that acts only where material is actually to be processed, or layers are to be deposited. This makes it possible, in the future, to flexibly process even complex or large-scale components. Restrictions imposed by the dimensions of process baths or potential masking and demasking steps are eliminated. At the same time, the use of chemicals, energy, and raw materials – as well as the generation of waste – is minimized.
Intelligent process control for complex component geometries
The platform is complemented by a modern robotics and automation infrastructure. In addition to high-precision industrial robots, autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) are used to flexibly support material and tool logistics and navigate their environment independently. This results in highly precise and reproducible processes that adapt to different component geometries and can be integrated into automated production lines.
“With our new system design, we combine selective electrochemical processes and robotics into a comprehensive system. Unlike with conventional systems, the process adapts to the component and its requirements – not the other way around,” explains Rowena Duckstein, a research scientist at Fraunhofer IST.
Diverse applications for high-tech industries
The new system technology is relevant wherever the highest precision, flexibility, and sustainability are required. For example, it enables the material-conserving production of microstructures with high deposition rates, as well as more targeted filling and thus better coating of, for instance, micro-holes. Localized deposition eliminates the need for stencils and masking.
A look to the future
In the future, the EJP platform is to be integrated even more closely with robotics, sensor technology, and data-driven control methods. The goal is an adaptive manufacturing system that continuously optimizes processes and reduces resource consumption and scrap. In this way, Fraunhofer IST is laying the foundation for adaptive manufacturing concepts that flexibly integrate local electrochemical processes into industrial production lines and open up new possibilities for micro-machining, repair processes, and functionalized surfaces.
“Our goal is to further develop a technology platform that not only meets current industrial requirements but also actively sets new standards – more precise, more sustainable, and more application-oriented than existing solutions,” Duckstein summarizes.

records.body_text:
Supercritical CO2 and kitchen-shelf lubricants could transform titanium machining
When carbon dioxide is squeezed past 74 bar and warmed above 31 degrees Celsius, it stops behaving like an ordinary gas or liquid and enters a strange middle state known as the supercritical phase. A team of French researchers at the Arts et Métiers Institute of Technology has now harnessed this exotic fluid to attack one of manufacturing’s most stubborn problems: the friction and heat that plague the machining of Ti6Al4V, the titanium alloy that holds together much of the aerospace industry. Their findings, published in Frontiers in Manufacturing Technology, suggest that cheap, sustainable additives dissolved in supercritical CO2 could rival industrial mineral oils, with ionic liquids delivering the most dramatic friction reductions of all.
The machining industry has long relied on flood coolants, minimum quantity lubrication, and cryogenic sprays such as liquid nitrogen to keep cutting tools alive and machined parts intact. These methods aim to tame the intense friction and heating that occur at the chip-tool and tool-part contact zones, where temperatures can soar high enough to soften the workpiece and destroy the tool edge. Supercritical CO2 has emerged as an intriguing alternative because it acts as a green solvent and, when delivered to the cutting zone, expands with a phase transformation that drops its temperature sharply, cooling both the tool and the part. Previous studies have shown that pairing supercritical CO2 with dissolved soybean oil roughly halved flank wear compared with emulsion flood cooling when milling compacted graphite iron, and that supercritical CO2 plus minimum quantity lubrication outperformed flood coolant in milling Ti6Al4V and turning AISI 1045 steel.
Yet supercritical CO2 alone often performs worse than flood cooling, which is why the lubricant carried within it matters so much. The research team, led by Koffi Samuel Koulekpa, set out to systematically test what happens when different lubricants are introduced into supercritical CO2 and delivered to a titanium-carbide contact under conditions mimicking real machining. They selected ionic liquids, vegetable oils, mineral oil, water, and polyethylene glycol, chosen for their solubility in supercritical CO2, their sustainable character, or their previous performances in machining-related friction analysis. The two ionic liquids tested, BMIM-PF6 and BMIM-BF4, are salts that stay liquid at room temperature and boast negligible volatility, high thermal stability, and non-flammability, making them fascinating candidates for machining applications.
Order Lab Supplies
To deliver these exotic mixtures, the researchers designed and built a dedicated machine that feeds CO2 from pressurized bottles, cools it to ensure a liquid phase before compression, then squeezes it to pressures up to 350 bar and heats it with four cartridges to reach the supercritical state in a mixing chamber. There, lubricants are injected at user-specified rates before the mixture sprays through a 0.25 mm round jet nozzle. For the experiments, the pressure was limited to 100 bar and the temperature set to 40 degrees Celsius, guaranteeing a supercritical state while minimizing CO2 consumption. The supercritical CO2 flowed at 0.185 kg/min, while lubricants were delivered at 1 mL/min and 4 mL/min, rates common in minimum quantity lubrication applications.
Shop Motor Oils
The friction tests themselves took place on a CNC lathe fitted with a Hedenqvist-type pin-on-cylinder tribometer, a setup chosen for easy and quick execution. Cylindrical carbide pins, instrumented with K-type thermocouples connected to a data acquisition system sampling at 2 kHz, pressed against a rotating Ti6Al4V bar with an initial diameter of 120 mm. The normal loads of 100 N, 250 N, and 400 N were selected based on a contact pressure of 1,300 MPa derived from finite element simulations, while sliding velocities of 20 m/min and 100 m/min covered the range of chip sliding velocities typical when machining difficult-to-cut alloys such as Ti6Al4V or Inconel 718. After each test, the workpiece surface was refreshed by a fresh machining pass to obtain a theoretical roughness of Ra 0.5 µm, and the pins were rotated by 25 degrees to expose a new contact surface.
The results revealed a striking pattern. At 20 m/min, adding lubricants to supercritical CO2 decreased friction, but the mixtures never outperformed the dry condition, with friction coefficients staying above the dry baseline for almost all loads. At 100 m/min, however, the story changed dramatically. The team observed a mean decrease of 0.1 in the apparent friction coefficient, and increasing the lubricant flow rate from 1 mL/min to 4 mL/min produced further reductions. The ionic liquids showed their lubricating prowess most clearly at 100 m/min with significant friction decreases at 4 mL/min and 400 N, demonstrating that the combined effect of lubrication by the additives and cooling from supercritical CO2 works best under the most demanding conditions.
The adhesive behavior of Ti6Al4V, notorious for sticking to counter-materials during friction, provided another revealing metric. After each test, the researchers examined the friction zone under an optical microscope and calculated the sticking area by assimilating it to an ellipse. Once again, the effects of the lubricants were clearly visible at 100 m/min. The ionic liquids, together with polyethylene glycol, led to the lowest sticking area values, with surface reductions of 54 percent and 55 percent for BF4 and PF6 respectively at the 1 mL/min rate. These values climbed to 74 percent at 4 mL/min, showing how strongly the delivery flow rate influences the protective action. The researchers attribute this to an adsorption layer that reduces direct contact between the two materials, and for the ionic liquids, to tribochemical reactions between the liquids and the tool-workpiece materials that form remarkably effective protective films.
Temperature measurements confirmed the cooling credentials of supercritical CO2. Pin temperatures dropped significantly compared with dry tests, with a maximum reduction of 80 degrees Celsius. Interestingly, no significant difference in cooling was provided by the presence of the lubricants compared with supercritical CO2 alone, suggesting that the additives’ contribution to heat removal was not activated under the tested speed conditions, possibly due to suboptimal delivery techniques or solubility issues that the team plans to investigate further.
Perhaps the most commercially significant finding concerns the cheap lubricants. Water, rapeseed oil, and sunflower oil performed similarly to the commonly used machining mineral oil when paired with supercritical CO2, and these biological alternatives are less expensive and less health-threatening than traditional emulsions. This could help develop future low-cost yet effective cooling and lubrication methods for the machining industry, a prospect with real sustainability appeal given that cryogenic minimum quantity lubrication methods have already been highlighted as superior to conventional flood coolants when considering toxicity, power consumption, and ozone depletion. The researchers caution that these lubricants would not suit applications where cleanliness is crucial, such as the biomedical and agri-food industries, but for aerospace-grade titanium machining the outlook is bright.
The study also demonstrates the fundamental need for lubrication when using supercritical CO2 in friction-related applications, since supercritical CO2 alone had almost no lubrication effect. The measured apparent friction coefficients could prove useful for supercritical CO2-assisted finite element simulations of machining processes, helping engineers model cutting operations more accurately. Solubility studies are already under investigation to find suitable supercritical conditions for better dissolving oils in supercritical CO2 and defining new efficient cutting fluids. If successful, this work could usher in a new generation of cutting fluids that combine the cooling power of an abundant, recyclable gas with the lubricating finesse of kitchen-shelf oils or laboratory-designed ionic liquids, transforming how the industry machines its most valuable alloys.

Article Title: Investigating the efficiency of mixtures based on supercritical CO2 and lubricants by friction tests under conditions similar to the machining of Ti6Al4V

original_evidence.body_text:
\# Supercritical CO2 and kitchen\-shelf lubricants could transform titanium machining

When carbon dioxide is squeezed past 74 bar and warmed above 31 degrees Celsius\, it stops behaving like an ordinary gas or liquid and enters a strange middle state known as the supercritical phase\. A team of French researchers at the Arts et Métiers Institute of Technology has now harnessed this exotic fluid to attack one of manufacturing’s most stubborn problems\: the friction and heat that plague the machining of Ti6Al4V\, the titanium alloy that holds together much of the aerospace industry\. Their findings\, published in Frontiers in Manufacturing Technology\, suggest that cheap\, sustainable additives dissolved in supercritical CO2 could rival industrial mineral oils\, with ionic liquids delivering the most dramatic friction reductions of all\.

The machining industry has long relied on flood coolants\, minimum quantity lubrication\, and cryogenic sprays such as liquid nitrogen to keep cutting tools alive and machined parts intact\. These methods aim to tame the intense friction and heating that occur at the chip\-tool and tool\-part contact zones\, where temperatures can soar high enough to soften the workpiece and destroy the tool edge\. Supercritical CO2 has emerged as an intriguing alternative because it acts as a green solvent and\, when delivered to the cutting zone\, expands with a phase transformation that drops its temperature sharply\, cooling both the tool and the part\. Previous studies have shown that pairing supercritical CO2 with dissolved soybean oil roughly halved flank wear compared with emulsion flood cooling when milling compacted graphite iron\, and that supercritical CO2 plus minimum quantity lubrication outperformed flood coolant in milling Ti6Al4V and turning AISI 1045 steel\.

Yet supercritical CO2 alone often performs worse than flood cooling\, which is why the lubricant carried within it matters so much\. The research team\, led by Koffi Samuel Koulekpa\, set out to systematically test what happens when different lubricants are introduced into supercritical CO2 and delivered to a titanium\-carbide contact under conditions mimicking real machining\. They selected ionic liquids\, vegetable oils\, mineral oil\, water\, and polyethylene glycol\, chosen for their solubility in supercritical CO2\, their sustainable character\, or their previous performances in machining\-related friction analysis\. The two ionic liquids tested\, BMIM\-PF6 and BMIM\-BF4\, are salts that stay liquid at room temperature and boast negligible volatility\, high thermal stability\, and non\-flammability\, making them fascinating candidates for machining applications\.

Order Lab Supplies

To deliver these exotic mixtures\, the researchers designed and built a dedicated machine that feeds CO2 from pressurized bottles\, cools it to ensure a liquid phase before compression\, then squeezes it to pressures up to 350 bar and heats it with four cartridges to reach the supercritical state in a mixing chamber\. There\, lubricants are injected at user\-specified rates before the mixture sprays through a 0\.25 mm round jet nozzle\. For the experiments\, the pressure was limited to 100 bar and the temperature set to 40 degrees Celsius\, guaranteeing a supercritical state while minimizing CO2 consumption\. The supercritical CO2 flowed at 0\.185 kg\/min\, while lubricants were delivered at 1 mL\/min and 4 mL\/min\, rates common in minimum quantity lubrication applications\.

Shop Motor Oils

The friction tests themselves took place on a CNC lathe fitted with a Hedenqvist\-type pin\-on\-cylinder tribometer\, a setup chosen for easy and quick execution\. Cylindrical carbide pins\, instrumented with K\-type thermocouples connected to a data acquisition system sampling at 2 kHz\, pressed against a rotating Ti6Al4V bar with an initial diameter of 120 mm\. The normal loads of 100 N\, 250 N\, and 400 N were selected based on a contact pressure of 1\,300 MPa derived from finite element simulations\, while sliding velocities of 20 m\/min and 100 m\/min covered the range of chip sliding velocities typical when machining difficult\-to\-cut alloys such as Ti6Al4V or Inconel 718\. After each test\, the workpiece surface was refreshed by a fresh machining pass to obtain a theoretical roughness of Ra 0\.5 µm\, and the pins were rotated by 25 degrees to expose a new contact surface\.

The results revealed a striking pattern\. At 20 m\/min\, adding lubricants to supercritical CO2 decreased friction\, but the mixtures never outperformed the dry condition\, with friction coefficients staying above the dry baseline for almost all loads\. At 100 m\/min\, however\, the story changed dramatically\. The team observed a mean decrease of 0\.1 in the apparent friction coefficient\, and increasing the lubricant flow rate from 1 mL\/min to 4 mL\/min produced further reductions\. The ionic liquids showed their lubricating prowess most clearly at 100 m\/min with significant friction decreases at 4 mL\/min and 400 N\, demonstrating that the combined effect of lubrication by the additives and cooling from supercritical CO2 works best under the most demanding conditions\.

The adhesive behavior of Ti6Al4V\, notorious for sticking to counter\-materials during friction\, provided another revealing metric\. After each test\, the researchers examined the friction zone under an optical microscope and calculated the sticking area by assimilating it to an ellipse\. Once again\, the effects of the lubricants were clearly visible at 100 m\/min\. The ionic liquids\, together with polyethylene glycol\, led to the lowest sticking area values\, with surface reductions of 54 percent and 55 percent for BF4 and PF6 respectively at the 1 mL\/min rate\. These values climbed to 74 percent at 4 mL\/min\, showing how strongly the delivery flow rate influences the protective action\. The researchers attribute this to an adsorption layer that reduces direct contact between the two materials\, and for the ionic liquids\, to tribochemical reactions between the liquids and the tool\-workpiece materials that form remarkably effective protective films\.

Temperature measurements confirmed the cooling credentials of supercritical CO2\. Pin temperatures dropped significantly compared with dry tests\, with a maximum reduction of 80 degrees Celsius\. Interestingly\, no significant difference in cooling was provided by the presence of the lubricants compared with supercritical CO2 alone\, suggesting that the additives’ contribution to heat removal was not activated under the tested speed conditions\, possibly due to suboptimal delivery techniques or solubility issues that the team plans to investigate further\.

Perhaps the most commercially significant finding concerns the cheap lubricants\. Water\, rapeseed oil\, and sunflower oil performed similarly to the commonly used machining mineral oil when paired with supercritical CO2\, and these biological alternatives are less expensive and less health\-threatening than traditional emulsions\. This could help develop future low\-cost yet effective cooling and lubrication methods for the machining industry\, a prospect with real sustainability appeal given that cryogenic minimum quantity lubrication methods have already been highlighted as superior to conventional flood coolants when considering toxicity\, power consumption\, and ozone depletion\. The researchers caution that these lubricants would not suit applications where cleanliness is crucial\, such as the biomedical and agri\-food industries\, but for aerospace\-grade titanium machining the outlook is bright\.

The study also demonstrates the fundamental need for lubrication when using supercritical CO2 in friction\-related applications\, since supercritical CO2 alone had almost no lubrication effect\. The measured apparent friction coefficients could prove useful for supercritical CO2\-assisted finite element simulations of machining processes\, helping engineers model cutting operations more accurately\. Solubility studies are already under investigation to find suitable supercritical conditions for better dissolving oils in supercritical CO2 and defining new efficient cutting fluids\. If successful\, this work could usher in a new generation of cutting fluids that combine the cooling power of an abundant\, recyclable gas with the lubricating finesse of kitchen\-shelf oils or laboratory\-designed ionic liquids\, transforming how the industry machines its most valuable alloys\.

records.title: Interpretable surrogate modeling for load-aware thermal risk assessment of bolted switchgear busbar joints using electro-thermal simulation
records.abstract: Thermal-risk assessment of bolted busbar joints is complicated by the coupled effects of electrical loading, contact condition, and heat dissipation. This study develops an interpretable forward-surrogate framework based on three-dimensional electro-thermal finite-element simulation. Physics enters through finite-element generation of the training data, physically defined input variables, and post hoc consistency checks, rather than through constraints embedded in the learning algorithm. Five prescribed inputs were considered: load current, contact resistance, effective contact ratio, ambient temperature, and convective heat-transfer coefficient. The effective-contact heating power was checked against P ≈ I 2 R c , with a maximum relative deviation of 0.173% across 400 simulated cases; 382 cases were retained within the intended applicability domain. Four candidate models were compared using 5 × 10 repeated cross-validation. The XGBoost regressor achieved R 2 = 0.990 ± 0.005 , R M S E = 1.877 ± 0.542 , and M A E = 1.042 ± 0.198 K , with performance comparable to random forest. For four-class simulation-oriented thermal-risk classification, XGBoost achieved an accuracy of 0.938 ± 0.026 and a macro F1-score of 0.941 ± 0.033 . SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified load current and prescribed contact resistance as the dominant contributors, while convection, ambient temperature, and effective contact ratio produced smaller, condition-dependent effects. The lower global importance of effective contact ratio reflects the area-averaged temperature-rise target and does not imply that current constriction is physically unimportant. Across three threshold schemes, all out-of-fold errors were between adjacent classes. The framework is geometry-specific and has not been experimentally validated. It predicts internal effective-contact temperature rise; relating this quantity to infrared surface measurements requires further validation.

1 Introduction
Bolted busbar joints are critical current-carrying components in switchgear, but their condition can deteriorate under mechanical relaxation, surface oxidation, contamination, and repeated thermal cycling. These processes reduce the real conducting area, increase electrical contact resistance, intensify current constriction, and promote localized Joule heating. The resulting temperature rise can accelerate insulation ageing and material degradation. Electrical-contact theory and recent multiphysics studies show that joint heating depends not only on bulk conductor properties, but also on contact state, current-transfer paths, surface films, and asperity deformation (Persson, 2022; Li et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024).
Infrared thermography is widely used for non-contact condition monitoring of electrical equipment (Xia et al., 2021; Balakrishnan et al., 2022; Bagavathiappan et al., 2013). Automated approaches have further extended thermal inspection to early fault detection, equipment localization, smart-camera diagnosis, image recognition and fusion, and machine-learning-assisted fault identification (Jaffery and Dubey, 2014; Gong et al., 2018; Han et al., 2021; Tang and Jian, 2024; Lu et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2021). However, a measured surface temperature is not determined by contact degradation alone. Load current, ambient temperature, enclosure airflow, conductor geometry, heat-transfer conditions, and contact resistance jointly shape the observed thermal field. Studies of insulated busbar joints and high-capacity switchgear have accordingly related accessible surface or enclosure temperatures to internal conductor temperature under specified operating conditions (Tang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021). This dependence limits the use of a single temperature value as a unique indicator of joint degradation.
To disentangle these coupled influences and resolve the internal electro-thermal response beyond surface observations, finite-element analysis can be used to calculate current density, interfacial heat generation, and three-dimensional temperature fields in busbar assemblies. Existing electro-thermal studies have examined how joint resistance, contact area, conductor dimensions, and cooling affect hotspot formation. However, the consistency between the simulated contact heating power and the theoretical Li et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024). Data-driven approaches have also been explored for predicting electrical contact resistance under wear-related conditions (Cai et al., 2024). These models are valuable for mechanism analysis, but repeated high-fidelity calculations become computationally demanding when many combinations of load, contact state, and thermal boundary conditions must be evaluated.
Simulation-trained surrogate models offer a practical means of reducing this computational burden. A surrogate learns the input–output mapping generated by a finite-element model and rapidly approximates the response within the sampled domain. Previous studies have used machine learning as a finite-element surrogate, including graph-based prediction of engineering responses and surrogate-supported digital-twin models for dynamic systems (Vurtur Badarinath et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2023; Chakraborty et al., 2021). Such approaches can support parameter exploration, sensitivity analysis, and scenario screening. Their predictions, however, inherit the assumptions, parameter ranges, and numerical limitations of the parent simulation and do not become experimentally validated merely because the surrogate accurately reproduces finite-element outputs.
This distinction is important when positioning the present method relative to physics-informed machine learning. Physics-informed approaches commonly embed governing equations, conservation laws, invariants, or related constraints directly into the loss function, training procedure, or model structure (Raissi et al., 2019; Karniadakis et al., 2021). The present study does not impose such constraints within the learning algorithm. Instead, physics enters through finite-element generation of the training data, physically defined predictors, and post hoc numerical consistency checks. The resulting model is therefore a simulation-trained forward surrogate with physically interpretable inputs, rather than a physics-informed neural network or an inverse diagnostic model.
Interpretability is nevertheless necessary for engineering use. Tree-based ensembles can capture nonlinear interactions among load, contact state, and cooling, but their predictive structure is not transparent from model coefficients. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provides a consistent framework for decomposing predictions into feature contributions, while TreeSHAP enables efficient explanation of tree ensembles and aggregation from local to global behaviour (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020). SHAP-based interpretation has also been adopted in engineering condition-monitoring applications to clarify feature contributions in machine-learning fault models (Brusa et al., 2023). Such attribution can clarify how a surrogate uses its inputs, but it does not establish causality, particularly when predictors are correlated.

First, a three-dimensional electro-thermal model is established in which prescribed contact resistance and effective contact ratio are controlled separately, allowing their roles in power dissipation and current distribution to be examined without treating them as interchangeable degradation indicators. Second, numerical consistency is assessed through mesh independence and an effective-contact power check against the theoretical relation
2 Electro-thermal model of the bolted busbar joint
This section describes the three-dimensional electro-thermal finite-element model of the bolted busbar joint, the equivalent representation of contact degradation, the governing equations, the boundary conditions, and the model-consistency assessment. The central modelling idea is that contact degradation is represented as a contraction of the effective conducting contact area rather than as a single high-resistance block, so that the current constriction and the resulting localized Joule heating are reproduced in a physically consistent manner.
2.1 Geometry and materials
The model consists of two overlapping copper busbars connected by steel bolts, washers and nuts, as shown in Figure 1B, which corresponds to the bolted joint of an actual switchgear busbar shown in Figure 1A. Each busbar is 300 mm long, 50 mm wide and 8 mm thick, and the overlap length of the lap joint is Lo = 80 mm. The two bolts are spaced 40 mm apart, each with a shank radius of 5 mm and a washer of 10 mm radius and 2 mm thickness. A contact layer of thickness 0.5 mm is inserted between the two busbars over the overlap region to represent the electrical contact interface, which is further divided into an effective conducting region and a degraded non-contact region as described in Section 2.2. The material properties used in the model are summarized in Table 1. The densities and specific heat capacities of copper and steel were 8,960 kg m-3 and 385 J kg-1 K−1, and 7,850 kg m-3 and 475 J kg-1 K−1, respectively.

2.2 Equivalent modelling of contact degradation
Contact degradation caused by mechanical loosening, oxidation, or surface contamination reduces the portion of the nominal overlap area that effectively carries current (Persson, 2022; Cheng et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2017). Rather than representing the entire degraded interface as a uniformly high-resistance block, the contact layer was divided into an effective conducting region and a degraded near-insulating region. In the notation used below, the subscripts “eff” and “deg” denote the effective conducting region and the degraded near-insulating region, respectively. This representation reflects the physical mechanism by which deterioration reduces the real conducting area and forces current through the remaining conductive contact spots, thereby intensifying current constriction and localized Joule heating. The steel bolts, washers, and nuts were included in the heat-transfer domain but excluded from the electric-current domain. This treatment prevented an electrical bypass through the fasteners and isolated the thermal consequences of current constriction at the busbar-to-busbar contact interface, which is the mechanism examined in this study. The fasteners nevertheless remained thermally coupled to the busbars and contributed to heat conduction and dissipation.

4 Surrogate-model framework
The finite-element simulations described in Sections 2 and 3 establish physically defined mappings from operating, environmental, and contact-degradation variables to the thermal response of the bolted busbar joint. However, repeated solution of the full three-dimensional electro-thermal model becomes computationally inefficient when dense evaluations are required across combinations of load current, contact condition, ambient temperature, and cooling intensity. Each finite-element case required a median solver time of approximately 8.4 s on the production mesh, as reported in Section 2.5. Once trained, a surrogate model evaluates the same prescribed input combination essentially instantaneously relative to the finite-element solution, making dense scans over
The present framework is formulated as a forward surrogate model. It predicts the simulated thermal response from prescribed operating, environmental, and degradation variables. The prescribed contact quantities are supplied as model inputs through direct measurement, calibration, estimation, or scenario specification, as summarized in Table 2.
All predictors represent explicitly defined operating, environmental, or degradation quantities, but the nonlinear mapping learned by the models is not transparent to direct inspection. SHAP analysis was therefore introduced to quantify global and case-specific feature attributions and to examine whether the learned relationships were consistent with the underlying electro-thermal mechanisms.
Two complementary learning tasks were considered: continuous prediction of the effective-contact temperature rise and classification into the simulation-oriented thermal-risk classes defined in Section 2.4. The following subsections describe the task formulation, leakage-controlled predictor design, candidate algorithms, validation workflow, evaluation metrics, model configurations, and interpretability procedure.
4.1 Surrogate-learning tasks
Both surrogate-learning tasks were developed using the retained 382-case dataset described in Section 3.1.
The first task was a regression problem in which the target variable was the effective-contact temperature rise
The second task was a four-class classification problem. Its target was the simulation-oriented thermal-risk class assigned from Section 2.4. The four classes—Normal, Warning, Serious, and Critical—were encoded as the ordered integers 0, 1, 2, and three for model implementation.
Although the labels possess a natural order, the candidate classifiers were evaluated using a multiclass formulation. This enabled consistent comparison across the four candidate classifier families within the same modelling framework. The ordered nature of the labels was assessed separately through the structure of the classification errors, distinguishing between adjacent-class errors and errors that crossed multiple thermal-risk classes.
The regression and classification tasks serve complementary purposes. Regression estimates the continuous finite-element temperature-rise response, whereas classification provides a compact representation of the corresponding simulation-oriented thermal-risk class. The classification output should not be interpreted as an independently established field defect grade because the labels are derived from simulation-oriented thresholds rather than standardized operational alarm limits or experimentally validated maintenance categories.

4.3 Candidate models and validation workflow
Four candidate algorithms were evaluated for each surrogate-learning task to compare linear and nonlinear model families within a common framework. For regression, the candidate models were linear regression, random-forest regression, XGBoost regression Chen and Guestrin, 2016, and support-vector regression. For classification, the candidates were multinomial logistic regression, random-forest classification, XGBoost classification, and support-vector classification. Their evaluation metrics, principal model configurations, and imbalance-handling settings are specified in Section 4.4.
The primary performance estimates were obtained using repeated cross-validation on the retained 382-case dataset. Regression used repeated five-fold cross-validation with 10 repeats, and classification used the stratified variant so that class proportions were approximately preserved within each fold; a random seed of 42 was used solely for reproducibility and has no physical significance. Across the resulting 50 train–validation iterations, each candidate model was fitted only on the training portion of the corresponding fold and evaluated on its held-out validation portion.
The repeated cross-validation results were used as the primary basis for comparing the candidate model families. The reported regression and classification metrics therefore represent the mean and standard deviation across the 50 validation folds rather than the result of a single partition. The earlier single five-fold results are retained only as a reproducibility comparison in Supplementary Table S6.
After the candidate model families had been compared, a separate stratified 80/20 split was generated using random seed 42 to support sample-level visualization and interpretation. The split contained 305 development cases and 77 held-out cases. The model fitted on the 80% development portion was used to generate the predicted-versus-simulated regression plot, the classification confusion matrix, and the selected case-level explanations. The 77 held-out cases were not used to fit the model that generated the corresponding predictions; training isolation therefore holds for these visualizations.
The 77 cases should not, however, be described as an independent or model-selection-independent test set: before the 80/20 split was constructed, all 382 cases had already participated in the repeated cross-validation comparison of the four candidate families. The two procedures therefore serve different purposes. The repeated cross-validation provides the primary quantitative comparison and supplies every performance value reported in the Abstract, Results, and Conclusions, whereas the 80/20 split supplies sample-level plots, a confusion structure, and representative local explanations. Because the model family retained for interpretation was selected using the same cross-validation results, its reported performance is conditional on that selection; differences between closely performing models are therefore described cautiously, and the 80/20 results are treated as descriptive supporting evidence rather than an estimate of post-selection generalization.
No automated hyperparameter search, grid search, Bayesian optimization, or cross-validation-guided tuning was performed. The principal model settings were specified before the final comparison, while parameters not explicitly set retained their software-package defaults, as detailed in Section 4.4. This avoids an additional tuning-induced source of optimism, although it does not eliminate the model-family selection bias described above.

4.4.2 Model configurations, preprocessing, and imbalance handling
As described in Section 4.3, no automated or cross-validation-guided hyperparameter search was performed. The model configurations were fixed before the final repeated-cross-validation comparison, and unspecified parameters retained the defaults of the corresponding software implementation.
StandardScaler was included in the pipelines for linear regression, support-vector regression, multinomial logistic regression, and support-vector classification. Within each cross-validation iteration, the scaler was fitted only on the training fold and then applied to the corresponding validation fold, preventing preprocessing information from crossing the fold boundary. Random-forest and XGBoost models were fitted without feature scaling.
The principal manually specified settings included 300 estimators for the random-forest and XGBoost models, C = 10 for the support-vector models, and the learning-rate, tree-depth, and subsampling settings reported in Supplementary Table S5. Logistic regression used max_iter = 2000 to support numerical convergence rather than to optimize predictive performance.
Class imbalance was addressed during model fitting without altering the sample distribution. Logistic regression, random-forest classification, and support-vector classification used balanced class weights, whereas balanced sample weights were supplied to the XGBoost classifier. No oversampling, undersampling, or synthetic sample generation was applied. Random seed 42 was used where supported to make stochastic estimation and resampling reproducible; it has no physical significance. Complete preprocessing, model, random-state, convergence, and imbalance-handling settings are reported in Supplementary Table S5.
Because nested cross-validation was not performed, the results represent the specified configurations rather than globally optimized versions of the candidate algorithms.
4.4.3 SHAP procedure
SHAP was used to interpret the XGBoost regression and classification surrogates (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020). SHAP decomposes a model output into a baseline and additive predictor contributions. Positive and negative values indicate contributions that increase or decrease the relevant model output relative to its baseline.
For regression, SHAP values are expressed in kelvin and quantify the contribution of each predictor to the predicted
Global regression importance was calculated as the mean absolute SHAP value across evaluated cases. Global classification importance was calculated by averaging absolute SHAP values across both cases and the four output classes, producing one overall value for each predictor. Class-specific results, including those for the Critical class, were analysed separately and were not combined with the all-class averages. Local explanations were generated for representative cases from the 77-case held-out visualization subset described in Section 4.3.
SHAP analysis was restricted to XGBoost to maintain one attribution procedure across the regression and classification tasks. Under its adopted feature-dependence formulation, TreeSHAP computes exact Shapley values for tree ensembles (Lundberg et al., 2020). Applying model-agnostic KernelSHAP to the support-vector or linear candidates would require sampling-based approximation and a different attribution framework, so the resulting magnitudes would not be directly comparable with the TreeSHAP values.
