5.4 Classification error structure and threshold sensitivity
The ordered structure of the four simulation-oriented thermal-risk classes was examined using out-of-fold predictions generated by a single stratified five-fold procedure with shuffling and random seed 42. Each of the 382 retained cases therefore received exactly one prediction from a classifier that had not been fitted using that case.
Under the reference thresholds of 5, 15, and 30 K, 21 of the 382 out-of-fold predictions were incorrect. All 21 errors occurred between adjacent classes, and no case crossed two or more class boundaries. Thus, no Normal case was assigned to Serious or Critical, and no Critical case was assigned to Warning or Normal. The classifier therefore generally preserved the ordinal structure of the labels when the exact class assignment was incorrect. However, adjacency alone does not demonstrate that every misclassified case was located immediately next to a numerical threshold.
These 21 out-of-fold errors should not be confused with the five errors shown in Figure 6. The former were obtained from the single five-fold out-of-fold analysis covering all 382 retained cases, whereas the latter arose from the separate 77-case held-out visualization subset. The repeated-cross-validation means and standard deviations in Table 6 remain the primary aggregate performance estimates; the two error counts are used only to characterize prediction behaviour under their respective resampling procedures.
Threshold sensitivity was assessed using the three schemes defined in Section 2.4. Under the lower thresholds of 4, 12, and 24 K, the class counts were 14, 141, 138, and 89. The corresponding repeated-cross-validation accuracy and macro F1 were 0.9251 ± 0.0317 and 0.8960 ± 0.0511, respectively. The single five-fold out-of-fold analysis contained 32 errors, all between adjacent classes, with no non-adjacent error.
For the reference thresholds of 5, 15, and 30 K, the class counts were 26, 174, 123, and 59. Accuracy reached 0.9377 ± 0.0266, and macro F1 reached 0.9407 ± 0.0337. The corresponding out-of-fold predictions contained 21 adjacent-class errors and no non-adjacent error.
Under the higher thresholds of 6, 18, and 36 K, the class counts became 39, 195, 106, and 42. Accuracy was 0.9346 ± 0.0274, while macro F1 was 0.9249 ± 0.0332. The out-of-fold analysis again produced 21 errors, all between adjacent classes. The complete threshold-sensitivity results are reported in Supplementary Table S2.
The lower scheme produced a particularly small Normal class of only 14 cases and exhibited both the lowest macro F1 and the greatest fold-to-fold variation in that metric. This result demonstrates why accuracy alone is insufficient for the present imbalanced classification problem. Raising the thresholds increased the number of Normal cases but reduced the Critical class to 42 cases, accompanied by a modest reduction in macro F1 relative to the reference scheme.
The diagnostics from the 5 × 10 repeated stratified cross-validation further clarify the observed variability. Across the 50 validation folds, macro F1 ranged from 0.794 to 0.991. In the lowest-performing fold (repeat 8, fold 3), Normal-class precision, recall, and F1 were 1.000, 0.200, and 0.333, respectively, whereas the F1-scores of the Warning, Serious, and Critical classes were 0.901, 0.941, and 1.000. Four of the five Normal cases in that fold were assigned to the adjacent Warning class, while all 12 Critical cases were correctly classified. The highest-performing fold (repeat 3, fold 4) reached a macro F1 of 0.991, with a Normal-class F1 of 1.000. The low-to-high variation therefore reflects the sensitivity of a macro-averaged metric to the small number of Normal cases within individual folds rather than a change in the dominant error mechanism.
Their comparatively balanced class distribution and stable macro-level performance support their use as the principal discretization in the present simulation study. Across all three schemes, the absence of non-adjacent errors indicates that the classifier retained the ordering of simulated thermal severity as the numerical class boundaries changed. These findings do not convert the classes into standardized field alarm levels; their operational interpretation, experimental validation requirements, and applicability limits are discussed in Section 5.5.
5.5 Applicability, limitations, and validation requirements
The present study establishes a numerically consistent simulation-to-surrogate workflow rather than an experimentally validated field-diagnostic system. The mesh-independence assessment, electrical-power consistency check, and comparison between the production mesh and the globally controlled sensitivity mesh support the internal numerical consistency of the finite-element implementation. These checks do not constitute experimental validation of the predicted temperatures, current-transfer paths, or contact-degradation states. Accordingly, the reported surrogate performance quantifies reproduction of the finite-element outputs within the simulated design space, rather than agreement with measurements from operating switchgear.
Several modelling assumptions delimit the interpretation of the electro-thermal results. This study developed an interpretable simulation-to-surrogate framework for load-aware thermal-risk assessment of bolted switchgear busbar joints. The proposed model remains a geometry-specific forward surrogate of finite-element outputs. It does not infer contact condition from infrared measurements and has not been experimentally validated. original_evidence.abstract: Thermal-risk assessment of bolted busbar joints is complicated by the coupled effects of electrical loading, contact condition, and heat dissipation. This study develops an interpretable forward-surrogate framework based on three-dimensional electro-thermal finite-element simulation. Physics enters through finite-element generation of the training data, physically defined input variables, and post hoc consistency checks, rather than through constraints embedded in the learning algorithm. Five prescribed inputs were considered: load current, contact resistance, effective contact ratio, ambient temperature, and convective heat-transfer coefficient. The effective-contact heating power was checked against P ≈ I 2 R c , with a maximum relative deviation of 0.173% across 400 simulated cases; 382 cases were retained within the intended applicability domain. Four candidate models were compared using 5 × 10 repeated cross-validation. The XGBoost regressor achieved R 2 = 0.990 ± 0.005 , R M S E = 1.877 ± 0.542 , and M A E = 1.042 ± 0.198 K , with performance comparable to random forest. For four-class simulation-oriented thermal-risk classification, XGBoost achieved an accuracy of 0.938 ± 0.026 and a macro F1-score of 0.941 ± 0.033 . SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified load current and prescribed contact resistance as the dominant contributors, while convection, ambient temperature, and effective contact ratio produced smaller, condition-dependent effects. The lower global importance of effective contact ratio reflects the area-averaged temperature-rise target and does not imply that current constriction is physically unimportant. Across three threshold schemes, all out-of-fold errors were between adjacent classes. The framework is geometry-specific and has not been experimentally validated. It predicts internal effective-contact temperature rise; relating this quantity to infrared surface measurements requires further validation.

Abstract
Thermal-risk assessment of bolted busbar joints is complicated by the coupled effects of electrical loading, contact condition, and heat dissipation. This study develops an interpretable forward-surrogate framework based on three-dimensional electro-thermal finite-element simulation. Physics enters through finite-element generation of the training data, physically defined input variables, and post hoc consistency checks, rather than through constraints embedded in the learning algorithm. 1 Introduction
Bolted busbar joints are critical current-carrying components in switchgear, but their condition can deteriorate under mechanical relaxation, surface oxidation, contamination, and repeated thermal cycling. These processes reduce the real conducting area, increase electrical contact resistance, intensify current constriction, and promote localized Joule heating. The resulting temperature rise can accelerate insulation ageing and material degradation. Electrical-contact theory and recent multiphysics studies show that joint heating depends not only on bulk conductor properties, but also on contact state, current-transfer paths, surface films, and asperity deformation (Persson, 2022; Li et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024).
Infrared thermography is widely used for non-contact condition monitoring of electrical equipment (Xia et al., 2021; Balakrishnan et al., 2022; Bagavathiappan et al., 2013). Automated approaches have further extended thermal inspection to early fault detection, equipment localization, smart-camera diagnosis, image recognition and fusion, and machine-learning-assisted fault identification (Jaffery and Dubey, 2014; Gong et al., 2018; Han et al., 2021; Tang and Jian, 2024; Lu et al., 2021; Choudhary et al., 2021). However, a measured surface temperature is not determined by contact degradation alone. Load current, ambient temperature, enclosure airflow, conductor geometry, heat-transfer conditions, and contact resistance jointly shape the observed thermal field. Studies of insulated busbar joints and high-capacity switchgear have accordingly related accessible surface or enclosure temperatures to internal conductor temperature under specified operating conditions (Tang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021). This dependence limits the use of a single temperature value as a unique indicator of joint degradation.
To disentangle these coupled influences and resolve the internal electro-thermal response beyond surface observations, finite-element analysis can be used to calculate current density, interfacial heat generation, and three-dimensional temperature fields in busbar assemblies. Existing electro-thermal studies have examined how joint resistance, contact area, conductor dimensions, and cooling affect hotspot formation. However, the consistency between the simulated contact heating power and the theoretical Li et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024). Data-driven approaches have also been explored for predicting electrical contact resistance under wear-related conditions (Cai et al., 2024). These models are valuable for mechanism analysis, but repeated high-fidelity calculations become computationally demanding when many combinations of load, contact state, and thermal boundary conditions must be evaluated.
Simulation-trained surrogate models offer a practical means of reducing this computational burden. A surrogate learns the input–output mapping generated by a finite-element model and rapidly approximates the response within the sampled domain. Previous studies have used machine learning as a finite-element surrogate, including graph-based prediction of engineering responses and surrogate-supported digital-twin models for dynamic systems (Vurtur Badarinath et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2023; Chakraborty et al., 2021). Such approaches can support parameter exploration, sensitivity analysis, and scenario screening. Their predictions, however, inherit the assumptions, parameter ranges, and numerical limitations of the parent simulation and do not become experimentally validated merely because the surrogate accurately reproduces finite-element outputs.
This distinction is important when positioning the present method relative to physics-informed machine learning. Physics-informed approaches commonly embed governing equations, conservation laws, invariants, or related constraints directly into the loss function, training procedure, or model structure (Raissi et al., 2019; Karniadakis et al., 2021). The present study does not impose such constraints within the learning algorithm. Instead, physics enters through finite-element generation of the training data, physically defined predictors, and post hoc numerical consistency checks. The resulting model is therefore a simulation-trained forward surrogate with physically interpretable inputs, rather than a physics-informed neural network or an inverse diagnostic model.
Interpretability is nevertheless necessary for engineering use. Tree-based ensembles can capture nonlinear interactions among load, contact state, and cooling, but their predictive structure is not transparent from model coefficients. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provides a consistent framework for decomposing predictions into feature contributions, while TreeSHAP enables efficient explanation of tree ensembles and aggregation from local to global behaviour (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020). SHAP-based interpretation has also been adopted in engineering condition-monitoring applications to clarify feature contributions in machine-learning fault models (Brusa et al., 2023). Such attribution can clarify how a surrogate uses its inputs, but it does not establish causality, particularly when predictors are correlated.

First, a three-dimensional electro-thermal model is established in which prescribed contact resistance and effective contact ratio are controlled separately, allowing their roles in power dissipation and current distribution to be examined without treating them as interchangeable degradation indicators. 2 Electro-thermal model of the bolted busbar joint
This section describes the three-dimensional electro-thermal finite-element model of the bolted busbar joint, the equivalent representation of contact degradation, the governing equations, the boundary conditions, and the model-consistency assessment. The central modelling idea is that contact degradation is represented as a contraction of the effective conducting contact area rather than as a single high-resistance block, so that the current constriction and the resulting localized Joule heating are reproduced in a physically consistent manner.
2.1 Geometry and materials
The model consists of two overlapping copper busbars connected by steel bolts, washers and nuts, as shown in Figure 1B, which corresponds to the bolted joint of an actual switchgear busbar shown in Figure 1A. Each busbar is 300 mm long, 50 mm wide and 8 mm thick, and the overlap length of the lap joint is Lo = 80 mm. The two bolts are spaced 40 mm apart, each with a shank radius of 5 mm and a washer of 10 mm radius and 2 mm thickness. A contact layer of thickness 0.5 mm is inserted between the two busbars over the overlap region to represent the electrical contact interface, which is further divided into an effective conducting region and a degraded non-contact region as described in Section 2.2. The material properties used in the model are summarized in Table 1. The densities and specific heat capacities of copper and steel were 8,960 kg m-3 and 385 J kg-1 K−1, and 7,850 kg m-3 and 475 J kg-1 K−1, respectively.

2.2 Equivalent modelling of contact degradation
Contact degradation caused by mechanical loosening, oxidation, or surface contamination reduces the portion of the nominal overlap area that effectively carries current (Persson, 2022; Cheng et al., 2023; Qiu et al., 2017). Rather than representing the entire degraded interface as a uniformly high-resistance block, the contact layer was divided into an effective conducting region and a degraded near-insulating region. In the notation used below, the subscripts “eff” and “deg” denote the effective conducting region and the degraded near-insulating region, respectively. This representation reflects the physical mechanism by which deterioration reduces the real conducting area and forces current through the remaining conductive contact spots, thereby intensifying current constriction and localized Joule heating. The nominal overlap area and the effective conducting area were defined by Equations 1, 2, respectively:c is the effective contact ratio, w is the busbar width and Lo is the overlap length.

Thus, decreasing ηc contracts the conducting annuli and forces the current through a smaller portion of the interface, increasing the degree of current constriction and the concentration of local Joule heating.
The adopted range of ηc was also checked against the physical dimensions of the overlap region. For c = 0.10, 0.30, and 0.50, the corresponding outer radii were approximately 9.42, 14.70, and 18.53 mm, respectively. At the upper bound ηc = 0.50, the annular diameter was approximately 37.1 mm, which remained smaller than the 40 mm bolt-centre spacing. In the adopted symmetric two-bolt geometry, the conducting patches therefore remained non-overlapping and within the physical overlap interface throughout the prescribed parameter range.
The prescribed joint contact resistance Rc was introduced through the equivalent resistivity of the effective contact layer, as described in Equation 5:c is the contact-layer thickness. This formulation assigns different physical roles to Rc and ηc. The parameter Rc specifies the target lumped resistance of the effective current path, whereas ηc determines the spatial extent of that path and hence the degree of current constriction. When ηc changes, ρeff is recalculated using Equation 5, so that the prescribed lumped resistance Rc is retained. This avoids counting the reduction in conducting area twice through both geometry and resistance.
Accordingly, Rc and ηc were independently controlled at the physical-model formulation level to represent resistance magnitude and conducting-area contraction, respectively. This does not imply statistical independence within the assembled simulation dataset. Because the main-design and extreme-design regions were concatenated, the sampled values exhibited moderate negative correlations, with Section 3.1. Nor does the formulation imply that Rc and ηc evolve independently during actual long-term contact degradation.

The steel bolts, washers, and nuts were included in the heat-transfer domain but excluded from the electric-current domain. This treatment prevented an electrical bypass through the fasteners and isolated the thermal consequences of current constriction at the busbar-to-busbar contact interface, which is the mechanism examined in this study. It should not be interpreted as a general assertion that metallic fasteners carry no current in all practical bolted assemblies. Accounting for current sharing through the bolt–busbar interfaces would require additional contact-resistance parameters that were unavailable and falls outside the present model scope. The fasteners nevertheless remained thermally coupled to the busbars and contributed to heat conduction and dissipation.

2.4 Definition of simulation-oriented thermal-risk classes
For the classification task, each simulated case was assigned an ordered thermal-risk class according to the effective contact temperature rise, defined as Section 2.3. The four simulation-oriented thermal-risk classes and their corresponding temperature-rise intervals are listed in Table 3.

The boundaries of 5, 15, and 30 K were adopted as modelling design choices for converting the continuous simulated response into an ordered classification target. They were intended to distinguish progressively increasing thermal responses while avoiding an excessively sparse lowest-risk class. The boundaries were specified before the model-performance comparison and were not selected by maximizing the cross-validation metrics. They were not derived from a field alarm standard and should therefore not be interpreted as universal operational limits for switchgear inspection.
To evaluate the sensitivity of the classification results to these design choices, the three boundaries were uniformly shifted by −20% and +20%. This produced three threshold schemes: 4/12/24 K, 5/15/30 K, and 6/18/36 K, referred to as the lower, reference, and higher schemes, respectively. All three schemes were evaluated using the same 382 simulated cases, the same repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation procedure with 10 repeats and a random seed of 42, and the same fixed model hyperparameters. No hyperparameter adjustment was performed for the alternative threshold schemes.
The corresponding classification results, class counts, and error structures for the three schemes are reported in Section 5.4 and Supplementary Table S2.
2.5 Mesh independence and model-consistency assessment

Four refinement levels—coarse, normal, fine, and extra fine—were evaluated. They contained 21,958, 54,394, 312,700, and 368,625 tetrahedral elements, respectively, corresponding to 83,307, 190,271, 1,003,469, and 1,155,331 degrees of freedom. 3 Simulation dataset and thermal descriptors
Using the electro-thermal model described in Section 2 and assessed for mesh independence and internal consistency in Section 2.5, a parametric simulation dataset was generated for surrogate-model development. This section describes the composition and screening of the dataset, examines the relationships among the sampled inputs, and defines the load-normalized thermal descriptors used for physical interpretation. The simulation-oriented thermal-risk classes were defined in Section 2.4.
3.1 Dataset generation, screening, and input relationships
The dataset was generated using the Latin hypercube design and parameter ranges specified in Section 2.3 and Table 2 (McKay et al., 1979). It comprised 350 main-design cases and 50 supplemental cases extending the ranges of load current, contact resistance, and effective contact ratio, giving 400 simulated cases in total. 4 Surrogate-model framework
The finite-element simulations described in Sections 2 and 3 establish physically defined mappings from operating, environmental, and contact-degradation variables to the thermal response of the bolted busbar joint. However, repeated solution of the full three-dimensional electro-thermal model becomes computationally inefficient when dense evaluations are required across combinations of load current, contact condition, ambient temperature, and cooling intensity. Each finite-element case required a median solver time of approximately 8.4 s on the production mesh, as reported in Section 2.5. Once trained, a surrogate model evaluates the same prescribed input combination essentially instantaneously relative to the finite-element solution, making dense scans over
The present framework is formulated as a forward surrogate model. It predicts the simulated thermal response from prescribed operating, environmental, and degradation variables. The prescribed contact quantities are supplied as model inputs through direct measurement, calibration, estimation, or scenario specification, as summarized in Table 2.
All predictors represent explicitly defined operating, environmental, or degradation quantities, but the nonlinear mapping learned by the models is not transparent to direct inspection. SHAP analysis was therefore introduced to quantify global and case-specific feature attributions and to examine whether the learned relationships were consistent with the underlying electro-thermal mechanisms.
Two complementary learning tasks were considered: continuous prediction of the effective-contact temperature rise and classification into the simulation-oriented thermal-risk classes defined in Section 2.4. The following subsections describe the task formulation, leakage-controlled predictor design, candidate algorithms, validation workflow, evaluation metrics, model configurations, and interpretability procedure.
4.1 Surrogate-learning tasks
Both surrogate-learning tasks were developed using the retained 382-case dataset described in Section 3.1.
The first task was a regression problem in which the target variable was the effective-contact temperature rise
The second task was a four-class classification problem. Its target was the simulation-oriented thermal-risk class assigned from Section 2.4. The four classes—Normal, Warning, Serious, and Critical—were encoded as the ordered integers 0, 1, 2, and three for model implementation.
Although the labels possess a natural order, the candidate classifiers were evaluated using a multiclass formulation. This enabled consistent comparison across the four candidate classifier families within the same modelling framework. The ordered nature of the labels was assessed separately through the structure of the classification errors, distinguishing between adjacent-class errors and errors that crossed multiple thermal-risk classes.
The regression and classification tasks serve complementary purposes. Regression estimates the continuous finite-element temperature-rise response, whereas classification provides a compact representation of the corresponding simulation-oriented thermal-risk class. The classification output should not be interpreted as an independently established field defect grade because the labels are derived from simulation-oriented thresholds rather than standardized operational alarm limits or experimentally validated maintenance categories.

4.3 Candidate models and validation workflow
Four candidate algorithms were evaluated for each surrogate-learning task to compare linear and nonlinear model families within a common framework. For regression, the candidate models were linear regression, random-forest regression, XGBoost regression Chen and Guestrin, 2016, and support-vector regression. For classification, the candidates were multinomial logistic regression, random-forest classification, XGBoost classification, and support-vector classification. Their evaluation metrics, principal model configurations, and imbalance-handling settings are specified in Section 4.4.
The primary performance estimates were obtained using repeated cross-validation on the retained 382-case dataset. Regression used repeated five-fold cross-validation with 10 repeats, and classification used the stratified variant so that class proportions were approximately preserved within each fold; a random seed of 42 was used solely for reproducibility and has no physical significance. Across the resulting 50 train–validation iterations, each candidate model was fitted only on the training portion of the corresponding fold and evaluated on its held-out validation portion.
The repeated cross-validation results were used as the primary basis for comparing the candidate model families. The reported regression and classification metrics therefore represent the mean and standard deviation across the 50 validation folds rather than the result of a single partition. The earlier single five-fold results are retained only as a reproducibility comparison in Supplementary Table S6.
After the candidate model families had been compared, a separate stratified 80/20 split was generated using random seed 42 to support sample-level visualization and interpretation. The split contained 305 development cases and 77 held-out cases. The model fitted on the 80% development portion was used to generate the predicted-versus-simulated regression plot, the classification confusion matrix, and the selected case-level explanations. The 77 held-out cases were not used to fit the model that generated the corresponding predictions; training isolation therefore holds for these visualizations.
The 77 cases should not, however, be described as an independent or model-selection-independent test set: before the 80/20 split was constructed, all 382 cases had already participated in the repeated cross-validation comparison of the four candidate families. The two procedures therefore serve different purposes. The repeated cross-validation provides the primary quantitative comparison and supplies every performance value reported in the Abstract, Results, and Conclusions, whereas the 80/20 split supplies sample-level plots, a confusion structure, and representative local explanations. Because the model family retained for interpretation was selected using the same cross-validation results, its reported performance is conditional on that selection; differences between closely performing models are therefore described cautiously, and the 80/20 results are treated as descriptive supporting evidence rather than an estimate of post-selection generalization.
No automated hyperparameter search, grid search, Bayesian optimization, or cross-validation-guided tuning was performed. The principal model settings were specified before the final comparison, while parameters not explicitly set retained their software-package defaults, as detailed in Section 4.4. This avoids an additional tuning-induced source of optimism, although it does not eliminate the model-family selection bias described above.

4.4.2 Model configurations, preprocessing, and imbalance handling
As described in Section 4.3, no automated or cross-validation-guided hyperparameter search was performed. The model configurations were fixed before the final repeated-cross-validation comparison, and unspecified parameters retained the defaults of the corresponding software implementation.
StandardScaler was included in the pipelines for linear regression, support-vector regression, multinomial logistic regression, and support-vector classification. Within each cross-validation iteration, the scaler was fitted only on the training fold and then applied to the corresponding validation fold, preventing preprocessing information from crossing the fold boundary. Random-forest and XGBoost models were fitted without feature scaling.
The principal manually specified settings included 300 estimators for the random-forest and XGBoost models, C = 10 for the support-vector models, and the learning-rate, tree-depth, and subsampling settings reported in Supplementary Table S5. Logistic regression used max_iter = 2000 to support numerical convergence rather than to optimize predictive performance.
Class imbalance was addressed during model fitting without altering the sample distribution. Logistic regression, random-forest classification, and support-vector classification used balanced class weights, whereas balanced sample weights were supplied to the XGBoost classifier. No oversampling, undersampling, or synthetic sample generation was applied. Random seed 42 was used where supported to make stochastic estimation and resampling reproducible; it has no physical significance. Complete preprocessing, model, random-state, convergence, and imbalance-handling settings are reported in Supplementary Table S5.
Because nested cross-validation was not performed, the results represent the specified configurations rather than globally optimized versions of the candidate algorithms.
4.4.3 SHAP procedure
SHAP was used to interpret the XGBoost regression and classification surrogates (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Lundberg et al., 2020). SHAP decomposes a model output into a baseline and additive predictor contributions. Positive and negative values indicate contributions that increase or decrease the relevant model output relative to its baseline.
For regression, SHAP values are expressed in kelvin and quantify the contribution of each predictor to the predicted
Global regression importance was calculated as the mean absolute SHAP value across evaluated cases. Global classification importance was calculated by averaging absolute SHAP values across both cases and the four output classes, producing one overall value for each predictor. Class-specific results, including those for the Critical class, were analysed separately and were not combined with the all-class averages. Local explanations were generated for representative cases from the 77-case held-out visualization subset described in Section 4.3.
SHAP analysis was restricted to XGBoost to maintain one attribution procedure across the regression and classification tasks. Under its adopted feature-dependence formulation, TreeSHAP computes exact Shapley values for tree ensembles (Lundberg et al., 2020). Applying model-agnostic KernelSHAP to the support-vector or linear candidates would require sampling-based approximation and a different attribution framework, so the resulting magnitudes would not be directly comparable with the TreeSHAP values.

5.4 Classification error structure and threshold sensitivity
The ordered structure of the four simulation-oriented thermal-risk classes was examined using out-of-fold predictions generated by a single stratified five-fold procedure with shuffling and random seed 42. Each of the 382 retained cases therefore received exactly one prediction from a classifier that had not been fitted using that case.
Under the reference thresholds of 5, 15, and 30 K, 21 of the 382 out-of-fold predictions were incorrect. All 21 errors occurred between adjacent classes, and no case crossed two or more class boundaries. Thus, no Normal case was assigned to Serious or Critical, and no Critical case was assigned to Warning or Normal. The classifier therefore generally preserved the ordinal structure of the labels when the exact class assignment was incorrect. However, adjacency alone does not demonstrate that every misclassified case was located immediately next to a numerical threshold.
These 21 out-of-fold errors should not be confused with the five errors shown in Figure 6. The former were obtained from the single five-fold out-of-fold analysis covering all 382 retained cases, whereas the latter arose from the separate 77-case held-out visualization subset. The repeated-cross-validation means and standard deviations in Table 6 remain the primary aggregate performance estimates; the two error counts are used only to characterize prediction behaviour under their respective resampling procedures.
Threshold sensitivity was assessed using the three schemes defined in Section 2.4. Under the lower thresholds of 4, 12, and 24 K, the class counts were 14, 141, 138, and 89. The corresponding repeated-cross-validation accuracy and macro F1 were 0.9251 ± 0.0317 and 0.8960 ± 0.0511, respectively. The single five-fold out-of-fold analysis contained 32 errors, all between adjacent classes, with no non-adjacent error.
For the reference thresholds of 5, 15, and 30 K, the class counts were 26, 174, 123, and 59. Accuracy reached 0.9377 ± 0.0266, and macro F1 reached 0.9407 ± 0.0337. The corresponding out-of-fold predictions contained 21 adjacent-class errors and no non-adjacent error.
Under the higher thresholds of 6, 18, and 36 K, the class counts became 39, 195, 106, and 42. Accuracy was 0.9346 ± 0.0274, while macro F1 was 0.9249 ± 0.0332. The out-of-fold analysis again produced 21 errors, all between adjacent classes. The complete threshold-sensitivity results are reported in Supplementary Table S2.
The lower scheme produced a particularly small Normal class of only 14 cases and exhibited both the lowest macro F1 and the greatest fold-to-fold variation in that metric. This result demonstrates why accuracy alone is insufficient for the present imbalanced classification problem. Raising the thresholds increased the number of Normal cases but reduced the Critical class to 42 cases, accompanied by a modest reduction in macro F1 relative to the reference scheme.
The diagnostics from the 5 × 10 repeated stratified cross-validation further clarify the observed variability. Across the 50 validation folds, macro F1 ranged from 0.794 to 0.991. In the lowest-performing fold (repeat 8, fold 3), Normal-class precision, recall, and F1 were 1.000, 0.200, and 0.333, respectively, whereas the F1-scores of the Warning, Serious, and Critical classes were 0.901, 0.941, and 1.000. Four of the five Normal cases in that fold were assigned to the adjacent Warning class, while all 12 Critical cases were correctly classified. The highest-performing fold (repeat 3, fold 4) reached a macro F1 of 0.991, with a Normal-class F1 of 1.000. The low-to-high variation therefore reflects the sensitivity of a macro-averaged metric to the small number of Normal cases within individual folds rather than a change in the dominant error mechanism.
Their comparatively balanced class distribution and stable macro-level performance support their use as the principal discretization in the present simulation study. Across all three schemes, the absence of non-adjacent errors indicates that the classifier retained the ordering of simulated thermal severity as the numerical class boundaries changed. These findings do not convert the classes into standardized field alarm levels; their operational interpretation, experimental validation requirements, and applicability limits are discussed in Section 5.5.
5.5 Applicability, limitations, and validation requirements
The present study establishes a numerically consistent simulation-to-surrogate workflow rather than an experimentally validated field-diagnostic system. The mesh-independence assessment, electrical-power consistency check, and comparison between the production mesh and the globally controlled sensitivity mesh support the internal numerical consistency of the finite-element implementation. These checks do not constitute experimental validation of the predicted temperatures, current-transfer paths, or contact-degradation states. Accordingly, the reported surrogate performance quantifies reproduction of the finite-element outputs within the simulated design space, rather than agreement with measurements from operating switchgear.
Several modelling assumptions delimit the interpretation of the electro-thermal results. The primary 400-case dataset was generated using constant material properties and one-way sequential electrical-to-thermal coupling. The thermal boundary conditions were also simplified. Convective cooling was represented by a prescribed heat-transfer coefficient, while detailed enclosure airflow, buoyancy-driven circulation, radiation exchange, nearby conductors, cabinet walls, and spatially varying ventilation were not explicitly resolved. These effects may alter both the absolute temperature field and the apparent contribution of h under operating conditions. In addition, the steel fasteners were included in the thermal domain but excluded from the electric-current domain. This assumption isolates the intended busbar-to-busbar current-transfer paths, but it may not apply to assemblies in which bolts, washers, surface coatings, or conductive contamination provide non-negligible parallel electrical paths.
The finite-element model describes one busbar geometry, material system, bolt arrangement, contact-patch representation, and set of boundary conditions. A separate sensitivity analysis of the assumed contact-layer thickness is provided in Supplementary Table S7. The surrogate is consequently geometry- and configuration-specific. Application to different conductor dimensions, overlap lengths, bolt spacings, materials, surface treatments, enclosure designs, or cooling arrangements would require additional simulations and preferably recalibration against measurements. Load current and ambient temperature can generally be measured directly, whereas Tang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021).
The machine-learning assessment has further limitations. The retained dataset comprised 382 simulated cases, including only 26 Normal cases under the reference threshold scheme. Repeated stratified cross-validation reduces dependence on a single partition but cannot replace evaluation on an external dataset. The learning curves in Supplementary Figure S3 show near-perfect training performance, including a classification training accuracy of 1.000, whereas validation performance remains lower and the validation curves have not fully plateaued at the largest training fraction. The remaining train–validation gap indicates that overfitting cannot be ruled out and further motivates evaluation with larger external datasets. As shown in Section 5.4, macro-averaged performance is also sensitive to the small number of Normal cases within individual folds, and a larger, more balanced dataset would be required to establish the stability of this error pattern.
The XGBoost family was selected after comparing four candidate algorithms on the same retained dataset, so its reported performance is conditional on that selection rather than a selection-independent estimate obtained from an external test set; the scatter plot and confusion matrix are correspondingly post-selection internal visualizations (Section 4.3).
The four thermal-risk classes were introduced as simulation-oriented modelling categories. Their thresholds were not derived from standards, maintenance records, insulation limits, experimentally established failure probabilities, or utility alarm criteria. The threshold-sensitivity analysis showed that the principal classification behaviour was not dependent on one exact set of boundaries, but this numerical robustness does not convert the labels into operational alarm levels. Field deployment would require application-specific thresholds linked to equipment design, loading history, allowable temperature limits, measurement uncertainty, and maintenance practice.

6 Conclusion
This study developed an interpretable simulation-to-surrogate framework for load-aware thermal-risk assessment of bolted switchgear busbar joints. A three-dimensional electro-thermal finite-element model was constructed to represent variations in load current, prescribed contact resistance, effective contact ratio, ambient temperature, and convective cooling. The contact formulation separately controlled
Of the 400 simulated cases, 382 were retained for surrogate development after excluding 18 cases with
SHAP analysis showed that load current and prescribed contact resistance dominated both continuous temperature-rise prediction and simulation-oriented class assignment. Convective cooling provided a smaller but physically meaningful contribution, while the global importance of
Across the lower, reference, and higher threshold schemes, all out-of-fold classification errors occurred between adjacent classes, with no non-adjacent error. The poorest repeated-cross-validation fold was primarily affected by upward misclassification of the sparsely represented Normal cases, while all Critical cases in that fold were correctly identified. These findings indicate preservation of the ordered thermal-severity structure, but they do not establish standardized operational alarm levels.
The proposed model remains a geometry-specific forward surrogate of finite-element outputs. It does not infer contact condition from infrared measurements and has not been experimentally validated. Future work should combine controlled bolted-joint experiments, calibrated thermal measurements, independently measured electrical quantities, evolving degradation states, and additional switchgear configurations to assess physical accuracy, transferability, and application-specific risk thresholds. Until such validation is completed, the framework should be used for simulation-based scenario assessment and interpretable sensitivity analysis rather than as a standalone field-diagnostic or maintenance-decision system.

records.body_text:
Celestica introduced the DS6005 at the OCP Global Summit, a co-packaged optics (CPO) data center switch that puts 102.4Tbps of switching capacity and 64 optically enabled 1.6TbE ports in a 1.5OU, fully liquid-cooled chassis for Open Rack v3. It is built on Broadcom’s Tomahawk 6 Davisson, the CPO version of the 102.4T Tomahawk 6, which integrates the optical engines onto the switch package so the front panel carries fiber connectors and laser modules in place of pluggable transceivers. Celestica is aiming it at AI/ML scale-up and scale-out fabrics.
The DS6005 lands in the same week as two other Tomahawk 6 CPO systems. Micas Networks put Davisson in a 1RU box with a Q1 2027 production date, and Supermicro’s 2OU CPO switch takes busbar power in an ORv3 rack. Celestica’s version is the one built for the OCP high-power rack from the start, with liquid cooling as the only cooling option and a chassis labeled for 46 to 56V DC input at 76A on the rear.
Optical Engine Integration
Co-packaging moves the optical engines from the faceplate onto the Tomahawk 6 Davisson package, which Celestica says removes the discrete digital signal processors and the long copper traces between the ASIC and a pluggable module, cutting link-level power and latency.
The lasers stay outside the package: the DS6005 carries 16 ELSFP external laser modules on the front panel that can be swapped in the field, so a failed laser does not take the switch out of service, and the 64 1.6TbE ports terminate in 16 MMC-16 fiber connectors. Celestica also cites CPO-aware software management for the platform, though it has not described what that covers.
“AI infrastructure is driving unprecedented demand for bandwidth, while power, thermal management, latency, and reach are becoming increasingly important constraints,” said Gavin Cato, SVP & GM Portfolio Solutions & AI Platform Engineering at Celestica. “The DS6005 brings co-packaged optics, liquid cooling, field-replaceable external laser modules, and CPO-aware software management together in a compact platform designed to help customers build scalable and power-efficient AI fabrics.”
Celestica has not published power or latency figures for the DS6005, so the savings over a pluggable-optics switch remain something to investigate further. Broadcom’s Manish Mehta, vice president of marketing and operations for its Optical Systems Division, said the partnership covers silicon, optical engines, packaging, thermal design, manufacturing, and system integration, and Dell’Oro Group’s Sameh Boujelbene noted in the same announcement that pluggable, near-package, and co-packaged optics will coexist as the ecosystem matures.
Thermal Management
The DS6005 is fully liquid-cooled in a 1.5OU chassis for ORv3-HPR, the OCP high-power rack, with the coolant quick-disconnects and the DC input on the rear panel. Celestica says the cooling keeps switch-level temperature stable, which improves reliability and allows denser racks, and its product page claims the design prevents thermal throttling. Beyond the switch ASIC and optics, the system runs an AMD Ryzen x86 host CPU with a BMC, carries TPM 2.0, a hardware root of trust, and post-quantum cryptography support, and has IEEE 1588 and SyncE timing hardware.
The switch runs SONiC with ONIE for installation, though Celestica has not named a SONiC release, and its specifications are preliminary and subject to change. The announcement and product documentation do not give sampling, shipping, or general-availability dates.

Silver Plating for Conductive Applications: Benefits and Limitations
Why Silver Shows Up in Conductive Work
When a part has to carry current with as little loss as possible, silver is one of the first finishes engineers consider. It conducts electricity better than any other metal and costs far less than gold.
That is why silver plating turns up on bus bars, switchgear contacts, and RF connectors. It also has limits, mainly tarnish and silver migration, and both are worth planning for before a part goes into production. Knowing those limits up front is what makes silver electroplating a sound choice and keeps it from becoming an expensive surprise.
Benefits of Silver Plating for Conductive Applications
Highest conductivity of any metal
Silver conducts electricity better than any other metal, slightly ahead of copper and well ahead of gold. As a plated surface, it gives current a low-resistance path right where parts meet. That surface is where losses can show up first, so finishing it with the best available conductor can make a real difference on parts that carry high current.
Low contact resistance
Clean silver has low contact resistance, which matters most at joints carrying high current. Less resistance at a joint means less heat, and less heat means less stress on the joint over time. In switchgear and power connectors, that can help a connection stay stable through years of service.
Performance at high frequencies
At high frequencies, current crowds into a thin layer near the surface of a conductor. This is called the skin effect. On RF and microwave parts, that surface layer may be the plating itself, so a silver finish can lower signal loss even when the base metal underneath conducts less well.
Solderability
Fresh silver plating solders well, which is one reason it is used on electronic parts that need a solderable surface. Solder wets clean silver readily, which helps form a sound joint. That advantage fades as the surface tarnishes, so parts meant for soldering are best soldered while the finish is fresh or protected as described later in this article.
Cost
Silver costs far less than gold. For larger parts, or for thicker deposits where gold would be too expensive, that difference can decide the finish. Bus bars are a good example: plating the whole surface of a large conductive part in gold would rarely make sense.
Where Silver Plating Is Used
As a conductive plating, silver shows up wherever the surface carries the current:
- Bus bars and power distribution components
- Switchgear and circuit breaker contacts
- High-current connectors, including battery and electric vehicle connections
- RF and microwave components, such as coaxial connectors and waveguides
- Electronic parts that need a solderable surface
- Medical devices, including electrosurgical electrodes, RF ablation devices, MRI and RF coil components, and contacts in wearable monitors
In each case, conductivity at the surface matters more than any other property of the finish. That is the job silver does best as an electrical contact plating. On medical devices, silver can also be applied selectively, so only the conductive areas of a part are plated.
Limitations of Silver Plating
Tarnish
Silver reacts with sulfur compounds in the air, such as hydrogen sulfide, and forms a dark film of silver sulfide. The film can raise contact resistance, especially on low-force contacts that cannot wipe through it, and it can reduce solderability.
Higher-force contacts may break through a light film on their own. That is part of why silver works well in power applications and less well on delicate signal contacts.
Silver migration
Under a DC voltage with moisture present, silver ions can move from one conductor toward another and grow thin, branching deposits called dendrites. If a dendrite bridges the gap, it can short the circuit. The risk rises with closer spacing, higher humidity, and higher voltage, so silver may be a poor fit for fine-pitch circuitry that will see moisture in service.
Wear and galling
Silver is soft. On sliding contacts that cycle many times, it can wear through or gall, which is when the two surfaces stick and tear. A harder bright silver deposit or a contact lubricant can extend life. For high-cycle sliding contacts, another finish may be a better match.
Underplate and adhesion
Silver plating normally starts with a silver strike, a thin first layer from a dilute bath that helps the deposit bond. On copper and copper alloys, a nickel underplate may be added as a barrier. Without it, copper can diffuse into the silver at elevated temperatures and weaken the bond.
RF parts call for more care. Nickel is magnetic and can add signal loss if the silver layer above it is thin, so some designers skip the nickel, specify enough silver to keep the current out of it, or use palladium as the underplate instead, since palladium is not magnetic.
Specifying Silver Plating
Standards
Engineering silver plating is commonly specified to ASTM B700, which classifies silver deposits by purity (type), appearance (grade), and whether a supplementary tarnish treatment is applied (class). Older drawings may still call out the federal spec QQ-S-365, and aerospace work may reference AMS 2410 or AMS 2411. Our article on the evolution of silver plating standards covers how these specs relate.
What a complete callout covers
A drawing that spells out these points gives the plater what it needs to quote and plate the part correctly:
- The specification, with type, grade, and class
- Minimum thickness, and where on the part it is measured
- Underplate, if any
- Packaging requirements
Leaving any of these open means the plater has to guess, and a guess on packaging can show up as tarnished parts at receiving inspection. Thickness deserves particular care, since it can drive both the cost and how long the finish holds up to wear.
Protecting parts from tarnish
Anti-tarnish treatments applied after plating can slow the reaction, and on an ASTM B700 callout the class sets whether one is used. Packaging matters too. Sulfur-free paper and sealed bags help, and plated parts should be kept away from rubber bands and some cardboard, which can give off sulfur compounds. A part that leaves the plater clean can still arrive tarnished if it is packed wrong.
Silver or Gold?
Gold does not tarnish, so it is a common choice for low-force signal contacts and for parts that may sit in storage before use. Silver conducts better and costs less, which makes it a strong option for power and high-current contacts with enough force to break through a light film. The better fit depends on contact force, current, operating environment, and how long parts will sit before they go into service.
Silver Plating at ProPlate
ProPlate provides medical silver plating and industrial silver plating, with a nickel underplate where the base metal calls for it and a tarnish-resistant treatment for parts that need one. Work can be done to specifications including ASTM B700, QQ-S-365, AMS 2410, and AMS 2411. If you are weighing silver against another finish, ask an expert early, while the spec can still be shaped around the part.

Integrated Laser Cleaning and Welding System for Automotive Busbars
Integrated Laser Cleaning and Welding System for Automotive Busbars
- October 16, 2026
Copper busbars are essential components in electric vehicle (EV) power distribution systems and electronic control units. They carry high currents between batteries, power electronics, and electrical connections. Consistent weld quality is critical to electrical conductivity, connection reliability, and overall system safety.
However, laser welding copper presents two major challenges: surface contamination and the material’s high thermal conductivity and reflectivity at infrared wavelengths. Oxide layers, oil residues, paint, and insulating coatings can interfere with laser energy absorption and weld formation. Copper also dissipates heat rapidly, making stable energy input and precise positioning essential.
Han’s Laser Integrated Laser Cleaning and Welding Gantry System for Automotive Busbars combines surface cleaning and laser welding in one machine. By integrating both processes with dual workstations, laser distance measurement, and welding data tracking, the system helps streamline production and improve process consistency.
Integrated Laser Cleaning and Welding
The system combines a laser cleaning unit and a laser welding unit on a single gantry platform. Before welding, the cleaning station removes paint, oxide layers, or other specified surface coatings from the busbar. The workpiece can then proceed directly to welding without intermediate transfer or secondary clamping.
This integrated approach reduces handling steps and repeated positioning, helping minimize alignment errors between cleaning and welding. It also supports a more efficient production sequence for busbars with multiple welding points.
Dual-Station Layout for Flexible Production
The left-right dual-station configuration allows cleaning and welding operations to be organized in alternating or coordinated production cycles, depending on the application.
This layout helps improve equipment utilization and supports continuous production across different product types. It is particularly useful for manufacturers processing multiple busbar designs or components that require both surface preparation and precision welding.
Gantry Design and Real-Time Distance Measurement
The gantry structure features a vertically downward-facing welding station, providing flexibility for different component geometries and fixture arrangements.
Laser distance measurement is integrated at each station to detect workpiece position and height variations in real time. This capability helps compensate for incoming-part variation and reduces the risk of welding deviations caused by inconsistent workpiece positioning.
For busbars with multiple weld locations, accurate positioning is especially important for maintaining consistent joint placement across production batches.
Semi-Automated Operation and Process Traceability
The system uses a semi-automated production approach that combines operator-assisted handling with automated cleaning and welding operations. This configuration helps balance production flexibility with repeatable processing.
Key capabilities include:
- Integrated process flow: Combines cleaning and welding within one machine.
- Reduced handling: Eliminates intermediate transfer and secondary clamping between the two processes.
- Real-time distance measurement: Detects workpiece position variations at both stations.
- Automated data recording: Saves welding data and uploads it to the designated system for traceability.
- Quality analysis: Provides historical welding parameters to support investigation of quality issues and process improvement.
- User-friendly operation: An intuitive human-machine interface simplifies routine operation and maintenance.
Data availability and system integration can be configured according to production management requirements.
Applications in EV Manufacturing and Beyond
Automotive Busbar Welding
The laser cleaning and welding system is designed for copper busbars used in EV battery packs, electronic control units, power distribution units (PDUs), and battery module connections. Online cleaning before welding helps prepare coated or oxidized surfaces for the joining process.
Laser Welding
Copper-to-Copper and Terminal Connections
It can be configured for overlapping copper busbars and connections between copper busbars and terminals. The downward-facing welding arrangement supports different workpiece orientations and joint configurations, subject to fixture and process validation.
Other Metal Components Requiring Pre-Weld Cleaning
The integrated architecture can also be evaluated for other metal components that require paint removal, coating removal, or oxide cleaning before laser welding.
Laser Cleaning
The system is particularly relevant to applications involving multiple weld points, variable incoming-part dimensions, frequent product changeovers, or production traceability requirements.
A More Integrated Approach to Busbar Welding
Reliable busbar welding depends not only on laser parameters but also on surface condition, positioning accuracy, and coordination between process steps.
By integrating laser cleaning and welding with dual-station operation, real-time distance measurement, and welding data tracking, Han’s Laser provides a coordinated solution for automotive busbar manufacturing. The system helps reduce unnecessary handling, manage workpiece variation, and support more consistent, traceable production.
Contact Han’s Laser to discuss an integrated cleaning and welding solution for your busbar components and production requirements.

records.body_text:
Combined Environmental Reliability Testing for EV Busbars: Temperature, Humidity, and 3-Axis Random Vibration
Oct 17, 2026 View: 109
EV battery-pack busbars cannot be qualified reliably through temperature, humidity, or vibration tests performed in isolation. A combined environmental profile exposes the actual interaction between thermal expansion, moisture, mechanical preload loss, fretting at bolted interfaces, and insulation stress, allowing failure mechanisms to be identified before vehicle-level durability testing.
For high-voltage battery applications, Apollo evaluates busbar assemblies under customer-defined combined profiles that can include -40°C to 125°C temperature cycling, up to 95% RH, and 3-axis random vibration, with vibration methodology referenced to ISO 16750-3 where applicable. Electrical resistance, fastening integrity, insulation condition, and post-test dimensional characteristics are correlated with the environmental load history.
-40°C to 125°C Thermal Cycling and 95% RH: Why Single-Factor Testing Misses Busbar Failures
Thermal Expansion at ΔT = 165°C: Copper, Aluminum, Insulation, and Fasteners
A busbar assembly contains materials with different coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE).
A temperature range from -40°C to 125°C produces a thermal span of 165°C. Copper, aluminum, polymer insulation, stainless-steel fasteners, and plated interfaces respond differently to this temperature change.
This differential expansion can generate:
Bolt preload variation
Contact-interface shear
Localized bending stress
Insulation movement
Cracking around formed sections
Fretting at bolted joints
A busbar that passes a static resistance test at 23°C may therefore show a different resistance profile after repeated thermal cycling.
95% RH and Condensation: Corrosion and Interface Degradation
High relative humidity creates an additional mechanism at exposed interfaces.
Potential failure locations include:
Plated copper terminals
Bolt and washer interfaces
Exposed conductor edges
Insulation defects
Crimped or welded transition areas
Moisture combined with temperature variation can accelerate surface oxidation and corrosion products. At a bolted electrical interface, even a small increase in contact resistance becomes significant at hundreds of amperes because
That 16 W is generated locally at the connection rather than distributed along the entire busbar.
ISO 16750-3 Vibration and Environmental Interaction: Mechanical Loading
ISO 16750-3 addresses mechanical loads for road vehicles and provides vibration-test approaches according to component location and vehicle application.
For an EV battery-pack busbar, the relevant mechanical environment may contain:
Broadband random vibration
Multiple vibration axes
Road-induced shocks
Resonance amplification
Fastener excitation
Local bending of flexible sections
The test profile must be established from the vehicle location, mounting structure, mass, and customer durability specification rather than assigning one universal vibration spectrum to every battery busbar.
3-Axis Random Vibration and 165°C Thermal Span: Combined Test Architecture
Three-Axis Excitation at X/Y/Z: Replicating Battery-Pack Mechanical Loads
A production busbar assembly should be mounted using the same:
Fasteners
Torque specification
Insulation components
Support brackets
Connector interfaces
Mounting points
used in the vehicle or battery-pack configuration.
The three principal directions are normally evaluated as:
Axis | Typical Mechanical Concern | Busbar Failure Mechanism
---|---|---
X-axis | Longitudinal excitation | Terminal/interface shear
Y-axis | Lateral excitation | Fastener loosening and bending
Z-axis | Vertical excitation | Support fatigue and resonance
Combined sequence | Multi-directional loading | Interaction of thermal and mechanical stresses
The objective is not simply to demonstrate that the copper conductor survives vibration. The complete assembly must maintain electrical and mechanical functionality.
Random Vibration PSD at Vehicle-Specific Frequencies: Resonance Control
Random vibration is normally defined using a power spectral density (PSD) profile in:
The highest mechanical stress may occur near a natural frequency rather than at the highest nominal acceleration.
For this reason, engineering validation should identify:
Natural frequency
Resonance frequency
Damping ratio
Mode shape
Acceleration response
Relative displacement between mounting points
A busbar with a long unsupported copper span can exhibit significantly higher dynamic displacement than a short rigid conductor.
Thermal-Vibration Interaction at -40°C and 125°C: Structural Resonance Shift
Temperature changes can alter polymer modulus, copper stress state, insulation flexibility, and joint stiffness.
At low temperature:
Polymer insulation may become less compliant
Flexible support elements can stiffen
Thermal contraction increases interface displacement
At high temperature:
Polymer modulus can decrease
Insulation may soften
Fastener preload can change
Differential thermal expansion increases
The vibration test should therefore include temperature states representative of the intended vehicle environment rather than relying exclusively on room-temperature vibration.
Fastener Preload at 400–800V and mΩ Resistance: Monitoring Bolted Busbar Interfaces
Belleville Washer Preload at High Vibration: Preventing Joint Loosening
Bolted busbar connections depend on stable clamping force.
A typical joint consists of:
Bolt → Belleville washer → terminal → busbar → mating terminal → nut
The preload creates the normal force required to maintain a low-resistance electrical interface.
A Belleville washer can provide controlled elastic displacement as the joint stack-up changes through thermal expansion and vibration.
Compared with a rigid flat washer, the spring characteristic of a Belleville washer can provide greater compensation for small changes in joint compression.
Preload Loss After 3-Axis Vibration: Torque Is Not Enough
Initial bolt torque does not prove long-term joint integrity.
Torque is an indirect indicator of preload because friction at the thread and bearing surface consumes a large portion of applied torque.
For reliability validation, Apollo can correlate:
Initial tightening torque
Initial bolt preload
Thermal cycling
Vibration exposure
Final preload
Contact resistance
Interface wear
A useful engineering acceptance criterion is therefore based on measured preload retention and electrical resistance, not torque alone.
Fretting Wear at <1 mΩ Interfaces: Resistance Growth Detection
Microscopic relative movement between two contacting surfaces can cause fretting.
The process may generate:
Removal of plating
Oxide formation
Metallic debris
Reduced real contact area
Increased contact resistance
Localized Joule heating
The failure can develop gradually, making continuous or periodic four-wire resistance measurement more informative than visual inspection alone.
For high-current EV busbars, resistance changes should be tracked against:
Cycle count
Temperature
Vibration axis
RMS acceleration
Joint preload
Interface condition
Flexible Copper Foil and Braided Transition Sections: Reducing Resonance-Induced Shear Stress
Multi-Layer Copper Foil at High Flexibility: Strain Distribution
Rigid copper busbars are efficient for short, fixed-distance connections but can transmit mechanical displacement directly between mounting points.
A flexible transition section changes the mechanical load path.
Common structures include:
Multi-layer copper foil
Laminated copper foil
Copper braided conductor
Stamped flexible links
Braided copper expansion connectors
The flexible section absorbs relative displacement between battery modules, busbar terminals, and structural supports.
Flexible Braided Copper at 100% IACS-Class Conductivity: Electrical and Mechanical Trade-Off
Electrical conductivity and mechanical flexibility must be evaluated together.
Structure | Electrical Path | Flexibility | Vibration Accommodation | Typical Use
---|---|---|---|---
Rigid C1100 copper bar | Low resistance | Low | Low | Fixed connection
Multi-layer copper foil | Low resistance | High | High | Battery interconnect
Braided copper conductor | Low resistance | Very high | Very high | Expansion/vibration transition
Laminated busbar | Low inductance potential | Medium | Medium | Power electronics
Flexible stamped copper link | Low resistance | Medium–High | High | Compact battery modules
High-purity copper such as C1100 can provide conductivity approaching 100% IACS, depending on material condition and specification.
Stray Inductance <10nH: Flexible Geometry in High-Speed Power Switching
For high-current switching systems, mechanical flexibility does not remove electrical design requirements.
A laminated or closely coupled conductor geometry can reduce loop area and associated parasitic inductance.
Even a small inductance becomes relevant when (di/dt) is high.
Therefore, flexible sections used around inverter or battery switching structures should be evaluated for both:
Mechanical strain relief
Electrical loop geometry
The final geometry depends on current rating, switching frequency, insulation system, mounting envelope, and customer electromagnetic compatibility requirements.
Insulation Sleeve at 125°C and Dielectric Strength >15kV/mm: Detecting Environmental Cracking
Thermal Stress at -40°C to 125°C: Polymer Insulation Failure Points
Busbar insulation can fail even when the copper conductor remains electrically functional.
High-risk locations include:
Sharp stamped edges
Formed corners
Bolt holes
Terminal transitions
Molded supports
Areas under mechanical compression
Repeated thermal expansion and contraction can produce tensile strain in the polymer.
At the same time, random vibration can create cyclic bending around the same location.
The combined mechanism is more severe than either load alone.
UL 94 V-0 Insulation and High-Voltage Dielectric Testing
For EV battery applications, insulation material selection may involve:
Operating temperature rating
Dielectric strength
Flame resistance
Chemical resistance
Tracking resistance
Environmental aging
Where specified by the material system, UL 94 V-0 can be used as a flammability classification.
A dielectric strength specification such as >15 kV/mm must be treated as a material or system-specific requirement and verified under the applicable test method.
The test program should also examine insulation after environmental exposure for:
Cracks
Pinholes
Delamination
Edge lifting
Abrasion
Carbonized areas
Post-Test Insulation Resistance at 400–800V: Electrical Safety Verification
Environmental testing should be followed by electrical inspection.
Depending on the customer's validation specification, measurements can include:
Insulation resistance
Dielectric withstand
Leakage current
Hi-pot test
Visual insulation inspection
Continuity testing
The electrical acceptance limits should be established from the vehicle architecture and applicable safety standard.
CMM Inspection at ±0.01mm and Resistance Mapping: Pre-Test and Post-Test Correlation
CMM Measurement at ±0.01mm: Detecting Permanent Deformation
Environmental testing should not end with a pass/fail electrical result.
A busbar may retain electrical continuity while experiencing permanent mechanical deformation.
CMM inspection can measure:
Terminal position
Hole-to-hole distance
Flatness
Bend angle
Mounting height
Flexible-section geometry
Connector alignment
Pre-test and post-test measurements are compared to identify permanent dimensional drift.
Four-Wire Resistance at mΩ Resolution: Mapping Joint Degradation
A four-wire Kelvin measurement separates voltage-sensing leads from current-carrying leads, reducing measurement error caused by lead resistance.
For busbar qualification, resistance should be recorded:
Before test → during defined intervals → after test
This creates a resistance-versus-cycle profile.
A resistance increase should then be correlated with:
Fastener preload loss
Fretting marks
Oxidation
Plating wear
Copper deformation
Thermal exposure
Cross-Section Analysis and Microscopy: Identifying Fretting and Fatigue
When resistance increases after vibration, destructive analysis can locate the failure mechanism.
Typical analysis includes:
Optical microscopy
Metallographic cross-section
SEM where required
Plating thickness measurement
Surface morphology analysis
Joint fracture analysis
The objective is to distinguish between electrical interface degradation and bulk conductor fatigue.
ISO 16750-3 Vibration and EV Battery Validation: From Component Test to Vehicle Durability
Battery-Pack Mounting at -40°C to 125°C: Test Fixture Fidelity
A test fixture must reproduce the mechanical boundary conditions of the production installation.
Fixture design should account for:
Mounting-point stiffness
Fastener type
Torque
Support spacing
Cable routing
Busbar mass
Connector constraints
An overly rigid fixture can suppress real vibration modes. An overly flexible fixture can introduce artificial resonance.
Therefore, fixture modal behavior should be checked before interpreting component test data.
Combined Environmental Test Matrix: Temperature × Humidity × Vibration
A structured validation matrix may be organized as follows:
Test Stage | Temperature | Humidity | Vibration | Primary Measurement
---|---|---|---|---
Baseline | 23°C | Ambient | None | Resistance + dimensions
Low-temperature exposure | -40°C | Defined by profile | Defined PSD | Resistance + function
High-temperature exposure | 125°C | Defined by profile | Defined PSD | Resistance + insulation
High-RH exposure | Defined by profile | Up to 95% RH | Defined PSD | Corrosion + insulation
Combined profile | -40°C to 125°C | Up to 95% RH | X/Y/Z random | Full electrical/mechanical data
Post-test | 23°C | Ambient | None | CMM + resistance + visual
Not every program requires simultaneous maximum temperature, maximum humidity, and maximum vibration. The test matrix should reflect the vehicle duty cycle and customer specification.
Failure Mode Analysis at IATF 16949: PFMEA-Driven Reliability Testing
Environmental reliability testing becomes more useful when each test condition is linked to a predefined failure mode.
For an automotive busbar program, PFMEA can identify:
Joint loosening
Fretting corrosion
Conductor fatigue
Insulation cracking
Plating degradation
Terminal deformation
Resistance increase
Dielectric failure
The Control Plan can then define the corresponding production controls and inspection frequencies.
This creates a closed engineering loop:
Design → FEA → Prototype → Environmental Test → Failure Analysis → DFM → Tooling → SPC → PPAP Level 3 → Mass Production
Apollo EV Busbar Reliability Engineering: C1100 Copper, Flexible Links, and PPAP Level 3
C1100 Copper at High Conductivity: Material and Forming Control
Apollo's EV busbar manufacturing process can incorporate precision copper stamping, bending, forming, surface treatment, insulation, and flexible transition structures according to the customer's drawing and electrical specification.
Typical engineering inputs include:
C1100/C10200 copper grades
Copper thickness
Plating specification
Bend radius
Hole diameter
Mounting pitch
Insulation requirement
Current rating
Temperature rise limit
Precision Stamping at ±0.01mm: Geometry and Assembly Fit
Critical busbar dimensions can be monitored using:
CMM inspection
Optical measurement
Go/no-go gauges
Flatness measurement
Burr inspection
SPC
Dimensional tolerances should be assigned according to functional requirements rather than applying ±0.01mm indiscriminately to every feature.
PPAP Level 3 and IATF 16949: Production Validation Documentation
For automotive programs, Apollo can structure project quality documentation around customer PPAP requirements, including:
Process Flow Diagram
PFMEA
Control Plan
Dimensional Inspection Report
Material Certification
MSA documentation
SPC data
Capability studies
Functional test results
Sample submission records
The final submission level and specific documents remain subject to the customer's purchasing and quality requirements.
FAQ
What temperature range should an EV busbar environmental reliability test use?
A customer-defined profile may include -40°C to 125°C for EV battery applications. The actual temperature limits, dwell time, transition rate, and number of cycles should be based on the battery-pack location and vehicle validation specification.
How is EV busbar random vibration testing performed?
The busbar assembly is mounted in its production configuration and exposed to vehicle-specific vibration profiles, commonly including X/Y/Z excitation. ISO 16750-3 can provide the mechanical test framework, while the customer defines the applicable PSD and duration.
How can Apollo detect busbar failure after combined thermal and vibration testing?
Apollo can compare pre- and post-test CMM dimensions, four-wire resistance, fastener preload, insulation condition, and interface wear. Metallographic analysis can then identify fretting, fatigue, corrosion, or joint degradation.
