\#\#\# 2\.3 Ionic liquid and DLLME extraction system

The recovery medium used throughout this work was 1\-butyl\-1\-methylpyrrolidinium bis\(trifluoromethylsulfonyl\)imide \(\[BMPyrr\]\[TFSI\]\)\, which served as the water\-immiscible receiving phase in the DLLME process\. The general procedure is summarized schematically in Figure 1\. The ionic liquid\, pre\-dissolved in a water\-miscible polar disperser\, was rapidly injected into the aqueous sample to generate a fine cloudy dispersion\. Centrifugation subsequently coalesced the dispersed droplets and produced a dense ionic\-liquid\-rich phase that could be collected for analysis\. Physicochemical measurements reported for \[BMPyrr\]\[TFSI\] show a density of approximately 1\.40 g cm−3 near room temperature\, together with well\-characterized viscosity and thermal behaviour\, properties that are advantageous for formation and sedimentation of a discrete receiving phase \(\)\.

FIGURE 1

\[BMPyrr\]\[TFSI\] functioned as the hydrophobic\, dense and chemically stable receiving phase in the DLLME system\. Its water immiscibility limits loss of the receiving phase during dispersion\, while a density of approximately 1\.40 gcm−3 near room temperature favours formation of a sedimented ionic\-liquid\-rich phase after centrifugation \(\)\. Pyrrolidinium\-TFSI systems also exhibit chemical and thermal stability under the mild conditions used here\, and the TFSI anion and pyrrolidinium cation provide characteristic FTIR bands for assessment of solvent integrity before and after extraction \(\; \; \)\. No comparative screening against alternative ionic liquids was performed\; consequently\, relative Cr\- or Ni\-specific affinity among ionic\-liquid families was not determined\.

TFSI− is a weakly coordinating anion\, and metal transfer in ionic\-liquid extraction depends on aqueous speciation\, complex formation\, ion pairing\, ionic strength and phase\-volume ratio\. Under the investigated conditions \[BMPyrr\]\[TFSI\] formed a separable dense receiving phase after dispersion and centrifugation\. Relative extraction performance against imidazolium\-\, ammonium\- or phosphonium\-based ionic liquids was not measured in the experimental programme \(\)\.

\#\#\# 2\.4 Chromium\-recovery experiments

For chromium recovery\, five parameters were screened sequentially\. Extractant volume was varied from 100 to 600 μL at an initial chromium concentration of 20 ppm\, pH 6\.0\, 3000 rpm and 10 min\. Feed concentration was examined from 10 to 60 ppm at 400 µL extractant\, pH 6\.0 and 3000 rpm\. Centrifugation speed was studied using a 10 ppm feed\, 400 µL extractant and pH 6\.0\, and centrifugation time was varied from 3 to 18 min at 3000 rpm\. Finally\, NaCl addition \(0\.1–0\.6 g\) was tested at pH 6\.0\, 2000 rpm and 15 min\. This sequential single\-factor design generated the response profiles used to identify the highest measured response within each operating range \(\; \)\.

\#\#\# 2\.5 Nickel aqueous\-phase removal experiments

The nickel aqueous\-phase removal experiments covered a wider concentration and ionic\-liquid\-volume range than the chromium experiments\. Initial Ni concentration was varied from 40 to 240 ppm and ionic\-liquid volume from 1 to 6 mL\, with pH maintained at 10\. Centrifugation speed was varied between 500 and 3000 rpm\, and NaCl addition between 0\.4 and 2\.4 g\. At pH 10\, aqueous Ni depletion can arise from ionic\-liquid partitioning together with hydroxo\-speciation\, complexation and solid formation\; the measured response therefore represents the combined decrease in dissolved aqueous Ni under each condition \(\; \)\.

\#\#\# 2\.6 Phase disengagement\, salting\-out and recovery calculation

Centrifugation was used to promote coalescence of the dispersed ionic\-liquid droplets and separation of the ionic\-liquid\-rich phase from the aqueous phase\. Sodium chloride was added in both single\-factor studies to examine ionic\-strength and salting\-out effects\. Recovery\/removal was calculated directly from the aqueous\-phase mass balance \(Equation 1\) using AAS\-measured concentrations before and after treatment\:

When the change in aqueous\-phase volume is negligible \(Vo ≈ Vf\)\, the expression reduces to Equation 2\,
R\%\=CoVo−CfVf\/CoVox100\(1\)
\(1\)
R\%\=Co−Cf\/Cox100\(2\)
\(2\)

Here\, C0 and Cf are the initial and final aqueous metal concentrations measured by AAS\, and V0 and Vf are the corresponding aqueous\-phase volumes\. The mass\-balance response quantifies the decrease in dissolved aqueous metal and does not distinguish ionic\-liquid transfer from precipitation or co\-sedimentation\. MATLAB served solely as a numerical calculation and plotting environment for the experimentally measured values\. No regression equation\, response\-surface model\, machine\-learning model\, fitted kinetic expression or independently optimized parameter set was used to generate the reported responses\. Lines connecting the measured points are visual guides and were not generated by regression\. Replicate\-level uncertainty estimates were not available for the screening dataset\; the figures therefore show the measured responses without error bars\, and inferential statistical tests were not performed\. R2 and RMSE were not calculated because no predictive model was fitted\.

\#\#\# 2\.7 AAS screening of real industrial samples

Five real industrial wastewaters were screened by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy \(AAS\)\: pharmaceutical wastewater \(S1\)\, industrial sewage \(S2\)\, leather\-industry wastewater \(S3\)\, paint\/coating wastewater \(S4\) and metal\-plating wastewater \(S5\)\. AAS was used to quantify total chromium in the screened samples\; no independent Cr\(III\)\/Cr\(VI\) speciation measurement was performed\. The Cr concentrations determined by AAS were used to select the plating wastewater matrix for the subsequent Cr recovery experiments \(\)\.

\#\#\# 2\.8 Ionic\-liquid recycling\, FTIR and SEM\-EDX characterization

Post\-extraction solvent and recovered solids were evaluated by reuse tests\, FTIR spectroscopy and SEM\-EDX analysis\. The reuse experiment tracked extraction performance over three consecutive cycles of \[BMPyrr\]\[TFSI\] without intermediate regeneration\. FTIR spectra recorded before and after extraction were used to assess retention of the principal functional\-group signatures of the ionic liquid\, providing qualitative evidence of structural stability \(\; \)\. SEM\-EDX was used for morphological examination and semi\-quantitative elemental assessment of the recovered chromium\-containing material using an UltraPlus instrument \(Carl Zeiss NTS\, Germany\) fitted with a Flash Quad 5060F EDX detector \(Bruker Nano GmbH\, Germany\)\, operated at 20 kV with a 50 s live time\.

\#\# 3 Results and discussion

\#\#\# 3\.1 Physicochemical properties of the source streams

The Cr\-bearing industrial wastewater and Ni\-bearing aqueous feed were alkaline and contained substantial dissolved and suspended solids\. Their measured pH values were 10\.0 and 9\.5\, respectively\. These chemically complex matrices can affect DLLME through ionic background\, particulate settling and phase\-separation behaviour \(\; \)\.

The Cr\-bearing stream contained TDS \= 9742\.47 mg\/L and TSS \= 3471\.38 mg\/L\, while the Ni\-bearing feed contained TDS \= 7835\.98 mg\/L and TSS \= 2987\.36 mg\/L\. Total hardness values were 568 and 479 mg\/L as CaCO3\, respectively\. These measurements indicate a substantial dissolved and particulate background\. In separation terms\, particulate material can sediment during centrifugation\, and added salt can alter solvation\, interfacial transfer and phase disengagement \(\; \)\.

\#\#\# 3\.2 Single\-factor screening for chromium and nickel

The operating variables investigated for Cr and Ni included initial metal concentration\, ionic\-liquid volume\, centrifugation conditions and NaCl addition\. Because the experimental ranges and fixed conditions differed between the two metals\, each response was evaluated within its own single\-factor operating window\. Table 2 consolidates the experimental ranges\, fixed conditions\, best observed values\, maximum observed response and qualitative response pattern\.

\#\#\# 3\.3 Chromium recovery as a function of extraction conditions

The chromium data showed distinct local maxima across the investigated single\-factor ranges\. Increasing the extractant volume from 100 to 400 µL raised Cr recovery from about 35\% to approximately 89\% \(Figure 2a\)\, whereas further increases to 500 and 600 µL reduced recovery to 73\% and 61\%\, respectively\. Thus\, 400 µL produced the highest measured recovery within the extractant\-volume series under the corresponding fixed conditions \(\; \)\.

FIGURE 2

Feed concentration strongly affected the measured Cr response \(Figure 2b\)\. Recovery was 86\% at a 10 ppm feed\, 46\% at 20 ppm and 13\% at 60 ppm\. Under the fixed solvent condition\, recovery therefore decreased as the initial Cr loading increased\, a trend consistent with finite receiving\-phase capacity and changes in the solute\-to\-solvent ratio \(\; \)\.

The highest Cr recovery in the centrifugation\-speed series occurred at 2000 rpm \(83\%\; Figure 2c\)\. Recovery was 46\% at 500 rpm and decreased to 71\% and 53\% at 2500 and 3000 rpm\, respectively\. In the centrifugation\-time series \(Figure 2d\)\, recovery increased from 49\% at 3 min to 93\% at 15 min and decreased to 71\% at 18 min\. The corresponding local maxima were therefore 2000 rpm for centrifugation speed and 15 min for centrifugation time under their respective fixed conditions\.

NaCl addition produced a non\-monotonic Cr response \(Figure 2e\)\. Recovery increased from 47\% at 0\.1 g to 86\% at 0\.4 g and then decreased to 68\% at 0\.5 g and 59\% at 0\.6 g\. Ionic\-strength changes can modify aqueous solvation\, interfacial transfer\, viscosity and phase disengagement\; within the tested range\, 0\.4 g NaCl gave the highest measured Cr recovery \(\; \)\.

Application of 400 µL ionic liquid\, pH 6\, 2000 rpm\, 15 min and 0\.4 g NaCl in a combined\-condition experiment produced approximately 89\% Cr recovery\. Because the preceding variable screening was conducted one factor at a time\, this result represents the measured response at the tested combination and not a statistically derived global optimum\.

\#\#\# 3\.4 Nickel aqueous\-phase removal as a function of extraction conditions

Ni aqueous\-phase removal was 94\.1\% at 40 ppm\, increased to 96\.1\% at 80 ppm and then decreased progressively to 56\.9\% at 240 ppm \(Figure 3a\)\. The Ni experiments were conducted in a separate aqueous feed and under a different pH and solvent\-volume range from the Cr experiments\.

FIGURE 3

At the fixed ionic\-liquid dose used in the concentration series\, the largest aqueous\-phase removal was observed at 80 ppm\, followed by a decrease at higher Ni concentrations\. In the separate ionic\-liquid\-volume series\, the response increased to 95\.4\% at 5 mL and remained essentially unchanged at 6 mL \(95\.1\%\)\, indicating a plateau within the investigated range \(Figure 3b\)\.

Ni aqueous\-phase removal increased from approximately 55\.9\% at 500 rpm to 87\.6\% at 2500 rpm and remained essentially unchanged at 3000 rpm \(Figure 3c\)\. The centrifugation\-speed response therefore approached a plateau at 2500–3000 rpm under the fixed conditions of this series\.

NaCl addition produced the largest change in the Ni aqueous\-phase response\, increasing removal from 70\.7\% at 0\.4 g to 98\.2\% at 2\.4 g \(Figure 3d\)\. The monotonic trend establishes an association between NaCl addition and aqueous Ni depletion within the tested alkaline range\. Because the response was calculated from residual aqueous Ni\, it includes ionic\-liquid partitioning together with pH\-dependent hydroxo\-speciation and precipitation\. The 98\.2\% value therefore quantifies overall aqueous\-phase removal rather than an isolated ionic\-liquid distribution coefficient \(\)\.

The highest Ni responses occurred in separate single\-factor series at approximately 80 ppm initial concentration\, 5–6 mL ionic liquid\, 2500–3000 rpm and 2\.0–2\.4 g NaCl\. These values were obtained under different fixed conditions and therefore represent local maxima within individual experimental series\. In the NaCl series\, 98\.2\% aqueous\-phase removal was measured at 40 ppm Ni\, pH 10\, 5 mL ionic liquid\, 2500 rpm and 2\.4 g NaCl\.

\#\#\# 3\.5 Comparative summary of chromium recovery and nickel aqueous\-phase removal

Cr and Ni exhibited different response patterns across the investigated single\-factor variables \(Table 2\)\. Cr recovery showed non\-monotonic maxima with ionic\-liquid volume\, centrifugation speed\, centrifugation time and NaCl addition\. Ni aqueous\-phase removal increased to a plateau with ionic\-liquid volume and centrifugation speed\, while the NaCl series increased monotonically over the tested range\.

Intrinsic \[BMPyrr\]\[TFSI\] selectivity cannot be inferred from the numerical difference between the maximum Cr recovery and Ni aqueous\-phase removal because the two metals were examined in different matrices and under different pH values\, feed concentrations\, ionic\-liquid volumes and salt loadings\. At pH 10\, Ni\(II\) hydroxo\-speciation and Ni\(OH\)2 formation can contribute to the decrease in dissolved Ni together with ionic\-liquid partitioning\; the 98\.2\% value consequently represents overall aqueous\-phase removal under the stated condition \(\)\.

The measured Cr recovery of approximately 89\% was lower than the 95\.40\% overall recovery reported for multistage amide solvent extraction \(\) and the 96\.67\% reductive desorption\/98\.6\% precipitation recovery reported for an integrated ion\-exchange process \(\)\. The maximum Ni aqueous\-phase removal of 98\.2\% was numerically higher than the 95\.6\% electrodeposition recovery reported after fixed\-bed ion exchange \(\) and the 94\.84\% recovery reported for coupled electrocatalytic oxidation\-electrodeposition \(\)\. These numerical comparisons describe the reported response magnitudes\; equivalence of process performance cannot be inferred because the studies differ in feed composition\, Cr oxidation\-state specificity\, recovery endpoint and separation mechanism\.

\#\#\# 3\.6 Real\-sample chromium screening by AAS

AAS was used to screen chromium in each of the five industrial wastewaters\. As shown in Table 3\, chromium concentrations varied widely among sources\. The lowest chromium concentration was measured in pharmaceutical wastewater \(S1\, 0\.28 ppm\) and the highest in industrial sewage \(S2\, 21\.42 ppm\)\. Plating wastewater \(S5\) contained 10\.31 ppm Cr and was selected for the recovery experiments because the Cr originated from a defined plating process stream\. The individual upstream contributors to the S2 industrial\-sewage sample were not separately traced\; therefore\, the measured value characterizes the composite sampled stream without assigning it to a specific upstream operation\.

The pharmaceutical\, leather and coating samples contained 0\.28\, 0\.41 and 0\.53 ppm Cr\, respectively\, substantially below the concentration measured in the plating wastewater\. Chromium is a functional process input to leather tanning\, but the measured S3 concentration is specific to the sampled stream and is not representative of untreated tannery effluent\. Among the samples screened\, plating wastewater \(S5\, 10\.31 ppm\) combined a comparatively high Cr concentration with a traceable process origin\. Selection of S5 for the recovery experiments was based on these measured characteristics \(\; \)\.

\#\#\# 3\.7 Ionic\-liquid recyclability and FTIR evidence of solvent integrity

Reuse of \[BMPyrr\]\[TFSI\] was evaluated over three consecutive extraction cycles without intermediate regeneration \(Figure 4\)\. Recovery decreased from 96\.1\% in the first cycle to 81\.8\% and 65\.6\% in the second and third cycles\, respectively\. The higher first\-cycle value relative to the Cr response in Section 3\.3 occurred at a lower metal loading\, consistent with the concentration\-response trend shown in Figure 2b\. The progressive decrease in recovery indicates loss of extraction performance during repeated use without regeneration \(\; \)\.

FIGURE 4

FTIR spectra recorded before \(Figure 5\) and after \(Figure 6\) extraction were compared to assess retention of the principal ionic\-liquid structural signatures\. Diagnostic TFSI\-anion bands occurred at essentially the same positions in both spectra\, including asymmetric SO2 stretching near 1201 cm−1\, C\-F stretching of the CF3 groups near 1059 cm−1\, and S\-N\-S\/SO2 bending near 619 cm−1\. Bands associated with the pyrrolidinium cation and ring framework were likewise retained\. The band near 3459 cm−1 is assigned to O\-H stretching of residual or adsorbed water\, while the weak feature near 2075 cm−1 is treated as a non\-diagnostic combination\/overtone feature\. The retained TFSI\-anion and pyrrolidinium bands show that major structural decomposition was not detectable by the FTIR comparison after extraction\. FTIR alone does not resolve the cause of the progressive recovery decrease during repeated use\; solvent loss\, water carry\-over and matrix fouling require separate phase mass\-balance\, washing and regeneration measurements \(\; \)\.

\#\#\# 3\.8 SEM\-EDX evidence for the chromium\-containing recovered material

SEM\-EDX analysis of the solid recovered after DLLME showed a collectable Cr\-containing solid\-associated phase\. The SEM micrograph \(Figure 7a\) shows an irregular\, aggregated particulate morphology\. The EDX spectrum \(Figure 7b\) contains Cr Kα and Kβ peaks at approximately 5\.41 and 5\.95 keV\, respectively\, and the semi\-quantitative EDX estimate \(Table 4\) gives 12\.9 wt\% Cr\. Carbon\, oxygen\, sodium and chlorine were also prominent\, with smaller amounts of aluminium\, sulphur\, potassium\, calcium\, manganese and iron\. The simultaneous detection of Cr and other matrix elements indicates Cr enrichment accompanied by co\-recovery rather than phase\-pure Cr separation\.

The elemental composition provides qualitative information on co\-recovery under the investigated conditions\. Alongside Cr\, EDX indicated Fe at 8\.6 wt\% and smaller amounts of Mn\, Ca and K \(Table 4\)\. These co\-detected elements reduce the compositional purity of the recovered material relative to Cr alone\. Quantitative Cr\/Fe selectivity coefficients cannot be obtained from the SEM\-EDX composition data and require controlled multicomponent extraction with phase\-specific mass balances\.

The EDX\-derived weight fractions are therefore treated as semi\-quantitative composition estimates rather than exact bulk\-phase assay values\. The SEM morphology describes the recovered particulate material\, whereas identification of the governing recovery pathways requires direct phase\-specific measurements\.

\#\#\# 3\.9 Integrated mechanistic interpretation

Cr and Ni exhibited distinct condition\-dependent response profiles under their respective experimental conditions\. Cr recovery at pH 6 showed local maxima for extractant volume\, phase\-separation conditions and salt loading\, whereas Ni aqueous\-phase removal at pH 10 increased strongly with ionic\-liquid dosage and NaCl addition\. Under the alkaline Ni condition\, hydroxo\-speciation and Ni\(OH\)2 precipitation\/co\-sedimentation can contribute to the decrease in dissolved Ni\. SEM\-EDX detected Cr together with Fe and other elements in the recovered solid\-associated material\. The measured responses thus represent process\-level aqueous\-phase depletion under defined conditions and do not provide metal\-specific distribution coefficients for a single extraction mechanism \(\; \; \)\.

\#\# 4 Conclusion

The present study evaluated \[BMPyrr\]\[TFSI\]\-based DLLME for the recovery and preconcentration of Cr and the aqueous\-phase removal of Ni under independently investigated operating conditions\. Chromium recovery from the electroplating\-type industrial wastewater reached approximately 89\% at 400 µL ionic liquid\, pH 6\, 2000 rpm centrifugation\, 15 min phase\-separation time and 0\.4 g NaCl\. The Cr system exhibited distinct condition\-dependent maxima with respect to extractant volume\, centrifugation conditions and salt addition\, indicating that phase ratio and phase\-disengagement characteristics strongly influenced the observed recovery\. In the Ni experiments\, aqueous\-phase removal increased with ionic\-liquid dosage and NaCl addition\, reaching 98\.2\% at 40 ppm Ni\, pH 10\, 5 mL \[BMPyrr\]\[TFSI\]\, 2500 rpm and 2\.4 g NaCl\. Under these alkaline conditions\, the measured Ni depletion represents the combined effect of aqueous\-phase removal mechanisms\, including ionic\-liquid partitioning and possible hydroxo\-speciation and precipitation\/co\-sedimentation\, rather than exclusive extraction into the ionic\-liquid phase\. Analysis of real industrial wastewater samples by AAS confirmed the occurrence of Cr in all five investigated streams\, with the selected plating wastewater containing 10\.31 ppm Cr\. FTIR spectra obtained before and after extraction retained the characteristic TFSI\-anion and pyrrolidinium signatures\, indicating preservation of the principal chemical structure of the ionic liquid during the investigated extraction step\. Reuse of \[BMPyrr\]\[TFSI\] without intermediate regeneration resulted in a progressive decrease in recovery from 96\.1\% in the first cycle to 81\.8\% and 65\.6\% in the second and third cycles\, respectively\, demonstrating the importance of solvent regeneration for repeated operation\. SEM\-EDX analysis of the recovered Cr\-containing material indicated approximately 12\.9 wt\% Cr together with 8\.6 wt\% Fe and smaller amounts of other elements\, confirming chromium enrichment while also revealing co\-recovery of competing species\.

Overall\, the results establish \[BMPyrr\]\[TFSI\] as a hydrophobic receiving phase capable of producing substantial Cr enrichment and high Ni aqueous\-phase removal under the investigated conditions\. The different response patterns of Cr and Ni further demonstrate the importance of metal\-specific operating conditions in ionic\-liquid\-based DLLME\. Further development of the process should focus on phase\-specific metal mass balances\, quantitative selectivity in multicomponent systems\, pH\-dependent speciation\, ionic\-liquid regeneration and back\-extraction\, reduction of the solvent\-to\-feed ratio for Ni treatment\, and validation at larger process scales\. Such investigations are necessary to establish the separation mechanism\, solvent efficiency and practical applicability of the process for metal recovery from industrial wastewater\.

records.abstract: Celestica Unveils DS6005 Co-Packaged Optics Switch for AI Data Centers Unite.AI
records.summary: Celestica announced the DS6005, a fully liquid-cooled data center switch that provides up to 102.4Tbps of switching capacity using co-packaged optics, per a company announcement dated October 12, 2026. The system is built on Broadcom's Tomahawk 6 – Davisson switch chip and places optical engines directly on the switch ASIC package rather than using front-panel pluggable optics. Celestica lists 64 ports of 1.6TbE, a 1.5OU enclosure for OCP ORv3 racks, SONiC support, and 16 ELSFP interfaces for field-replaceable external laser modules. The company claims the design reduces link power consumption, lowers latency, and improves bandwidth density and cluster efficiency for AI scale-up and scale-out networks. These are vendor claims from a product announcement; the source reports no independent measurements or benchmark data for the DS6005 itself.
records.why_it_matters: The DS6005 illustrates the shift toward co-packaged optics and liquid cooling as a way to raise per-rack bandwidth density for AI fabrics, but its power and latency benefits remain vendor-stated until independently measured.

score_details.reason: The article describes Celestica's DS6005, a fully liquid-cooled co-packaged optics switch built on Broadcom's Tomahawk 6-Davisson silicon, with concrete system-level details: 64x1.6TbE ports for 102.4Tbps, optical engines on the ASIC package, a 1.5OU ORv3-HPR liquid-cooled enclosure, 16 ELSFP external laser interfaces, MMC-16 connectors, and SONiC support. records.body_text:
Celestica introduced the DS6005, a fully liquid-cooled data center switch that delivers up to 102.4Tbps of capacity through co-packaged optics, in a company announcement dated October 12, 2026. The system is built on Broadcom’s Tomahawk 6 – Davisson switch chip, and Celestica is showcasing it at the 2026 OCP Global Summit in San Jose, which runs October 12–15, 2026.
The Toronto-based company described the DS6005 as a co-packaged optics (CPO) switching system designed around the bandwidth density, power, latency, and reach requirements of next-generation AI data center networks. Celestica said the switch is purpose-built for AI and machine learning scale-up and scale-out networking, and that it reduces power consumption, lowers latency, and improves cluster efficiency and reliability in next-generation AI clusters.
Gavin Cato, Celestica’s senior vice president and general manager of portfolio solutions and AI platform engineering, said AI infrastructure is driving demand for bandwidth while power, thermal management, latency, and reach become increasingly important constraints. “The DS6005 brings co-packaged optics, liquid cooling, field-replaceable external laser modules, and CPO-aware software management together in a compact platform designed to help customers build scalable and power-efficient AI fabrics,” Cato said.
DS6005 Hardware and Design
The DS6005 places its optical engines directly on the switch ASIC package instead of using conventional front-panel pluggable optics. Celestica said the co-packaged layout is intended to help data center operators optimize bandwidth density, reduce latency, and improve power efficiency. The company listed 64 ports of 1.6TbE providing the system’s 102.4Tbps switching capacity, and said the fully liquid-cooled 1.5OU enclosure, designed for OCP ORv3 racks, improves temperature stability and reliability while increasing overall rack density. The switch also supports SONiC, which Celestica said enables faster time to production on a proven, open architecture.
The DS6005 product page lists an AMD Ryzen x86 CPU alongside the Broadcom TH6-Davisson chip. The 64 optical interconnects run through 16x 4x MMC-16 connectors, and the system also carries one 100GbE QSFP28 port, RJ45 console and out-of-band GbE management ports, one USB 3.0 Type A port, one USB-C console port, and 16 ELSFP interfaces for external laser modules. The unit complies with the ORv3-HPR rack specification.
On the product page, Celestica said the switch reduces link power consumption, delivers ultra-low latency, and reduces latency relative to retimed optics. The page names AI and machine learning scale-up and scale-out networks, high-performance computing, frontier cloud and enterprise domain AI models, and hyperscale cloud infrastructure as the deployment types the system is optimized for.
Broadcom’s Tomahawk 6 – Davisson Silicon
Broadcom announced on October 8, 2025 that it was shipping Tomahawk 6 – Davisson, its third-generation CPO Ethernet switch, which it described as the industry’s first to deliver 102.4Tbps of optically enabled switching capacity. For the BCM78919 device, Broadcom listed 16 Davisson DR optical engines of 6.4Tbps each, 200Gbps of bandwidth per link, field-replaceable ELSFP laser modules, and support for scale-up clusters of 512 XPUs as well as over 100,000 XPUs in two-tier networks at 200Gbps per link. According to Broadcom, the chip complies with IEEE 802.3 and interoperates with existing 400G and 800G standards.
Broadcom said TH6-Davisson heterogeneously integrates optical engines based on TSMC’s COUPE technology with advanced substrate-level multi-chip packaging, and reported a 70% reduction in optical interconnect power consumption, a level it described as more than 3.5 times lower than traditional pluggable solutions. Cato provided a supporting statement in that 2025 announcement, saying the chip’s optical integration, power efficiency, and performance aligned with Celestica’s strategy for next-generation AI infrastructure and workload deployments.
Supporting Statements and Summit Showcase
Manish Mehta, vice president of marketing and operations in Broadcom’s Optical Systems Division, said moving co-packaged optics from an advanced architecture to a production-ready system requires collaboration across silicon, optical engines, packaging, thermal design, manufacturing, and system integration. Mehta said Celestica’s system engineering and platform execution helped translate Broadcom’s technology into a platform designed for high-density AI fabrics.
Sameh Boujelbene, vice president of research at Dell’Oro Group, said AI networking is shifting the constraint from compute to the physical infrastructure around it, where power, density, reach, and deployment complexity increasingly matter. Boujelbene described co-packaged optics as one of the industry’s important paths to address those challenges, and said pluggable, near-package, and co-packaged approaches will continue to coexist as the ecosystem matures.
Alan Weckel, founder and technology analyst at 650 Group, said co-packaged optics is moving from an industry theme toward production for AI networking, with an important near-term opportunity in controlled, high-density scale-out fabrics. Cliff Grossner, chief innovation officer of the Open Compute Project Foundation, said open collaboration across silicon photonics, hardware, software, and management is essential to building scalable, interoperable AI fabrics that can be deployed and supported at scale.
Celestica said it will exhibit the DS6005 in booth C2 at the 2026 OCP Global Summit, which the Open Compute Project Foundation is holding October 12–15, 2026 in San Jose, California. The foundation’s event page states that the 2026 summit is sold out, that registration is closed, and that onsite registration will not be offered. Celestica directed readers to its event landing page for more information about its participation at the summit, which concludes October 15, 2026.

TORONTO, Oct. 12, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Celestica Inc. (NYSE: CLS) (TSX: CLS), a global leader in data center infrastructure and advanced technology solutions, today introduced the Celestica DS6005, a co-packaged optics (CPO) data center switching system designed to address the bandwidth density, power, latency, and reach requirements of next-generation AI data center networks.
Built on the Broadcom Tomahawk 6 – Davisson switch chip, the DS6005 is designed to deliver up to 102.4Tbps of switching capacity in a compact 1.5OU form factor designed for OCP ORv3 racks. By co-packaging optical engines with the switch ASIC, the DS6005 eliminates the need for traditional front-panel pluggable optics, helping data center operators optimize bandwidth density, reduce latency, and improve power efficiency in the AI data center.
"AI infrastructure is driving unprecedented demand for bandwidth, while power, thermal management, latency, and reach are becoming increasingly important constraints," said Gavin Cato, SVP & GM Portfolio Solutions & AI Platform Engineering, Celestica. "The DS6005 brings co-packaged optics, liquid cooling, field-replaceable external laser modules, and CPO-aware software management together in a compact platform designed to help customers build scalable and power-efficient AI fabrics."
Purpose-built to support AI/ML scale up and scale out networking, the DS6005 is a fully liquid-cooled, co-packaged optics data center switch that slashes power consumption and improves cluster efficiency while lowering latency and increasing reliability for next-generation AI clusters.
Key DS6005 features include:
- Up to 102.4Tbps of switching capacity based on the Broadcom Tomahawk 6 – Davisson switch chip
- CPO Architecture: Integrates optical engines directly onto the switch ASIC
- 64 x 1.6TbE Ports (102.4T Capacity): Optically enabled 102.4Tbps of switching capacity to deliver bandwidth needs of AI clusters
- Fully Liquid-Cooled ORv3 1.5OU: Improves temperature stability and reliability with increased overall rack density
- SONiC Support: Achieves faster time to production using proven, open architecture that delivers AI fabric features and operational simplification
Supporting Quotes
"Moving co-packaged optics from an advanced architecture to a production-ready system requires collaboration across silicon, optical engines, packaging, thermal design, manufacturing, and system integration. By combining Broadcom's Tomahawk 6 – Davisson platform and optical expertise with Celestica's system engineering and platform execution, the DS6005 demonstrates how our partnership is helping bring CPO to market for AI networking. Celestica's work has been instrumental in translating our technology into a platform designed for high-density AI fabrics," said Manish Mehta, Vice President of Marketing and Operations, Optical Systems Division, Broadcom.

records.body_text:
Wistron Corporation and Wiwynn Corporation are participating in the 2026 OCP Global Summit in San Jose, California, under the theme “Create AI Beyond Limits,” showcasing a range of AI solutions and technology applications.
The showcase focuses on “Powering the AI Factory: Next-Generation AI Compute and Storage Systems,” featuring next-generation AI compute and storage systems, including:
- NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Platform
Wistron and Wiwynn are among the first in line with readiness for NVIDIA’s latest generation rack-scale platform, unifying 72 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs, 36 NVIDIA Vera CPUs with NVIDIA NVLink, NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, and NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPU. Built for the resiliency, energy efficiency, and scalability AI factories demand, the fully liquid-cooled platform is optimized for frontier AI model training, inference, and reasoning, delivering breakthrough performance and efficiency for AI factories.
- NVIDIA Vera CPU Rack: Built for Agentic AI and Reinforcement Learning at Scale
NVIDIA Vera CPU rack delivers the CPU infrastructure required to scale reinforcement learning and agentic AI systems. Built on the NVIDIA MGX architecture and integrated with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking, it supports over 22,500 concurrent execution environments per rack—completing workloads twice as fast with twice the efficiency of traditional CPU infrastructure. To secure these environments, NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform combines OpenShell runtime controls on Vera CPUs with NVIDIA Sentry on BlueField-4 DPUs for host-independent monitoring and policy enforcement.

E-Archive
Articles
in Vol. 15 - March Issue - Year 2014
SFCHINA Did Perform Once Again In Shanghai 2013!
In the Spotlight
Sinostar International Ltd. is a Hong Kong-based company specialized in organizing industrial exhibitions, publishing bilingual (Chinese & English) technical magazines and offering direct marketing services to a clientele worldwide. Sinostar International has been organizing the "Surface Finishing" & "Coatings" series of Exhibitions since 1983. From 1996 onwards, these two exhibitions have been held concurrently, and alternate between Guangzhou and Shanghai. Sinostar International is also the publisher of "China Coatings Journal (CCJ)" and "Surface Finishing Journal (SFJ)" - the only official publications for the CHINACOAT and SFCHINA series of exhibitions.
SFCHINA2013 (The 26th China International Exhibition for Surface Finishing & Coating Products) ended on Nov 22 at the Shanghai New International Expo Centre (SNIEC) with results that exceeded all its past editions.
SFCHINA2013 Facts & Statistics
China maintains the momentum of economic growth. SFCHINA continues to create success together with the industry in the following areas:
Gross exhibition area over 14,000
10,695 visitors, including 9,473 domestic and 1,222 overseas visitors;
298 exhibitors from 22 countries/regions, including 64 new exhibitors ;
2,356 representatives of exhibiting companies attended the show
797 visitors attended a total of 18 sessions of on-site technical programmes
Visitors' Comments
Mr. CHEN Lianzhong, Senior Engineer & Technical Director, Changchun Anchor Precision Electronic Industry Co., Ltd., P.R. China
"The exhibition has been widely recognized by the industry..."
Mr. Raj GOPAL, Manager, Triad Exports Pvt. Ltd., India
"SFCHINA offers me adequate information to make purchasing decisions�"
Ms. Echo LIN, Finish Test Engineer, SRAM Taiwan, Asia Development Centre, Taiwan Region
"Exhibits are novel and diversified. The concurrent technical programmes are knowledgeable."
An on-site visitor survey conducted has confirmed qualified visitors roamed the show floor:
93% agreed SFCHINA2013 was successfully organized;
89% agreed SFCHINA2013 had wide range/diversified scope of exhibits;
77% were plant managers/management, engineers, R&D and purchasing personnel;
76% were manufacturers, processing enterprises/job shops with production or purchasing background;
50% wanted to source new suppliers/products
Exhibitors' Comments
Mr. HUNG Hsilin, General Manager, Ean Sheng Enterprises Co., Ltd.
"Basically, our company only exhibits in this event as it is an excellent promotional channel."
Mr. Bob GEISSLER, General Manager, Greater China, MacDermid Technology (Suzhou) Co., Ltd.
"SFCHINA is one of our most important marketing tools which helps find many quality visitors."
Mr. Roy DONG, General Manager, Industrial Coating Systems Group, Nordson (China) Co., Ltd.
"The show continues with good visitor traffic and quality. We are very satisfied with the participation this year."
Concurrent Technical Programmes
In addition to showcase the latest products and technologies on the exhibition floor, SFCHINA2013 also featured 18 sessions of technical programmes, including Technical Seminars and New-Tech Corner. Many attendees expressed that they benefited tremendously by acquiring useful knowledge, developing networks of contacts and meeting with experts.
"Environmental Innovation" Competition
An "Environmental Innovation" Competition was organized during the exhibition with a view to commending the contribution of the industry to environmental protection. Mr. Darrell J. Reeve, an environmental expert from Australia, was invited as the adjudicator. A total of 15 companies participated. Assessment criteria were based on environmental need, scope of application, originality, availability, financial savings and marketability. The First Prize went to CTS Technology International Ltd. for its nano-plating technology being able to replace some traditional surface treatment technologies and 3D laser transfer printing. The Second and Third Prizes were awarded to Gema (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. and MacDermid Industrial Solutions respectively.
SFCHINA2014 Guangzhou
Being the world's largest finishing market, China maintains the focus of the global finishing industry. SFCHINA2014 Guangzhou will be held on Dec 3-5, 2014 in the China Import and Export Fair Complex (Canton Fair Complex). For the past 30 years, SFCHINA has stayed vibrant and will continue to provide vast opportunities to both exhibitors and visitors.

Microscopy also revealed a needle-like dense network on the Al side growing toward the steel interface, described as Fe-Al intermetallics formed by Fe diffusion into molten Al, with cracks along the reaction layer due to these brittle phases. records.body_text:
Comparative Investigation of Autogenous and Cu-Interlayer-Assisted Laser Welding of Dissimilar Steel-Aluminum Overlap Joints
- Original Research Article
- Published:
Abstract
In this study, steel-aluminum dissimilar metals were joined with and without a Cu interlayer in an overlap configuration using a laser welding process. The mechanical performances of the welded joints were evaluated in terms of lap shear strength and microhardness. The welding performances of the steel-aluminum joints with a Cu interlayer were also compared with autogenously welded joints by maintaining the same experimental and testing conditions. The ASTM D1002 for the lap shear test and ASTM E92 for the Vickers microhardness test were followed to assess the mechanical properties of the joints. The interfacial shear strength of the Cu interlayer-added steel-aluminum joints showed ~ 14% enhancement compared to autogenously welded joints. The microhardness at the fusion zone of Cu interlayer-added joints showed a ~ 7% reduction compared to autogenously welded samples due to ductile phase formation at the joint interface. The spectroscopic and microscopic analysis also revealed that the ductile intermetallic phases, such as Al-Cu and Al2-Cu, enhanced the overall mechanical performance of Cu interlayer-added joints. A needle-like dense network is visible on the Al side growing toward the steel interface. These phases are a characteristic feature of Fe-Al intermetallics formed during laser welding due to Fe diffusion into molten Al. Cracks are generated along the reaction layer due to these brittle phases.

They connect cooling loops in data centers, EV battery thermal management, energy storage and industrial power electronics.
records.summary: This CHX Metal product page describes the company's manufacture of liquid cooling connectors for data center cooling loops, EV battery thermal management, energy storage, and industrial power electronics. The connectors are CNC-machined from aluminum (6061), stainless steel (SUS316), and brass (C3604), with O-ring sealing and sealing surfaces held to a stated tolerance of ±0.005 mm. The page states that every connector undergoes 100% pressure-decay leak testing and CMM dimensional inspection, and that the plant is ISO 9001:2015 and ISO 14001:2015 certified. Offered types include quick-disconnect couplings, threaded coolant fittings, cold plate connectors, manifold connectors, and blind-mate connectors for server racks. All performance and quality statements are manufacturer claims from a company webpage, not independently verified experimental results.
records.why_it_matters: For engineers specifying coolant-loop hardware, the page indicates that sealing-surface tolerance (±0.005 mm) and 100% pressure-decay leak testing are the manufacturer's stated controls for leak risk, which are the parameters to verify in incoming inspection or supplier qualification.

About CHX Metal — Precision CNC Manufacturer Since 2013
Shenzhen Changhexin Precision Hardware Co., Ltd. (CHX Metal) is an ISO 9001:2015 & ISO 14001:2015 certified precision CNC machining manufacturer based in Shajing, Bao'an, Shenzhen — one of China's most concentrated precision manufacturing clusters. Founded in 2013, CHX Metal operates 220 production machines including:
- 100 5-axis machining centers
- 50 CNC lathes (46-type, dia. 1–300mm, concentricity ±0.005mm)
- 70 Swiss-type automatic lathes (dia. 1–300mm)
Monthly capacity: 5,000,000 pieces (5 million PCS). Tolerance ±0.005mm. All products include CMM inspection reports (coordinate measuring machine) and material test reports (MTR).
Contact: mc@chxmetal.com | +86 18138850989 (WhatsApp) | Mon–Sat 09:00–18:00 UTC+8
Liquid Cooling Connector | Precision CNC Cooling Connectors
CHX Metal manufactures Liquid Cooling Connector at its own factory in Shenzhen Bao’an, China: standard tolerance ±0.005mm (or better on request), MOQ 1 piece, prototypes in 3–7 days and batch production in 7–15 days. The 5,000 m² plant runs 220 CNC machines, is ISO 9001:2015 and ISO 14001:2015 certified, and inspects every lot on a CMM.
CHX Metal (Shenzhen Changhexin Precision Hardware) produces liquid cooling connectors for data center cooling and EV battery thermal management, with dimensional tolerance ±0.005mm and 100% leak testing. ISO 9001:2015 certified. Engineering teams review drawings and return manufacturability feedback within 24 hours.
Liquid Cooling Connector Types
- Quick-disconnect couplings
- Threaded coolant fittings
- Cold plate connectors
- Manifold connectors
- Blind-mate connectors for server racks
Manufacturing for Sealing
- CNC machining of aluminum, stainless steel, brass
- Tolerance ±0.005mm on sealing surfaces
- 100% leak testing (pressure decay)
- Surface treatment: anodizing, passivation
- Cleanroom-compatible cleaning available
Applications
- Data centers: server liquid cooling loops
- EV batteries: thermal management connectors
- Energy storage: battery pack cooling
- Industrial: laser and power electronics cooling
Quality Assurance
ISO 9001:2015 certified. Every cooling connector undergoes 100% leak testing and dimensional inspection to ensure zero failure in thermal loops.
Frequently Asked Questions
What are liquid cooling connectors used for? They connect cooling loops in data centers, EV battery thermal management, energy storage and industrial power electronics.
How do you ensure leak-free connectors? Sealing surfaces are machined to ±0.005mm and every connector is fully leak tested by pressure-decay before shipment.
Which materials are used? Aluminum, stainless steel and brass, with anodizing or passivation for corrosion resistance.
Do you make custom connector geometries? Yes. We manufacture to customer drawings, including quick-disconnect, blind-mate and manifold connectors.
Get a Quote → Upload your drawing/3D model for a process plan and quotation within 24 hours.
Materials & Specifications
We machine liquid cooling connectors from Brass C3604, 6061, SUS316, O-ring sealed. Typical accuracy is ±0.005mm sealing surfaces. Parts are manufactured to your 2D drawing or 3D model, in sizes from a few millimeters up to 1000mm envelopes, from single prototypes to hundreds of thousands of pieces per year.
Typical Applications
- server cooling loops
- EV battery cooling
- laser and medical chillers
These are representative examples; we regularly take on custom geometries outside this list. Send your drawing for a feasibility check.
Our Machining Capability
Production runs on 3-axis and 5-axis vertical machining centers, CNC lathes, and Swiss-type automatic lathes. Fixtures are designed in-house for repeatable clamping, and programs are simulated before cutting to protect tight tolerances. Every order ships with in-process inspection records. Our CMM verifies critical dimensions against your drawing on first article, at batch start, and at final release. Material certificates (EN 10204 3.1) and full dimensional reports come standard; PPAP and FAIR documentation are available on request for automotive and industrial programs.
Surface Finishing Options
Available finishes include Type II and Type III anodizing (clear, black, and custom colors), sandblasting, wire drawing, laser engraving and silk-screen marking, zinc and nickel plating, passivation, and black oxide. Cosmetic parts are inspected under standardized lighting with defined surface criteria.
MOQ, Lead Time & Packaging
Standard lead time is 3-7 days for prototypes and 7-15 days for production batches, with surface treatment adding 3-7 days. Parts are cleaned, protected against corrosion and scratching, and packed in customized trays or EPE foam for international shipping. DFM feedback on RFQs is returned within 24 hours.
Why Choose CHX Metal
One supplier from drawing to finished part: milling, turning, 5-axis and Swiss-type machining are all in-house, together with anodizing, plating, laser marking, and silk-screen coordination. You get one accountable partner instead of a chain of subcontractors.

records.title: Joining of Transparent Substrates Through a Combination of Laser-Induced Forward Transfer and Laser Micro-Welding
records.source_name: Journal of Micro and Nano Science and Engineering
records.abstract: Abstract Transparent materials like glass are widely used in consumer electronics, optoelectronic devices, electrical insulation, and lab-on-a-chip devices due to their superior physical and chemical stability and high optical transparency. In recent years, significant effort has been directed toward achieving high-precision laser-based joining of optically transparent materials. Due to the laser's poor absorption in transparent glass substrates, thin-film absorptivity coatings are typically used to enhance absorption and facilitate welding. However, this reduces the optical transparency of the processed zone. To avoid this, we selectively coated two quartz substrates with an absorptive film via laser-induced forward transfer (LIFT) and then welded them using the same laser source. This enabled the successful welding of the two quartz plates while maintaining the transparency of the unprocessed zone. Initially, the substrate was spin-coated with copper nano-ink, serving as a transfer layer(donor). A pulsed laser beam was directed perpendicularly onto the donor, which precisely transferred a layer of material to a specific location on the surface beneath it (the receiver). The donor was then replaced with a fresh, uncoated quartz substrate. The laser was scanned over the previously transferred zone. High laser fluence caused the melting of the interface and enabled successful welding. The shear strength test also shows an excellent shear strength of 57.04 MPa ± 7.19 MPa. Thus, a combination of LIFT and laser micro-welding techniques provides a low-cost, practical solution for precise, selective laser welding of transparent materials.
records.summary: The source is a journal abstract describing a two-step laser process for joining quartz substrates while preserving optical transparency outside the processed zone. Because quartz absorbs laser light poorly, the authors first use laser-induced forward transfer (LIFT) to selectively deposit an absorptive copper nano-ink film from a spin-coated donor onto a receiver substrate, then replace the donor with a fresh uncoated quartz plate and scan the same laser over the transferred zone. The high laser fluence melts the interface and welds the two quartz plates. The abstract reports a shear strength of 57.04 MPa ± 7.19 MPa and frames the combined LIFT plus laser micro-welding route as a low-cost, practical method for selective welding of transparent materials. Only the abstract was available, so experimental details and comparisons cannot be independently assessed.
records.why_it_matters: Selective absorptive coating by LIFT confines laser energy to the joint region, potentially allowing transparent-substrate welding without sacrificing transparency of the surrounding device area.

Prof.Rajendra Mathur , Khushbu Yadav, Poonam Sandu
Vol. 15 Issue 4 Pages 509 - 523

Quaternized-Carbohydrate Ionic Liquid Assisted Green synthesis of Silver Nanoparticles
Authors
PM
Prof.Rajendra Mathur
Department of Chemistry, Jai Narain Vyas University, JODHPUR-342001(INDIA
rajendra\_mathur@rediffmail.com
Co-Authors
Khushbu Yadav, Poonam Sandu
Abstract
Carbohydrate-based ionic liquids (ILs) offer a promising sustainable platform for nanoparticle synthesis because of their low volatility, high polarity, solvation capacity, and potential for biodegradability. In this study, glucose- and lactose-based quaternized ionic liquids containing chloride, sulfate, nitrate, and acetate counter anions were synthesized and investigated as reaction media for the preparation and stabilization of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs). The synthesized ionic liquids were characterized by FTIR and NMR spectroscopy and subsequently employed for the aqueous synthesis of AgNPs without the addition of external capping or stabilizing agents. Formation of AgNPs was initially indicated by characteristic colour changes and was further confirmed by UV–Vis spectroscopy, which showed surface plasmon resonance bands in the 420–460 nm region. FTIR and ¹H NMR analyses indicated the association of carbohydrate-derived functional groups with the synthesized nanoparticles. Dynamic light scattering revealed a Z-average hydrodynamic diameter of 65.73 nm for glucose-based AgNPs and 475 nm for lactose-based AgNPs, with polydispersity indices of 0.3608 and 0.4713, respectively. The particle size and dispersion characteristics varied with the carbohydrate component and counter anion. Among the investigated systems, sulfate-containing ionic liquids produced comparatively smaller and more uniformly distributed nanoparticles. SEM and EDS analyses further confirmed the presence and distribution of silver in the synthesized materials. Notably, the aqueous AgNP dispersions remained visually stable for more than 100 days under ambient conditions without an external stabilizing or capping agent. Overall, the findings demonstrate that carbohydrate-based ionic liquids can serve as multifunctional reaction media for the synthesis and stabilization of AgNPs and provide a potentially sustainable alternative to conventional nanoparticle synthesis systems.

SEM and EDS analyses further confirmed the presence and distribution of silver in the synthesized materials\. Notably\, the aqueous AgNP dispersions remained visually stable for more than 100 days under ambient conditions without an external stabilizing or capping agent\. Overall\, the findings demonstrate that carbohydrate\-based ionic liquids can serve as multifunctional reaction media for the synthesis and stabilization of AgNPs and provide a potentially sustainable alternative to conventional nanoparticle synthesis systems\.

The review is described as covering principal factors influencing Al–Cu joint properties, common defects, the effect of material properties on laser joining, and laser–material interaction during welding. It further indicates that process parameter adjustment (e.g., laser power or speed), laser operational mode, and material selection (base metals, alloying elements, filler metals) may enhance mechanical and electrical joint properties. Only the abstract and introductory text were retrieved, so specific reported values, comparisons and conclusions from the full review are not available here.

E-Archive
Good Vibrations
in Vol. 19 - January Issue - Year 2018
Professional Mass Finishing Engineer
Objects for surface finishing training
Surface finishing training practical foundations
Workshop surface finishing theoretical foundations
Which are the main topics when you qualify as a mass finishing engineer?
The lack of an accredited vocational training course for mass finishing engineers at technical schools and advanced technical colleges has been a problem for the mass finishing industry for many years. Even though the technology has entered all areas of the metal and plastics processing industry in the past 20 years, no specific training is available.
And so it is the responsibility of companies to provide professional training. The problem is that training content and intensity vary considerably and there are no overall training standards. There is some specialist literature, but it is very technical and theoretical and therefore of limited use for training purposes.
This column provides a concise overview of the main topics and can serve as a professional training guide. The application engineers and trainers of the well-known industry specialists provide a more in-depth understanding of the specific subject areas.
• Metal expertise
A basic knowledge of metals and plastics and their properties is essential and constitutes the basic qualification. This includes knowing which metals and plastics are available, how they are processed and what their areas of application are. To gain a realistic understanding of the possibilities and limits of processes and the resulting products, it is important to have knowledge of the properties of metals (and their alloys) and plastics.
• Grinding, polishing, deburring and cleaning processes
It is important to have a comprehensive overview of the many available grinding, polishing and deburring processes and the differences between them.
Which process is suitable for which requirement? What are the pros and cons of the processes and what are the key areas of application?
• Systems technology for grinding, polishing, deburring and cleaning
Which systems technology is available for grinding, polishing, deburring and cleaning? Which systems are used for which applications and what are the limits of the individual systems? Which equipment options are available, which equipment is necessary, which useful and which of advantage? What automation options are there for the different systems?
• Process agents/consumables for grinding, polishing, deburring and cleaning
There exists a vast number of different agents/consumables for grinding, polishing, deburring and cleaning. Which process agents are used for which applications and what are the advantages and limits of the individual agents.
Mechanical as well as chemical products are used in mass finishing; therefore, in order to understand and influence the processes, the relationships between mechanical and chemical modes of action have to be taught. A mass finishing engineer has to have a thorough understanding of these things to be able to establish stable and reproducible processes in a company.
• Peripheral devices
In addition to the main production machinery, a variety of peripheral devices are available for industry, which are used to extend the machining task itself or to improve or automate handling and processes. These include transport systems (e.g. feeders and conveyor belts), drying systems, separating devices, process water treatment systems (wastewater treatment plants), automation equipment (e.g. robots). A planning engineer should have extensive knowledge of the available systems in order to decide what is required and useful for his production environment. Only then will he be able to optimally configure the individual components and thus develop a strong overall concept.
Serious planning errors can result in unstable processes, inefficient production runs and economic inefficiency.
• Upstream and downstream processes
In order to be able to plan and execute mass finishing operations, it is of benefit to know and understand the original manufacturing operation. The manufacturing operation tells you what the properties of the workpiece surface and the workpiece edges are.
To be able to deliver a perfectly prepared surface for the subsequent process (e.g. electroplating), it makes sense to know what the main criteria of the downstream processes are.
This may include workpiece cleanliness requirements or a definition of the workpiece edges.
• Assessing surface finish and quality assurance
An essential part of quality assurance after a mass finishing process is the assessment of the surface properties. This may be about defining roughness, or measuring surface tension or edge roundness. Here, standards or specific specifications might have to be met and the processing results have to be tested. Most companies have their own measuring equipment to do this, and sometimes measurements and tests are carried out by accredited external laboratories. Over the course of his training, the mass finishing engineer should acquire the basic knowledge necessary to be able to assess the practical results from the production processes and the measurement results.
These days, every industrial company has to have an effective quality management system in place. The surface finish is critical for quality, and in most cases, the mass finishing engineer is directly or indirectly involved in the quality assurance of his production area. It is therefore a key element of this demanding profession to keep an eye on all the standard quality assurance measures (stability, documentation, reproducibility, traceability).
A well-qualified mass finishing engineer can perform many roles within a company. Production, development, process planning and quality assurance departments are always looking for qualified staff who have the right training or are prepared to undergo such training. To meet the growing demand, major specialist companies, such as Rösler Oberflächentechnik GmbH (https://de.rosler.com/de-de/service/roesler-academy/) also offer specialist training courses and workshops.

records.title: Optical illusion: Is co-packaged optics the savior the data center industry has been waiting for? - Data Center Dynamics
records.abstract: Optical illusion: Is co-packaged optics the savior the data center industry has been waiting for? Data Center Dynamics
records.summary: This Data Center Dynamics article examines co-packaged optics (CPO), which integrates optical engines and switching ASICs on a single packaged substrate to move electrical-to-optical conversion onto the silicon and reduce the power and cost burden of pluggable DSP-based transceivers. It reports that early industry reaction to Cisco's 2023 OFC demonstration was indifferent or negative, largely due to vendor lock-in concerns and questions about cost, manufacturability, and laser reliability, with hot-swappable ELSFP lasers described as a partial remedy. The article attributes renewed momentum largely to Nvidia's GTC 2026 announcements of Spectrum-X CPO switches in production in H2 2026 and NVLink 8 CPO in the 2028 Feynman architecture, alongside Broadcom, Marvell, Lightmatter, Coherent, and others, plus formation of the Open CPX MSA. It reports Meta's deployment of Broadcom's Tomahawk 5 'Bailly' CPO switch showed a 0.34 percent annual link failure rate over the first million hours, roughly five times more reliable than pluggable control groups. Cisco's Gartner cautions that the CPO ecosystem remains immature and that CPO becomes more compelling at 400G per line SerDes than at today's 200G.
records.why_it_matters: The reported Meta link-failure data and Nvidia's stated production timelines suggest CPO may shift from vendor-pushed demos to a deployable option, but the article indicates the decision hinges on SerDes rate: at 200G per line CPO and LPO are described as a toss-up, while at 400G per line LPO becomes much more challenging and CPO becomes more necessary.

score_details.reason: Full extracted article directly addresses co-packaged optics (CPO) for data center high-speed interconnects, a core High-Speed Connectivity problem. It supplies concrete engineering context: CPO integrates optical engines and switching ASICs on one packaged substrate, removes DSPs, and cites a measured reliability datapoint (Meta/Broadcom Tomahawk 5 'Bailly' CPO switch: 0.34% annual link failure rate over first million hours, ~5x more reliable than pluggable transceivers). It also covers ELSFP hot-swappable lasers, LPO/NPO alternatives, ecosystem immaturity, and the 200G vs 400G per-lane SerDes threshold where CPO becomes necessary. Quality is moderate: largely analyst/vendor commentary with one quantitative reliability result and no test methodology. Novelty is low-moderate; it is a news/analysis piece summarizing existing announcements rather than disclosing new technical contributions. Engineering value is solid for design trade-offs (power, reliability, vendor lock-in, ecosystem maturity).

records.body_text:
When Cisco took to the stage at the Optical Fiber Conference (OFC) 2023 to demonstrate co-packaged optics (CPO) on a 3.2TB switch, it is fair to say the technology did not receive a rapturous reception.
“I would say the industry response at that time ranged from indifference or a yawn to fairly negative,” Bill Gartner, SVP & GM, optical systems and optics at Cisco, tells DCD.
It wasn’t that three years ago the world didn’t care about the potential benefits of CPO. Rather, as Gartner explains it, the negative response stemmed from a number of concerns, one being that the technology would introduce vendor lock-in to an environment that traditionally allowed for a multi-vendor approach.
“There’s a switch, which makes up the bulk of the router and its costs, and then there are ports on the face plate into which you plug these pluggable optics,” Gartner explains. “But a customer has a choice of which pluggable optic they want to use, and there are many providers of pluggable optics. That gives them negotiating leverage and the ability to make sure that they've got supply chain diversity, which gives them a lot of benefit.”
In 2023, customers were fearful that CPO would force them into an all-Cisco or all Broadcom world, Gartner says, although he stresses that while Cisco is one of the aforementioned providers of pluggable optics, the company is not in the habit of forcing its customers to buy Cisco.
“Multi-vendor gives customers leverage, and customers like that leverage. It gives them peace and comfort that they're not going to be held hostage by a single source.”
While vendor lock-in remains an issue that CPO has yet to fully resolve three years later, it appears that the indifference Gartner witnessed on the OFC stage has vanished, replaced by an industry ready to shrug off all concerns and welcome the technology with open arms.
What is co-packaged optics?
Co-packaged optics emerged as a concept around the start of the decade, when the data center industry began discussing the need for a solution to the power and bandwidth bottlenecks it was increasingly experiencing.
“In the old days, your electrical connections were copper. Your data center networks were connected by Ethernet, and everything was good,” says Roy Chua, founder and industry analyst at AvidThink. “Then, as speeds increased, copper became unable to handle the volume of traffic, so the industry turned to fiber optics,” which Chua notes was also good, until it wasn’t quite good enough anymore.
Fiber optics requires the use of lasers to convert electrical signals into optics, or photons, so they can be transported over the glass fiber, then reconverted from optical signals back to electrical ones when they reach the other side. “So that's all wonderful, except that all takes a certain amount of energy,“ Chua says.
In today’s data center environments, most electrical-to-optical conversions take place via pluggable optical transceivers, known as digital signal processors (DSPs), which connect to the switch. However, DSPs are expensive and power-hungry, meaning that although they have clear benefits over copper interconnects, they are not quite the power-efficient option the industry is looking for.
Enter: Co-packaged optics. On a very basic level, unlike pluggable optics, where the transceivers are kept separate from the main chips, CPO integrates optical and electrical components, such as optical engines and switching ASICs, on a single packaged substrate.
“What co-packaged optics does is move the conversion onto the actual silicon itself. It moves those lasers onto the silicon, eliminating the need for any external units,” Chua explains. “And by putting those lasers inside the silicon, you are able to save power. By co-packaging these elements, it allows for more consolidation while lowering costs and energy use.”
However, while the concept might seem relatively straightforward, the practicalities are less so. “As you can imagine, manufacturing of co-packaged optics can be complicated because you have to manufacture everything – your wave guides and your modulators – all together.”
Therefore, it's unsurprising that another early concern regarding the technology was its potential cost, with Chua noting that “people felt it would not be sufficiently reliable and cost-effective enough to produce and take to market. “
The reliability of the technology has also come under scrutiny from customers, with questions arising as to how to go about replacing a laser that has failed when it's part of a monolithic structure, particularly given the so-called blast radius of optics, and the high failure rate of lasers.
The industry has responded by developing a hot-swappable laser source known as an External Laser Small Form-Factor Pluggable (or ELSFP) while keeping everything monolithically integrated. Gartner says that although this solution certainly helps to address the challenge, it’s something of a half-measure that doesn’t succeed in solving the issue entirely.
The shifting optical landscape
According to AvidThink’s Data Center Networking in 2026 report, CPO is one of several new architectures that are driving a “structural shift” in the optical interconnect landscape, namely removing the need for DSPs from optical transceiver modules.
In addition to CPO, there’s what Chua describes as a half-step, known as linear pluggable optics (LPO), and a three-quarter step called near-packaged optics, with LPO currently the most popular of the three. There’s also eXtra-dense pluggable optics, or XPO, which was developed by Arista but described by Chua as less of a pure technology and more of a packaging form factor. [See Box Out].
While co-packaged optics is not a new concept, AvidThink’s report notes that the technology reached a milestone this year, transitioning from “perpetual promise to production deployment,” with both Chua and Gartner agreeing this has been largely driven by announcements made by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at GTC 2026.
At the March conference, Huang indicated that Nvidia’s Spectrum-X CPO switches would be in production in H2 2026, and officially announced that the chip giant’s 2028 Feynman architecture would introduce NVLink 8 CPO, bringing silicon photonics directly to the GPU-to-GPU scale-up interconnect for the first time.
AvidThink says this is architecturally significant as, until now, CPO has been applied to scale-out switch-to-switch connections. Applying it to the latency-critical scale-up domain signals that CPO technology has achieved the maturity and performance required for the most demanding interconnect tier.
“Until Jensen said CPO, no one cared about CPO. No one had any idea what CPO was, and now I get asked that question all the time,” Chua laughs. He also questions whether anyone in the industry would have been saying widespread adoption of the technology would take place in 2028 had Huang not gotten on stage and made the Feynman announcement.
“Without Jensen sort of stoking the fire, I think it would have been the 2027 - 2028 conversation, and Jensen basically made it the 2025 - 2026 conversation,” Chua says, adding that “to be frank, I wasn't expecting it.”
While Chua says Huang has put a rocket under the industry – with Broadcom in particular being incredibly aggressive around its timelines for deployment in the wake of Huang’s comments – the AvidThink report does highlight that there have been a number of other notable CPO announcements from the last 18 months.
These include AMD’s January 2025 acquisition of Enosemi; Lightmatter unveiling Passage L200, the world’s first 3D co-packaged optics product; Broadcom announcing its Tomahawk 6 CPO variant ‘Davisson’; Marvell’s acquisition of Celestial AI; Coherent demonstrating multi-technology CPO at OFC 2026; and Ayar Labs and Wiwynn announcing a joint reference design for optically connected, rack-scale AI systems.
Furthermore, in March 2026, Ciena, Coherent, Marvell, Molex, Samtec, and TeraHop announced the formation of the Open CPX MSA (Open Co-packaging Multi-Source Agreement) to develop the specifications for optical engines “required to enable a broad ecosystem of interoperable co-packaged and near-package interconnect solutions.”
Where are we now?
While all of these announcements appear to indicate significant demand, Gartner says it's important to note that a lot of work in the CPO space was initially vendor, not customer, driven, as demonstrated by those poor early responses.
“[In 2023] Cisco and Broadcom announced these CPO demos and didn't get a great customer response. Then Nvidia announced that they were going to deploy CPO and, quite honestly, stimulated a lot of excitement in the industry – I think maybe irrational exuberance is the way I would characterize it though.”
Although Cisco had already demoed a co-packaged optics prototype back in 2023, Gartner says the company has not yet announced a commercial CPO line, although he says that it does have CPO technology under development.
“We're playing this a bit cautiously,” he explains. “We don't want to come across to our customers like we're not going to give them a choice.”
Gartner says Cisco’s initial CPO offering will likely be in the 100-terabit switch capacity range, and the company will continue to give customers a choice between pluggables and an embedded option, be that CPO or NPO.
“Again, we have not announced a product yet; this is something that's under development, and we're really going to be cautious about launching it based on customer demand. We want to see the customers are really pulling for this, as opposed to it being a vendor push.”
In the meantime, the company is developing LPO options for its Silicon One portfolio, with the first commercially available 800G LPO modules for its Nexus 9000 series switches and 8000 series routers released in February 2026.
“I think the challenge that we have to acknowledge here is that the industry ecosystem is evolving around CPO, but it’s not mature. The ecosystem around silicon is highly mature – we know how to put a package and substrates around silicon, and we know how to do that around optics, and build a pluggable optics module, but we don’t have an ecosystem that’s mature and can put those two together,” Gartner says.
“There's a lot of invention right now around things like connectors for CPO, substrates that support the optics, and optical chiplets, but that's an immature ecosystem, and it really has to mature pretty significantly before we'll see this technology make sense at volume. Anybody can produce a hundred of these things, but when we have to talk about delivering thousands or millions, that ecosystem really needs to be mature, and that's going to take some time.”
Despite all the excitement, Chua also acknowledges that, at the moment, CPO is being deployed at “a very small scale.” However, he says all early signs are promising, and the data show that the technology will be able to scale up and be deployed into production.
In particular, Meta’s deployment of the Broadcom Tomahawk 5 ‘Bailly’ CPO switch in its data centers resulted in a 0.34 percent annual link failure rate during the first million hours of testing, making it roughly five times more reliable than traditional pluggable transceivers that were used as control groups.
As a result, Chua says he can’t see anything on the horizon that would block the mass adoption of co-packaged optics in the near future, and he expects to see some level of volume shipments from Broadcom of its Tomahawk 6 ‘Davisson’ CPO variant.
For Gartner, however, whether the reality of CPO lives up to the hype remains to be seen, especially with regard to the timelines being touted by vendors such as Nvidia and Broadcom. While shiny and new will be enough for some people to jump on board the co-packaged optics train, for him, the real turning point for the technology will be when all the other technologies currently on offer hit their ceiling, making CPO a necessity.
“Today, the SerDers rate coming off the silicon is 200G per line, and at that rate, in my view, it's a toss-up as to whether CPO or LPO makes sense,” he says. “Once we get to 400G per line, then LPO becomes much more challenging ... that is where the ability for LPO to continue serving the market diminishes, and the need for CPO becomes more real.”

records.title: Lubricant-Engine Suitability Evaluation for Fuel Efficiency in Fishing VesselUsing Temperature and Color Degradation
records.source_name: Marine Fisheries : Journal of Marine Fisheries Technology and Management
records.abstract: Engine performance in fishing vessel depends on the reliability and efficiency of diesel engine, in which the lubrication system plays a key role in reducing friction, controlling operating temperature, and minimizing component wear. However, field observations in small-scale fisheries indicate that many fishermen select lubricants based on habit, price, or availability rather than manufacturer specifications, which may reduce engine efficiency and increase fuel consumption. This study evaluated the suitability of three lubricants (S40, SC SAE 15W-40, and SX SAE 15W-40), each matched to a different Mitsubishi diesel engine (6D14, 6D15, 6D16) under real purse seine fishing conditions in Majene Regency, Indonesia, using engine temperature and lubricant color degradation as practical field indicators. Because operating duration varied substantially among engines (76-180 minutes per trip), fuel consumption was expressed as a rate (L hour-1) for fair comparison. S40 produced the lowest, most stable rate (21.97 L hour-1) and lowest final temperature (36.22°C); SC SAE 15W-40 recorded the highest rate (37.51 L hour-1) despite a moderate final temperature (46.00°C); SX SAE 15W-40 showed the most fluctuating temperature (up to 50.80°C) with an intermediate rate (31.19 L hour-1). Kruskal-Wallis tests confirmed significant differences among groups (p < 0.001). Multiple regression showed operating duration and final temperature jointly explained 30.5% of the variance in total fuel consumption (R2 = 0.305, p < 0.001). These findings indicate that rate-based, engine-specific lubricant matching is essential for improving fuel efficiency and thermal stability in small-scale fishing vessels. Keywords: Fishing vessels; fuel efficiency; lubricant degradation; marine engines; operating temperature

The authors address the problem that small-scale fishers often choose lubricants by habit, price, or availability rather than manufacturer specification, which may reduce efficiency and raise fuel consumption. Because trip durations varied widely (76–180 minutes), fuel consumption was normalized to a rate (L hour-1). Engine performance in fishing vessel depends on the reliability and efficiency of diesel engine\, in which the lubrication system plays a key role in reducing friction\, controlling operating temperature\, and minimizing component wear\. However\, field observations in small\-scale fisheries indicate that many fishermen select lubricants based on habit\, price\, or availability rather than manufacturer specifications\, which may reduce engine efficiency and increase fuel consumption\. This study evaluated the suitability of three lubricants \(S40\, SC SAE 15W\-40\, and SX SAE 15W\-40\)\, each matched to a different Mitsubishi diesel engine \(6D14\, 6D15\, 6D16\) under real purse seine fishing conditions in Majene Regency\, Indonesia\, using engine temperature and lubricant color degradation as practical field indicators\. Because operating duration varied substantially among engines \(76\-180 minutes per trip\)\, fuel consumption was expressed as a rate \(L hour\-1\) for fair comparison\. Kruskal\-Wallis tests confirmed significant differences among groups \(p \< 0\.001\)\. Multiple regression showed operating duration and final temperature jointly explained 30\.5\% of the variance in total fuel consumption \(R2 \= 0\.305\, p \< 0\.001\)\.
