Ionic conductivity is strongly influenced by viscosity\, but additional factors such as ion association\, charge correlations\, specific coordination\, and\, in protic ionic liquids \(ILs\)\, proton\-transfer mechanisms\, also affect charge transport\. Clough et al\. found that most of the 11 investigated IL mixture series were well described by a logarithmic conductivity–composition relation\. However\, no clear correlation was found between the non\-ideality parameters derived independently for viscosity and conductivity \[111\]\. Annat et al\. similarly observed approximately logarithmic mixing for several systems\, whereas structurally distinct mixtures showed more complex behavior\; for example\, the conductivity of \[P666\,14\]\[TFSI\]\+\[MPPyr\]\[TFSI\] remained close to that of the phosphonium parent even at xMPPyr \= 0\.5 \[109\]\. Ning et al\. found the conductivities of \[OMIm\]\[BF4\]\+\[OMIm\]\[Cl\]\, \[HMIm\]\[BF4\]\+\[HMIm\]\[Cl\]\, and \[HMIm\]\[PF6\]\+\[HMIm\]\[Cl\] to remain between those of the corresponding neat ILs and to vary inversely with viscosity\. Their fractional Walden slopes were below unity\, indicating appreciable ion association \[115\]\. More pronounced non\-additivity was reported by Zhang et al\. \[116\]\. The authors observed positive deviations for \[DEME\]x\[BMMIm\]1−x\[TFSI\]\, \[DEME\]x\[BMMIm\]1−x\[BF4\]\, and \[BMMIm\]\[TFSI\]x\[BF4\]1−x\. For the latter system\, conductivity peaked at x \= 0\.9\, exceeding the values of both parent ILs\. In contrast\, \[DEME\]\[TFSI\]x\[BF4\]1−x showed a negative deviation\, with conductivity values remaining between those of the parent compounds\. Pameté et al\. demonstrated a strong interdependence among conductivity\, viscosity\, and phase behavior\. At 293 K\, the conductivities of pure \[EMIm\]\[FSI\]\, \[EMIm\]\[BF4\]\, and \[EMIm\]\[TFSI\] were 15\.26\, 12\.16\, and 7\.14 mS cm−1\, respectively\. The mixture \[EMIm\]\[FSI\]0\.6\[BF4\]0\.4 exhibited the highest conductivity among the mixtures at 12\.62 mS cm−1 and also had the lowest viscosity\. Although the room\-temperature conductivity of the mixture was lower than that of pure \[EMIm\]\[FSI\]\, it maintained a conductivity of 0\.46 mS cm−1 at 233 K\, a temperature at which the pure FSI\-based IL was no longer in the liquid state \[71\]\. A similar benefit was observed for the \[EHIm\]\[TFO\]\+\[EHIm\]\[TFSI\] system by Abdurrokhman and Martinelli \[78\]\. They found only small changes in conductivity with composition\; however\, the addition of \[EHIm\]\[TFSI\] strongly suppressed crystallization and widened the liquid\-state temperature range\. In conclusion\, while high conductivity is typically associated with low viscosity\, the relationship is not strictly proportional\. Positive conductivity deviations are advantageous\, although exceeding the conductivity of both parent ILs is not essential\. Suppression of crystallization and preservation of ion transport over a wider temperature range may be equally important\.

\#\#\# 4\.4\. Surface Tension and Interfacial Composition

Surface tension is highly sensitive to the composition of the interfacial layer\, which may differ significantly from the bulk composition \[117\,118\]\. As a result\, IL mixtures can exhibit pronounced deviations from linear mixing behavior\, particularly when the components possess markedly different surface affinities \[40\,119\,120\,121\]\. Koller et al\. reported that adding small amounts of the fluorinated 3\-methyl\-1\-\(3\,3\,4\,4\,4\-pentafluorobutyl\)imidazolium hexafluorophosphate \(\[PFBMIm\]\[PF6\]\) to \[BMIm\]\[PF6\] led to a substantial decrease in surface tension\, consistent with preferential enrichment of the fluorinated component at the interface \[122\]\. Comparable behavior was observed for 1\,3\-bis\(2\-\(2\-methoxyethoxy\)ethyl\)imidazolium iodide \(\[\(mPEG2\)2Im\]\[I\]\)\+\[OMIm\]\[PF6\]\, for which Zhai et al\. identified a negative deviation of approximately −5\.3\% at equimolar composition \[123\]\. An even greater effect was found for the common\-cation mixture \[EMIm\]\[OAc\]\+\[EMIm\]\[TFSI\]\, for which the equimolar mixture showed a −7\.7\% deviation from linear additivity\. Angle\-resolved X\-ray photoelectron spectroscopy \(ARXPS\) confirmed preferential enrichment of \[TFSI\]− at the interface\, especially at low bulk concentrations\, thereby directly linking macroscopic surface tension to microscopic surface composition \[8\]\. Both positive and negative surface tension deviations have been reported\. Buarque et al\. observed positive surface tension deviation for \[2\-HEA\]\[OAc\]\+\[BHEA\]\[OAc\]\, while \[2\-HEA\]\[OAc\]\+\[BHEA\]\[Bu\] showed negative values across the investigated temperature range \[108\]\. Direct evidence for the microscopic origin of such non\-linear behavior was also provided by Paap et al\.\, who combined pendant\-drop measurements with angle\-resolved X\-ray photoelectron spectroscopy to correlate surface tension with surface composition \[117\]\. Overall\, surface tension cannot be reliably predicted from bulk composition alone\, because preferential interfacial segregation may allow even small amounts of a surface\-active IL to exert a disproportionately large influence on interfacial properties\. This behavior provides an additional strategy for tuning wetting\, interfacial mass transfer\, and supported\-liquid\-phase applications without necessarily inducing comparably large changes in bulk properties\.

\#\#\# 4\.5\. Hydrogen Bonding\, Polarity\, Solvatochromism\, and Acid–Base Descriptors

Polarity in ionic liquid mixtures results from Coulombic interactions\, hydrogen bonding\, polarizability\, dispersion forces\, and local ionic organization\. Mixing can redistribute cation–anion contacts and alter both the accessibility and residence time of ions around a solute\, even when macroscopic properties such as density are nearly additive\. Existing studies confirm that hydrogen\-bond structure and dynamics may vary non\-linearly with composition \[22\]\. Molecular simulations indicate that strongly coordinating anions preferentially occupy the hydrogen\-bonding sites of suitable cations and mixing may strengthen specific interactions rather than simply dilute them \[20\]\. Spectroscopic and computational results for \[BMIm\]\[TFSI\]\+\[BMPyr\]\[TFSI\] showed that imidazolium–anion hydrogen bonding is stronger than pyrrolidinium–anion coordination\. Increasing the pyrrolidinium fraction weakened the overall hydrogen\-bond network and changed the cis\/trans conformational distribution of \[TFSI\]− \[22\]\.

Solvatochromic probes offer an effective method for examining these changes\. Reichardt\-type dyes yield the normalized polarity parameter\, while multiprobe approaches provide the Kamlet–Taft parameters\: \(α\) hydrogen\-bond\-donor acidity\, \(β\) hydrogen\-bond\-acceptor basicity\, and \(π\*\) dipolarity\/polarizability\. Thawarkar et al\. reported pronounced positive deviations of the polarity parameter for mixtures of the protic ionic liquid \[HMIm\]\[OAc\] with either \[BMIm\]\[TFSI\] or \[BMPyr\]\[TFSI\]\. At intermediate compositions\, the apparent polarity exceeded that of both parent liquids\. This “hyperpolarity” was attributed to hydrogen\-bond\-mediated restructuring and preferential solvation of the dye\, whereas analogous protic–protic mixtures did not exhibit the same synergistic effect \[124\]\.

Acid–base descriptors can also be related directly to application performance\. In common\-acetate double\-salt ionic liquids containing \[EMIm\]\+\, \[Ch\]\+\, and \[N2222\]\+\, a modified multiparameter relationship incorporating \(α\)\, \(β\)\, \(π\*\)\, and Hammett basicity described catalytic activity with \(R2 \> 0\.994\)\. Hydrogen\-bond basicity was the dominant factor in two mixture families\, whereas dipolarity\/polarizability became more important in the choline–tetraethylammonium system \[82\]\.

Overall\, polarity and acid–base parameters should be treated as composition\-\, temperature\-\, water\-\, and probe\-dependent characteristics of the complete formulation\. No single descriptor fully represents the solvation environment\, and parameters obtained for the parent ionic liquids should not be assumed to mix linearly\.

\#\# 5\. Conclusions and Future Perspective

Ionic liquid \(IL\) mixtures extend the designer\-solvent concept by introducing composition as an additional\, continuously adjustable variable\. Mixing can suppress crystallization\, modify ion association and hydrogen\-bond networks\, alter preferential coordination\, and change interfacial organization\. Consequently\, the application\-optimal composition is not necessarily equimolar or eutectic and generally cannot be predicted by linear interpolation of the properties of the parent ILs\.

The most relevant composition–property relationships depend strongly on the intended application\. In low\-temperature batteries and supercapacitors\, for example\, crystallization suppression and the preservation of conductivity over a broad temperature range may be more important than achieving the highest conductivity at room temperature\. Mixed\-anion systems can additionally modify Li\+ coordination\, proton\-transfer pathways\, and ion packing within electrode pores\. In aromatic extraction and extractive distillation\, polarity and preferential solvation determine capacity and selectivity\, whereas viscosity\, phase disengagement\, and solvent recovery ultimately govern process feasibility\. In cellulose processing\, chloride and acetate can cooperatively disrupt cellulose hydrogen bonding\, although the outcome depends strongly on their relative proportions and on the cation structure\. Replacing part of the acetate with a less basic anion\, such as thiocyanate\, may improve fluidity but can substantially reduce cellulose dissolution\. In catalysis\, composition can be used to adjust acidity\, basicity\, polarity\, and the accessibility of active ions\. Electrospray propulsion depends on the combined effects of conductivity\, viscosity\, surface tension\, and cluster formation\, whereas luminescent mixtures exploit composition\-dependent nanoheterogeneity around the emitting species\. Biological activity and toxicity must likewise be assessed directly because mixtures may exhibit additive\, antagonistic\, or synergistic effects\.

Gas separation is a particularly important example of the possibilities offered by IL mixtures\, as the composition can be used to tune gas solubility\, selectivity\, phase behavior\, viscosity\, and transport properties simultaneously\. However\, the available evidence shows that the effect of mixing is highly system\-specific\. CO2 solubility may show positive deviations from linear mixing at selected compositions and pressures\, whereas CO2\/N2 or CO2\/CH4 selectivity may remain intermediate between the values of the pure ILs\. Improved CO2 uptake alone should therefore not be regarded as evidence of superior separation performance\. Instead\, capacity\, selectivity\, permeability\, diffusivity\, and regeneration behavior should be evaluated together\. A central priority for future studies is to move from pure\-gas measurements towards realistic mixed\-gas testing\. Predictions based solely on single\-gas Henry’s law constants may therefore fail to represent solvent behavior adequately in biogas upgrading\, natural\-gas sweetening\, pre\-combustion capture\, or flue\-gas treatment\. Experiments should consequently employ representative gas mixtures containing CO2\, N2\, CH4 and\, where relevant\, acid gases and water vapor\, across realistic ranges of pressure\, temperature\, and feed composition\.

A central priority for future studies is to move from pure\-gas measurements towards realistic mixed\-gas testing\. Predictions based solely on single\-gas Henry’s law constants may therefore fail to represent solvent behavior adequately in biogas upgrading\, natural\-gas sweetening\, pre\-combustion capture\, or flue\-gas treatment\. Experiments should consequently employ representative gas mixtures containing CO2\, N2\, CH4 and\, where relevant\, other feed components such as acid gases and water vapor\, across realistic ranges of pressure\, temperature\, and composition\. Because the effects of water were not systematically evaluated in the studies reviewed here\, no general conclusions regarding its influence on IL mixture performance can be drawn\. Nevertheless\, for applications involving humid gas streams\, water content should be reported and controlled so that its possible influence on phase behavior\, viscosity\, gas sorption\, and transport can be distinguished from the intrinsic effects of IL mixture composition\.

The trade\-off between reactivity and mass transfer likewise requires systematic consideration\. Basic\, acetate\-containing\, amino\-functionalized\, or otherwise reactive components can enhance CO2 affinity through chemisorption\, but may simultaneously increase viscosity\, slow transport\, complicate regeneration\, or introduce absorption–desorption hysteresis\. Less reactive components\, in contrast\, may improve fluidity and favor physical sorption\, particularly at elevated pressures\. For these reasons\, future solvent development should rely on multi\-objective optimization rather than maximizing a single equilibrium property\. Relevant objectives include CO2 capacity at the intended partial pressure\, selectivity against relevant co\-gases\, absorption and desorption kinetics\, viscosity\, diffusivity\, thermal and oxidative stability\, susceptibility to water\, liquid\-phase stability\, membrane retention where supported ionic liquid membranes are used\, and the energy required for solvent regeneration\.

Molecular\-level characterization should be integrated with macroscopic separation measurements\. Combining spectroscopic methods\, scattering techniques\, molecular simulations\, and gas\-sorption experiments would help establish direct structure–property relationships relevant to gas separation\.

The development of reliable machine learning models for IL mixtures is still limited by the amount and consistency of available experimental data\. Many datasets cover only a few compositions\, narrow temperature or pressure ranges\, or a limited number of IL families\. Future studies should therefore report the full ionic composition\, several mixture compositions including the pure\-component endpoints\, temperature\, pressure\, water content\, purity\, and experimental uncertainty\. It would also be useful to measure several relevant properties for the same compositions under the same conditions\, for example density\, viscosity\, conductivity\, phase behavior\, solubility\, selectivity\, and application performance\. Reporting both high\-performing and poor\-performing compositions is important to avoid biased datasets\. More standardized and machine\-readable data would improve model training\, validation\, and multiobjective optimization of IL mixtures\.

records.body_text:
High-Performance Ethernet Switch Connectors
As data centers evolve, the demand for high-speed performance, reliable signal integrity and efficient heat management in Ethernet switches continues to grow. Navigating these challenges while maximizing port density requires innovative interconnect solutions. Molex delivers advanced technologies that enhance signal performance and optimize thermal efficiency, aligned with the next generation of networking infrastructure.
Overcoming Data Center Ethernet Switch Challenges with Advanced Interconnects
For data centers to meet the demands of high-speed, data-intensive applications and avoid bottlenecks, switches need to support lower latency and increased throughput. Additionally, physical space constraints often require switches and components to optimize port density and maintain compact designs. Efficient heat dissipation across the system is also critical for ensuring long-term operational reliability.
Advanced interconnects and high-performance cabling deliver the bandwidth and low latency required for next-generation data rates. High-density connectors, like QSFP-DD and SFP-DD, allow for greater port density in limited spaces. To manage heat dissipation and maintain system stability, system designers look to liquid cooling and heat sinks as effective solutions.
Molex provides the advanced Ethernet switch components that overcome these obstacles, supporting the latest standards like PCIe Gen 6 and Ethernet 224Gbps PAM4. With superior signal integrity (SI) even at high frequencies, compact form factors and innovative thermal management options, Ethernet switch components from Molex empower data centers to perform at peak efficiency.
Featured Products
High-Speed Internal I/O Connectors
As data rates increase, maintaining signal integrity becomes critical for handling high frequencies without loss or distortion. High-density connectors from Molex are designed to support leading-edge standards like PCIe Gen 6 and 224Gbps PAM4, to support reliable signal integrity and high-speed performance across complex data environments.

records.body_text:
Aluminum Busbar vs. Copper Busbar in EV Battery Modules: Weight Savings, Ampacity, and Cost Trade-offs
Oct 09, 2026 View: 114
Aluminum Busbar can reduce conductor mass and material costs in electric vehicle (EV) battery modules, but require careful evaluation of conductivity, temperature rise, joint resistance, and corrosion protection. Commercially pure aluminum has approximately 61% IACS conductivity, compared with approximately 100% IACS for standard high-conductivity copper. The final choice depends on electrical performance, installation space, manufacturing requirements, and total component cost.
Aluminum vs. Copper Busbar: Key Material Differences
Material selection affects conductor dimensions, battery pack weight, forming processes, and connection reliability. C1100 copper, 1060 aluminum, and 6061 aluminum offer different combinations of conductivity, strength, and formability.
Property
| C1100 Copper | 1060 Aluminum | 6061 Aluminum
---|---|---|---
Density | Approx. 8.9 g/cm³ | Approx. 2.70 g/cm³ | Approx. 2.70 g/cm³
Electrical conductivity | Approx. 100% IACS | Typically above 60% IACS | Generally lower than 1060
Main advantage
| High conductivity | Low mass and high conductivity among aluminum grades | Higher structural strength in suitable tempers
Main consideration | Higher density and material cost | Larger cross-section may be required | Conductivity and forming behavior depend on temper
For equal conductor length and comparable DC resistance, aluminum may require approximately 1.6 times the copper cross-sectional area. Despite the larger area, its lower density can result in a conductor mass roughly 50% lower under simplified room-temperature assumptions.
Actual savings depend on geometry, operating temperature, joint design, and thermal conditions. Engineers must validate the complete assembly rather than compare materials by density alone.
Ampacity, Temperature Rise, and Battery Pack Weight
The current-carrying capacity of an EV battery busbar depends on conductor cross-section, current duty, ambient temperature, cooling conditions, insulation, and connection resistance.
For initial sizing, conductor resistance can be estimated using:
R=ρL/A
where R is resistance, ρ is electrical resistivity, L is conductor length, and A is cross-sectional area.
A larger aluminum cross-section can compensate for its higher resistivity, but engineers must also evaluate:
- Continuous and peak current requirements.
- Temperature rise under representative operating cycles.
- Joint resistance at bolted or welded interfaces.
- Available installation space and insulation clearances.
- Mechanical loads from vibration and thermal expansion.
Weight savings at battery pack level will be smaller than the percentage reduction in busbar mass. For example, if busbars account for 2% of pack mass and their mass is reduced by 50%, the total pack mass decreases by approximately 1%, assuming other components remain unchanged.
Aluminum Busbar Plating and Corrosion Protection
Aluminum naturally forms a stable oxide film that can interfere with electrical contact. For battery applications, surface preparation and interface design are important to maintaining low contact resistance.
A qualified plating process may include:
- Degreasing and surface cleaning.
- Controlled oxide removal and pretreatment.
- Zincate treatment where required by the selected process.
- Copper or nickel underplating where specified.
- Tin plating or another approved surface finish.
- Coating inspection and electrical contact validation.
The appropriate process depends on alloy, geometry, plating chemistry, and application requirements. Tin plating can support selected contact applications, but does not eliminate all corrosion risks. Aluminum-to-copper connections require assessment of galvanic corrosion, moisture exposure, contact pressure, and coating integrity.
Recommended validation may include coating-thickness measurement, adhesion testing where applicable, four-wire joint-resistance measurement, and temperature-rise testing under defined conditions.
Stamping, Bending, and Welding for OEM Production
An Aluminum Busbar Manufacturer must control both electrical performance and manufacturing consistency. Stamping, CNC machining, bending, and joining processes affect dimensional accuracy, contact quality, and production yield.
Important design considerations include:
- Bend radius relative to material thickness.
- Burr height and direction near insulation or contact surfaces.
- Hole position, flatness, and terminal alignment.
- Cracking risk at formed edges.
- Tool wear and dimensional variation during production.
Laser welding and resistance welding may both be suitable, depending on the joint geometry and materials.
Factor
| Laser Welding | Resistance Welding
---|---|---
Heat input | Localized and controlled by laser parameters | Generated through current, resistance, and electrode force
Main process variables | Power, speed, focus, and joint fit-up | Current, force, weld time, and electrode condition
Typical risks | Porosity, lack of fusion, distortion | Inconsistent weld formation and electrode wear
Validation | Weld inspection, resistance, and mechanical testing | Weld monitoring, resistance, and mechanical testing
Copper-to-aluminum laser welding requires particular attention to brittle intermetallic compounds, cracking, and joint resistance. The process must be qualified using representative parts and agreed acceptance criteria.
For automotive programs, production documentation may include process flow, PFMEA, control plans, dimensional inspection reports, and PPAP submissions where required. ISO 9001 or IATF 16949 certification should be verified against the supplier's actual certification scope and customer requirements.
How to Select the Right Busbar Supplier
A Custom Aluminum Busbar Supplier should evaluate the drawing, material grade, electrical duty, surface finish, and production volume before confirming feasibility and pricing.
Procurement and engineering teams should verify:
- Material control: Alloy, temper, thickness, and material traceability.
- Manufacturing capability: Stamping, bending, machining, joining, and plating.
- Inspection capability: Dimensional accuracy, coating quality, and electrical resistance testing.
- Quality documentation: Applicable ISO 9001, IATF 16949, and customer-specific requirements.
- Production readiness: Sample approval, process validation, change control, and PPAP where required.
The RFQ should include a 2D drawing or 3D model, current and voltage requirements, temperature limits, connection details, surface-finish specifications, annual volume, and required quality documents. Complete specifications help suppliers evaluate manufacturability and reduce design changes during production.
FAQ: Aluminum Busbars for EV Battery Modules
Q: How much lighter is an aluminum busbar than a copper busbar?
A: For equal length and comparable DC resistance, a simplified calculation suggests aluminum conductor mass may be approximately 50% lower. Actual results depend on geometry, operating temperature, joints, and thermal requirements.
Q: Can an aluminum busbar carry the same current as copper?
A: Yes, when conductor dimensions and thermal performance are properly engineered. Aluminum generally requires a larger cross-section, and the finished assembly must meet specified temperature-rise and electrical performance limits.
Q: Does every aluminum busbar require tin plating?
A: No. Surface treatment depends on the contact interface, operating environment, corrosion risk, and customer specification. Any selected coating system should be validated for adhesion, thickness, and electrical performance.
Q: What information is needed for an aluminum busbar quotation?
A: Provide drawings, alloy and temper requirements, current duty, voltage, temperature limits, connection details, surface finish, annual quantity, and applicable quality documentation.
Contact Us
Xiamen Apollo Stamping Welding Technology Co., Ltd. manufactures precision metal stamping and welded components for EV, energy storage, photovoltaic, and electrical applications. For aluminum busbar projects, provide your drawings, electrical requirements, surface-finish specifications, and estimated order volume for a manufacturing feasibility review.

For equal conductor length and comparable DC resistance\, aluminum may require approximately 1\.6 times the copper cross\-sectional area\. Despite the larger area\, its lower density can result in a conductor mass roughly 50\% lower under simplified room\-temperature assumptions\.

Actual savings depend on geometry\, operating temperature\, joint design\, and thermal conditions\. Engineers must validate the complete assembly rather than compare materials by density alone\.

\#\# Ampacity\, Temperature Rise\, and Battery Pack Weight

The current\-carrying capacity of an EV battery busbar depends on conductor cross\-section\, current duty\, ambient temperature\, cooling conditions\, insulation\, and connection resistance\.

For initial sizing\, conductor resistance can be estimated using\:

R\=ρL\/A

where R is resistance\, ρ is electrical resistivity\, L is conductor length\, and A is cross\-sectional area\.

A larger aluminum cross\-section can compensate for its higher resistivity\, but engineers must also evaluate\:

\- Continuous and peak current requirements\.
\- Temperature rise under representative operating cycles\.
\- Joint resistance at bolted or welded interfaces\.
\- Available installation space and insulation clearances\.
\- Mechanical loads from vibration and thermal expansion\.

Weight savings at battery pack level will be smaller than the percentage reduction in busbar mass\. For example\, if busbars account for 2\% of pack mass and their mass is reduced by 50\%\, the total pack mass decreases by approximately 1\%\, assuming other components remain unchanged\.

\#\# Aluminum Busbar Plating and Corrosion Protection

Aluminum naturally forms a stable oxide film that can interfere with electrical contact\. For battery applications\, surface preparation and interface design are important to maintaining low contact resistance\.

A qualified plating process may include\:

\- Degreasing and surface cleaning\.
\- Controlled oxide removal and pretreatment\.
\- Zincate treatment where required by the selected process\.
\- Copper or nickel underplating where specified\.
\- Tin plating or another approved surface finish\.
\- Coating inspection and electrical contact validation\.

The appropriate process depends on alloy\, geometry\, plating chemistry\, and application requirements\. Tin plating can support selected contact applications\, but does not eliminate all corrosion risks\. Aluminum\-to\-copper connections require assessment of galvanic corrosion\, moisture exposure\, contact pressure\, and coating integrity\.

Recommended validation may include coating\-thickness measurement\, adhesion testing where applicable\, four\-wire joint\-resistance measurement\, and temperature\-rise testing under defined conditions\.

\#\# Stamping\, Bending\, and Welding for OEM Production

An Aluminum Busbar Manufacturer must control both electrical performance and manufacturing consistency\. Stamping\, CNC machining\, bending\, and joining processes affect dimensional accuracy\, contact quality\, and production yield\.

Important design considerations include\:

\- Bend radius relative to material thickness\.
\- Burr height and direction near insulation or contact surfaces\.
\- Hole position\, flatness\, and terminal alignment\.
\- Cracking risk at formed edges\.
\- Tool wear and dimensional variation during production\.

Laser welding and resistance welding may both be suitable\, depending on the joint geometry and materials\.

Factor
 \| Laser Welding \| Resistance Welding 
\-\-\-\|\-\-\-\|\-\-\-
Heat input \| Localized and controlled by laser parameters \| Generated through current\, resistance\, and electrode force 
Main process variables \| Power\, speed\, focus\, and joint fit\-up \| Current\, force\, weld time\, and electrode condition 
Typical risks \| Porosity\, lack of fusion\, distortion \| Inconsistent weld formation and electrode wear 
Validation \| Weld inspection\, resistance\, and mechanical testing \| Weld monitoring\, resistance\, and mechanical testing 

Copper\-to\-aluminum laser welding requires particular attention to brittle intermetallic compounds\, cracking\, and joint resistance\. The process must be qualified using representative parts and agreed acceptance criteria\.

For automotive programs\, production documentation may include process flow\, PFMEA\, control plans\, dimensional inspection reports\, and PPAP submissions where required\. ISO 9001 or IATF 16949 certification should be verified against the supplier\'s actual certification scope and customer requirements\.

\#\# How to Select the Right Busbar Supplier

A Custom Aluminum Busbar Supplier should evaluate the drawing\, material grade\, electrical duty\, surface finish\, and production volume before confirming feasibility and pricing\.

Procurement and engineering teams should verify\:

\- Material control\: Alloy\, temper\, thickness\, and material traceability\.
\- Manufacturing capability\: Stamping\, bending\, machining\, joining\, and plating\.
\- Inspection capability\: Dimensional accuracy\, coating quality\, and electrical resistance testing\.
\- Quality documentation\: Applicable ISO 9001\, IATF 16949\, and customer\-specific requirements\.
\- Production readiness\: Sample approval\, process validation\, change control\, and PPAP where required\.

The RFQ should include a 2D drawing or 3D model\, current and voltage requirements\, temperature limits\, connection details\, surface\-finish specifications\, annual volume\, and required quality documents\. Complete specifications help suppliers evaluate manufacturability and reduce design changes during production\.

\#\# FAQ\: Aluminum Busbars for EV Battery Modules

Q\: How much lighter is an aluminum busbar than a copper busbar\?

A\: For equal length and comparable DC resistance\, a simplified calculation suggests aluminum conductor mass may be approximately 50\% lower\. Actual results depend on geometry\, operating temperature\, joints\, and thermal requirements\.

Q\: Can an aluminum busbar carry the same current as copper\?

A\: Yes\, when conductor dimensions and thermal performance are properly engineered\. Aluminum generally requires a larger cross\-section\, and the finished assembly must meet specified temperature\-rise and electrical performance limits\.

Q\: Does every aluminum busbar require tin plating\?

A\: No\. Surface treatment depends on the contact interface\, operating environment\, corrosion risk\, and customer specification\. Any selected coating system should be validated for adhesion\, thickness\, and electrical performance\.

Q\: What information is needed for an aluminum busbar quotation\?

A\: Provide drawings\, alloy and temper requirements\, current duty\, voltage\, temperature limits\, connection details\, surface finish\, annual quantity\, and applicable quality documentation\.

records.body_text:
Functionally Speaking: A Bright Future for Surface Finishing is in Our Hands
Earlier this year I wrote the article “Fabrication to Finishing to Assembly: A Stronger Voice by Aligning Affiliated Industries.”
That piece was about the metals ecosystem—fabricators, finishers, assemblers—and the strength that comes from lining up together. This one is about a different kind of voice: how our industry talks about itself.
Ask anyone in automotive, airlines, aerospace, defense, space, or medical devices where they would be without chemical surface treatment. The answer: out of luck. That’s the polite version, since I couldn’t print the F-word everyone is thinking.
Surface finishing makes the part look right, resist corrosion, and take the wear in all kinds of environments. It’s not a nice-to-have. Think about that the next time you’re driving a car, flying in a plane, talking to someone with an artificial limb, or wondering what is keeping a satellite working in space.
Why are Regulators Aggressive Towards Finishers?
If the work we provide is that essential, why do the public, regulators, and localities so often take an aggressive stance against the shops that do it? Why the hearings, the “not in my backyard,” the assumption that finishing is a problem to be contained rather than a capability manufacturing cannot fly without?
Maybe it’s because we keep inviting them into the wrong room.
Think about the finest steak restaurant. Guests don’t have the appetite for the slaughterhouse or what goes on in the kitchen. It’s all about the dining room—the plate that arrives, that well-prepared, juicy steak.
To many people, surface finishing is the slaughterhouse and the kitchen. Tanks. Chemistry. Airborne exposure. Wastewater. That is the story they already think they know. They never see the satellite, the airframe, the implant. They see the tank. Then they vote, write the rule, and tell their kids to look for work somewhere else. Sometimes we are our own worst enemy. How many times have you heard, even in the shop, “who wants to be a plater?”
There’s a story, probably embellished and maybe made up, that got me thinking about how we should be talking. During the early 1960s, as part of the space race, President Kennedy visited a NASA center and introduced himself to a janitor sweeping the floor. When Kennedy asked what he did at NASA, the janitor didn’t say he cleaned the building. He said he was helping put a man on the moon.
Why a car lasts, why a plane flies, why a satellite stays on station, why a device can go in a body. That’s our story. But telling it through public relations, marketing, and recruiting the next generation was never anyone’s main assignment.
I got a chance to try that thinking. On the way to SUR/FIN, a TSA agent asked what I was going to Chicago for. I said a trade show for surface finishing. When he asked what that was, I didn’t mention chemicals or plating. I said it was the work that helps keep aircraft doing what they are supposed to do. Much to my surprise, he started talking about how a wing flexes in flight. He got it.
It happened again in my driveway on a Saturday. A maintenance guy from one of our plating-shop customers was looking for some weekend work, and believe me, I had projects for him. My neighbor—young, family, homebrews his beer, used to jump out of planes before the kids—works for a large company that builds satellites. He saw the shop name on the guy’s shirt, came over, and said, “Hey, your company does some of our plating.” They talked for a while. He wasn’t thinking about the tanks and the processes. He saw the parts that keep a satellite on station.
What’s Missing in All of This?
A lot of good work is already happening. Suppliers are doing their part with alternative chemistries. Platers are doing their part by installing air-handling and water-treatment systems in their facilities. Associations, nationally and locally, are doing their part through advocacy, government relations, technical education, and funding sound science. The primes are doing their part by approving those alternative chemistries so shops can run them. Back to the restaurant: the kitchen is getting cleaner, safer, and easier to defend. That’s real progress. But it isn’t what’s missing.
What’s missing is something we never really had to focus on in the past: promoting and marketing surface finishing itself, and the value it delivers. You know, the dining room.
Why a car lasts, why a plane flies, why a satellite stays on station, why a device can go in a body. That’s our story. But telling it through public relations, marketing, and recruiting the next generation was never anyone’s main assignment.
The next generation—students and people early on in their careers—need to hear something else: this is a good gig, with real careers at every level
The industry around us has changed and is still changing. Surface finishing is contracting, as are other trades. Perception is part of it. So is reality: the cost of staying in compliance and the cost of doing business keep climbing. In the past, the work found you. Even today, many finishers have a website and maybe a LinkedIn or Instagram page, but they are operating without a sales force. When our associations rally members, it’s usually to fight a new regulation or a city council deciding whether to regulate us or eliminate us. We are always playing defense. It’s time to go on offense, positively.
Learning From Other Industries
If we look at other industries facing some of these same challenges, we can learn from them. Trucking still fights hours-of-service rules and the public’s view of diesel and wrecks. They also sold the dining room: if you bought it, a truck brought it—and later, Nothing Without Trucking. Beef still has packing plants. They didn’t advertise the kill floor. They advertised dinner. Mining’s association says Minerals Make Life. Paper and packaging went with How Life Unfolds. None of them stopped advocating or doing the science. They just stopped letting the plant be the only story.
We can fill the gap the same way I did with the TSA agent, and the way my neighbor did in my driveway: start with the finished product. With officials, that means jobs, tax base, defense readiness, and supply chain. The next generation—students and people early on in their careers—need to hear something else: this is a good gig, with real careers at every level. You can come in from high school, a trade program, or a four-year degree. You can stay on the line, move into quality or EHS, run a process, run a plant, or own one. Attracting them takes more than promoting the industry to the public. It means showing up at high schools, trade schools, and community colleges (counselors, CTE teachers, chem labs) with a career ladder in hand and a plant tour on the calendar.
Here’s what that ladder can look like. And that’s only the plant floor. A finishing plant also hires in sales, estimating, customer service, shipping, HR, finance, and IT. It’s a company, not a tank room.
Career Ladder: Same Plant, Many Paths
Start here: High school; 0–2 yrs | Skilled:
2–5 yrs
| Lead/Specialist:
4–8 yrs
| Manager & Up:
7+ yrs
---|---|---|---
Plating & anodizing | Racker / Masker; Entry Plater | Multi-Process Plater; Anodize Tech | Lead Plater | Production Mgr → Plant Mgr / GM → VP Ops
Paint & prep | Blast / Deburr Prep Tech | Painter (liquid or powder) | Paint Supervisor | Production Manager
Quality | Quality Inspector; NDT Level I | NDT Level II | QC Lead; Quality Engineer | Quality Manager
Lab & process | Lab Technician | Technical Service Rep | Process Engineer | Lab Manager / Chief Chemist
EHS & wastewater | Waste Treatment Assistant | Certified Wastewater Operator | Compliance Specialist | EHS Manager
Maintenance | — | Maintenance Technician | Lead Multi-Craft Tech | Maintenance Manager
How you move up | On-the-job training; safety certs (HAZWOPER) | AESF CEF; NDT Level II; CWEA wastewater cert | Supervisor training; Six Sigma Green Belt; CQE | Experience plus leadership; degree helps; not always required
Whatever Someone’s Background, There’s a Path
That’s the school packet: one table, one tour, and one sentence like the one that worked on the TSA agent. Whatever someone’s background, there’s a path. Some will be drawn to the lab, some to running the process, some to estimating, and some to keeping a satellite contractor’s parts in spec.
I wish I could snap my fingers and everyone would say this is a great industry to be in. That is not how it works. If we mean Made in the USA—and staying in the USA—local and national associations have to add promotion and the next generation to the mission. I’m not saying instead of advocacy, government relations, and the science. I’m saying in addition to.
The good news is we don’t have to invent the whole toolbox. The AESF Foundation, NASF’s education arm, already trains and certifies—CEF, CAF, MSF—and runs scholarships for students in chemistry and materials. Chapters add their own awards. Shops can pay for the course and put a bonus on passing, which some already do. Manufacturing Day is on the calendar every October: open the door, walk a class through, talk about the part that goes on the plane.
Keep the suppliers on chemistry. Keep the platers on air and water treatment. Keep the associations on advocacy, government relations, and the science. Keep the primes on approvals. Then market the value.
Other associations already invest in schools. SME’s education foundation runs PRIME—manufacturing labs, curriculum, and teacher training inside high schools, free to the school. FMA’s foundation, SparkForce, funds summer camps and scholarships that include trade school and community college, not only the four-year. AWS SENSE is the welding curriculum high schools and tech colleges use, including to line up Perkins dollars. Those programs are running now. We don’t need a new organization. We need to copy the on-ramp.
Public money is available if someone will fill out the paperwork. In California, the Employment Training Panel reimburses manufacturers for training people already on the clock and people just hired. Workforce boards under WIOA can fund on-the-job training. Perkins dollars sit in the high-school CTE and community-college system, waiting for an employer to help design the class. Registered apprenticeships exist; manufacturing is a priority sector. None of that money shows up on its own. It shows up when a shop or an association asks for it.
Promotion and Workforce Should Be in the Written Mission
So the snap-your-fingers list is actually short and doable. Put promotion and workforce in the written mission. Build a one-page school packet and a speaker list. Host a Manufacturing Day tour. Get two shops onto an ETP or WIOA contract this year. Fund a scholarship that includes trade school, not just the college junior year. Lead with the finished product, the way I did with the TSA agent, at every hearing, every counselor visit, and every plant tour. That’s not pie in the sky. That’s work.
Keep the suppliers on chemistry. Keep the platers on air and water treatment. Keep the associations on advocacy, government relations, and the science. Keep the primes on approvals. Then market the value. Cars that last. Planes that fly. Satellites that stay on station. Devices that can be implanted. If we want a future that looks like that, we have to stop leading with the kitchen.
It’s time to go on offense. Who’s in?
Dan Zinman is the Chief Commercial Officer for Miles Chemical in Arleta, California. He has been active in industry trade groups for decades, and currently sits on the board of the Metal Finishing Association of Southern California.

EHS \& wastewater \| Waste Treatment Assistant \| Certified Wastewater Operator \| Compliance Specialist \| EHS Manager 
Maintenance \| — \| Maintenance Technician \| Lead Multi\-Craft Tech \| Maintenance Manager 
How you move up \| On\-the\-job training\; safety certs \(HAZWOPER\) \| AESF CEF\; NDT Level II\; CWEA wastewater cert \| Supervisor training\; Six Sigma Green Belt\; CQE \| Experience plus leadership\; degree helps\; not always required 

\#\#\#\# Whatever Someone’s Background\, There’s a Path

That’s the school packet\: one table\, one tour\, and one sentence like the one that worked on the TSA agent\. Whatever someone’s background\, there’s a path\. Some will be drawn to the lab\, some to running the process\, some to estimating\, and some to keeping a satellite contractor’s parts in spec\.

I wish I could snap my fingers and everyone would say this is a great industry to be in\. That is not how it works\. If we mean Made in the USA—and staying in the USA—local and national associations have to add promotion and the next generation to the mission\. I’m not saying instead of advocacy\, government relations\, and the science\. I’m saying in addition to\.

The good news is we don’t have to invent the whole toolbox\. The AESF Foundation\, NASF’s education arm\, already trains and certifies—CEF\, CAF\, MSF—and runs scholarships for students in chemistry and materials\. Chapters add their own awards\. Shops can pay for the course and put a bonus on passing\, which some already do\. Manufacturing Day is on the calendar every October\: open the door\, walk a class through\, talk about the part that goes on the plane\.

\#\#\#\# Keep the suppliers on chemistry\. Keep the platers on air and water treatment\. Keep the associations on advocacy\, government relations\, and the science\. Keep the primes on approvals\. Then market the value\.

Other associations already invest in schools\. SME’s education foundation runs PRIME—manufacturing labs\, curriculum\, and teacher training inside high schools\, free to the school\. FMA’s foundation\, SparkForce\, funds summer camps and scholarships that include trade school and community college\, not only the four\-year\. AWS SENSE is the welding curriculum high schools and tech colleges use\, including to line up Perkins dollars\. Those programs are running now\. We don’t need a new organization\. We need to copy the on\-ramp\.

Public money is available if someone will fill out the paperwork\. In California\, the Employment Training Panel reimburses manufacturers for training people already on the clock and people just hired\. Workforce boards under WIOA can fund on\-the\-job training\. Perkins dollars sit in the high\-school CTE and community\-college system\, waiting for an employer to help design the class\. Registered apprenticeships exist\; manufacturing is a priority sector\. None of that money shows up on its own\. It shows up when a shop or an association asks for it\.

\#\#\#\# Promotion and Workforce Should Be in the Written Mission

So the snap\-your\-fingers list is actually short and doable\. Put promotion and workforce in the written mission\. Build a one\-page school packet and a speaker list\. Host a Manufacturing Day tour\. Get two shops onto an ETP or WIOA contract this year\. Fund a scholarship that includes trade school\, not just the college junior year\. Lead with the finished product\, the way I did with the TSA agent\, at every hearing\, every counselor visit\, and every plant tour\. That’s not pie in the sky\. That’s work\.

Keep the suppliers on chemistry\. Keep the platers on air and water treatment\. Keep the associations on advocacy\, government relations\, and the science\. Keep the primes on approvals\. Then market the value\. Cars that last\. Planes that fly\. Satellites that stay on station\. Devices that can be implanted\. If we want a future that looks like that\, we have to stop leading with the kitchen\.

It’s time to go on offense\. Who’s in\?

Dan Zinman is the Chief Commercial Officer for Miles Chemical in Arleta\, California\. He has been active in industry trade groups for decades\, and currently sits on the board of the Metal Finishing Association of Southern California\.

records.title: Optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system and method
assignees: 四川天邑康和通信股份有限公司
records.abstract: The invention relates to an optical fiber insertion loss return loss test management system and method, wherein an optical power detection module comprises an input optical power detection unit, an output optical power detection unit, a reflected optical power detection unit, an optical emission module, an optical switch matrix and a data processing module, wherein the optical emission module is a quantum dot tunable laser module, the optical switch matrix is a bionic optical switch matrix, multi-channel optical path reconstruction is realized, a multi-physical field sensing array is arranged in the optical power detection module, optical power data is detected in real time, the data processing module is used for receiving the optical power data to perform data processing, and the optical power detection system comprises a test module, acquires the optical power data based on the optical power detection module, and calculates optical fiber insertion loss and optical fiber return loss according to the acquired optical power data. The optical switch switching time is overlong, the requirement of the 5G carrier network on the rapid detection of batch optical fibers is difficult to meet, and the technical problems of inaccurate test results and the like in complex environments due to the lack of real-time sensing and compensation capability are solved.
records.summary: The disclosure describes an optical fiber insertion-loss and return-loss test management system and method intended to address slow optical-switch switching and the lack of real-time sensing/compensation in complex environments. The system combines an optical power detection module (input, output and reflected power detection units), a quantum-dot tunable laser emission module with a wavelength control unit, a bionic optical switch matrix for multi-channel optical path reconstruction, and a data processing module. A multi-physical-field sensing array integrating a distributed fiber acoustic sensor, a Brillouin optical time-domain analyzer and a micro thermal imaging unit is described for real-time optical power detection. A test module computes insertion loss and return loss from the acquired input, output and reflected optical power data. The claims present architecture and formulas; no measured performance results are supplied in the available text.

records.abstract: Translated from Chinese 本发明属于润滑材料技术领域，具体涉及一种化合物作为润滑剂凝胶因子的应用、超分子凝胶润滑剂及其制备方法。本发明提供了式I所示结构的化合物作为润滑剂凝胶因子的应用。本发明中，式I所示结构的化合物作为凝胶因子能够很好地阻止润滑油的泄露与爬移，同时通过磷酸酯结构引入减摩抗磨元素P，从而提高全氟聚醚润滑油的减摩与抗磨性能。由实施例的结果表明，本发明提供的磷酸酯功能化全氟聚醚型凝胶因子作为润滑添加剂提高了全氟聚醚润滑油的减摩、抗磨及极压条件下的摩擦学性能；作为凝胶因子使全氟聚醚润滑油凝胶化，得到类固体的超分子凝胶润滑剂，阻止了全氟聚醚润滑油的爬行迁移行为，同时突破了全氟聚醚润滑油摩擦系数较高的瓶颈； This invention belongs to the field of lubricating materials technology, specifically relating to the application of a compound as a lubricant gelling factor, a supramolecular gel lubricant, and its preparation method. This invention provides the application of a compound with the structure shown in Formula I as a lubricant gelling factor. In this invention, the compound with the structure shown in Formula I, as a gelling factor, can effectively prevent the leakage and creep of lubricating oil. Simultaneously, by introducing the friction-reducing and anti-wear element P through the phosphate ester structure, it improves the friction-reducing and anti-wear properties of perfluoropolyether lubricating oil. The results of the examples show that the phosphate ester-functionalized perfluoropolyether gelling factor provided by this invention, as a lubricating additive, improves the friction-reducing, anti-wear, and tribological properties of perfluoropolyether lubricating oil under extreme pressure conditions; as a gelling factor, it gels the perfluoropolyether lubricating oil to obtain a solid-like supramolecular gel lubricant, preventing the creeping and migration behavior of the perfluoropolyether lubricating oil, and simultaneously overcoming the bottleneck of the high friction coefficient of perfluoropolyether lubricating oil.
records.summary: The disclosure describes use of a phosphate-ester-functionalized perfluoropolyether compound of Formula I as a gelator for lubricants, and a supramolecular gel lubricant made by heating the gelator in a base oil (notably a perfluoropolyether lubricant) to at least 150 °C and cooling. The stated aims are to prevent leakage and creep/migration of perfluoropolyether oils and, through the phosphorus-containing phosphate ester structure, to improve friction-reducing and anti-wear behavior. The abstract reports that examples show improved friction-reducing, anti-wear and extreme-pressure tribological performance as an additive, and gelation into a solid-like lubricant that suppresses creep while addressing the high friction coefficient of perfluoropolyether oils. Only the abstract and claims were retrieved; the description, figures and experimental data are not available, so reported results are as summarized in the abstract rather than independently verifiable here.
records.why_it_matters: The claimed approach combines two functions in one molecule—a perfluoropolyether-compatible gelator that immobilizes the oil against creep and a phosphorus-containing phosphate ester intended to lower friction and wear—potentially allowing perfluoropolyether lubricants to be used as semi-solid gels in applications where oil migration is a problem.

records.title: An optical probe and related methods
records.abstract: The present invention relates to optical coupling between optical components and, more particular, to an optical probe (1) configured for optical testing of at least one micro-optical component (50), to a method for producing an optical probe (1), and to a method for simultaneously optical testing of at least one micro-optical component (50). The optical probe (1) is comprising: a probe head (10), wherein the probe head (10) comprises a test component (2); a plurality of micro-optical elements (20), wherein each micro-optical element (20) is a separate element with regard to the test component (2) and in mechanical contact with the test component (2), wherein each micro-optical element (20) is individually aligned with regard to the test component (2); and wherein each micro-optical element (20) is configured to generate a mode-field diameter of up to 100 µm, wherein the micro-optical elements (20) are configured to optically couple at least one light beam (3) between the test component (2) and the micro-optical component (50), thereby being configured to determine an emission characteristics of a coupling location (52) comprised by the micro-optical component (50), wherein the micro-optical component (50) further comprises a beam-shaping element (51a), wherein the beam-shaping element (51a) is arranged in a manner that at least a portion of the light beam (3) is travelling through the beam-shaping element (51a).
records.summary: The disclosure describes an optical probe for optically testing micro-optical components, particularly for determining emission characteristics of a coupling location on such a component that includes a beam-shaping element through which at least part of the light beam travels. The probe head contains a test component and a plurality of micro-optical elements that are separate from, but in mechanical contact with, the test component; each micro-optical element is individually aligned to the test component and is configured to generate a mode-field diameter of up to 100 µm. The micro-optical elements optically couple at least one light beam between the test component and the micro-optical component. Related methods are described for producing the probe, including direct-write generation of the micro-optical elements and a sensor structure, and for simultaneously testing micro-optical components. The source is abstract-and-claims only, so no experimental performance data are available.
records.why_it_matters: The claimed architecture separates the micro-optical coupling elements from the test component while keeping them in mechanical contact and individually aligned, which may allow probe heads to be built with direct-write processes rather than monolithic optics.

score_details.reason: The claims disclose an optical probe for testing micro-optical components: a probe head with a test component plus multiple separately aligned micro-optical elements (mode-field diameter up to 100 µm) that couple light to a micro-optical component and determine emission characteristics of a coupling location, with alignment markers, distance sensing, and direct-write/additive manufacturing of the elements and sensor structures. This is relevant to high-speed connectivity as an optical coupling/test method, but it is an adjacent test/inspection technology rather than a core interconnect design. Mechanism is concretely claimed (independent claims 1, 9, 11), but no measured outcomes, tolerances, or performance data are supplied, and the description/figures are absent, limiting quality and confidence. Novelty is apparent in the combination of individually aligned micro-optical elements with position-referenced emission measurement, but prior-art comparison is not possible from the text.

technical_points: Independent claim 1 defines an optical probe with a probe head comprising a test component and a plurality of micro-optical elements, each separate from the test component, in mechanical contact with it, and individually aligned to it.
Each micro-optical element is claimed to generate a mode-field diameter of up to 100 µm and to optically couple at least one light beam between the test component and the micro-optical component.

The probe is configured to determine an emission characteristic of a coupling location on the micro-optical component, which further comprises a beam-shaping element through which at least a portion of the light beam travels.

Dependent claims describe a sensor structure for detecting alignment markers on the micro-optical component, a distance sensor, and detection of beam deviation via first and second measurements of probe-head position and emission characteristics.

Independent method claim 9 describes producing the probe by direct-write generation of the micro-optical elements and a sensor structure; dependent claim 10 specifies additive manufacturing, and independent claim 11 describes a simultaneous testing method.
limitations: Only the abstract and claims were retrieved; the description and figures are not included, so mechanism details and embodiments beyond the claims cannot be assessed.
No experimental results, measured performance, or comparative data are supplied in the source text.
The English view may be machine translated, and no legal conclusions about claim scope or validity are drawn.

records.title: Rotary electric converter with preferred lubricant
records.abstract: Translated from Korean A rotary converter that transmits current between a stationary position and a rotating position uses pairs of conductive sintered discs, one stationary and one rotating, wherein the rotating sintered disc rotates on the stationary sintered disc and is lubricated with a boundary layer conductor of triglyceride.
records.summary: The disclosure describes a rotary electric converter that transfers current between a stationary external environment and a rotating internal environment using pairs of conductive sintered discs, one stationary and one rotating. The rotating sintered disc rotates on the stationary sintered disc, and a boundary layer conductor applied to both sintered metal contact surfaces both permits current flow between the non-rotating and rotating conductors and facilitates movement of the rotating surface during rotation. The claims recite that the boundary layer conductor is a pure triglyceride, a pure hydroxyl and unsaturated triglyceride, or pure castor oil. Independent claims cover a single pair of conductors and multiple isolated pairs separated by electrical insulating members, and a disc-based embodiment with a spindle housing and inner/outer periphery electrical connections. The source is limited to the abstract and claims; no experimental performance data, figures, or full description are available, and the English text may be machine translated.
records.why_it_matters: The disclosure frames the lubricant/conductive boundary layer as a functional element of the rotary electrical joint, so material selection of the triglyceride is presented as directly tied to both electrical conduction and sliding wear behavior rather than as a mere lubricant additive.

score_details.reason: The claims disclose a rotary electrical converter (slip-ring-like power transfer between stationary and rotating members) using paired sintered metal contact surfaces lubricated by a boundary-layer conductor of pure triglyceride, hydroxyl/unsaturated triglyceride, or castor oil. This directly touches the Advanced Lubricants theme and contact-surface/plating concerns, and is relevant to rotating electrical interconnect design. However, the text is abstract-and-claims only, machine-translated, with no description, figures, or measured data (contact resistance, wear rate, current density, temperature rise). Claims are largely repetitive variants differing only in lubricant identity, and no comparative performance versus prior art is established.

records.abstract: Provided is a female terminal. The female terminal includes a spring member and a terminal main body. The spring member is electrically connected to a male terminal to be connected. The terminal main body includes a base portion which has electrical conductivity and is electrically connected to the spring member. The base portion has a pair of side walls spaced apart by an insertion space that is inserted with a part of the male terminal. The spring member is arranged between the pair of side walls in the base portion, and the spring member is fixed to the side wall with a conductive welded portion with which the spring member is conductively welded to the side wall.
records.summary: The disclosure describes a female terminal in which a conductive spring member is arranged between a pair of side walls of a conductive terminal main body base portion and fixed to a side wall by a conductive welded portion. The spring member has multiple arm springs extending along the insertion depth direction and arranged along a direction intersecting that depth direction; the conductive welded portion runs in a line intersecting the depth direction and spans a region corresponding to all arm springs when viewed in the depth direction. The terminal main body may be more conductive and thicker than the spring member, and may have an unplated surface portion. Dependent claims add variants such as spring members on one or both side walls, a gripping plate welded on the outer side of a side wall, and a protruding portion on the opposite side wall. The disclosure also describes a connector, terminal-equipped electric wire, connector-equipped electric wire, wire harness, and busbar incorporating the female terminal. No experimental performance data are supplied in the retrieved abstract and claims.
records.why_it_matters: The claimed line-shaped conductive weld spanning all arm springs is intended to provide a continuous conductive path between the spring member and the terminal main body across the full spring array, which is relevant to current-carrying capacity and contact reliability in high-power connector designs.

records.abstract: Translated from Chinese 本发明涉及光学测量技术领域，提供一种光纤阵列适配器以及基于阵列通道的光谱测量装置。该光纤阵列适配器的输入端由多根光纤的输入端精密排列并固定形成二维阵列，且光纤输入端设为磨砂端面；其输出端由所述多根光纤的输出端重新排列并固定形成一维线性阵列。该光谱测量装置包括该光纤阵列适配器和光谱分析模块，光谱分析模块的入射狭缝与一维线性阵列光学耦合，其将来自各光纤通道的光信号经色散元件分光后，独立地成像在成像探测器的不同位置，通过单次曝光同步获取所有通道的光谱信息。该装置通过单一光谱分析模块实现多通道同步测量，降低了成本与复杂度；光纤磨砂端面抑制了反射与杂散光；模块化设计提升了适应不同测量场景的灵活性。 This invention relates to the field of optical measurement technology, providing a fiber optic array adapter and a spectral measurement device based on array channels. The input end of the fiber optic array adapter consists of multiple fiber optic input ends precisely arranged and fixed to form a two-dimensional array, with the fiber input ends having frosted end faces. Its output end consists of the output ends of the multiple fiber optics rearranged and fixed to form a one-dimensional linear array. The spectral measurement device includes the fiber optic array adapter and a spectral analysis module. The entrance slit of the spectral analysis module is optically coupled to the one-dimensional linear array. It disperses the light signals from each fiber channel through a dispersive element and independently images them at different positions on the imaging detector, simultaneously acquiring the spectral information of all channels in a single exposure. This device achieves multi-channel synchronous measurement through a single spectral analysis module, reducing cost and complexity; the frosted end faces of the fibers suppress reflection and stray light; and the modular design enhances flexibility in adapting to different measurement scenarios.

original_evidence.abstract: Translated from Chinese 本发明涉及光学测量技术领域，提供一种光纤阵列适配器以及基于阵列通道的光谱测量装置。该光纤阵列适配器的输入端由多根光纤的输入端精密排列并固定形成二维阵列，且光纤输入端设为磨砂端面；其输出端由所述多根光纤的输出端重新排列并固定形成一维线性阵列。该光谱测量装置包括该光纤阵列适配器和光谱分析模块，光谱分析模块的入射狭缝与一维线性阵列光学耦合，其将来自各光纤通道的光信号经色散元件分光后，独立地成像在成像探测器的不同位置，通过单次曝光同步获取所有通道的光谱信息。该装置通过单一光谱分析模块实现多通道同步测量，降低了成本与复杂度；光纤磨砂端面抑制了反射与杂散光；模块化设计提升了适应不同测量场景的灵活性。 This invention relates to the field of optical measurement technology, providing a fiber optic array adapter and a spectral measurement device based on array channels. The input end of the fiber optic array adapter consists of multiple fiber optic input ends precisely arranged and fixed to form a two-dimensional array, with the fiber input ends having frosted end faces. Its output end consists of the output ends of the multiple fiber optics rearranged and fixed to form a one-dimensional linear array. The spectral measurement device includes the fiber optic array adapter and a spectral analysis module. The entrance slit of the spectral analysis module is optically coupled to the one-dimensional linear array. It disperses the light signals from each fiber channel through a dispersive element and independently images them at different positions on the imaging detector, simultaneously acquiring the spectral information of all channels in a single exposure. This device achieves multi-channel synchronous measurement through a single spectral analysis module, reducing cost and complexity; the frosted end faces of the fibers suppress reflection and stray light; and the modular design enhances flexibility in adapting to different measurement scenarios.

records.title: A multiphoton fiber array endoscopic imaging device and method based on hollow …
records.abstract: The invention discloses a multi-photon optical fiber array endoscopic imaging device and method based on hollow spiral scanning, and belongs to the technical field of biological imaging. The device comprises a laser collimation beam expansion module, a pulse chirp module, a beam switching module, an endoscopic detection module and a fluorescence acquisition module. The inner detection module drives the optical fiber array to execute hollow spiral scanning through the resonance driver, and the track starting point is not positioned at the view field origin, so that central dense sampling is avoided. The method comprises the steps of switching optical fibers through an optical switch, enabling each optical fiber to execute hollow spiral scanning with misaligned space, collecting multi-photon signals such as fluorescence, second harmonic, fluorescence service life and the like, and obtaining a complete field imaging result through image reconstruction and fusion to complement a central cavity. The invention obviously reduces the photodamage of the central area, improves the uniformity of imaging resolution, ensures reality and reliability based on physical sampling of the fused image, and has high system stability.

The micro-objective is used to focus the excitation light onto the sample and couple the multiphoton signal of the sample to the fiber array. records.title: New copper-aluminum composite terminal
assignees: Changchun Jetty Automotive Technology Co., Ltd.
records.abstract: A novel copper-aluminum composite terminal, including a connecting part and a functional part which are connected to each other, the functional part is made of an aluminum-clad copper composite material which comprises an inner copper layer and an outer aluminum layer encapsulating the copper layer, the connecting part is connected to a conductive portion of the aluminum cable, and at least part of the copper layer of the functional part is connected to the electric device. The design of this structure enables weight reduction and cost savings.
records.summary: The disclosure describes a copper-aluminum composite terminal for electrically connecting an aluminum cable to an electric device. The terminal has a connecting part joined to the aluminum cable's conductive portion and a functional part made of an aluminum-clad copper composite material, with an inner copper layer encapsulated by an outer aluminum layer; at least part of the copper layer connects to the electric device. The stated aim is weight reduction and cost savings from this structure. The available text covers the abstract and all 19 claims only; the description and figures were not retrieved, and no experimental performance data are supplied.
records.why_it_matters: It proposes a terminal architecture that places copper only where device contact occurs while using aluminum for cable-side connection, potentially reducing copper content and mass in aluminum-cable terminations.

records.abstract: Translated from Korean 패키지는 브리징 요소(OMIB)와 제1 및 제2 광자 경로를 포함하여, 양방향 광자 경로를 형성한다. OMIB는 하나 이상의 다이와 연결되기 위한 제1 및 제2 상호 연결 영역을 갖는다. 제3 및 제4 단방향 광자 경로는 제1 상호 연결 영역과 광 인터페이스(OI) 사이를 결합할 수 있다. 광자 트랜시버는 OMIB에서의 제1 부분, 및 다이 중 하나에서의 제2 부분을 갖는다. 제1 및 제2 부분은 길이가 2㎜ 미만인 전기 상호 연결부를 통해 결합될 수 있다. 다이는 제2 부분에 인접한 중앙 영역 주위에 있는 컴퓨팅 요소를 포함한다. OMIB는 게르마늄, 실리콘, 게르마늄의 합금, 실리콘의 합금, 인듐 인화물(InP)을 기반으로 하는 III-V족 재료 또는 갈륨 비소화물(GaAs)을 기반으로 하는 III-V족 재료로 제작된 전기 흡수 변조기를 포함할 수 있다. OMIB는 변조기에 대한 온도 보상을 포함할 수 있다. The package includes an OMIB and first and second photonic paths, forming a bidirectional photonic path. The OMIB has first and second interconnect regions for connecting to one or more dies. Third and fourth unidirectional photonic paths can couple between the first interconnect region and an optical interface (OI). The photonic transceiver has a first portion in the OMIB and a second portion in one of the dies. The first and second portions can be coupled via electrical interconnects less than 2 mm in length. The dies include computing elements around a central region adjacent to the second portion. The OMIB can include an electroabsorbing modulator fabricated from germanium, silicon, an alloy of germanium, an alloy of silicon, a group III-V material based on indium phosphide (InP), or a group III-V material based on gallium arsenide (GaAs). The OMIB can include temperature compensation for the modulator.
records.summary: The disclosure describes an optical multi-die interconnect bridge (OMIB) that optically and electrically couples two dies. The bridge contains a photonic network with waveguides, a modulator, a photodetector, and an edge coupler providing an optical interface to fibers, plus analog/mixed-signal (AMS) blocks with serializer/deserializer circuits that connect to each die via an electrical interface supporting a communication protocol. A photonic channel forms a data path from serializer through modulator, photonic path, photodetector, and parallelizer between the joined dies. The abstract further describes a photonic transceiver split between the OMIB and a die, coupled by electrical interconnects under 2 mm, with computing elements arranged around a central die region, and modulators fabricated from germanium, silicon, Ge/Si alloys, InP-based III-V, or GaAs-based III-V materials, optionally with temperature compensation. No measured performance data are supplied; the text is abstract and claims only.
records.why_it_matters: It suggests an architecture for chiplet-to-chiplet links that places the optical transceiver partly in a silicon bridge and partly in the die, keeping the electrical interface short (under 2 mm) while using WDM photonics for the longer reach.

records.title: High-power shielded busbars for electric vehicle charging and power distribution
records.abstract: Translated from Korean A unitary busbar transmits power from one connection point to another in an electric vehicle. A unitary busbar comprises a central solid-core conductor, an insulating layer over the solid-core conductor, and an electromagnetic shield fitted around the insulation. The unitary busbar can be bent into specific configurations to fit the electric vehicle body.
records.summary: The disclosure describes a unitary busbar for electric-vehicle power distribution that combines a solid-core conductor, an insulating layer, and a conductive shielding layer compressed against the insulation, with at least one connector formed from the solid core itself. The busbar is described as bendable to follow the vehicle's internal configuration and is grounded to the vehicle through a rigid ground conductor connected to the shielding layer. The claims describe a system in which the busbar links a first connection point, such as a charging port, to a second connection point, such as a battery connector. Dependent claims recite materials and dimensions, including aluminum or copper conductors and shields, XLPE/PVC/silicone insulation, conductor cross-sections of 3–300 mm², insulation thickness of 0.9–1.1 mm, and shield thickness of 0.5–2 mm. One dependent claim states the busbar can support 350 kW charging at 400 V while keeping the shielding layer at or below 120 °C; this is a claim feature, not a demonstrated experimental result in the supplied text.
records.why_it_matters: The disclosure describes integrating shielding and grounding into a single bendable busbar, which could simplify routing and EMI containment in high-power EV charging and distribution architectures.

records.title: Demountable coupling of optical connector and optoelectronic device
assignees: 美商扇港元器件有限公司
records.abstract: Optical alignment of a receptacle at an aligned position on an optoelectronic device body is accomplished using an alignment optical connector that is demountably attached to the receptacle by matching passive alignment features on the facing surfaces between the receptacle and the alignment optical connector. The device body includes a first row of at least two data optical ports, and a second row of alignment input and output ports parallel to and spaced from the first row of data optical ports by a parallel spacing. The data optical ports communicate with the optoelectronic device. The alignment ports correspond to a loopback waveguide. The aligned position of the receptacle is determined from the loopback waveguide. The receptacle is permanently attached to the device body at this aligned position. A data optical connector is similarly configured as the alignment optical connector, in the manner in which optical fibers are supported to input/output optical signals and with similar passive alignment features, but the passive alignment features are referenced to the optical fibers by an offset equivalent to the parallel spacing between the first and second rows. The second row is same or shorter than the first row. The number of data optical ports is greater or equal to the number of alignment optical ports. The data optical ports and the alignment optical ports are arranged in a 2 x N matrix.
records.summary: The disclosure describes an optoelectronic device body with a first column of at least two active data optical ports (e.g., grating couplers) and a second, parallel column of alignment input/output ports spaced from the data ports by a defined parallel spacing. The alignment ports correspond to a loopback/feedback waveguide, so an alignment optical connector with matching passive alignment features can be demountably attached and used to actively determine the correct alignment position of a receptacle on the device body. Once aligned, the receptacle is permanently attached to the device body, and the alignment connector is removed. A data optical connector is configured similarly but with its passive alignment features referenced to its fibers by an offset equal to the parallel spacing between the two rows, enabling passively aligned detachable coupling of data fibers. The abstract states the ports are arranged in a 2 x N matrix, with the second row same or shorter than the first and data ports numbering at least as many as alignment ports. No measured performance data are supplied; the text is limited to abstract and claims.
records.why_it_matters: It separates the one-time active alignment of a permanently fixed receptacle from routine connector mating, so subsequent data connectors can be attached and detached using only passive alignment features referenced by a fixed offset.

records.summary: The disclosure describes a lubricant composition built around an ionic liquid whose cation is a quaternary structure of general formula (B), with R5, R6 and R7 each independently a linear or branched alkyl group of 1 to 22 carbon atoms and R8 either a linear or branched alkyl group of 1 to 22 carbon atoms or a hydroxyalkyl group —CnH2n—OH with n from 1 to 22, paired with an anion of general formula (C) in which R9 and R10 are each independently linear or branched alkyl groups of 1 to 10 carbon atoms. The independent claim covers this ionic-liquid-containing lubricant composition; dependent claims add a base oil and specify that the base oil is at least one of a poly-α-olefin and a polyol ester. The available text is a search snippet with claims only, so no measured friction, wear, thermal-stability or viscosity data are reported here. The filing is assigned to Minebea Mitsumi and carries publication number JP7757242B2.
